candidates/disulfiram_due_diligence.title: Disulfiram — Due Diligence Review
candidates/disulfiram_due_diligence.content:
Disulfiram for Maureen — Due Diligence Review
Prepared: 2026-08-07
Context: A physician outside her care team has written an Rx for disulfiram. This document is
pre-start due diligence: chemistry, pharmacology, risks, patient-specific relevance,
and monitoring strategy.
Status: Research memo. Not medical advice. Every actionable item below is framed as
a question for the prescribing physician, not a recommendation to override her.

0. Bottom line up front
Three things matter more than everything else in this document:


⚠ The dose almost certainly isn’t 25/50 mg. US disulfiram is manufactured only
as 250 mg and 500 mg tablets. There is no 25 mg or 50 mg product. “Start smaller,
then go up” maps exactly onto the standard 250 mg → 500 mg titration. This is a
10× difference and it flips the entire risk profile — verify before the first dose.


Her prior oxaliplatin exposure is the single biggest patient-specific risk. She
has had oxaliplatin twice (FOLFOXIRI+bev, then FOLFOX+cetuximab+encorafenib). Disulfiram
causes a dose-dependent axonal sensorimotor neuropathy that is rare below 250 mg/day
and reported almost exclusively at ≥250 mg/day. That is additive with oxaliplatin
neuropathy, which is often already present and can be permanent.


The Rx appears to be disulfiram alone, but the preclinical effect depends on copper.
Essentially all of the anticancer literature — including the March 2026 APC paper driving
the current buzz — uses disulfiram + copper. Disulfiram monotherapy is the weaker arm
in nearly every experiment. This needs an explicit decision, not a default.


⚠ Her ctDNA has been negative since 2025-12-05, so there is no headroom to demonstrate benefit.
Undetectable cannot become more undetectable. The risks below are all measurable; the
benefit, structurally, is not. See §8.3 — this is the finding that most changes the
shape of the decision.


Overall assessment: at standard dose with proper monitoring this is a reasonable,
reversible, low-cost thing to try in a setting with few good options — but the honest
evidence grade for benefit is preclinical only, and the clinical track record across
~21 human trials is poor. Given point 4, this would be a bet taken on mechanism, entered
as prophylaxis against recurrence — not a trial you can read out. The case for it rests
on low cost and reversibility, not on strength of evidence, and not on any expectation of
being able to tell whether it worked.

1. What the news actually said
The “metabolic way to treat certain cancers” story traces to a single preclinical paper:

Liang, T., et al. (2026). ALDH2 inhibition induces synthetic lethality in APC-deficient
colorectal cancer via ROS/ASK1/JNK pathway. Genes & Diseases.
DOI: 10.1016/j.gendis.2026.102057

The claim: APC-mutant colorectal cells run a higher baseline load of toxic aldehydes
from lipid peroxidation. ALDH2 is the enzyme that clears them. Block ALDH2 → aldehydes
accumulate → ROS spike → ASK1/JNK stress cascade → apoptosis. Normal cells, with intact
APC, have headroom and are spared. That is a synthetic-lethal framing, and APC status
is the proposed patient-selection biomarker.
Reported results: 50–70% reduction in cancer cell survival with disulfiram alone;
near-complete with added copper; ~60% tumour shrinkage in APC-mutant mouse models without
apparent normal-tissue harm.
What it is not:

Not a clinical trial. Cell lines, organoids, and mouse xenografts only.
Not a high-impact venue. Genes & Diseases is a legitimate peer-reviewed journal but
not Nature/Cell/NEJM tier.
Not independently replicated yet.
The authors themselves flag “important differences between animal models and human
pharmacology that must be resolved before the strategy can reach patients.”

Much of the amplification you likely saw came through secondary outlets
(news-medical.net
and aggregator blogs) rather than primary coverage. The absence of cautions you noticed
is a property of the coverage, not of the drug. The cautions are real and well documented;
they just don’t make headlines.

2. Chemistry and how it works
Disulfiram (tetraethylthiuram disulfide, “Antabuse”) is a small-molecule dithiocarbamate
— two diethyldithiocarbamate (DDC) halves joined by a disulfide bond. It has been in
clinical use since 1951. It is a promiscuous metal chelator, and essentially all of its
biology flows from that.
Metabolic cascade
Disulfiram  ──(rapid reduction in stomach/blood)──▶  2 × DDC (diethyldithiocarbamate)
                                                        │
                    ┌───────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┐
                    ▼                                   ▼                          ▼
              DDC-methyl ester              +Cu²⁺ ──▶ CuET                    free DDC
                    │                       bis(diethyldithiocarbamate)-copper
              ──(CYP3A4/5)──▶ DETC-MeSO              │
                    │                                 │
                    ▼                                 ▼
         ALDH inhibition (irreversible)      NPL4/p97 inhibition
         → the alcohol reaction              → the main anticancer mechanism
         → the ALDH2/APC mechanism

Mechanism A — ALDH inhibition (the APC/ALDH2 story)
DETC-MeSO covalently and irreversibly inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase. Because the
inhibition is covalent, enzyme activity only returns as new protein is synthesised —
which is why the alcohol reaction persists up to 14 days after the last dose. This is
also the mechanism the new APC paper exploits.
Mechanism B — CuET / NPL4-p97 (the better-established anticancer mechanism)
This is the mechanism from Skrott et al., Nature 2017 — the work that started the modern
disulfiram-oncology field. DDC complexes with copper to form CuET, which preferentially
accumulates in tumour tissue. CuET immobilises NPL4, the adaptor of the p97/VCP
segregase — the cell’s central machine for pulling ubiquitinated proteins out of complexes
and membranes for degradation. NPL4 aggregates, p97-dependent protein turnover collapses,
the unfolded protein response fires, and the cell dies of proteotoxic stress.
Structural work (Nature Communications 2020)
refined this: cupric ions released from CuET under oxidative conditions disrupt NPL4’s
zinc-finger motifs, locking a conformational switch. That release is oxidation-dependent —
which is elegant, because tumour tissue is already under oxidative stress, giving a degree
of tumour selectivity.
Both mechanisms require copper. Mechanism B obviously so. Mechanism A is potentiated
by it.

3. Pharmacokinetics


















































ParameterValueWhy it mattersDisulfiram t½~7.3 hParent drug is transientDDC t½~15.5 hDDC-Me ester t½~22.1 hDrives once-daily dosingTmax (drug + metabolites)8–10 hEvening dosing is conventionalElimination~90% in 3 daysBut ALDH inhibition long outlasts thisALDH recoveryup to 14 daysCovalent inhibition — the alcohol ban extends 2 weeks past the last doseBioactivationCYP3A4/5 (plus 1A2, 2A6, 2D6)⚠ See §6 — interacts with encorafenibInhibitsCYP2E1 strongly (mechanism-based); 1A2, 2B6Relatively selective for 2E1
The central pharmacological problem for oncology: oral disulfiram has poor and
erratic bioavailability, and is largely degraded before reaching systemic circulation.
Achieved plasma CuET concentrations in humans sit well below the levels that produce the
dramatic effects in cell culture. This — more than any failure of the underlying biology —
is the leading explanation for why ~21 clinical trials have produced no breakthrough
despite spectacular preclinical data. An enormous amount of current work is on nanoparticle
and cyclodextrin formulations precisely to solve this.
Read this honestly: the mouse data may be real and the oral drug may still not reach
the tumour at meaningful concentration in a human.

4. Relevance to Maureen’s cancer specifically
Her profile













































FeatureValueSourceDiagnosisColorectal adenocarcinoma, Stage IVMODSAPCp.T1556fs, pathogenic — VAF 12% (2024) → 24% (2025)Caris ×2, Guardant, AlteraBRAFV600E — VAF 37% → 41%Caris ×2, Guardant, AlteraATMsomatic p.S151fsCarisMSI / TMBStable / 3 (Low)Caris, AlteraOtherTGFBR2 D522fs, MGA I945fs, MYC amp, NTRK2 VUSCarisSecond primaryMelanoma (specimen the melanoma specimen) — confirmed by expressionCaris WTS
She is APC-mutant, which is exactly the stratifier the new paper proposes. On the
paper’s own selection criterion, she qualifies.
⚠ Her ALDH2 expression — the key personalized finding
I pulled ALDH2 directly from her Caris whole-transcriptome data, benchmarked against the
colorectal adenocarcinoma reference cohort:

































SpecimenDateSiteALDH2 TPMPercentile vs CRCthe 2024 colorectal specimenJan 2024Ascending colon46.831stthe 2025 colorectal specimenAug 2025Colon, NOS49.636ththe melanoma specimen2026(melanoma — not CRC)43.225th
Her tumour is not ALDH2-high. It sits below the median for colorectal adenocarcinoma,
stably, across 20 months and two independent specimens.
How to read that — carefully, because it cuts both ways:

Argument it weakens the case: less target enzyme to inhibit; in most dependency
models, higher target expression predicts greater sensitivity to inhibiting it.
Argument it strengthens the case: less ALDH2 reserve means she may already sit
closer to the aldehyde-clearance cliff, so a smaller reduction could tip the balance.

The paper does not resolve which applies, because it stratified on APC status, not ALDH2
expression. The honest summary: she has the paper’s selection biomarker (APC), but she
does not have a positive enrichment biomarker on the target enzyme itself. This is worth
showing the prescribing physician — it’s real data on her actual tumour, and it’s the kind of thing that
would otherwise never enter the conversation.
Supporting pathway genes (colorectal-cohort percentiles)





























































GeneRoleTN24 (2024)TN25 (2025)ReadNPLOC4 (NPL4)direct CuET target87th86th✅ Consistently high — favourable for Mechanism BVCP (p97)partner segregase94th4th⚠ Wildly discordant — see caveatALDH1A1stem-cell ALDH, disulfiram target26th95th⚠ 14× rise (15→214 TPM)ALDH3A1ALDH isoform47th93rdRisingSLC31A1 (CTR1)copper importer42nd43rdAverageATP7A / ATP7Bcopper exporters8th / 1st53rd / 74thLow export in 2024 = copper retentionSOD1, NQO1oxidative-stress handling86th / 86th51st / 64thFalling
The most encouraging signal here is NPLOC4 at the 86th–87th percentile in both specimens —
the direct molecular target of CuET is consistently over-expressed in her tumour. That
supports the better-established mechanism, independent of the ALDH2 question.
The ALDH1A1 shift is notable: a 14-fold rise (26th → 95th percentile) between 2024 and
2025 suggests drift toward an ALDH-high, stem-like phenotype. ALDH1A1-high tumours are a
long-proposed disulfiram-target population, since disulfiram inhibits ALDH1A1 as well as
ALDH2. This is arguably a better argument for disulfiram in her case than the ALDH2 story is.

Caveat on the 2024→2025 comparison: VCP swinging 94th → 4th percentile is too large to
be straightforward biology. Different specimens, likely different sites, differing tumour
purity, and possible batch effects all contribute. Treat single-gene percentile shifts as
hypothesis-generating, not established. The genes I’d trust most here are the ones that
are stable across both specimens — ALDH2 (31/36) and NPLOC4 (87/86).


5. Risks and side effects
5.1 The alcohol reaction — absolute and non-negotiable
Acetaldehyde accumulation produces flushing, throbbing headache, nausea, violent vomiting,
tachycardia, chest pain, profound hypotension, and — in severe cases — arrhythmias,
cardiovascular collapse, MI, seizures, and death. Onset within ~10 minutes.
It persists up to 14 days after the last dose.
Hidden ethanol sources that catch people out:

⚠ Her “Magic Mouthwash” (diphenhydramine-lidocaine-Maalox-nystatin) — many
compounded formulations and diphenhydramine elixirs contain ic ethanol (up to ~14%).
This is on her active med list. Verify the exact formulation with the pharmacy.
Liquid/elixir medications, many cough syrups
Mouthwash (Listerine ~21% ethanol), some toothpastes
Vanilla and other extracts; wine/beer in cooking (not fully cooked off); vinegars
Sauces, marinades, some desserts, kombucha
Hand sanitiser and alcohol-based topicals (absorption is possible with heavy use)
Some IV drug diluents — anaesthesia and ER staff must be told she is on disulfiram


Cardiac note: her LVEF is currently normal (67% biplane, Feb 2026, up from 59% in
January), which is reassuring. But binimetinib carries a cardiomyopathy risk requiring
ongoing echo surveillance, and a disulfiram-ethanol reaction causes profound vasodilation
and hypotension. If LVEF drops on binimetinib, the consequences of an accidental exposure
get materially worse. Worth linking these two surveillance streams.

5.2 Hepatotoxicity — the risk that needs active monitoring
Per NIH LiverTox, disulfiram carries
Likelihood Score A — a well-established cause of clinically apparent liver injury.





































Mild ALT/AST elevationup to 25% of chronic users>3× ULN≤4%Clinically apparent injury~1 per 10,000–30,000 patient-yearsLatency2–12 weeks (the critical monitoring window)PatternHepatocellular, resembles acute viral hepatitisMortality/transplant once jaundiced~16%RechallengeRapid recurrence — never re-challenge
⚠ Additive risk in her case. She is on encorafenib (hepatotoxicity warning) and
binimetinib (hepatotoxicity warning), plus scheduled acetaminophen 1000 mg q6h and
ibuprofen. That is already a meaningful hepatic load.
✅ The good news: her baseline is excellent and gives clean signal to monitor against.













































Lab2026-02-242026-03-092026-03-232026-04-062026-04-27ALT (U/L)1617161611AST (U/L)2225232317Bilirubin, total0.30.40.30.40.4Albumin (g/dL)3.13.73.53.94.1
Pristine, and albumin has recovered nicely (3.1 → 4.1). Any drift will be obvious.
One genuine caution from LiverTox: routine monitoring may not reliably prevent severe
outcomes, because injury can develop fast between draws. Symptom vigilance matters as
much as scheduled labs — new fatigue, anorexia, nausea, right-upper-quadrant discomfort,
dark urine, or scleral icterus should trigger immediate cessation and same-day LFTs, not
“wait for the next appointment.”
5.3 Peripheral neuropathy — her highest-salience risk

Dose- and duration-dependent, large-fibre axonal sensorimotor pattern
Essentially all reported cases occur at ≥250 mg/day; rare below that
Onset typically 15 days to 6 months (most within 2 months)
Incidence roughly 1 in 15,000 patient-years overall
Usually reversible on discontinuation — but not always
Mechanism: axonal degeneration plus direct Schwann-cell/myelin toxicity

⚠ She has had oxaliplatin in two separate regimens. Oxaliplatin-induced peripheral
neuropathy is cumulative, frequently persistent, and sometimes permanent. Layering a second
axonal toxin on a nerve population already damaged by platinum is the risk I would weight
most heavily at 250–500 mg/day.
This makes a documented baseline neuro exam essential — if she has existing numbness,
tingling, or proprioceptive loss, that needs to be graded and written down before the
first dose, or you will have no way to attribute any later change.
5.4 Other adverse effects

Neuropsychiatric: drowsiness, fatigue, headache; at 500 mg, reversible delirium and
psychosis (notably reported in the glioblastoma trials at continuous 500 mg)
Optic neuritis — rare but reported. Note she is already on Maxitrol eye drops and
binimetinib carries ocular toxicity (retinopathy/uveitis) warnings; any visual change
needs prompt ophthalmology review with both drugs in the differential
Metallic/garlic aftertaste — very common, benign
Dermatologic: acneiform eruption, rash. ⚠ Confounded — she is already managing
cetuximab acneiform rash with doxycycline and topical clindamycin
Contraindications: severe myocardial disease, coronary occlusion, psychosis, active
alcohol use, existing significant liver disease

5.5 Drug interactions with her actual regimen


















































Her drugInteractionSeverityEncorafenib⚠ Bidirectional — see below. Encorafenib is a CYP3A4 inhibitor; disulfiram requires CYP3A4/5 for bioactivation. ⚠ Corrected 2026-10-05 (#830): the current label calls encorafenib a strong CYP3A4 inducer at steady state; see the note below the callout.Important, under-appreciatedBinimetinibAdditive hepatotoxicityHigh — monitorAcetaminophen 1 g q6hAdditive hepatic load. (Mechanistically, CYP2E1 inhibition should reduce toxic NAPQI formation — but total burden still matters)ModerateOndansetron + encorafenibQT prolongation. Her Mg is low-normal (1.7–1.8) on cetuximab, which worsens QT risk. Disulfiram isn’t a major QT drug but the baseline is already tightModerate (pre-existing)MetforminBoth carry rare lactic-acidosis associationsLowFerrous gluconateIron and copper compete for absorption (DMT1) — matters if copper is added; separate the dosesLow, but relevant to §7Magic Mouthwash⚠ Possible ethanol content — verify formulationPotentially highCaffeineReduced clearance — more jitterinessTrivial

⚠ The encorafenib interaction is the subtle one worth raising explicitly
Disulfiram is a prodrug. It must be bioactivated to DETC-MeSO, and that step runs
principally through CYP3A4/5. Encorafenib is “a relatively potent reversible inhibitor
of CYP3A4 and also a time-dependent inhibitor of CYP3A4” (FDA label).
Plausible consequence: her BRAF inhibitor may substantially blunt the conversion of
disulfiram into its active metabolite — reducing both the anticancer effect and,
paradoxically, the alcohol-reaction intensity.
Two practical implications:

Disulfiram may simply do less in her than in a patient not on encorafenib. If it’s
going to be tried, this is a reason it might fail for pharmacological rather than
biological reasons.
Do not let a blunted alcohol reaction be interpreted as “she tolerates alcohol fine.”
CYP3A4 inhibition is not reliable protection, and encorafenib dosing changes could
restore full reaction intensity without warning.

I have not found this specific pair studied directly — I’m reasoning from each drug’s
documented CYP profile. It’s a hypothesis worth putting to the prescribing physician or a pharmacist,
not an established finding.

⚠ Corrected 2026-10-05; sources checked 2026-10-06 (#830).
The callout’s premise is wrong for her.

In patients, encorafenib is a strong CYP3A4 inducer at steady state. Taken with
binimetinib, it cut the exposure of midazolam, a sensitive CYP3A4 substrate, by 82%
(Piscitelli et al., Clin Pharmacol Ther 119(2):375–380, online 2025-11-10, PMID 41215578).
The regulators agree. The FDA label says so in §7.2 and §12.3 (versions of 10/2023 and
3/2025), and so does the EU product information (§4.5).
Where the quote came from.

The words match the in-vitro paragraph of the EU product information (§5.2) and of that study’s
protocol. None of the FDA labels checked (2018, 2023, 2025) uses them.
Every one of those sources, the 2018 FDA label included, follows the in-vitro inhibition with
in-vitro induction of CYP3A4.
The review took the sentence from a web search’s summary and never opened a label.


So implication 1 runs the wrong way. If CYP3A4 governs disulfiram’s activation, encorafenib
points toward faster activation, not a blunted one.
Implication 2 still stands, for a different reason. The pair is unstudied, so an absent
or altered alcohol reaction proves nothing, and a change to her encorafenib dose could shift it.

The original text is kept above.

6. ⚠ The dose question — resolve this first
You recalled “25 mg, then up to 50 mg.”
US disulfiram is manufactured only in 250 mg and 500 mg tablets. No 25 mg or 50 mg
product exists.
Meanwhile the standard regimens are:

























SettingRegimenAlcohol-aversion (FDA label)500 mg/day × 1–2 weeks, then 250 mg/day maintenanceCancer trials (most common)250 mg/day + copper gluconate 2–8 mg elemental CuCancer trials (MTD)500 mg/day — but continuous use caused reversible delirium or neuropathy prompting discontinuation in some patientsPhase II alternative80 mg TID + copper gluconate 1.5 mg TID
“Start smaller to see if she tolerates it, then go up” is a precise description of the
250 → 500 mg titration. The most likely explanation is a dropped zero in recall.
Why this matters so much:



































25/50 mg (as recalled)250/500 mg (as manufactured)Neuropathy riskEssentially nilReal — and she has 2× prior oxaliplatinAlcohol reactionAttenuated but present (covalent, accumulates)Full strengthHepatotoxicityLowerMeaningful — needs scheduled LFTsDelirium riskNilPresent at 500 mgAny anticancer plausibilityVery unlikely — 10× below every studied doseMatches trial dosing
Note the asymmetry: at 25–50 mg the safety concerns mostly evaporate, but so does any
realistic expectation of anticancer effect. A genuinely low dose would be close to taking
nothing. So the dose isn’t just a safety question — it determines whether the whole exercise
has a point.
→ Call the pharmacy and read the label. This is a five-minute task and everything else
depends on it.

7. The copper question
The Rx as described is disulfiram alone. But:

Mechanism B (CuET/NPL4) is copper — no copper, no CuET, no p97 inhibition
The March 2026 APC paper’s headline result — “nearly complete” kill — is the +copper arm
Essentially every modern trial pairs them: 250 mg disulfiram + 2–8 mg elemental copper
as copper gluconate, with a Phase 1 dose-escalation study
concluding 8 mg elemental copper/day as the projected optimum, well tolerated in solid
tumours involving the liver with no DLTs

But copper is genuinely double-edged, and this deserves real caution rather than
enthusiasm:

Copper is a well-documented driver of angiogenesis and metastasis (“cuproplasia”).
Copper chelation — the opposite intervention — has itself been trialled as an
anti-angiogenic cancer therapy.
There is specific evidence that copper improves disulfiram’s anti-angiogenic activity
via the EGFR/Src/VEGF pathway in glioma — mechanistically interesting for her, since
she is on cetuximab (anti-EGFR). Whether that’s synergistic or antagonistic in an
EGFR-blocked patient is genuinely unknown.
Her copper-exporter expression (ATP7A/ATP7B) was very low in the 2024 specimen
(8th/1st percentile), suggesting copper retention — which could amplify both the intended
effect and any off-target copper toxicity.
⚠ She takes ferrous gluconate; iron and copper compete for absorption. Doses would
need separating.

This is exactly the kind of judgement call to hand to the prescribing physician rather than resolve at
home. The question to put to her is not “should we add copper?” but “the preclinical
effect you’re targeting is copper-dependent — is copper part of your plan, and if not, what
mechanism are we expecting to engage?“

8. What metric tells us whether it’s doing anything

⚠ Revised 2026-08-07 after user correction. An earlier draft of this section read
the database at face value and drew two wrong conclusions — that her CTC was detectable,
and that her CEA had gone unmeasured for eleven months. Both were data-pipeline
artifacts, not clinical facts. The corrected picture is below, and it changes the
answer to the monitoring question substantially.


⚠ Corrected 2026-10-01. Earlier versions of this section said her ctDNA had been
undetectable since September 2025, and that it disagreed with her rising CEA. The
Signatera reports say otherwise:

positive and rising through 2025-10-01: 7.26 MTM/mL on 2025-01-29, 20.74 on 2025-10-01;
0.15 on 2025-10-27, after FOLFOX + cetuximab + encorafenib began;
negative from 2025-12-05 to the last report on file, 2026-03-03.

CEA and ctDNA agreed. Both rose through the August 2025 recurrence. §8.3’s conclusion
still holds for her situation now.

8.1 The two markers, correctly attributed
Natera ctDNA: negative since 2025-12-05. Her tumour-burden testing comes from Natera,
whose oncology product is Signatera: a tumour-informed ctDNA (circulating tumour DNA)
assay reporting in MTM/mL. It is not a CTC (circulating tumour cell) count, despite the
colloquial shorthand. Maple holds 21 Signatera reports (2025-01-29 to 2026-03-03) as documents,
but they are not yet parsed into structured rows (#131). Reports after March 2026 haven’t
arrived (#512). ⬅ See §8.4.
RGCC CTC 2.6–2.7 — a different assay entirely. The numbers in the database came from
RGCC (Onconomics Plus / OncoTrace, ordered by the integrative physician, reported 2025-02-15 and 2025-09-19). RGCC’s assay counts circulating tumour
cells per mL. It is a separate measurement on a separate scale from Signatera, is not
FDA-cleared, and its analytic validity is contested. The two are not comparable and should
never be plotted together.
In February and September 2025, RGCC counted 2.7 and 2.6 cells/mL, while Signatera was positive
and rising (7.26 MTM/mL in January, 20.74 by 2025-10-01). The two assays measure different things
on different scales. Where they ever need reconciling, Signatera is the far better-validated
test.
8.2 CEA — the gap was ours, not the lab’s
Her CEA is drawn roughly every two weeks. The eleven-month gap is an ingest bug, not a
gap in her care — filed as #256. Her
panel-mate CA 19-9 kept arriving through 2026-04-27 on the same cadence; CEA alone stopped
landing after 2025-09-16. The lone later row (2026-03-16) is not a lab value at all — it is
a computed “trailing 3-period average” that leaked into the observation series.
So the trend below is real but stale, and should not be extrapolated past September 2025:





































DateCEA (ng/mL)2025-02-272.82025-03-262.62025-04-253.32025-05-093.62025-05-194.02025-08-084.52025-09-164.8 (last real value)
CEA rose ~85% between February and September 2025, and so did her ctDNA: 7.26 MTM/mL on
2025-01-29, 20.74 on 2025-10-01. The two markers agreed. The recurrence was confirmed in
August–September 2025, when nodes were enlarged on CT and the pathology came back. After
FOLFOX + cetuximab + encorafenib began, ctDNA fell to 0.15 (2025-10-27), and it has been
negative since 2025-12-05. CEA stopped landing in Maple after 2025-09-16 (the ingest gap
above). So the recent comparison that matters is ctDNA against CA 19-9, not CEA.
8.3 ⚠ The finding that actually changes the decision
Her ctDNA has been negative since 2025-12-05 (the last report on file is 2026-03-03), so
there is no headroom in which disulfiram could demonstrate benefit. She is already at the
floor of the most sensitive tumour-burden assay available.
The consequences are worth stating plainly:

You cannot show it helped. Undetectable cannot become more undetectable. The only
observable movement is upward — i.e. the assay can register failure, never success.
You can still show it harmed. New neuropathy or rising LFTs in the 2–12 week window
after starting, on an otherwise stable regimen, is attributable.
So the ledger is asymmetric in the unfavourable direction: the risks are fully
measurable, the benefit is structurally unmeasurable.

This also reframes her clinical situation. Negative ctDNA since 2025-12-05, first on FOLFOX +
cetuximab + encorafenib and then on cetuximab + encorafenib + binimetinib maintenance, is a
deep, durable response. Adding a drug with
real neuropathy and hepatotoxicity risk to someone in deep remission is a materially
different proposition from adding it to someone visibly progressing — the first is
prophylaxis against recurrence, and the endpoint of successful prophylaxis is “nothing
happens,” which is unfalsifiable in a single patient.
None of this makes disulfiram wrong. Preventing recurrence is a legitimate goal, and
BRAF V600E MSS mCRC recurs often enough that wanting to do something is entirely
reasonable. But it should be entered with clear eyes: this would be a bet taken on
mechanism, not a trial you can read out. That argues for weighting tolerability heavily
and for pre-committing to a stopping rule, since “is it working?” will not answer itself.
8.4 Recommended monitoring framework (revised)
Before starting:





































ItemWhyCurrent Signatera result + full historyThe primary endpoint. Establishes that undetectable is still true today.Parse the Natera reports Maple already holds (#131), and fetch those after March 2026 (#512) ⬅Maple stores 21 reports as documents but has no structured series. Without one, the record shows only the contested RGCC numbers.Current CEARe-anchor after the ingest gap — worth one draw even if ctDNA is the real endpointCMP incl. ALT/AST/bilirubin/albuminHepatotoxicity baseline (current values excellent)Documented neuro exam⚠ Grade existing oxaliplatin neuropathy — otherwise later change is unattributableConfirm mouthwash formulation⚠ Rule out ethanolConfirm exact prescribed dose⚠ See §6
On treatment:


Signatera at its existing surveillance interval. The primary endpoint, and the one
that matters. Conversion from undetectable → detectable is the signal to act on —
and note it would signal disease recurrence, not disulfiram failure specifically.


⚠ CA 19-9 — currently your only live tumour marker, and you may not be tracking it.
Unlike CEA, it is flowing: n=17 since Sept 2025, through 2026-04-27, stable at
20–27 U/mL. That is a usable, current, every-2-week trend available at no extra cost.
⚠ One value needs checking: 2026-03-16 = 78, a >3× outlier against 20–27 on every
surrounding draw. Same date as the corrupted CEA row, so it may well be a parse error —
but if it is real it deserves attention, and it should be confirmed against the source
report either way.


CEA every 4–6 weeks, once ingestion is fixed. Secondary to ctDNA, and interpret
cautiously given the discordance noted above.


LFTs every 2 weeks through the 2–12 week hepatotoxicity window, then monthly.
Given additive risk with binimetinib and encorafenib, this is the monitoring that
actually earns its keep.


Neuro check at each visit — targeted questions about numbness, tingling, and balance,
compared against the documented baseline.


Imaging at its existing interval.


A pharmacodynamic option worth asking about: the Phase 1 disulfiram/copper trial used
S-glutathionylation as a target-engagement biomarker — a direct readout of whether the
drug is doing anything biochemically, independent of tumour response. Almost certainly not
orderable clinically, but given that tumour-burden endpoints are floored, target engagement
is the only category of evidence that could tell you the drug is doing anything at all.
Worth one question.
8.5 ⚠ Confounding compounds the problem
Beyond the floored-endpoint issue, she is on active therapy — encorafenib + binimetinib

cetuximab. Even if there were headroom to show improvement, any change would be
confounded between disulfiram, her existing regimen, and natural variation.

With n=1, no washout, and an endpoint already at its floor, “did it work?” is not an
answerable question. That is not by itself a reason to skip it — but it is a reason to
decide in advance what would make you stop, rather than deciding later while staring at
ambiguous numbers.

9. Questions for the prescribing physician
Resolve before the first dose:

⚠ What is the exact prescribed dose? 25 mg and 50 mg tablets do not exist; the
standard titration is 250 → 500 mg. Confirm from the label.
⚠ Is copper part of the plan? The mechanism being targeted is copper-dependent.
If not, what mechanism is expected to engage?
⚠ Does her Magic Mouthwash contain ethanol? Pharmacy can confirm the formulation.
⚠ Can we get a baseline neuro exam documented, given two prior oxaliplatin regimens?
⚠ Confirm the current Signatera result. The whole risk/benefit framing below depends
on whether undetectable is still true today.

Worth raising:

⚠ Given her ctDNA is undetectable, what would we expect to observe if disulfiram is
working? If the honest answer is “nothing we can measure,” is that an acceptable basis
for accepting neuropathy and hepatotoxicity risk — and if so, for how long? (This is the
central question. Everything else is detail.)
Encorafenib inhibits CYP3A4, which disulfiram needs for bioactivation — does that
blunt the expected effect, and does it change how much to trust an absent alcohol reaction?
⚠ Corrected 2026-10-05 (#830): the current label calls encorafenib a strong CYP3A4
inducer, so the question becomes whether it speeds activation. The second half stands.
LFT monitoring schedule — given additive hepatotoxicity with binimetinib/encorafenib,
would every 2 weeks through the 2–12 week high-risk window be appropriate?
CEA rose 2.6 → 4.8 through Sept 2025 while ctDNA went undetectable. How does she
read that discordance, and is CEA worth continuing to follow at all?
(Corrected 2026-10-05: there was no discordance. Her ctDNA was positive and rising through
2025-10-01, as her CEA was, and has been negative since 2025-12-05 (§8). Whether CEA is
worth following still stands.)
CA 19-9 on 2026-03-16 read 78 against 20–27 on every surrounding draw — real spike
or lab/parse artifact? Worth confirming against the source report.
Her tumour’s ALDH2 sits at the 31st–36th percentile for colorectal adenocarcinoma
(data attached) — does that change her read on the ALDH2-dependency rationale?
NPLOC4 is at the 86th–87th percentile across both specimens — is the CuET/NPL4
mechanism a better rationale here than the ALDH2 one?
Stopping rules — what would constitute enough evidence of harm, or of futility,
to discontinue? Given there is no efficacy readout, this needs deciding up front.


10. Balanced summary
Arguments for trying it:

She has the APC mutation that is the new paper’s own selection biomarker
NPLOC4 (the direct CuET target) is at the 86th–87th percentile in both her CRC
specimens — a genuinely supportive, stable, patient-specific finding
ALDH1A1 rose to the 95th percentile in the 2025 specimen — an ALDH-high/stem-like drift
that disulfiram also targets
75 years of human safety data; risks are known, monitorable, and largely reversible
Inexpensive; her oncologist is on board; readily stopped
Baseline LFTs are excellent, giving clean signal to monitor against
BRAF V600E MSS mCRC is a hard subtype with limited options — the calculus for a
low-cost, reversible addition is different than it would be in a curable setting

Arguments for caution:

Evidence for benefit is preclinical only. No completed trial supports use in CRC.
~21 human trials across many tumour types have produced no breakthrough, most likely
because oral disulfiram cannot achieve tumour CuET concentrations that work in a dish
Her ALDH2 is below median — no positive enrichment on the specific target the news
story is about
Two prior oxaliplatin regimens make additive neuropathy the standout risk at 250–500 mg
Additive hepatotoxicity with binimetinib + encorafenib + scheduled acetaminophen
Encorafenib may blunt disulfiram bioactivation via CYP3A4 inhibition. ⚠ Corrected
2026-10-05 (#830): the current label calls encorafenib a strong CYP3A4 inducer, so the
expected direction is faster activation. The pair is unstudied either way (§5.5).
The absolute alcohol restriction, extending 14 days past the last dose, is a real quality-of-life
and safety burden with genuine hidden-exposure hazards
⚠ Her ctDNA is already undetectable — there is no headroom to show benefit, and
confounding with active therapy compounds it. Risks are measurable; benefit is not.
She is in a deep, durable response (~11 months undetectable on encorafenib +
binimetinib + cetuximab). Adding neuropathy and hepatotoxicity risk to a patient in
remission is a different proposition from adding it to one who is progressing.
(Corrected 2026-10-05: negative since 2025-12-05, about eight months when this review was
written; see §8.)

My read: this is a defensible thing to try, provided the dose is confirmed, copper is
decided deliberately, and neuro/hepatic monitoring is set up properly beforehand. The
evidence is far thinner than the coverage implies — but the risk is bounded, detectable,
and reversible, which is the actual argument in its favour.
What the corrected data changes is the framing, not the verdict. This is not “try it and
watch the markers” — the markers are already at the floor. It is prophylaxis against
recurrence, taken on mechanistic faith, with no available readout. That is a legitimate
thing to choose; it just needs to be chosen deliberately rather than backed into. The
practical consequence is that tolerability becomes the whole decision, which puts
disproportionate weight on getting the dose right (§6) and on the baseline neuro exam (§5.3).
If I had to name the single highest-value output of this review: confirm the dose, and
then ask the prescribing physician question 6 in §9 — what, concretely, would we expect to see if this is
working?

Sources
Primary study driving the news

Liang, T., et al. (2026). ALDH2 inhibition induces synthetic lethality in APC-deficient colorectal cancer via ROS/ASK1/JNK pathway. Genes & Diseases. DOI: 10.1016/j.gendis.2026.102057
News-Medical coverage

Mechanism

Skrott et al., Alcohol-abuse drug disulfiram targets cancer via p97 segregase adapter NPL4 (Nature 2017)
Seesaw conformations of Npl4 in the human p97 complex (Nature Communications 2020)
CuET, translational arrest, p53 aggregation and ribosome biogenesis stress (Cell Death & Differentiation)
Copper improves anti-angiogenic activity of disulfiram via EGFR/Src/VEGF

Safety

NIH LiverTox — Disulfiram
Clinical characteristics and prognostic markers in disulfiram-induced liver injury (J Hepatology)
Disulfiram neuropathy: two cases of distal axonopathy
Disulfiram neuropathy — MedLink Neurology
Disulfiram — StatPearls

Pharmacology and dosing

Duration of CYP2E1 inhibition after single-dose disulfiram (JPET)
Lack of single-dose disulfiram effects on CYP2C9/2C19/2D6/3A4
Disulfiram dosage guide — Drugs.com
BRAFTOVI (encorafenib) FDA label

Clinical trials

Phase 1 disulfiram + copper gluconate, solid tumours involving liver (BMC Cancer)
Disulfiram + copper + chemo vs chemo in recurrent glioblastoma — RCT (JAMA Netw Open)
Phase IIb disulfiram + chemo in metastatic NSCLC
NCI — clinical trials using disulfiram
Leveraging disulfiram to treat cancer: mechanisms, delivery, regimens

Monitoring

Signatera — clinician information (Natera)
ctDNA-based molecular residual disease and survival in resectable CRC (Nature Medicine 2024)

Patient data — Maple MODS database: Caris MI Tumor Seek+ (the 2024 colorectal specimen, the 2025 colorectal specimen,
the melanoma specimen WTS), Guardant360 CDx (the 2025 liquid biopsy), Invitae (the germline panel report), Altera
(the tumour-informed ctDNA profile), RGCC Onconomics Plus / OncoTrace, Kaiser medication and lab imports.

candidates/maureen_candidate_treatments.content:
Candidate treatments Maureen is considering
Tracking issues: #28 (the catalog) and
#565 (moving it into the database).
Not medical advice. Every entry is something to discuss with her treating physicians, not
something to act on. Nothing here recommends starting anything.
What this file is for
Maple records treatments Maureen has had in ModsTreatmentEpisode / ModsTreatmentDrug,
shown in the TRT Dashboard. This file covers the treatments she is considering: options
under research that she has not started. It also holds tests that would decide between
them, such as live-tissue drug testing or a more sensitive ctDNA assay. They are listed
because they gate a treatment decision, not because they treat anything. Several near
neighbours in the code look similar, but none of them fits:





















Existing structureWhy it is not thisModsInterventionCurated drug/supplement knowledge base. It has no status field, so a candidate is indistinguishable from any other catalog row.ModsTreatmentSuggestionHas a review status, but only for AI-generated suggestions parsed from reports. It is not her own shortlist.ModsTreatmentResponseEpisodeLabels past treatments for contrastive learning. It looks backward.
Why markdown first. Several candidates, dendritic cell therapy among them, are not one
drug. They are a procedure, a manufacturing process and often a combination, so they do not
map onto one ModsIntervention row. The plan was to wait for 5–10 entries, see which fields
they actually need, and then move the catalog into the database with a “Considering” view
in MODS Lab. There are now eight. The fields they needed are written up under
Schema notes for #565. The migration itself belongs to #565 and is
not decided here.
Rules for an entry

Patient facts trace to her data (Mission Spec §7.1). Anything stated about her tumor
or her clinical state has to come from a real report row or from the Mission Spec’s
verified sections, with the source named. Nothing gets in because it is “typical” for
colorectal cancer. A bare ”§” refers to docs/MODS_MISSION_SPEC.md.
Trial status comes from the ClinicalTrials.gov v2 API (overallStatus and
whyStopped), never from a press release. Record the date it was checked.
Evidence carries its level. Preclinical, phase 1/2, randomized, or approved for
another indication. Say which, and give the citation.
Unknowns stay visibly unknown. Write not yet recorded. Do not fill a gap with a
guess.
Status is one of researching, discussed with clinician, pursuing, declined
or parked. A candidate that starts moves to ModsTreatmentEpisode and stays here only
as a link.
No germline content. Never her call or zygosity at a heritable variant, nor the gene
of one she carries (the project’s publishing rules). Somatic tumor findings are fine.

Index
Trial statuses below were read from the ClinicalTrials.gov v2 API on 2026-10-01 unless
an entry says otherwise.



























































CandidateStatusAddedLast reviewedDendritic cell therapyresearching2026-09-302026-10-06Botensilimab and balstilimab (BOT/BAL)discussed with clinician2026-10-012026-10-01Disulfiram, with or without copperdiscussed with clinician2026-10-012026-10-01Live-tissue drug testing at her next biopsyresearching2026-10-012026-10-01A more sensitive ctDNA assaydiscussed with clinician2026-10-012026-10-01Mebendazoleresearching2026-10-012026-10-01Neoantigen and personalized cancer vaccinesparked2026-10-012026-10-01Bacterial oncolyticsparked2026-10-012026-10-01

Dendritic cell therapy





















StatusresearchingAdded2026-09-30Last reviewed2026-10-06
What it is and how it works
Dendritic cells are the immune system’s antigen-presenting cells: they show fragments of a
target to T cells and activate them against it. Dendritic cell therapy (a “DC vaccine”) is
an autologous cell therapy, typically made like this:

The patient’s monocytes are collected by leukapheresis.
In the lab they are matured into dendritic cells and loaded with tumor antigen:
whole tumor lysate, defined peptides (e.g. CEA-derived), mRNA, or predicted neoantigens.
The loaded cells are injected back, usually as a series of doses. The intent is a
T-cell response against cells that carry those antigens.

“Dendritic cell therapy” is a family of products, not one product. Antigen source,
maturation protocol, route and schedule all differ between providers, and the evidence for
one does not transfer automatically to another. Any specific offer needs to be pinned down
on each of these points.
Why she is interested
Not yet recorded: what she hopes it would add, and who first raised it. Two facts bear on
it:

She is in contact with three providers. Her emails, forwarded to Richard and read on
2026-10-06, name them: IOZK in Cologne, which set a Zoom call for 2026-09-29; Dr. Frank
Gansauge’s clinic near Munich, which replied on 2026-09-23 and 09-25; and Immunocine in
Mexico, which sent an introduction on 2026-10-06. What each offers is under Who would
give it.
An earlier list. In September 2025, after the recurrence, she listed three clinics among the treatment facilities she was considering (clinical
journal archive). None of the three providers above is on that list.

Fit to her disease
Facts below are from the verified sections of docs/MODS_MISSION_SPEC.md (§2.2–§2.5) unless
a row names another source. The consequences drawn from them are inferences, marked as
such.

































Her fact (source)Relevance, as inferenceMSS, TMB 2–3 mut/Mb, PD-L1 0 (Caris, §2.4)Few mutations means few neoantigens. A product built on predicted neoantigens has little to work with. Lysate- or shared-antigen-loaded products do not rely on neoantigen count, but shared antigens tend to give weaker responses.Recurrence nodal-predominant, no liver metastases (§2.5)Liver involvement is the strongest known negative predictor for immunotherapy in MSS CRC. Its absence is a reason immunotherapy is worth considering for her at all. Whether that transfers from checkpoint blockade to DC vaccines is not established.NED on BREAKWATER maintenance; Signatera negative from 2025-12-05 to the last report on file, 2026-03-03 (§2.3). Kaiser CT of 2026-08-13: no evidence of metastatic disease (oncology note of 2026-08-17)A vaccine that primes immunity is, in principle, best suited to low disease burden. But there is no measurable disease and, at present, no positive ctDNA to measure a response against. A response would be hard to see.Maintenance cetuximab + encorafenib + binimetinib (§2.2)Any DC schedule would run alongside, or instead of, this regimen. See open questions.All her stored tumor is formalin-fixed, in three Kaiser pathology cases. None was frozen or kept alive (the three surgical pathology reports, read 2026-10-06)Products loaded with tumor lysate or RNA cannot use it, and IOZK and Immunocine both confirmed this (below). A product designed from sequencing could use the blocks; a blood-derived one (Gansauge) needs no tumor.A small mass above the right collarbone, along her old port’s catheter, was left in place at the 2025-08-25 excision. The surgeon called it “highly suspicious for malignancy” and offered to remove it (operative note 2025-08-25; surgical follow-up 2025-09-08). In Jan 2026 her oncologist found a rice-sized nodule next to the removed port site, receding on treatment (note of 2026-01-26). Richard, 2026-10-06: a chest site where the tumor was not completely removedIt is the one known site that could give fresh tissue. At about 5 mm it would likely yield well under Immunocine’s 250 mg minimum (estimate). Whether to sample or remove it is a clinical decision for her oncologist and the surgeon.
Evidence
Level: investigational for colorectal cancer. No dendritic cell product is approved for
CRC in the US.

Closest approved precedent: sipuleucel-T (Provenge), an autologous antigen-presenting-cell
product, FDA-approved in 2010 for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer. It shows
the manufacturing model can reach approval. It says nothing about efficacy in CRC.
CRC trials: DC vaccines have been tested in colorectal cancer in small phase 1/2 studies.
Two randomized phase II trials, both verified against the papers on 2026-10-06:

After complete resection of CRC liver metastases: Rodríguez et al., J Immunother
Cancer 2018, PMID 30268156. Among 15 randomized patients, median disease-free survival
was 25.3 vs 9.5 months, p = 0.067, not significant. The trial was planned for 56
patients and stopped early for lack of funding.
Tumor-lysate DCs in pretreated advanced CRC: Caballero-Baños et al., Eur J Cancer
2016, PMID 27428073. It stopped for futility, with no progression-free or overall
survival benefit.


Not yet done: a systematic literature and ClinicalTrials.gov pass. That means CRC and
MSS subgroups, adjuvant or NED settings, and combinations with checkpoint inhibitors.
No trial status is asserted in this entry.

Who would give it, and access path
Three providers are in contact. The table draws on her emails (read 2026-10-06) and, for
IOZK and Immunocine, their own published documents. How each loads its cells decides
whether her stored tissue matters.





































ProviderCountryProduct (antigen, protocol)Regulatory statusCostAnswers to the questions belowIOZK (Immun-Onkologisches Zentrum Köln)Germany (Cologne)IO-VAC: her dendritic cells loaded with tumor components and combined with a virus. It is part of a multimodal program that can add checkpoint inhibitors, modulated hyperthermia and oncolytic viruses. Treatment is about monthly, 5–8 days a stayAn individual treatment attempt (individueller Heilversuch); the vaccine is made under GMP (email of 2026-09-18)An overview is on its website; not yet recordedQ1: needs tumor “dry, sterile, and frozen at –80°C”, so her paraffin blocks cannot serve. Its brochure (p.13) says tumor components can be isolated from blood if no tumor material is available, and that stored tumor stays the patient’s property. A Zoom call with Dr. Ksouri was set for 2026-09-29; outcome not yet recordedDr. Frank Gansauge, LDG (Laboratories Dr. Gansauge), clinic in Berg near MunichGermanyLANEX-DC: her dendritic cells loaded with antigens from her own blood cells (PBMC), with no tumor tissue. Three visits: consent, a blood draw, then the cells returned 7 days laternot yet recorded€18,800Q1: blood only. Q5: pause binimetinib 1 week before the blood draw. Q3: claims NED within 5 years for 85% of adjuvant patients and no MSS/MSI difference, without a citation. Hb must be above 10 g/dL. Appointments offered for the second half of October (emails of 2026-09-23 and 09-25)Immunocine Cancer Center (Immunocine LLC, Texas)Mexico (Cancún, San José del Cabo)Her dendritic cells, collected by apheresis after filgrastim and loaded with RNA and lysate from her own fresh tumor. Three injections near lymph nodes, two weeks apart, each with pegylated interferonUnapproved, with no ClinicalTrials.gov record (checked 2026-10-06). It cites three Mexican health licenses. The FDA Fast Track designations it is associated with belong to Diakonos Oncology, which its CEO founded at BaylorAbout 120,000; boosters 9,000 each; tissue banking (Immunocine Preserve) $4,000–6,000, as its pages disagreeQ1: at least 250 mg of fresh, never-fixed tumor in its refrigerated kit, or lesions totalling 2 cm that its own team biopsies in Mexico. Paraffin blocks and sequencing data are excluded (Preserve instructions, inclusion criteria), and tissue becomes Immunocine’s on receipt. Q3: one case series of 5 patients, none colorectal. Its patient coordinator sent an introduction on 2026-10-06
The other routes are a clinical trial and an academic center’s compassionate or
expanded-access program. No trial has been identified, because the ClinicalTrials.gov pass
under Evidence has not been done. Whether her treating team would co-manage is an open
question for any route. Her oncologist (conventional) and the integrative clinic are the
likely first conversations (§2.7).
Contraindications, interactions and open questions

Interaction with maintenance. Does MEK inhibition (binimetinib) or anti-EGFR therapy
blunt the T-cell priming a vaccine depends on? Would a provider require a washout, and
would her oncologist accept pausing maintenance? Partly answered:

Dr. Gansauge would pause binimetinib for 1 week before his blood draw.
Immunocine’s criteria call EGFR inhibitors potentially compatible, say nothing about
BRAF or MEK inhibitors, and require 21 days off strong immunosuppressants.
her oncologist has not been asked (question 5 below).


Measuring response. With NED status and negative ctDNA, what endpoint would show
whether it is working? Immune-monitoring assays (e.g. antigen-specific T-cell response)
could be one answer (question 6).
Immune state. RGCC IMMUNE-FRAME reported down-regulated immunity via CD25/CTLA4
overproduction (§2.6, not yet parsed into structured rows). Does that argue for combining
with checkpoint blockade, and is such a combination available anywhere? (question 4)
Product identity. Which antigen, and made from which specimen? The 2024 and 2025 tumors
predate and straddle the BREAKWATER course (question 1).
Leukapheresis tolerance given albumin and blood counts on maintenance. Check current
labs at the time.

Questions for every provider
Put the same questions to each clinic, ideally in writing, and record the answers in the
provider table above so the offers can be compared on the same terms.

Antigen source. What is the product loaded with: whole-tumor lysate, defined
peptides, mRNA, or neoantigens predicted from sequencing? Lysate protocols generally
start from fresh or frozen tumor rather than formalin-fixed tissue. IOZK (2026-09-18) and
Immunocine (its Preserve instructions) have both confirmed this. Her archived tumor is the pathology blocks behind the 2024
and 2025 Caris reports. Do archived blocks suffice? If fresh tissue is needed, this
option is tied to the live-tissue plan
for her next biopsy.
Manufacturing and regulatory status. Where are the cells processed, and is the
facility GMP-certified? What is the product’s legal status in that country: an approved
product, an exemption, a registered trial, or none? Will they put that in writing?
Published colorectal outcomes. For this exact product, is there a registered trial
(with a registry number), a published case series, or only testimonials? How many MSS
colorectal patients have they treated, and in what setting: measurable disease, or NED?
Her immune profile. RGCC IMMUNE-FRAME (February 2025) reported down-regulated
immunity via CD25/CTLA4 overproduction (§2.6). The report is not parsed into structured
data (#326), the assay’s validity is not
established, and it predates both the recurrence and BREAKWATER. Do they measure immune
function before treating, and with what assay? Would a poor result change the protocol
(for example, adding a checkpoint inhibitor) or lead them to decline?
Scheduling around BRAF/MEK inhibitors. She takes encorafenib and binimetinib with
cetuximab (§2.2). Must she pause any of them, and for how long, before leukapheresis and
around each dose? Have they treated patients on BRAF/MEK inhibitors? Will they coordinate
with her oncologist? For comparison only: two of the BOT/BAL trials read on 2026-10-01 require
14 days off targeted small-molecule therapy before their first dose.
Measuring response. She has no measurable disease, and her ctDNA has been negative
since 2025-12-05 (last report on file 2026-03-03). What would they measure to tell
whether it is working, and will they share the raw results?
Cost and data sharing. What is the total cost? That means leukapheresis, manufacture,
every dose and booster, monitoring and travel. What is refunded if manufacture fails?

What it is and how it works
Disulfiram (Antabuse) is an oral drug, in use since 1951 for alcohol-use disorder. Two
anticancer mechanisms are proposed (due diligence §2):

ALDH inhibition. A metabolite formed through CYP3A4/5 irreversibly blocks aldehyde
dehydrogenase. A 2026 preclinical paper argues that APC-deficient colorectal cells depend
on ALDH2 to clear toxic aldehydes, so blocking it is synthetic-lethal.
CuET and NPL4. With copper, its breakdown product forms a complex, CuET. CuET disables
NPL4, the adaptor of the p97 protein-disposal machine, and the cell dies of proteotoxic
stress (Skrott et al., Nature 2017). This is the better-established mechanism.

Both mechanisms depend on copper or are enhanced by it. The prescription described in the
review is for disulfiram alone.

In spring 2026, news coverage of the APC/ALDH2 paper prompted the May brief
(docs/maureen_apc_disulfiram_brief.md).
A physician outside the care team listed in the Mission Spec (§2.7) then wrote a
prescription (the review, 2026-08-07).

She has not started it (Richard, 2026-10-01: prescription written, not taken). If she
starts, the review’s dose and neuropathy questions come first, and the entry moves to
ModsTreatmentEpisode, staying here only as a link.
