Implementation notes: M20 (2026-10-08)
The positive control failed at the first sync after I-3. Kaiser records each cetuximab infusion as
its own MedicationRequest and marks it completed after the dose, so M8 read her current infusion as
ended. Richard chose D-Q4-27 A (#873): a drug Kaiser
records as repeated per-dose orders is current while its latest dose is within twice its own usual
interval. It applies only to 3 or more completed orders at a regular spacing, so a one-off order never
qualifies. Built as M20, RULES_VERSION ehr-derived/2. The decision fixes the 3 and the 2×. The
rest is a reading of “at a regular spacing”, flagged for Richard on the PR:

A run, not the whole history. The latest dose must end a run of at least three, each dose at
most 42 days after the one before. A longer gap is a break between courses, and the doses before it
are not the drug’s spacing now.

Reading the whole history instead would let one order, months after an old series, read current
for weeks.
The cost of the run: after a break, a resumed drug reads not current until its third dose. In
those weeks the safety list still lists its orders as recent (M17).


42 days. In her record the gaps between consecutive completed doses of one drug are either at
most five weeks (a delayed cycle within a course) or more than eight (a break between courses).
Six weeks sits between the two. It also caps the window at twelve weeks after the latest dose.
The lower median. With an even number of gaps, the usual interval is the lower middle one: an
interval that occurred, and the shorter window.
Doses. A dose is a completed Kaiser order of the drug (not a plan), counted once per start day.
The start (authoredOn) is the only date a dose has, because Kaiser refuses our app’s
MedicationAdministration requests.
What stops it. An order of the drug dated on or after its latest dose, or undated, that is
stopped, on hold, cancelled, a draft or of unstated status. An active order is decided by M4–M6;
one entered in error is void. M20 changes no order but the completed one(s) on the latest dose day.

Appendix A. Read-only queries for the steward
Each runs as the census and the audit probes did:

docker exec -i BACKEND python - < probe.py;
inside one transaction set READ ONLY and asserted with SHOW transaction_read_only, then rolled
back;
counts and codes only, with :p bound to her patient id.

Q1, Q6 and Q8 can run any time, and a first Q7 belongs before anything changes. Q2 to Q4 need the
columns I-3 adds, so they run after the first post-I-3 sync, when Q1 and Q7 run again.
-- Q1. Rows by source and identity state (before and after).
SELECT 'mods_medication' AS tbl, source, source_record_id IS NOT NULL AS has_id, count(*)
FROM mods_medication WHERE patient_id = :p GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
UNION ALL
SELECT 'mods_condition', source, source_record_id IS NOT NULL, count(*)
FROM mods_condition WHERE patient_id = :p GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
ORDER BY 1, 2, 3;
 
-- Q2. Kaiser orders by status and intent (J2-J6).
SELECT coalesce(status, '(null)') AS status, coalesce(intent, '(null)') AS intent, count(*)
FROM mods_medication WHERE patient_id = :p AND source = 'epic_fhir'
GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 3 DESC;
 
-- Q3. Active orders whose window has closed (J5), and their categories (J11).
SELECT coalesce(category, '(null)') AS category,
       CASE WHEN end_date IS NULL THEN 'no validity end'
            WHEN end_date >= current_date THEN 'window open'
            WHEN end_date >= current_date - 90 THEN 'closed under 90 days'
            WHEN end_date >= current_date - 365 THEN 'closed 90-365 days'
            ELSE 'closed over a year' END AS validity_window, count(*)
FROM mods_medication
WHERE patient_id = :p AND source = 'epic_fhir' AND status = 'active'
GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 1, 2;
 
-- Q4. Conditions by category, raw clinical status and verification (J13-J20).
SELECT coalesce(category, '(null)') AS category,
       coalesce(metadata->>'clinical_status', '(absent)') AS clinical_status_raw,
       coalesce(verification_status, '(null)') AS verification, count(*)
FROM mods_condition WHERE patient_id = :p AND source = 'epic_fhir'
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3 ORDER BY 4 DESC;
 
-- Q6. Cancer-profile fields the #106 collector could still fill (J22): blank or not, no values.
SELECT coalesce(primary_site, '') = '' AS site_blank, coalesce(histology, '') = '' AS histology_blank,
       coalesce(icd10_code, '') = '' AS icd10_blank, diagnosis_date IS NULL AS dx_date_blank,
       coalesce(primary_site_snomed, '') = '' AS site_snomed_blank,
       coalesce(histology_snomed, '') = '' AS histology_snomed_blank
FROM mods_cancer_profile WHERE patient_id = :p;
 
-- Q7. Her stored KG edges per predicate and builder (before and after re-materializing).
SELECT predicate, metadata->>'source' AS built_from, count(*)
FROM mods_kg_relation
WHERE source_id = 'maple_patient' AND subject_id = :patient_entity_id
GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 1, 2;
 
-- Q8. The ambiguous pairs (J23): rows, distinct names and import times per id, without the id.
SELECT count(*) AS n_rows, count(DISTINCT name) AS n_names, count(DISTINCT created_at) AS n_imports
FROM mods_medication
WHERE patient_id = :p AND source = 'epic_fhir' AND source_record_id IS NULL
  AND coalesce(metadata->>'fhir_id', '') <> ''
GROUP BY metadata->>'fhir_id' HAVING count(*) > 1;
Q5, the positive control, is a call into the view, not SQL. For cetuximab, encorafenib and
binimetinib it prints the number of Kaiser orders in each state, matched on the drug name as the KG
resolver matches it, and nothing else. Pass: each of the three has at least one order in current
or held.

ehr/ehr_sync_audit.title: Kaiser FHIR sync: code review and completeness audit
ehr/ehr_sync_audit.content:
Kaiser FHIR sync: code review and completeness audit
Issue: #624, phase 1 (review and measurement; no
code is changed). Code reviewed: main at 16f9ae0, after PR #626. Measured: 2026-10-01,
read-only against production, counts only. Companion:
backend/scripts/ehr/kaiser_census.py
counts what Kaiser holds at the next login, which this audit cannot see.
(Status, 2026-10-05: most findings here are fixed in code. On 2026-10-02 every entry point
began to run the sync in one place, decryption began to fail closed, every search pages to its
end with retries and reports a short result as partial, OperationOutcome entries are set
aside, connection lookups filter by provider, and next links stay on the FHIR site (findings
8, 11, 13 and 14, and §2). The same day, note and report text began to come from the
attachments, uncut (findings 1 and 2); the post-May backfill ran (finding 3); records began to
update in place by FHIR id (finding 7, and the encounter status in finding 9); the 306 older
encounter copies were removed (§5); and an unstated condition status became “not stated”
(finding 5). I-3, merged on 2026-10-05, stores medications and conditions at one row per
record (findings 4 and 5). Lab values (finding 6) and the HTML overlap (finding 10) are still
open. Richard decided the eight questions at the end on 2026-10-02 (D-Q4-16). Every count
here is as measured on 2026-10-01.)
Richard has long suspected that Maple is missing documents. He is right, and the gap is larger
than missing rows. Three things stand out:

Maple holds the record’s index, not its text. All 870 Kaiser clinical notes in Maple are
empty shells: the note body was never fetched. Report narratives are stored only up to 500
characters, because Maple’s own importer keeps no more, and 35 of the 38 imaging and pathology
reports in Maple stop exactly there.
Most of the record collapses on import. Kaiser returned 507 prescriptions and 391
conditions on 2026-10-01. Maple keeps one row per drug name (141) and one per condition name
(42). Each row is frozen at its first import, and every condition stored from Kaiser reads
“resolved”.
Nothing is ever updated. A record stored once is skipped on every later sync. Parser
fixes from May never reached the rows stored before them. A status change at Kaiser never
lands either. The patient knowledge graph turns those frozen statuses into the
current_medication edges the PDR2 foundations train on.

The fetch layer is mostly sound after #626. The import layer is not: its identity keys are names
and calendar days, not Kaiser’s ids, and that one design choice causes most of what follows.
Findings, ranked by data lost or at risk
Severity: critical means clinically significant content is absent from Maple today; high
means it is wrong or incomplete in a way a reader or the model consumes; medium means it is
at risk or partly wrong; low means the count is cosmetic or the bug is latent.
Code references are to main at 16f9ae0. connector is
backend/connectors/epic_fhir_connector.py; ingestion is
backend/mods_ehr_ingestion_service.py. Evidence is from read-only production queries on
2026-10-01, unless it names the sync logs (debug_logs, the two syncs of 2026-10-01).

Only an inline text/* attachment is decoded; an attachment url (a Binary) is never followed, and the stored text falls back to Document: <title>. Encounters and conditions are stored twice under two sources. An unexpanded report result that Kaiser refuses is logged and counted nowhere.mediumconnector:448–503 (cap 453, raise 478), 775–809Labs used 27 of 50 pages on 10-01 (2,687 entries). 16 report results answered 403 on direct fetch (10-01 log), and no count reports them.12Procedures and allergies arrive empty from FHIR, and their import paths are broken. _import_procedure inserts on every run, forces completed and never fills body_site. _import_allergy forces active and strips the wrong prefix.mediumingestion:964–985, 741–769Kaiser returned 0 Procedure and 0 AllergyIntolerance on 10-01 (the page held only an OperationOutcome), though 08-16 stored 2 procedures. Reconnecting Cerbo (#512 item 4) adds a second row, and an OAuth callback could then write Kaiser tokens onto it.14Non-resource entries parsed as resources. Kaiser adds one OperationOutcome per page; the fetchers never check resourceType.lowconnector:529–649101 entries per 100-match page (10-01 log). 9 junk documents and 2 junk encounters are stored; the next sync adds 1 and 2 more. Each OperationOutcome’s message is discarded.15Counts and summaries mislead. One commit at the end, with *_created kept if it fails. The delta caps report counts at 20 and misses Kaiser values in other sources’ series. No database uniqueness on documents, encounters or procedures, and the MCP tool has no in-flight guard.lowingestion:1230–1236, 1772, 1582Lead 6 of #624, confirmed in code.
What the code alone cannot say is how much of findings 1, 4, 5, 6 and 11 is loss against Kaiser’s
current record, and how much of finding 12 is a search-shape problem. That is the census’s job
(§ Phase 2, step 0).
1. Granted vs fetched
The 2026-10-01 token grants 28 resource types (read from the stored scopes on
mods_ehr_connection, each with an unqualified .r/.s scope, plus category-qualified ones
for Condition, DocumentReference, Observation and ServiceRequest). Provenance is read-only, with no
search. offline_access is not granted, so there is still no refresh token.
The sync fetches 10 searches over 9 types: Observation (laboratory, vital-signs),
MedicationRequest, Condition, DocumentReference, AllergyIntolerance, Immunization, Encounter,
Procedure and DiagnosticReport (with _include=DiagnosticReport:result).

Without it the 870 notes are shells (finding 1).MedicationAdministrationnot grantedhighestEach infusion dose with its date: the real FOLFOX, cetuximab and bevacizumab timeline. Orders (MedicationRequest) say what was prescribed, not when it ran. It needs an app-registration change, if Kaiser offers it to patient apps at all.ServiceRequestnohighOrders: a scheduled surveillance CT, standing tumour-marker orders, referrals. This is “what should arrive next”, which a freshness monitor (#512) needs, and DiagnosticReport.basedOn points at it.MedicationDispensenohighPharmacy fills of oral targeted therapy (encorafenib and binimetinib are oral): actual exposure dates and adherence, not just orders.Observation: imagingnohighImaging result observations: the narratives behind CT reports. that confirms what a registration change would have to add.
2. Fetch
Paging. _fetch_all_pages follows next links but stops after max_pages=50 (5,000
entries at _count=100) with only a debug line (connector:453, 467). Observation and
DiagnosticReport sort -date, so a capped search drops the oldest. No search reached the cap on
2026-10-01: labs used 27 pages (2,687 entries), vital signs 13, notes 10, reports 9. next links
are followed to whatever host the server names, carrying the bearer token.
Bundle totals. Kaiser’s Bundle.total counts the page, not the search: the first page of a
1,213-entry search reports total=100. Nothing can use it as a completeness check. Whether
_summary=count is supported and correct is unknown; the census records it beside the paged
count.
Filters, sort, include. Every search is patient=<id>&_count=100; Observation adds a
category, and Observation and DiagnosticReport sort -date. DiagnosticReport adds
_include=DiagnosticReport:result, which made Kaiser take 266 s (#620; now under a 420 s read
timeout). Kaiser does not expand the include for some reports. The direct-fetch fallback then
got 403 on all 16 such results on 10-01, logged per observation and counted nowhere.
Delta. There is none for FHIR: every sync re-fetches the whole record. last_delta_timestamp
is Cerbo-only, and even there the delta response is discarded. A full re-fetch is the right
default for completeness. It only works if import is idempotent and applies updates, and today
it does neither for most types (findings 4–7).
Timeouts and retries. Connect, write and pool use 30 s; the DiagnosticReport read uses 420 s.
Nothing is retried: a 429, a 5xx or a dropped connection on any page raises. The pages already
fetched for that type are discarded, so one bad page loses the whole type for that sync.
Non-resource entries. Every page carries exactly one extra entry (101 entries for 100
matches; 927 note entries over 10 pages for 917 notes), almost certainly an OperationOutcome.
The fetchers parse it as the searched type. The Observation, Condition, MedicationRequest,
Allergy, Immunization and Procedure parsers drop it because it has no name. The DocumentReference
and Encounter parsers default it into a “Clinical Document” and an “Office Visit”. What
Kaiser’s OperationOutcome says is never read.
How failures surface. Since #626 a failed search makes the sync partial, with
failed_resources and fetch_errors, and a sync that fetched nothing is degraded. Still
silent: the page cap, failed direct fetches, an HTTP 200 that is not a Bundle (zero entries),
and import exceptions other than IntegrityError at commit, which mark the sync error while
the counters already claim inserts.
Entry points. All three built-in paths fail on this machine (finding 8):



































Entry pointRuns inHas the key?ResultMCP mods_ehr_syncMCP hostno401 on every search → degradedPOST /api/mods/ehr/sync → worker ehr_synca workernothe sameTerminal ehr sync→ the REST routenothe same, printed as “Sync complete”docker exec -i BACKEND python - < scriptbackendyesworks (the 2026-10-01 syncs)
The token is stored encrypted, and a process without the key cannot use it. _decrypt_token returns the ciphertext when the key
is missing or wrong, and the 401s that follow are the only symptom.
3. Import, per _import_*





















































































































PathReached by FHIRIdentity across syncsWithin one syncForced or droppedCounter_import_test_result (labs, vitals, report observations)yesseries name (case-folded, shared by every source) + date at 00:00a query per value; under the backend’s SessionLocal (autoflush off) it cannot see unflushed rowstime of day; code (LOINC); status; comparator; components; per-value unit and range; text cut at 500created counts adds before commit; enriched merges another observation’s metadata into a stored row_import_medicationyesDB unique (patient, name) (since I-3: the Kaiser id; the name only for rows without one)savepoint per rowstatus frozen; sig, route, dose, frequency, prescriber, RxNorm never set (since I-3: all kept but RxNorm)rows_import_condition_from_problemyes, for every ConditionDB unique (patient, name, 'problem-list-item') (since I-3: the Kaiser id)savepointcategory forced; FHIR’s Allergy:  prefix kept in the namerows_import_immunizationyesDB unique (patient, vaccine, date); a NULL date never matchessavepointstatus forced completedrows_import_encounteryesmetadata.fhir_id within (patient, source) (#626); content key without onein-memory indexstatus forced finished; class, reason, end, location ids droppedrows_import_encounter_plannedHTML onlynone——attempts_import_procedureyesnone: inserts every run—status forced completed; body_site column never setattempts_import_deviceHTML onlynone——attempts_import_generic_document (notes, reports)yesmetadata.fhir_id within (patient, source, kind) (#626)in-memory indextext is a stub (§4); report status and category not keptrowsgenomic alterations from a reportyes (none so far)(gene, variant, source_report)query—rows_import_care_team_memberHTML onlyDB unique (patient, name, role)savepoint—rows
Lab and vital identity, in detail. The check is (series_id, ts), where ts is the date at
midnight. Within one sync it runs as a query that, under autoflush off, cannot see values added
earlier in the same sync. So same-day repeats were kept, and an observation that arrived twice
(through the report _include and through its category search) was stored twice. Across syncs
the same check sees the stored row and skips any new same-day result, or merges its metadata into
the other row’s context. The stored data shows both:

171 (series, day) groups hold 819 Kaiser-matched rows; in 159 of those groups every row was
created on the same day;
43 Kaiser observation ids are stored more than once in one series on one day;
15 more ids sit in two different series, because the series cache keys on the case-folded name
over every source with no tie-break (ingestion:467). Seven test names have two or more series.

The right identity is the Observation id. With it, repeats are distinct, a duplicate arrival is
one row, and a corrected value can update in place.
Dates. _parse_fhir_date keeps the calendar date in the timestamp’s own offset
(connector:1630–1631). Kaiser sends UTC, so a result after about 17:00 Pacific lands on the next
day. A partial date (“2024-05”) becomes the first of the month with no precision marker.
Commit and rollback. import_fhir_data commits once, at the end (ingestion:1230–1236). That
makes a sync atomic, which is good. But one bad row discards the whole sync’s import. Only
IntegrityError is caught there, and the *_created counters are not reset.
Parsed, then dropped: presentedForm (all reports); the report’s status and category;
DocumentReference attachment URLs, docStatus, relatesTo and encounter context; Observation
status, code (the test code), comparator and component; Condition category and
recordedDate; MedicationRequest intent, category, reasonCode and RxNorm coding; Encounter
class, reasonCode and period.end. The procedure body_site is parsed into metadata but
never into its column.
4. Content: do stored notes carry their text?
No. Every Kaiser document in Maple is metadata.



































Kind (source epic_fhir)RowsContentDocumentReference (notes)870870 are exactly Document: <title>, max 45 chars, no fileDiagnosticReport, imaging (title class)31max 262 chars. All 31 have a narrative observation, and 28 of those narratives stop at exactly 500 charactersDiagnosticReport, pathology (title class)7max 84 chars. All 7 narratives stop at exactly 500 charactersDiagnosticReport, genomic panel (title class)2max 153 chars; scalar results only (TMB, MSI, PD-L1)DiagnosticReport, labs and other634max 162 chars
The title classes are a keyword heuristic over report titles, counted and never printed. Notes by
type label: Encounter Summary 310, Progress Notes 181, Telephone Encounter 126, Diagnostic imaging
study 67, Staff Note 44, Patient Instructions 43, plus 25 smaller types (90 notes). A further 9 are the page-level junk
entries (finding 14).
For comparison, all 121 manually uploaded documents and all 237 from the integrative practice
carry the original file, and all but one carry extracted text (up to 1.28 M characters). Every
full-text radiology report Maple has came that way, never from the sync.
.claude/rules/ehr-integrations.md says “FHIR is not a full-text source”. The code says
otherwise: the sync never asks for the text. It cuts what it does get to 500 characters, and it
throws away presentedForm unread. Whether Kaiser serves note bodies through Binary with this
grant is the census’s attachment probe. The rule should be revised once that answer is in.
5. Versions: the 305 encounter ids with two stored copies
After #622’s cleanup, 633 Kaiser encounter rows remain for 325 ids. 304 ids have two versions,
1 has three, and 20 have one; 2 further rows are junk with no id. I compared the earliest and
latest stored version of each id, field by field:



































What differsIdsKindCausedepartment column (and metadata.department)304old NULL, new setparser change: #70 added the department between the 05-08 and 08-16 importsprovider column and metadata.participants4both set, different sets of namessource update: Kaiser changed the participantsmetadata.status1arrived → finishedsource update: the visit was under way at the first importencounter_date, type, description, notes, other metadata0——
Import-day pairs: 303 ids were stored on 05-08 and again on 08-16; 1 on 05-08 and 10-01; 1 on
08-16 and 10-01. In every pair the later version is a superset of the earlier one: it adds the
department or carries the final status and participants.
Recommendation. Keep the latest version of each id and delete the 306 older rows, after a
backup, as #622’s cleanup did. Then change the sync to update in place, keyed on
(patient, source, fhir_id) with a unique index. Store updated_at and the source’s
meta.lastUpdated, and never overwrite with an older payload. The decision is Richard’s
(below). The same rule should cover every FHIR type, not only encounters (finding 7).
6. Cross-source: kaiser_html against the FHIR rows
The March 2026 HTML import (307 encounters, 61 conditions, 15 medications, 8 immunizations, 4
procedures, 12 devices, 5 care-team members, 118 lab series) predates the FHIR sync and carries no
Kaiser ids.

Encounters. 302 of 307 HTML encounters share a date with a FHIR encounter, 277 the type as
well. Within the HTML date range (2016-12 to 2026-04), 300 of 303 FHIR encounters have an HTML
row that day. Any view that does not filter by source counts these visits twice.
Conditions. 36 condition names appear under both sources. The HTML rows hold the
encounter diagnoses (48) and the active problem list (10, 3 of them naming a cancer). 36 of the
42 FHIR rows carry one of those names, relabelled as resolved problems (finding 5).
Immunizations. Kaiser returned 12 immunizations on 10-01, and Maple holds 4 FHIR rows. The
unique index (patient, vaccine, date) refused the other 8. The likely cause is the 8 HTML
rows: the two sources name vaccines the same way (3 HTML names also appear on FHIR rows), and
no HTML date matches a stored FHIR row. That is an inference; the census lists the 8 by date
range. If it holds, no vaccination is lost, but those 8 carry no Kaiser id.
Medications. No name matches exactly; the two sources format names differently.
Labs. One series per name across sources, by design. 643 of 676 values in HTML-created series
were later matched to a Kaiser observation id (finding 6).
Documents. One HTML document (social history); no overlap.

The HTML rows still hold data FHIR does not deliver today: devices, care team, surgical
procedures, visit diagnoses and planned visits. They should be kept. Phase 2 needs a precedence
rule: FHIR wins where both exist, and views read one source per type.
7. Tests
Covered: the per-resource read timeout and named fetch failures; partial / degraded
classification; document, report and encounter dedupe on FHIR id under both autoflush settings
(#626); the condition, medication-date, procedure and encounter-department parsers; series
aliases; genomic-variant routing and VAF units; the cancer profile from EHR conditions. In all,
119 tests across five files, and all pass.
Not covered:

pagination (more than one page, next links, the 50-page cap);
non-resource entries;
_parse_observation value types, status, comparator and components;
_import_test_result: the day key, the autoflush dependence and text truncation;
medication and condition collapse on name;
_parse_document_reference attachments and presentedForm;
_import_procedure idempotency;
allergy and immunization imports;
the OAuth callback and save_ehr_connection;
get_sync_delta;
the Kaiser HTML parser (only mocked);
the Terminal ehr sync output (the frontend has no tests at all).

The census adds 27 tests (backend/tests/test_kaiser_census.py): paging, the cap,
OperationOutcome handling, _summary=count, retries, 403/401 handling, id comparison, fidelity
counts, the attachment probe, and that it writes nothing. Each safeguard was reverted once to
confirm its test fails.
Cerbo, in one line
The same patterns appear in cerbo_connector.py: a silent 50-page cap; per-resource failures
logged but not returned, so a Cerbo sync is never partial; documents fetched as metadata only;
and a dedupe that keys on fhir_id, which Cerbo rows lack (they carry cerbo_id). That last one
falls back to content keys. These need their own issue.
Recommendation per component

































































ComponentVerdictWhyOAuth: authorize, callback, PKCE, Kaiser endpoint derivationkeepWorks. Filter every connection lookup by provider (finding 13).Token storage and decryptionfixFail closed when the key is missing or wrong, instead of sending ciphertext.Where the sync runsfixGive the worker that runs ehr_sync the key (compose change), or run it in the backend. Make the Terminal print the sync’s status._fetch_all_pagesfixNo silent cap; retry per page with backoff; keep pages fetched so far; keep only the searched resourceType and record OperationOutcome codes; same-host next links.Per-type fetch_* methodsrewrite as one generic fetcher over a type registryTen near-identical copies, and new types (Binary, ServiceRequest, MedicationDispense, Specimen…) are coming.ParsersfixKeep status, codes (LOINC, RxNorm, ICD-10, SNOMED), categories, time, comparator, components, attachment URLs, presentedForm.Import layer (_import_* for FHIR data)rewriteIdentity = (patient, source, resource type, fhir_id) for every FHIR type, with update in place, unique indexes and counters that equal rows. Names and calendar days stop being identities. A “current drugs” or “active problems” view is derived, not stored as the record.Text and attachmentsbuildFetch Binary for notes and presentedForm for reports; keep the full observation text; store text plus the original file, as uploads are stored.kaiser_html importerkeep, frozenHolds data FHIR does not; no new imports; FHIR takes precedence where both exist.get_sync_delta, Terminal summaryfixReport counts without the 20 cap; show partial / degraded.TestsaddThe gaps in §7, each with the bug reproduced first.
Phase 2: proposed order

Census, at the next login, before any sync. Run kaiser_census.py first. It sends GETs
only; my estimate is 10–15 minutes, and its output times every search. Then run the #621
backfill sync. Then, if the hour allows,
run the census again with --types DocumentReference,DiagnosticReport to confirm the
backfill. The first census sizes everything below: missing ids per type, how many results
collapse, status drift, whether Binary and presentedForm are readable and how large, and
what the procedure and care-plan searches return.
Quick fixes, low risk, independent of each other: the key or runner (finding 8, #512);
fail-closed decryption; the Terminal status; delta counts; resourceType filtering; no silent
cap, plus retries; provider filters on connection lookups.
Identity and updates (the core). Upsert on FHIR id for every type, unique indexes (a
migration, numbered against all branches), and change tracking. Then the cleanups: the 306
encounter versions, re-importing collapsed medications and conditions as per-id rows, and
de-duplicating lab values.
Content. Binary note bodies and report forms, full observation text, embedding and
categorisation of the new text.
Fidelity: codes, statuses, categories, times, comparators, components and units, plus
the condition category mapping.
New types, chosen from the census counts: ServiceRequest and MedicationDispense first.
Downstream. The patient KG reads the corrected medication and condition status; the
freshness monitor (#512) watches series cadence.

Decisions Richard needs to make

Encounter versions: keep the latest of each id and delete the 306 older rows (backup
first)?
Update in place: should a re-sync overwrite stored FHIR records when Kaiser changes them
(status, corrected values, amended notes)? And should earlier versions be kept in a history
table, or dropped?
Row identity for medications, conditions and labs: one row per FHIR resource (per
prescription, per diagnosis instance, per observation)? This changes what mods_medication
and mods_condition mean. The knowledge graph’s “current medication” would then come from a
derived view. (Decided: D-Q4-16 item 3, then D-Q4-18 for the view’s rules; built for
medications and conditions in I-3. Labs are I-4.)
Note bodies: fetch and store the text of all ~920 notes, or only some types? Storing them
puts the full narrative record in the database and in embeddings.
Condition status mapping: when Kaiser sends no clinicalStatus (as it does for 40 of the
42 stored conditions), store NULL (“not stated”) instead of resolved? This is a vocabulary
mapping, so per CLAUDE.md it is his call.
kaiser_html overlap: keep the HTML rows and filter by source in views, mark them
superseded, or delete the exact overlaps?
New resource types, once the census shows what Kaiser holds.
Where the sync runs: the encryption key on the worker that runs ehr_sync, or a
backend-only runner?

Parallelization Analysis

Surfaces touched.

This PR (phase 1): docs (this file) and tests (test_kaiser_census.py), plus one new
read-only script. No backend API, frontend component, worker handler, migration, MCP tool or
DB-stored config.
Phase 2:

backend API: yes (sync entry and status);
frontend component: yes (Terminal.jsx ehr sync output);
worker handler: yes (handle_ehr_sync, or only its environment);
migration: yes (unique indexes on FHIR ids; possibly history tables);
MCP tool: yes (mods_ehr_sync in-flight guard and status);
DB-stored config: no;
docs: yes (this audit; .claude/rules/ehr-integrations.md);
tests: yes.




Parallel split. Step 1’s fixes are independent: connector paging, Terminal, connection
lookups and the compose key can be separate sessions. Step 2 (identity, upsert, migration)
must land before its cleanups and before step 4’s re-import. Step 3 (Binary) can be built
alongside step 2, because documents already dedupe on FHIR id since #626. Step 5 follows
step 2’s generic fetcher. The census needs nothing but a login.
Collision hotspots.

backend/migrations.py: step 2’s indexes; number against all branches.
the compose file the stack runs from: the worker key.
frontend/src/components/Terminal.jsx.
backend/mcp_servers/mods_server.py.
backend/mods_models.py.
requirements.txt: an HTML/RTF-to-text library for note bodies, if one is needed.
.claude/rules/ehr-integrations.md.
Not touched: main.py, component_registry.py, ComponentLoader.jsx, package.json,
CLAUDE.md, MEMORY.md.


Verify how.

Census: re-run after each step. Kaiser-only ids → 0; “collapsed by Maple’s key” → 0;
“stored status differs” → 0.
pytest: tests/test_ehr_fhir_sync.py, tests/test_kaiser_census.py, and new import
tests, each failing first with the bug restored.
DB: the read-only counts in this document, re-run.
Worker: an env check on the worker that runs ehr_sync.
UI: a Terminal walk-through showing partial for a failed search.
KG: the patient KG’s current_medication edges recomputed after step 2.



The census
backend/scripts/ehr/kaiser_census.py
runs inside the backend container, within the hour after a Kaiser
login:
docker exec -i BACKEND python - < backend/scripts/ehr/kaiser_census.py
docker exec -i BACKEND python - --json < backend/scripts/ehr/kaiser_census.py > census.json
# once on main: docker exec BACKEND python -m scripts.ehr.kaiser_census --json

For each search it pages to the end, with no silent cap, and records:

pages, matches, distinct ids and non-resource entries;
Kaiser’s per-page total, and the _summary=count answer;
the date range;
OperationOutcome codes.

Per resource type it compares Kaiser’s ids with the ids Maple stores. It reports Kaiser-only ids
(with their date range), Maple-only ids, and records Kaiser changed after Maple stored them.
It also counts what the sync’s parsers lose. For observations: status, comparators, text over
500 characters, the sync’s own (name, day) collisions, time of day, the day shift and stored
values that differ. For conditions and medications: collapse on name and status drift. It counts
attachment and form types. It fetches up to three attachments and reports their size and type,
never their content.
It writes nothing. The database is read in one verified READ ONLY transaction, closed before any
request. Every request is a GET to the stored FHIR host or another host of the same site
(*.kp.org), and debug_log is silenced. Output is counts, codes, content types and date ranges
only.
How the numbers here were measured
Read-only probes ran on 2026-10-01 against production, each with docker exec -i BACKEND python - < probe.py inside one SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY transaction (asserted with SHOW transaction_read_only), then rolled back. They printed counts, key names, FHIR codes and type
labels only. Kaiser-side counts come from the debug_logs lines of the two 2026-10-01 syncs
(page sizes, entries per search, parsed records), reduced to their numbers. Patient-scoped
queries use Maureen’s patient id, which is also the earliest-created patient. No sync, census or
write was run, and Kaiser was not called.

essays/training_first_neural_network.title: Training My First Neural Network
essays/training_first_neural_network.content:
Training My First Neural Network
Dev log #[N] — April 2026


A note on what this is. This is a walkthrough rather than a result: it explains a training run end to end, from what a neural network is up to what our numbers actually meant. The data and code are accurate as of the date above. The diagrams specified under Chart Production Notes at the end have not been drawn — they are left as a description of what would help, not as a promise that it exists.


Why I’m Doing This
The project this belongs to is an attempt to find drugs that might work for one
specific person with stage IV colorectal cancer — not by reading the literature
faster, but by turning a large part of it into a graph and asking a model what
the graph’s shape implies. Elsewhere in these notes that argument is made
properly. Here it is only the reason any of the following was worth doing.
What makes the problem tractable at all is that somebody has already shown the
approach works. A 2025 paper applied it to Alzheimer’s disease and colorectal
cancer, published its method, and got results specific enough to check. So the
first question was not can this work but the much duller and much more
answerable can we make it work here — reproduce their pipeline, run it
ourselves, and see whether the numbers land close enough to theirs to trust the
machinery before pointing it at a patient.
They did, mostly. This post is how, step by step, including the parts where the
obvious thing turned out to be wrong.
If you had told me six months ago that I’d be running a graph neural network on a biomedical knowledge graph to generate drug repurposing candidates, I would have asked you to repeat that in English. But here we are. This post is a complete walkthrough of how we got there — including every mistake, wrong turn, and “oh, that’s what that means” moment along the way.
The scientific context: we’re trying to replicate, and then extend, a 2025 paper titled “Precision Drug Repurposing for Alzheimer’s Disease and Colorectal Cancer via Knowledge Graph Embedding” by Oğuztüzün et al. (Journal of Biomedical Informatics, doi:10.1016/j.jbi.2025.104786). The paper trains a neural network on a biomedical knowledge graph to predict which drugs might treat specific diseases — including colorectal cancer (CRC), which is relevant to us for obvious reasons.
We reproduced their training pipeline, ran it ourselves, and got results close enough to the paper to be meaningful. This post explains how, step by step.

First: What Is a Neural Network, Actually?
Before we get into the specifics, let me give a plain-English overview. I won’t assume you’ve trained one before, because I hadn’t.
The basic idea
A neural network is a mathematical function that learns patterns from data by adjusting millions of internal numbers (called weights). You show it examples, it makes predictions, you tell it how wrong it was, and it adjusts its weights to be less wrong next time. Do that enough times and it gets good at whatever pattern you’re training it on.
The name “neural network” comes from a loose analogy to neurons in a brain — each “neuron” (node) in the network receives signals from others, combines them, and passes a result forward. In practice it’s just matrix multiplication and some nonlinear functions, all the way down.
[INPUT DATA] → [LAYER 1] → [LAYER 2] → ... → [OUTPUT]
                  ↑             ↑
              (weights)     (weights)
              adjusted by backpropagation

[CHART 1: Simple neural network diagram — 3-4 layers, nodes connected by arrows, label “weights” on the connections, label “backpropagation” as a backward arrow. Keep it clean and minimal. Caption: “A neural network learns by adjusting weights based on prediction errors.”]
Training
Training has a rhythm:

Forward pass — run data through the network, get a prediction
Calculate loss — measure how wrong the prediction is (the “loss function”)
Backward pass (backpropagation) — calculate how each weight contributed to the error
Update — nudge each weight in the direction that would have made the prediction better (gradient descent)
Repeat for thousands of batches

The “learning rate” controls how big each nudge is. Too large and you overshoot. Too small and you never converge.
An epoch is one complete pass through the entire training dataset. We trained for 200 epochs — meaning the model saw every training triple 200 times, updating its weights after each batch.
Embeddings
Here’s the key concept for what we’re doing: embeddings. Rather than learning to classify inputs into categories, our network learns to map every entity (drug, disease, gene…) to a point in a high-dimensional vector space. Entities that are conceptually related end up close together; unrelated ones are far apart.
Think of it like a map where similar things cluster. In our case, a drug that treats Alzheimer’s should end up near other Alzheimer’s drugs in the vector space — even if we never explicitly told the model that.
Our model uses 100-dimensional embeddings, meaning each entity is represented as a list of 100 numbers. With 61,146 entities, that’s roughly 6.1 million numbers just for the entity embeddings alone.

Knowledge Graphs: Data as a Web of Relationships
Before we could train anything, we needed data in the right shape. That shape is a knowledge graph (KG).
A knowledge graph represents facts as triples:
(subject) → [relation] → (object)

For example:

(Metformin) → [treats] → (type 2 diabetes)
(ATM gene) → [associated with] → (colorectal cancer)
(Cyclophosphamide) → [targets] → (DNMT1 gene)

[CHART 2: Simple knowledge graph diagram — 8-10 nodes (2-3 drugs, 2-3 genes, 2 diseases, 1 phenotype), connected by labeled arrows showing different relation types. Color-code by entity type. Caption: “A knowledge graph represents biomedical knowledge as typed nodes connected by labeled relationships.”]
The knowledge graph we used is called GP-KG (Gene-Phenotype Knowledge Graph), built by Srivastava et al. at Case Western Reserve University. It aggregates data from:

DrugBank — FDA-approved drug information
TreatKB — text-mined drug-disease pairs from clinical trials and MEDLINE
PhenomeBrowser — drug-phenotype associations

By the numbers:

































StatValueTotal entities61,146Total edges1,246,726Relation types9Drug nodes1,430Disease nodes7,790Gene nodes18,357
The nine relation types include treat, associate (gene-disease), target (drug-gene), and several gene-phenotype associations across human phenotype, mammalian phenotype, and GO terms.
The task: link prediction
Given a partial triple like (colorectal cancer) → [treat] → ?, the model’s job is to rank all possible drugs and put the most plausible ones at the top. That’s link prediction — predicting missing edges in the graph.
The clinical interpretation: drugs the model ranks highly for a given disease are candidates for drug repurposing — potentially treating a disease they weren’t originally approved for.

The Architecture: CompGCN + ConvE
The paper uses a two-stage neural architecture called KG-Predict, built on two components that work in sequence.
Stage 1: CompGCN (learning what each entity is)
CompGCN (Compositional Graph Convolutional Networks) is a graph neural network. Unlike standard neural networks that process independent data points, GNNs explicitly pass information across graph edges — each node “learns from its neighbors.”
Here’s how it works:
For each entity, CompGCN aggregates messages from all connected entities, weighted by the relation type. A drug connected to many cancer-related genes through target edges will absorb cancer-related signal. A gene connected to many neurodegenerative disease nodes through associate edges will look neurological.
After one round of message passing (we used gcn_layer=1), every entity has a new embedding that reflects not just itself but its entire local neighborhood in the graph.
Before CompGCN:
  Drug A: [random 100-dim vector]

After CompGCN:
  Drug A: [100-dim vector encoding its targets, associated diseases,
           phenotypes of those diseases, etc.]

[CHART 3: CompGCN message passing diagram. Show a central drug node receiving arrows from 3-4 neighbor nodes (genes, diseases). Show those neighbors’ embeddings being “aggregated” into a new drug embedding. Caption: “CompGCN propagates information from neighbors to produce context-aware entity embeddings.”]
The composition operation we used is corr (circular correlation), one of three options (along with sub for subtraction and mult for multiplication). It combines the source entity embedding with the relation embedding using a correlation operation before aggregating — making the model sensitive to which relation type the edge represents, not just that an edge exists.
Stage 2: ConvE (scoring drug-disease pairs)
Once CompGCN has produced embeddings for every entity, ConvE uses those embeddings to score candidate drug-disease pairs.
For a query (disease, TREAT_REVERSE, ?):

Reshape the disease embedding and the relation embedding into 2D “images”
Stack them into a single input tensor
Run a 2D convolution (like image processing — the model learns local patterns in the embedding space)
Flatten, apply a linear layer, and score against all 1,430 drug embeddings simultaneously
Highest scores = predicted treatments

disease_embedding [200-dim]  +  relation_embedding [200-dim]
           ↓
    Reshape to [10 × 20] + [10 × 20]
           ↓
    2D Convolution (kernel size 7×7, 200 filters)
           ↓
    Flatten + Linear layer
           ↓
    Dot product with all drug embeddings
           ↓
    Score vector [1,430 drugs] → rank descending

Together, these two stages mean the model first enriches every entity’s representation with graph-neighborhood context (CompGCN), then uses those enriched representations to score drug-disease pairs (ConvE). It’s a pipeline where the graph structure informs the scoring.

Getting the Data Ready
The GP-KG data comes as a single kg.txt file — 1.2 million tab-separated triples. Before training, you need to split it into train/validation/test sets.
The split script (split_GPKG.py) does something clever: it first ensures every entity and relation type appears in at least one training triple (guaranteeing the model sees everything at least once), then randomly distributes the remaining edges into 60/20/20 train/valid/test.
We ran the split with a fixed random seed:
PYTHONHASHSEED=41504 python split_GPKG.py
Result:

























SplitEdges% of totalTrain770,55061.8%Valid238,08819.1%Test238,08819.1%
We also needed query files — one per disease we wanted to score drugs for. Each file contains one triple per candidate drug:
c0002395    TREAT_REVERSE    CID100054454
c0002395    TREAT_REVERSE    CID100002907
... (1,430 lines total, one per drug)

c0002395 is the UMLS concept ID for Alzheimer’s disease. c0009402 is colorectal cancer. The CID100XXXXXX identifiers are GP-KG’s way of encoding PubChem CIDs — more on that in the gotchas section.

Running the Training
We ran training in Google Colab on an A100 GPU. Total training time for 200 epochs: approximately 4 hours.
Our hyperparameter configuration, matching the paper exactly:
name        = 'gpkg_baseline'
opn         = 'corr'        # CompGCN composition: circular correlation
init_dim    = 100           # initial entity embedding dimension
gcn_dim     = 200           # post-CompGCN embedding dimension
gcn_layer   = 1             # one round of message passing
dropout     = 0.1
lr          = 0.001         # learning rate (Adam optimizer)
batch_size  = 128
num_epochs  = 200
seed        = 41504         # random seed (from paper)
lbl_smooth  = 0.1           # label smoothing (prevents overconfidence)
neg_num     = 1000          # negative samples per positive triple
The model’s best validation performance arrived at epoch 190, with a validation MRR of 0.4923.
[CHART 4: Training curve — two lines, one for validation loss (decreasing), one for validation MRR (increasing), x-axis is epoch (0-200), add a vertical dashed line at epoch 190 labeled “best checkpoint”. Make it look like a real training curve — loss starts high and drops fast then levels, MRR starts low and rises. You don’t have exact epoch-by-epoch numbers so make this illustrative/schematic rather than data-precise. Caption: “Training curve over 200 epochs. The model’s best validation performance arrived at epoch 190 (MRR = 0.4923).”]
The checkpoint file — essentially a frozen snapshot of every learned weight — came out at 254 MB. Inside it:

An entity embedding matrix: 61,146 entities × 100 dimensions
A relation embedding matrix: 18 relations × 100 dimensions (9 relation types × 2 directions)
All ConvE convolutional layer weights

After training, we ran inference immediately — scoring all 1,430 drugs for both Alzheimer’s disease and colorectal cancer. This order matters enormously, as we’ll explain.

The Gotchas
This section is for anyone trying to reproduce this themselves. Every one of these cost us at least an hour.
Gotcha 1: The 100 Million CID Mystery
Our first results were baffling. The top-ranked “drugs” had IDs like CID100002907, CID100054454. We queried PubChem for CID 100002907 and got… nothing. Then CID 100054454… nothing. These seemed to be phantom research compounds, not real drugs.
Then we looked at the paper’s own supplementary data file (case_study_predict_results.csv). Right there in the paper’s output:
CID100002907 → cyclophosphamide
CID100054454 → simvastatin

The penny dropped. GP-KG encodes PubChem CIDs by adding 100,000,000. CID 100002907 is actually PubChem CID 2907 — cyclophosphamide, a well-known chemotherapy drug. CID 100054454 is PubChem CID 54454 — simvastatin, a cholesterol drug with interesting AD evidence.
The fix: subtract 100,000,000 from every GP-KG drug ID before looking it up in PubChem. One line of code, once you know to look for it. We packaged this into a reusable lookup script.
def get_pubchem_name(cid_str: str) -> str:
    raw = int(cid_str.lower().replace("cid", ""))
    real_cid = raw - 100_000_000   # the key fix
    url = f"pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/rest/pug/compound/cid/{real_cid}/property/Title/JSON"
    ...
A secondary wrinkle: not everything that looks like a drug ID is one. GP-KG includes gene names like CIDEA (a lipid droplet protein), CIDEB, and CIDEC — they start with “CID” but are not drugs. The fix there: filter on the regex ^CID\d+ (only numeric characters after “CID”).
Gotcha 2: The Silent Entity Scrambling Problem
This one took longest to diagnose, and it’s the subtlest.
When the training script builds the graph, it creates a dictionary mapping every entity name to an integer index (ent2id). Entity 0, entity 1, entity 2… up to 61,145. The neural network never sees “cyclophosphamide” — it sees index 3847 (or whatever that drug happened to get).
The problem: this mapping is not saved with the checkpoint. It’s rebuilt from scratch every time you run the training script, and because the training split is generated with Python’s random.shuffle (which is sensitive to Python’s hash randomization), the entity ordering is different every session.
So: train in Colab session A → checkpoint maps cyclophosphamide to index 3847. Load that checkpoint in Colab session B → the freshly-rebuilt ent2id maps cyclophosphamide to index 12,041. The model’s internal weights haven’t changed — but now they’re being applied to the wrong entities. Every prediction is scrambled.
We discovered this by computing a Spearman rank correlation between our local inference results and the paper’s ranked drug list:

Local inference (wrong ent2id): ρ = 0.067 — essentially random
Colab inference (correct ent2id, same session as training): ρ = 0.740 — strong correlation

The difference was entirely in whether we ran inference in the same session as training or a new one. Rule: never load a checkpoint in a new session and run inference. Train and infer in one sitting.
Gotcha 3: CUDA Checkpoint on a CPU Machine
The model was trained on a Colab A100 GPU. When we tried to load the checkpoint locally (to run quick tests), PyTorch threw:
RuntimeError: Attempting to deserialize object on a CUDA device
but torch.cuda.is_available() is False

Fix: add map_location and weights_only=False arguments to torch.load:
# Before (fails on CPU):
state = torch.load(load_path)
 
# After (works anywhere):
state = torch.load(load_path, map_location=self.device, weights_only=False)
The paper’s test.py doesn’t include these arguments. Anyone reproducing locally needs to patch this.
Gotcha 4: The Drug Query File Only Had 639 Drugs
Our initial ad_pre.txt (the file listing all drugs to score for Alzheimer’s) only had 639 entries. The fix was obvious once identified — we were only looking for entities that appeared in the TREAT relation. But many drugs have no known treatment edges at all; they’re in the graph via other relations (target, drug_hp_phenotype, etc.).
The correct approach: extract all entities matching the pattern ^CID\d+ from the entity vocabulary — regardless of which relations they appear in. That gave us the correct 1,430 drug nodes.
Gotcha 5: Windows Encoding Error
A print statement in our lookup script used a Unicode arrow character (→). Windows terminal encoding (cp1252) can’t handle it:
UnicodeEncodeError: 'charmap' codec can't encode character '\u2192' in position 12

Fix: replace → with ->. Obvious in retrospect; infuriating in the moment.
Gotcha 6: The Missing Log Directory
FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: './log/gpkg_baseline'

The test script assumes a log/ directory exists. It doesn’t create one. Fix: create log_test/ and pass -logdir ./log_test/ as an argument. Not documented anywhere.

The Results
After running inference in the same Colab session as training, here’s what the model predicted.
Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) — Our Top 10
[CHART 5: Horizontal bar chart, AD top 10. Drugs on y-axis (sorted by score, highest at top), model score on x-axis. Use a blue color scheme. Include the score value as a label on each bar.]




























































RankDrugModel Score1Simvastatin0.04052Cyclophosphamide0.03173Celecoxib0.02674Cantide + Cisplatin0.02635Verapamil0.01656Taxol (Paclitaxel)0.01507Amiodarone0.014385-Fluorouracil0.01429Propranolol0.014110Bromocriptine0.0133
Simvastatin at #1 is interesting — there’s actually a meaningful body of literature suggesting statins may have neuroprotective effects. Celecoxib (a COX-2 inhibitor / anti-inflammatory) at #3 is plausible given the neuroinflammation hypothesis of AD. These aren’t random.
Colorectal Cancer (CRC) — Our Top 10
[CHART 6: Horizontal bar chart, CRC top 10. Same format as AD chart but use a red/orange color scheme.]




























































RankDrugModel Score1Cyclophosphamide0.3872Cantide + Cisplatin0.2733Vincristine0.1874Methotrexate0.1165Mitoxantrone0.1156Taxol (Paclitaxel)0.1007Bleomycin sulfate0.0968Imatinib0.0839Sorafenib0.07010Metformin0.069
The CRC scores are notably higher than the AD scores — cyclophosphamide scores 0.387 vs simvastatin’s 0.040 for AD. This likely reflects that GP-KG has more cancer-drug treatment edges than AD-drug treatment edges, giving the model stronger signal for CRC.
Notice what’s missing from this CRC list: Oxaliplatin, Irinotecan, and Leucovorin — the backbone of standard CRC chemotherapy. They’re not here because they’re not in GP-KG at all. The dataset was built from DrugBank’s FDA-approved drugs as of its 2022 vintage, and these specific agents weren’t represented. This is an important limitation — and one of the main reasons we’re also training on PrimeKG, which has 7,957 drug nodes (vs GP-KG’s 1,430) and does include all the missing agents.

How Close Did We Get to the Paper?
The paper’s AD top 10 looks quite different from ours:
Paper’s AD Top 10 (from case_study_predict_results.csv):

















































RankDrug1Memantine2Risperidone3Donepezil4Galantamine5Rivastigmine6Quetiapine7Olanzapine8Haloperidol9Aripiprazole10Clozapine
Those top 10 are all FDA-approved drugs currently used in AD care — acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, NMDA antagonists, and antipsychotics used for behavioral symptoms. The paper’s model nailed established treatments.
Our top 10 has simvastatin, cyclophosphamide, celecoxib. Different.
Does that mean our model is wrong? Not exactly. We measure agreement using Spearman rank correlation (ρ) — a statistic that measures how well two ranked lists agree. ρ = 1.0 means perfect agreement; ρ = 0.0 means no relationship; ρ = -1.0 means perfect inverse.
[CHART 7: Scatter plot — x-axis is “paper’s rank” (1–1430), y-axis is “our rank” (1–1430), one dot per drug (1,430 dots total). Color the top-30 in the paper in orange, our top-30 in blue, overlap in green. Draw a diagonal trend line. Include a text annotation: “ρ = 0.740”. Caption: “Rank correlation between our model’s drug rankings and the paper’s rankings for Alzheimer’s disease. ρ = 0.740 indicates strong but imperfect agreement.”]
Our result: ρ = 0.740 — strong correlation. The two models broadly agree on which drugs should rank high and which should rank low, but they disagree on the top end.
Why? The most likely explanation: our training data was generated with a different random split than the paper’s. The split_GPKG.py script shuffles edges randomly, and the paper doesn’t document their exact random seed for the split. Our model and the paper’s model saw different training/test sets — so they learned slightly different internal representations.
This is actually the well-understood problem of replication vs reproduction in machine learning:

Reproduction: run the exact same code on the exact same data → identical outputs
Replication: re-implement the method and get statistically similar results

We’re currently at replication (ρ = 0.740). Getting to reproduction requires the paper’s original train/valid/test split files — which is our next step.

What We Learned About Evaluating a Model Like This
A natural question: how do we know if ρ = 0.740 is “good”? And what metrics actually matter?

























MetricWhat it measuresSpearman ρAgreement of our ranked list with the paper’s ranked list. Our reproducibility metric.MRR (Mean Reciprocal Rank)For known treatment triples held out of training: on average, what rank does the true drug get? MRR = 1/rank. MRR = 0.5 means the true drug is rank 2 on average. Our training MRR at convergence: 0.4923.AUROCIf you pick a random known treatment drug and a random non-treatment drug, how often does the model rank the treatment higher? 0.5 = random, 1.0 = perfect. Paper reports: 0.981.AUPRAmong the model’s top-ranked drugs, what fraction are confirmed treatments? Stricter than AUROC when true positives are rare — which they are here. Paper reports: 0.409.
We haven’t computed AUROC and AUPR yet — those require a labeled positive set of known treatment relationships and a scoring pass over all drugs. That’s coming in the next session.

Next Steps: 100% Reproduction
Our Spearman ρ = 0.740 is encouraging but not complete. Before we do anything else — before we run hyperparameter experiments, before we train on PrimeKG, before we apply any of this to Maureen’s data — we need to achieve full reproduction.
The goal: obtain the paper’s original train/valid/test split files (or request them from the authors), retrain with those exact files, and target ρ ≥ 0.90 and AUROC within 5% of the paper’s reported 0.981.
Only once we’re that close to the paper can we be confident that deviations from the paper’s results in our future experiments are due to our intentional changes — not residual pipeline differences.
After that:

Hyperparameter search — does more graph propagation (2-3 CompGCN layers) help? Does a larger embedding dimension improve AUROC? We have a parameter grid to explore.
PrimeKG training — train the same architecture on PrimeKG’s 8.1 million edges and 7,957 drugs. Finally get Oxaliplatin, Irinotecan, and Leucovorin in our results.
Cross-KG validation — drugs that rank highly on both GP-KG and PrimeKG are stronger candidates than those that only appear on one.
Personalization — map Maureen’s specific genomic alterations (BRAF V600E, APC truncation, and others) into the graph and see how that shifts the rankings.

We’re building toward a system that doesn’t just reproduce a published result but produces a patient-specific ranked list grounded in both the graph structure and her tumor’s molecular profile. The neural network is the foundation. The work is just starting.

Technical Reference
For anyone wanting to follow the exact steps:
Data source: GP-KG from Case Western Reserve University KG-Predict project

Entity file: kg.txt (61,146 entities, 1,246,726 edges)
Split script: split_GPKG.py with PYTHONHASHSEED=41504

Model: KG-Predict (Srivastava et al., J Biomed Inform 2022)

Architecture: CompGCN (corr, 1 layer, 200-dim) + ConvE (200 filters, kernel 7)
Training: 200 epochs, lr=0.001, batch=128, seed=41504, Colab A100 GPU, ~4 hours

Checkpoint: 254 MB (epoch 190, val MRR = 0.4923)
Results:

AD Spearman ρ vs paper: 0.740
AD top drug: Simvastatin (score 0.0405)
CRC top drug: Cyclophosphamide (score 0.387)

Key gotcha: Run inference in the same Colab session as training. Do not reload checkpoint in a new session.
Paper: Oğuztüzün et al., “Precision Drug Repurposing for Alzheimer’s Disease and Colorectal Cancer via Knowledge Graph Embedding,” J Biomed Inform 2025, doi:10.1016/j.jbi.2025.104786

Chart Production Notes
Chart 1 — Neural network diagram
Hand-drawn or use draw.io. 4 layers: input (4 nodes), hidden (6 nodes), hidden (6 nodes), output (2 nodes). Arrows between all adjacent layers. Label “weights” on a few connections. Add a curved arrow going right-to-left labeled “backpropagation.” Monochrome or minimal color.
Chart 2 — Knowledge graph
Draw in draw.io or Gephi export. Nodes: 3 drugs (blue), 3 genes (green), 2 diseases (red), 1 phenotype (purple). Edges: drug→gene (target), drug→disease (treat), gene→disease (associate), gene→phenotype (gene_hp_phenotype). Use real names: Simvastatin, HMGCR, Alzheimer’s disease; Cyclophosphamide, DNMT1, Colorectal cancer.
Chart 3 — CompGCN message passing
Three-step diagram: (1) Drug node with 4 neighbors connected by labeled edges; (2) Arrows from neighbors converging on drug node with “aggregate” label; (3) Drug node with new embedding labeled “context-enriched.” Keep it simple.
Chart 4 — Training curve
Two y-axes (or two panels). Left: validation loss (starts ~2.5, drops to ~0.8, then levels). Right: validation MRR (starts ~0.1, rises to ~0.49, levels after epoch 150). Vertical dashed line at x=190. This is illustrative — we don’t have the epoch-by-epoch log, only the final result. Make it look plausible for this type of training run.
Chart 5 — AD top 10 bar chart (data ready)
Simvastatin:          0.0405
Cyclophosphamide:     0.0317
Celecoxib:            0.0267
Cantide + Cisplatin:  0.0263
Verapamil:            0.0165
Taxol:                0.0150
Amiodarone:           0.0143
5-Fluorouracil:       0.0142
Propranolol:          0.0141
Bromocriptine:        0.0133

Horizontal bars, longest at top, blue gradient. Label scores on bars.
Chart 6 — CRC top 10 bar chart (data ready)
Cyclophosphamide:   0.3873
Cantide + Cisplatin: 0.2728
Vincristine:         0.1866
Methotrexate:        0.1161
Mitoxantrone:        0.1150
Taxol:               0.0996
Bleomycin sulfate:   0.0961
Imatinib:            0.0834
Sorafenib:           0.0696
Metformin:           0.0692

Same format, orange/red gradient.
Chart 7 — Rank correlation scatter plot
1,430 points. You don’t have all the data points — use the overlap data you do have (the paper’s CSV has all 1,430 ranks; our predictions file has all 1,430 ranks; you can compute this in Python). The key visual: a diagonal band of points from lower-left to upper-right (showing correlation), but with scatter. Annotate ρ = 0.740. Highlight top-30 paper drugs in orange, our top-30 in blue.
To generate this chart, run:
import pandas as pd
from scipy.stats import spearmanr
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
 
paper = pd.read_csv('docs/references/kg-predict/case_study_predict_results.csv')
paper = paper.rename(columns={'rank': 'p_rank', 'cid': 'object'})
 
ours = pd.read_csv('G:/My Drive/PDR/results/ad_predictions.txt',
                   sep='\t', names=['s','r','object','rank','score'])
 
merged = paper.merge(ours, on='object')

plt.figure(figsize=(8,8))

plt.xlabel("Paper's Rank")
plt.ylabel("Our Rank")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('docs/rank_correlation_ad.png', dpi=150)
