human and porcine secretin; human and ovine corticotropin-releasing hormone; factor VIII of human and of porcine sequence;
isosorbide and its mononitrate; pentaerythritol and its tetranitrate; adenosine and AMP;
two ferric pyrophosphate complexes; inositol and inositol nicotinate; almasilate and magnesium aluminium silicate;


2 salts whose counter-ion is a second active drug: procaine benzylpenicillin and ambroxol acefyllinate. Choline salicylate is a third, in a group whose split also needs J4;
12 Reactome pairs with different events: ten SARS-CoV-1/SARS-CoV-2 pairs and two disease pathways;
the disease pair, which PrimeKG itself links parent to child.

The six unclear groups. The CSV’s partition column gives the split I lean to for each.

Calcium phosphate and its dihydrate. DrugBank’s “Calcium Phosphate” does not say which calcium phosphate it is. The dihydrate (MW 172.09) is dicalcium phosphate.
D-glucose, dextrose, and beta-D-glucose. J5 merges the first two, which carry the same DrugBank text. Beta-D-glucose is an anomer, and anomers interconvert in water.
Dihydroergocryptine and dihydro-alpha-ergocryptine. DrugBank’s own text calls the alpha form “usually … the mixture”.
Camphor and synthetic camphor. Neither entry states its stereochemistry.
Two influenza vaccine antigen groups (A/California/7/2009 X-181, two entries; B/Brisbane/60/2008, four entries). Each group’s entries differ in antigen type or inactivation method and have identical PrimeKG edges.

A caution that cuts both ways. In 38 drug groups, PrimeKG lists drug–drug interactions between two members of the same group: 82 pairs, such as estradiol with each of its esters. The merges deleted those rows as self-loops. For a distinct group they are real assertions, and a split restores them. Three same groups have them too: CT-011 with pidilizumab, magnesium acetate with its tetrahydrate, and PEG-uricase with pegloticase. DrugBank generates interactions by drug class, so there they are a product interacting with itself, and they stay deleted. An interaction between two entries proves two DrugBank entries, not two drugs.

5. Surprises

Node Normalizer conflates unrelated drugs. Guanabenz, an alpha-2 agonist, shares an entity with icodextrin, a glucose polymer for peritoneal dialysis. Ethanol shares one with ipecac, a plant emetic. Its cliques also join different molecules: human insulin with four analogues and beef insulin, three Tc-99m agents that share only the radionuclide, and Lu-177 dotatate (therapy) with Ga-68 dotatate (imaging).
SARS-CoV-1 and SARS-CoV-2 pathways are merged. Reactome builds both virus hierarchies with the same pathway names. Pass 2 merged ten such pairs by name, along with 8 disease-pathway pairs that share a name.
One entity’s CURIE names a third antigen. Entity 88504 carries DRUGBANK:DB14432, an A/Singapore/gp1908/2015 IVR-180 antigen. Its members are two A/California/7/2009 X-181 antigens, and PrimeKG has no node for DB14432. The merge script gave each surviving entity Node Normalizer’s preferred CURIE.
Name and CURIE disagree on 47 of the 101 drug entities. The name comes from the member with the most edges; the CURIE comes from Node Normalizer. Sometimes they name different substances:

“Choline salicylate” carries CHEBI:15354, choline;
“Procaine benzylpenicillin” carries CHEBI:17334, penicillin;
“Technetium Tc-99m exametazime” carries CHEBI:33353, the technetium atom;
“Levonorgestrel” carries CHEBI:231594, norgestrel.


Rows lost understate the harm. 16 drug groups lost no row to their own merge. They include both tartaric acids, guanabenz with icodextrin, and ketoconazole with levoketoconazole. Each still serves two drugs’ edges as one node, and a split is what fixes that.
A re-run would merge them again. For 228 of the 237 drug members, mods_kg_curie_cache maps the standard DRUGBANK: spelling of the id to the merged entity’s CURIE. Pass 1 groups on exactly that. A split therefore needs a guard, or the next run of the script, or a fresh backfill with Node Normalizer on, will merge them again. Pass 2 would re-merge the pathway pairs by name.
A PrimeKG mapping question sits behind two correct gene merges. The node PrimeKG names “COX2” (NCBI Gene 4513, MT-CO2) has disease edges to colorectal cancer, colorectal carcinoma and colorectal neoplasm, beside MELAS and cytochrome-c oxidase deficiency. The colorectal ones look like PTGS2 (COX-2) associations filed under MT-CO2 by symbol, the COX2 homonym of #752. “COX1” (MT-CO1) shows the same pattern. The merges are right, since each pair shares one id, and a split would not touch these edges. They are worth their own check, because colorectal cancer is the index disease.

6. Before any split: open points for the follow-up
These are notes for whoever implements the approved splits. None is decided here.

Other sources’ rows on these entities were not measured. This review read PrimeKG rows only. Node Normalizer answers for an id, not for a source, so any source that met one of these DrugBank ids sits on the merged entity too. The split must route those rows as well.
The patient overlay. Maureen’s drug objects that resolved to one of these entities need re-checking, and materialize_patient_kg() must run after the split. The overlay was out of scope here: no maple_patient row was read.

One check needed no patient data. Paclitaxel, one of the RGCC taxanes the mission spec names, is merged with paclitaxel poliglumex. Every poliglumex row duplicated a paclitaxel row or joined the two, so the paclitaxel node carries no foreign edge today.


The re-merge guard (surprise 6): pass 1 and pass 2 of apply_canonical_entity_merges.py, and the cache rows behind them.
Which member keeps the entity row. A natural choice is the member the entity’s CURIE names, or the parent compound; each other member gets its own entity under its standard CURIE. First check whether an entity with that CURIE already exists. Entity 88504’s CURIE has to change whichever member keeps it.
Expected counts. For any approved set of partitions, primekg_merge_review.py replays the expected rows restored by relation (§8). The proposal as written gives 106,818.
Backup, dry run, expected count, per the plan in #438’s 2026-10-05 comment.

Save §8.4 and §8.5 as files, then, from Git Bash on the host:

docker exec -i BACKEND python - < primekg_merge_snapshot.py > primekg_merge_snapshot.json
 
# 2. Replay and table (local only, about 40 s). Feeding the committed CSV back in
#    carries its proposal columns over and recomputes every measured column.
python primekg_merge_review.py --snapshot primekg_merge_snapshot.json \
    --kg-csv C:/Maple/worker/data/kg/prime_kg/kg.csv \

On 2026-10-05, step 2 run against the 15:06 PDT snapshot reproduced the committed CSV byte for byte. The script writes LF line endings, and a Windows checkout with core.autocrlf on holds CRLF, so compare with diff --strip-trailing-cr. Its console line reports two checks, and both held:

the stored relations match the replay on all 33 relation keys;
they match on all 183 entities, relation by relation.

A later snapshot gives the same table until the store changes.
The proposal columns are written by hand: verdict, partition, rules, reason and basis. The script only carries them over, by group key. The key is the group’s PrimeKG x_index values joined by +, which do not change between environments. A partition lists the proposed nodes after a split: blocks separated by |, members of a block joined by +. To test another proposal, edit those columns and re-run step 2. The JSON’s scenarios then gives the rows each split restores, by relation.

8.4 primekg_merge_snapshot.py
"""#438 item 2: read-only snapshot of the PrimeKG entity merges on the canonical KG.
 
Reads only KG tables, only PrimeKG rows (source_id = 'prime_kg'), and only
aggregates or the merged groups themselves. Every transaction is read-only.
Writes one JSON document to stdout.
 
    docker exec -i BACKEND python - < primekg_merge_snapshot.py > primekg_merge_snapshot.json
"""
import datetime
import json
import os
import sys
 
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, text
 
# PrimeKG's x_source label -> standard CURIE prefix, and the zero-padded
# prefixes: the rules of connectors/prime_kg_connector.primekg_curie (#53, #704),
# inlined so the snapshot does not depend on the running container's code.
_PREFIX = {"NCBI": "NCBIGene", "DrugBank": "DRUGBANK", "HPO": "HP"}
_PAD = {"HP": 7, "MONDO": 7, "UBERON": 7, "GO": 7}
 
 
def hint_spellings(src, oid):
    """Every spelling of a node's CURIE the store has used: PrimeKG's own label
    (before #53), the standard prefix (#53), padded and unpadded (#704)."""
    src, oid = (src or "").strip(), (oid or "").strip()
    if not src or not oid:
        return set()
    out = {f"{src}:{oid}"}
    p = _PREFIX.get(src, src)
    out.add(f"{p}:{oid}")
    if _PAD.get(p) and oid.isdigit():
        out.add(f"{p}:{oid.zfill(_PAD[p])}")
        out.add(f"{p}:{int(oid)}")
    return out
 
 
GROUPS = """
    SELECT entity_id FROM mods_kg_entity_source WHERE source_id = 'prime_kg'
    GROUP BY entity_id HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT external_id) > 1
"""
 
engine = create_engine(os.environ["DATABASE_URL"])
out = {"taken_at": datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc).isoformat()}
with engine.connect() as conn:
    conn.execute(text("SET SESSION CHARACTERISTICS AS TRANSACTION READ ONLY"))
    conn.commit()
    conn.execute(text("SET statement_timeout = '600s'"))
    assert conn.execute(text("SHOW transaction_read_only")).scalar() == "on"
 
    r = conn.execute(text("""
        SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT external_id), COUNT(DISTINCT entity_id)
        FROM mods_kg_entity_source WHERE source_id = 'prime_kg'
    """)).one()
    out["prime_kg_source_rows"] = {"rows": r[0], "external_ids": r[1], "entities": r[2]}
    out["external_ids_on_two_entities"] = conn.execute(text("""
        SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT external_id FROM mods_kg_entity_source
            WHERE source_id = 'prime_kg' GROUP BY external_id
            HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT entity_id) > 1) t
    """)).scalar()
 
    ents = conn.execute(text(f"""
        WITH g AS ({GROUPS})
        SELECT e.id, e.curie, e.name, e.domain, e.is_synthetic_curie
        FROM mods_kg_entity e JOIN g ON g.entity_id = e.id ORDER BY e.id
    """)).fetchall()
    ids = [e.id for e in ents]
    out["entities"] = [{"entity_id": e.id, "curie": e.curie, "name": e.name,
                        "domain": e.domain, "is_synthetic_curie": e.is_synthetic_curie}
                       for e in ents]
 
    mem = conn.execute(text("""
        SELECT entity_id, external_id, source_name, source_entity_type, source_metadata
        FROM mods_kg_entity_source
        WHERE source_id = 'prime_kg' AND entity_id = ANY(:ids)
        ORDER BY entity_id, external_id::bigint
    """), {"ids": ids}).fetchall()
    out["members"] = [{"entity_id": m.entity_id, "external_id": m.external_id,
                       "source_name": m.source_name, "source_entity_type": m.source_entity_type,
                       "original_source": (m.source_metadata or {}).get("original_source"),
                       "original_id": (m.source_metadata or {}).get("original_id")}
                      for m in mem]
 
    # Where each member sat in the pre-merge snapshot that
    # scripts/apply_canonical_entity_merges.py requires before it runs.
    pre = conn.execute(text("""
        SELECT es.external_id, es.entity_id, e.curie
        FROM mods_kg_entity_source_premerge es
        LEFT JOIN mods_kg_entity_premerge e ON e.id = es.entity_id
        WHERE es.source_id = 'prime_kg' AND es.external_id = ANY(:x)
    """), {"x": [m.external_id for m in mem]}).fetchall()
    out["premerge"] = [{"external_id": p.external_id, "entity_id": p.entity_id,
                        "curie": p.curie} for p in pre]
 
    # What Node Normalizer answered for each spelling (mods_kg_curie_cache).
    queries = set(e.curie for e in ents) | set(p.curie for p in pre if p.curie)
    for m in out["members"]:
        queries |= hint_spellings(m["original_source"], m["original_id"])
    cache = conn.execute(text("""
        SELECT query_curie, preferred_curie, preferred_name
        FROM mods_kg_curie_cache WHERE query_curie = ANY(:q)
    """), {"q": sorted(queries)}).fetchall()
    out["cache"] = [{"query_curie": c.query_curie, "preferred_curie": c.preferred_curie,
                     "preferred_name": c.preferred_name} for c in cache]
 
    # Stored PrimeKG relations, for the reconciliation against kg.csv.
    out["stored_by_source_predicate"] = {sp: n for sp, n in conn.execute(text("""
        SELECT source_predicate, COUNT(*) FROM mods_kg_relation
        WHERE source_id = 'prime_kg' GROUP BY 1
    """)).fetchall()}
    out["stored_self_loops"] = conn.execute(text("""
        SELECT COUNT(*) FROM mods_kg_relation
        WHERE source_id = 'prime_kg' AND subject_id = object_id
    """)).scalar()
    # Stored PrimeKG relations touching each merged entity, for a per-group check.
    out["stored_touching_entity"] = [[e, sp, n] for e, sp, n in conn.execute(text(f"""
        WITH g AS ({GROUPS})
        SELECT g.entity_id, r.source_predicate, COUNT(*)
        FROM g JOIN mods_kg_relation r
          ON r.subject_id = g.entity_id OR r.object_id = g.entity_id
        WHERE r.source_id = 'prime_kg'
        GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 1, 2
    """)).fetchall()]
    conn.rollback()
 
json.dump(out, sys.stdout, indent=1, default=str)
8.5 primekg_merge_review.py
"""#438 item 2: the review table for PrimeKG nodes merged onto one canonical entity.
 
Replays PrimeKG's kg.csv under the merges recorded on prod, and measures what
each merge costs. Local only: reads two or three files, writes two, touches no
database.
 
Inputs
  --snapshot  JSON from primekg_merge_snapshot.py (read-only on prod)
  --kg-csv    PrimeKG kg.csv (Harvard Dataverse file 6180620)
  --proposal  optional: the review CSV (or a JSON of the same fields). Its
              hand-written columns (verdict, partition, rules, reason, basis)
              are carried over by group key; every other column is recomputed.
Outputs
  --out-csv   one row per merged PrimeKG node
  --out-json  the totals the review doc quotes
 
    python primekg_merge_review.py --snapshot primekg_merge_snapshot.json \
        --kg-csv C:/Maple/worker/data/kg/prime_kg/kg.csv \
        --proposal docs/kg_primekg_merge_review.csv \
        --out-csv docs/kg_primekg_merge_review.csv --out-json review_totals.json
 
Units: rows are directed kg.csv rows, the unit mods_kg_relation stores
(PrimeKG writes every edge in both directions). A drug_protein row's relation
key is its role (display_relation), as stored since #696.
"""
import argparse
import csv
import hashlib
import json
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
 
import numpy as np
 
SHIFT = 1 << 21        # node ids < 2**21 (PrimeKG x_index < 129,375; entity block ids offset)
ENT_OFFSET = 1_000_000  # merged entity -> 1e6 + entity_id (< 2**21)
BLOCK_OFFSET = 1_500_000  # a kept-together block of a split group -> 1.5e6 + its smallest x_index
PROPOSAL_COLS = ["verdict", "partition", "rules", "reason"]
 
 
def sha256(path):
    h = hashlib.sha256()
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        for chunk in iter(lambda: f.read(1 << 20), b""):
            h.update(chunk)
    return h.hexdigest()
 
 
def read_kg(path, members):
    """kg.csv as int arrays (x, y, relation key code), plus node info for members."""
    codes, xs, ys, rs, info = {}, [], [], [], {}
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8", newline="") as f:
        rd = csv.reader(f)
        ix = {h: i for i, h in enumerate(next(rd))}
        for row in rd:
            rel = row[ix["relation"]]
            key = row[ix["display_relation"]] if rel == "drug_protein" else rel
            c = codes.setdefault(key, len(codes))
            x, y = int(row[ix["x_index"]]), int(row[ix["y_index"]])
            xs.append(x); ys.append(y); rs.append(c)
            if x in members and x not in info:
                info[x] = {k: row[ix["x_" + k]] for k in ("id", "type", "name", "source")}
    names = [None] * len(codes)
    for k, v in codes.items():
        names[v] = k
    return np.array(xs, np.int64), np.array(ys, np.int64), np.array(rs, np.int64), names, info
 
 
def keys(gx, gy, r):
    return (gx * SHIFT + gy) * 64 + r
 
 
def kept_by_rel(gx, gy, r, nrel):
    """Distinct stored keys per relation code, self-loops dropped."""
    m = gx != gy
    u = np.unique(keys(gx[m], gy[m], r[m]))
    return np.bincount(u % 64, minlength=nrel)
 
 
def fmt(counter):
    return "; ".join(f"{k} {v:,}" for k, v in sorted(counter.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0])) if v)
 
 
def load_proposal(path):
    if not path:
        return {}, {}
    if path.endswith(".json"):
        p = json.load(open(path, encoding="utf-8"))
        return ({g: {c: v.get(c, "") for c in PROPOSAL_COLS} for g, v in p.items()},
                {int(x): b for v in p.values() for x, b in v.get("basis", {}).items()})
    groups, basis = {}, {}
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8", newline="") as f:
        for row in csv.DictReader(f):
            groups[row["group_key"]] = {c: row.get(c, "") for c in PROPOSAL_COLS}
            basis[int(row["x_index"])] = row.get("basis", "")
    return groups, basis
 
 
def parse_partition(text_, xs):
    """'a+b | c' -> [[a, b], [c]]; empty -> one block (the merge as it stands)."""
    if not text_.strip():
        return [sorted(xs)]
    return [[int(v) for v in blk.split("+")] for blk in text_.split("|")]
 
 
def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__, formatter_class=argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter)
    ap.add_argument("--snapshot", required=True)
    ap.add_argument("--kg-csv", required=True)
    ap.add_argument("--proposal")
    ap.add_argument("--out-csv", required=True)
    ap.add_argument("--out-json", required=True)
    a = ap.parse_args()
 
    snap = json.load(open(a.snapshot, encoding="utf-8"))
    ents = {e["entity_id"]: e for e in snap["entities"]}
    mem = {int(m["external_id"]): m for m in snap["members"]}
    pre = {int(p["external_id"]): p for p in snap["premerge"]}
    cache = {c["query_curie"]: c for c in snap["cache"]}
    groups = defaultdict(list)
    for x, m in mem.items():
        groups[m["entity_id"]].append(x)
    for g in groups.values():
        g.sort()
    proposal, basis = load_proposal(a.proposal)
 
    x, y, r, rel_names, info = read_kg(a.kg_csv, mem)
    nrel = len(rel_names)
    nmax = int(max(x.max(), y.max())) + 1
    ident = np.arange(nmax, dtype=np.int64)
    cur = ident.copy()
    for xi, m in mem.items():
        cur[xi] = ENT_OFFSET + m["entity_id"]
 
    # ── Reconciliation: kg.csv replayed under the merges vs what prod stores ──
    raw = np.bincount(r, minlength=nrel)
    assert len(np.unique(keys(x, y, r))) == len(r), "kg.csv has duplicate (x, y, relation) rows"
    assert not (x == y).any(), "kg.csv has native self-loops"
    replay = kept_by_rel(cur[x], cur[y], r, nrel)
    loops = np.bincount(r[(cur[x] == cur[y])], minlength=nrel)
    stored = snap["stored_by_source_predicate"]
    recon = [{"relation": rel_names[c], "kg_csv_rows": int(raw[c]), "replayed": int(replay[c]),
              "stored_on_prod": int(stored.get(rel_names[c], 0)),
              "lost_to_merges": int(raw[c] - replay[c]), "of_which_self_loops": int(loops[c])}
             for c in np.argsort(-raw)]
    mismatch = [row for row in recon if row["replayed"] != row["stored_on_prod"]]
 
    # ── Per-node neighbours and row counts (rows touching a member) ──────────
    touch = np.isin(x, list(mem)) | np.isin(y, list(mem))
    ti = np.nonzero(touch)[0]
    tx, ty, tr = x[ti], y[ti], r[ti]
    rows_by = defaultdict(Counter)
    nbrs = defaultdict(set)
    for a_, b_, c_ in zip(tx.tolist(), ty.tolist(), tr.tolist()):
        if a_ in mem:
            rows_by[a_][rel_names[c_]] += 1
            nbrs[a_].add((c_, b_))
        if b_ in mem:
            rows_by[b_][rel_names[c_]] += 1
 
    def restored(mapping, sel):
        """Rows restored, per relation, when `mapping` replaces the current one on rows `sel`."""
        before = kept_by_rel(cur[tx[sel]], cur[ty[sel]], tr[sel], nrel)
        after = kept_by_rel(mapping[tx[sel]], mapping[ty[sel]], tr[sel], nrel)
        return after - before
 
    def split_map(mapping, xs, partition):
        for blk in partition:
            for v in blk:
                mapping[v] = v if len(blk) == 1 else BLOCK_OFFSET + min(blk)
        return mapping
 
    stored_touch = defaultdict(dict)
    for eid, sp, n in snap["stored_touching_entity"]:
        stored_touch[eid][sp] = n
    touch_mismatch = []
    out_rows, gsum = [], []
    order = sorted(groups, key=lambda e: (ents[e]["domain"], ents[e]["entity_id"]))
    for gi, eid in enumerate(order, 1):
        e, xs = ents[eid], groups[eid]
        gkey = "+".join(str(v) for v in xs)
        pre_ents = {pre[v]["entity_id"] for v in xs}
        prefs = [cache.get(pre[v]["curie"] or "", {}) for v in xs]
        pref_set = {p.get("preferred_curie") for p in prefs}
        if len(pre_ents) == 1:
            step = "backfill: one CURIE hint for all members"
            src_ids = sorted({f"{info[v]['source']}:{info[v]['id']}" for v in xs})
            key_txt = f"every member carries the same PrimeKG id {', '.join(src_ids)}"
        elif None not in pref_set and len(pref_set) == 1:
            step = "apply_canonical_entity_merges pass 1: Node Normalizer"
            p0 = prefs[0]
            key_txt = (f"Node Normalizer gives {', '.join(pre[v]['curie'] for v in xs)} "
                       f"one preferred CURIE, {p0['preferred_curie']} ('{p0.get('preferred_name')}')")
        else:
            step = "apply_canonical_entity_merges pass 2: name match"
            key_txt = (f"same name, same domain; Node Normalizer knows none of "
                       f"{', '.join(pre[v]['curie'] for v in xs)}")
        anchor = next((v for v in xs if info[v]["name"].lower() == e["name"].lower()), xs[0])
        sel = np.isin(tx, xs) | np.isin(ty, xs)
        # Rows touching the group that the merges collapsed (a row between two
        # merged groups counts in both), and rows that splitting this group
        # alone, with every other merge left in place, would restore.
        kept = kept_by_rel(cur[tx[sel]], cur[ty[sel]], tr[sel], nrel)
        g_lost = np.bincount(tr[sel], minlength=nrel) - kept
        g_restore = restored(split_map(cur.copy(), xs, [[v] for v in xs]), sel)
        g_loops = int(((cur[tx[sel]] == cur[ty[sel]])).sum())
        prod_touch = stored_touch.get(eid, {})
        if {rel_names[c]: int(n) for c, n in enumerate(kept) if n} != prod_touch:
            touch_mismatch.append(eid)
        prop = proposal.get(gkey, {c: "" for c in PROPOSAL_COLS})
        gsum.append({"group": gi, "group_key": gkey, "entity_id": eid, "domain": e["domain"],
                     "step": step, "lost_touching": {rel_names[c]: int(n) for c, n in enumerate(g_lost) if n},
                     "restored_if_only_this_split": {rel_names[c]: int(n) for c, n in enumerate(g_restore) if n},
                     "self_loop_rows": g_loops, **prop})
        for v in xs:
            inter = len(nbrs[v] & nbrs[anchor]); union = len(nbrs[v] | nbrs[anchor])
            out_rows.append({
                "group": gi, "group_key": gkey, "entity_id": eid, "entity_curie": e["curie"],
                "entity_name": e["name"], "domain": e["domain"], "merge_step": step,
                "merge_key": key_txt, "x_index": v,
                "primekg_id": f"{info[v]['source']}:{info[v]['id']}", "primekg_type": info[v]["type"],
                "primekg_name": info[v]["name"], "premerge_curie": pre[v]["curie"],
                "nn_preferred": cache.get(pre[v]["curie"] or "", {}).get("preferred_curie") or "",
                "anchor": "yes" if v == anchor else "",
                "rows": sum(rows_by[v].values()), "rows_by_relation": fmt(rows_by[v]),
                "shared_with_anchor": "" if v == anchor else inter,
                "jaccard_with_anchor": "" if v == anchor else (f"{inter / union:.3f}" if union else ""),
                "group_rows_lost": int(g_lost.sum()),
                "group_lost_by_relation": fmt({rel_names[c]: int(n) for c, n in enumerate(g_lost)}),
                "group_rows_restored_if_only_this_split": int(g_restore.sum()),
                "group_self_loop_rows": g_loops,
                **prop, "basis": basis.get(v, ""),
            })
 
    # ── Scenarios: what a split restores, by relation ─────────────────────────
    allm = np.ones(len(tx), bool)
    all_split = restored(ident, allm)
    scen = {"split_all_183": {rel_names[c]: int(n) for c, n in enumerate(all_split) if n}}
    def cites(p, rule):
        return rule in [t.strip() for t in p.get("rules", "").split(",")]
 
    # A rule that some `same` group cites keeps nodes together (a merge rule);
    # any other rule separates them.
    merge_rules = {t.strip() for p in proposal.values() if p.get("verdict") == "same"
                   for t in p.get("rules", "").split(",") if t.strip()}
 
    def proposal_restores(split_verdicts, flip_rule=None):
        """Rows restored, per relation, by splitting the groups whose verdict is in
        `split_verdicts` (a distinct group along its partition). With `flip_rule`,
        the groups citing that rule are treated as if it were rejected: for a merge
        rule they split into single nodes, for any other rule they stay merged.
        A group citing several rules flips whole, so for those three groups the
        figure is an upper bound. Unclear groups are never flipped."""
        mp = cur.copy()
        for eid in order:
            xs = groups[eid]
            p = proposal.get("+".join(map(str, xs)), {})
            v = p.get("verdict")
            if flip_rule and cites(p, flip_rule) and v != "unclear":
                v = "split-whole" if flip_rule in merge_rules else "same"
            if v == "split-whole":
                split_map(mp, xs, [[x_] for x_ in xs])
            elif v == "distinct" and v in split_verdicts:
                split_map(mp, xs, parse_partition(p.get("partition", ""), xs))
            elif v in split_verdicts:
                split_map(mp, xs, [[x_] for x_ in xs])
        return restored(mp, allm)
 
    per_rule = {}
    if proposal:
        for name, verdicts in (("split_distinct", {"distinct"}), ("split_distinct_and_unclear", {"distinct", "unclear"})):
            res = proposal_restores(verdicts)
            scen[name] = {rel_names[c]: int(n) for c, n in enumerate(res) if n}
        base = sum(scen["split_distinct"].values())
        rules_seen = sorted({t.strip() for p in proposal.values() for t in p.get("rules", "").split(",") if t.strip()})
        for rule in rules_seen:
            flipped = int(proposal_restores({"distinct"}, flip_rule=rule).sum())
            per_rule[rule] = {"groups": sum(1 for p in proposal.values() if cites(p, rule)),
                              "kind": "merge" if rule in merge_rules else "split",
                              "rows_restored_if_rejected": flipped, "change_vs_proposal": flipped - base}
 
    cols = ["group", "group_key", "entity_id", "entity_curie", "entity_name", "domain", "merge_step",
            "merge_key", "x_index", "primekg_id", "primekg_type", "primekg_name", "premerge_curie",
            "nn_preferred", "anchor", "rows", "rows_by_relation", "shared_with_anchor",
            "jaccard_with_anchor", "group_rows_lost", "group_lost_by_relation",
            "group_rows_restored_if_only_this_split", "group_self_loop_rows", *PROPOSAL_COLS, "basis"]
    with open(a.out_csv, "w", encoding="utf-8", newline="") as f:
        w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=cols, lineterminator="\n")
        w.writeheader()
        w.writerows(out_rows)
    totals = {
        "kg_csv": {"path": a.kg_csv, "sha256": sha256(a.kg_csv), "rows": int(len(r))},
        "snapshot_taken_at": snap["taken_at"],
        "prime_kg_source_rows": snap["prime_kg_source_rows"],
        "groups": len(groups), "member_nodes": len(mem), "surplus_nodes": len(mem) - len(groups),
        "by_domain": {d: {"groups": sum(1 for e in groups if ents[e]["domain"] == d),
                          "nodes": sum(len(g) for e, g in groups.items() if ents[e]["domain"] == d)}
                      for d in sorted({e["domain"] for e in ents.values()})},
        "by_step": dict(Counter(g["step"] for g in gsum)),
        "reconciliation": recon, "reconciliation_mismatches": mismatch,
        "replayed_total": int(replay.sum()), "stored_total": sum(stored.values()),
        "stored_self_loops": snap["stored_self_loops"],
        "groups_whose_stored_rows_differ_from_replay": touch_mismatch,
        "scenarios": scen, "per_rule": per_rule, "groups_detail": gsum,
    }
    json.dump(totals, open(a.out_json, "w", encoding="utf-8"), indent=1)
    print(f"{len(groups)} groups, {len(mem)} nodes; replayed {int(replay.sum()):,} rows vs "
          f"{sum(stored.values()):,} stored; mismatched relations: {len(mismatch)}; "
          f"groups whose stored rows differ from the replay: {len(touch_mismatch)}")
    for k, v in scen.items():
        print(f"{k}: {sum(v.values()):,} rows  {fmt(Counter(v))}")
 
 
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

kg/pdr_phase8.5_variant_kg_planning.title: Variant-Aware Knowledge Graph Extension
kg/pdr_phase8.5_variant_kg_planning.content:
Phase 8.5 — Variant-Aware KG Extension — Planning Document
Status: PARTIAL — schema landed, CIViC ingested, Phase 12 V1 patient-as-node done for Maureen. OncoKB + PharmGKB connectors coded but not ingested. Patient→variant edges are still gene-level — fix pending.
Created: 2026-05-07
Last updated: 2026-05-14 (post-canonical-cutover audit)
Owner: whafa
Master plan reference: PDR_PIPELINE_PLAN.md § Phase 8.5
Companion writeup template: pdr_phase0_gpkg_writeup.md

This document is the seed for a dedicated planning session. It contains: (1) the problem statement and why this work matters, (2) a draft Phase 8.5 plan with checklist sub-phases, (3) context on how biomedical KG merging actually works in practice, (4) open questions to be resolved in the planning session, and (5) suggested next steps to convert this from “draft” to “executable.”


Status snapshot (2026-05-14, against the canonical KG mods_kg_entity / mods_kg_relation)
Audit triggered after the 2026-05-13 canonical-cutover; reality is materially ahead of the original “PLANNING” status:

4,124 variant entities in the canonical KG (domain='variant', biolink:SequenceVariant), all from the CIViC source. Schema is therefore first-class for variants — mods_kg_entity.biolink_category='biolink:SequenceVariant'. 8.5.1 schema work is done.
CIViC connector is live (backend/connectors/civic_connector.py, 541 lines). Already shipped: 3,142 biolink:predicts_sensitivity_to, 1,651 biolink:predicts_resistance_to, 33 biolink:predicts_toxicity_for, 960 biolink:gene_associated_with_condition, 945 biolink:biomarker_for, 4,124 biolink:has_sequence_variant. 8.5.5 is done.
CAID coverage on CIViC variants: 780 / 4,124 (19%) carry CAID:* CURIEs; 3,302 (80%) still on civic:civic_variant:*; 25 on CLINVAR:*; 17 on HGVS:*. The 80% un-normalized chunk is the remaining 8.5.3 polish.
Maureen is already a patient node (MAPLE_PATIENT:maureen-1173a8db, biolink:IndividualOrganism) with 250 outbound edges: 5/48/48 sensitive/partial/resistant RGCC drugs (MAPLE:sensitive_to_drug family), 45 over_expresses + 14 under_expresses (genomics), 9+59+8 medication history, 6 phenotypes, 8 MAPLE:has_genetic_alteration_in (gene-level). Phase 12 V1 (patient-as-a-node) is therefore partially landed.
Patient→variant gap: all 8 has_genetic_alteration_in edges point to gene entities (NCBIGene:324 APC, NCBIGene:673 BRAF, etc.) — the variant detail lives only in the edge metadata. Even when CAID:CA123643 (BRAF V600E) exists in the canonical KG, Maureen isn’t linked to it as a node. This is the lift Phase 8.5.2 was supposed to deliver and remains the open structural work for Maureen.
OncoKB connector is coded (backend/connectors/oncokb_connector.py, 403 lines) but NOT ingested — zero oncokb rows in mods_kg_entity_source. Same for PharmGKB.
Maureen variant inventory (run 2026-05-14): 19 variants across 8 genes from 3 source documents (Caris ×14, Guardant360 ×4, Invitae ×1). No RGCC variant rows (as expected — RGCC is drug-sensitivity, not variant calls). 100% gene symbols, 79% HGVS-p, 74% HGVS-c, 0% transcripts / hgnc_id / chromosomal coords.
Translator/ClinGen spike result (run 2026-05-14): with HGNC-driven transcript inference + version-fallback, 10/14 eligible variants resolved to CAIDs (71.4%), passing the 8.5.3 ≥70% gate on the eligible denominator. 4 unique CAIDs across 10 row hits — including CAID:CA123643 (BRAF V600E, present in the KG) and one inherited variant NOT present in the KG (identifiers withheld; CIViC doesn’t curate it). Scripts at backend/scripts/maureen_variant_inventory.py and backend/scripts/translator_clingen_spike_v3.py. Results: runs/2026-05-14_phase8.5_spike/translator_clingen_spike_v3.json.

Net read: Phase 8.5 is roughly half-landed. What’s left: (a) OncoKB + PharmGKB ingest, (b) patient→variant resolver fix in mods_patient_kg_service.py::_resolve_variant_canonical + variant-upsert path so we can connect Maureen to CAIDs that the public KBs don’t carry, (c) CAID back-normalization for the 80% civic-internal CURIEs (defer), (d) 8.5.9 retrain — currently underway on Maureen-noded + CIViC + PrimeKG (no OncoKB yet).

1. Problem statement
What we have
PrimeKG and GP-KG operate at gene-level granularity. Variant-specific information exists in PrimeKG only as free text inside drug and disease description fields. Verified counts in docs/References/PrimeKG/:

drug_features.csv: 6 mentions of “V600” (in vemurafenib, cobimetinib, encorafenib, dabrafenib descriptions)
disease_features.csv: 4 mentions of “V600” (in BRAF-driven disease descriptions)
nodes.csv: zero variant-typed nodes — none of PrimeKG’s 10 node types is variant or mutation
edges.csv: zero variant-keyed edges — none of PrimeKG’s 30 relation types operates at variant granularity

What this costs us
The CompGCN+ConvE and ULTRA models we train see node IDs and edge types — not text. So variant signals from drug descriptions are invisible to the link-prediction model. Concretely, the graph cannot reason about:


Mechanism-coupled drug selection. Maureen’s inherited variant raises a mechanism-coupled drug question (a nuanced call). The graph would need to traverse Maureen → variant → gene → pathway → drug class. Without variant nodes, the inference path collapses at the gene level.


Combinatorial filtering. Maureen has KRAS / BRAF / MSI / MLH1 / MSH2 status from her Caris and RGCC reports, plus 73 expression genes and 224 drug sensitivities (112 drugs x 2 draws). Hand-coding a rule for every combination (“if BRAF wild-type AND KRAS wild-type AND MSS then EGFR inhibitors are eligible”) is brittle. Graph reasoning composes naturally.


Subtype-specific drug sensitivity. PrimeKG knows “vemurafenib treats melanoma” but not “vemurafenib treats BRAF V600E-positive cancers.” With BRAF_V600E as a graph entity, the model could surface vemurafenib for any V600E-positive tumor, including CRC subtypes.


Pharmacogenomic safety filtering. DPYD-deficient patients can have fatal toxicity to 5-FU and capecitabine. UGT1A1*28 homozygotes have severe irinotecan toxicity. Both are CRC chemotherapy concerns. Without variant-keyed contraindication edges, the graph ranks these drugs without regard to patient genotype — currently mitigated only by patient-side filtering, which is fragile.


Workarounds that exist (and what they recover)

Text embedders (Phase 7.6/7.7) pick up V600E and similar mentions from drug descriptions. They can recover variant-aware ranking via post-hoc combination, but only as good as the description text — sparse for non-cancer variants and absent for most PGx.
Patient-side filtering against mods_genomic_alteration can hard-filter or hard-promote at inference time. Real and useful, but ad hoc and doesn’t scale across patients or new evidence sources.
RAG / LLM re-ranking can layer variant context on top of the model’s top candidates. Limited because the LLM doesn’t see graph structure.

These together recover meaningful practical value, but they are workarounds. Variant-as-graph-entity is the principled architecture.
Why now

Phase 9 (Maureen personalization) becomes more powerful with variant nodes. Without them, every variant has to be hand-engineered into a scalar feature vector, losing all the public evidence linking variants to drugs.
Phase 12 (patient-as-node) makes the same gene-level mistake. Its DYSREGULATED_GENE patient→gene edges can’t distinguish BRAF V600E from BRAF V600K, even though the drug response differs.
The schema work (8.5.1, 8.5.2) is model-independent and can proceed in parallel with whatever PDR1/PDR2 training is happening.

Why not now

Engineering cost is real — see § 4 cost estimate. 6-18 weeks depending on path.
PrimeKG’s own authors didn’t include variants by design. We’re forking the philosophy as well as the data. Worth being deliberate about this.
Phase 11 (PDR2/ULTRA) makes 8.5.9 retraining cheaper. If PDR2 is on track, we may want to schedule the retrain step after Phase 11 closes.


2. Closure criteria (aggregate)

Schema supports variant entity type and at least three new relation types covering predict-response, predict-toxicity, and variant-of-gene.
All of Maureen’s parsed variants from mods_genomic_alteration are present as graph nodes with edges to the appropriate gene nodes.
At least one public variant-evidence KB (OncoKB or CIViC for cancer; PharmGKB for PGx) is ingested and connected to the variant nodes.
A retrained or fine-tuned model on the variant-extended KG meets two regression gates:

(a) Phase 7.5 RGCC validation numbers do not degrade.
(b) At least one validation track shows ≥ 0.03 AUROC or ≥ 0.05 Spearman ρ improvement.


Documentation captures the identifier-normalization decisions, the merge methodology, and the architectural choice for retrain vs fine-tune.


3. Sub-phases
8.5.1 — Schema extension (low cost, immediate value) — DONE in canonical schema
The canonical schema (mods_kg_entity / mods_kg_entity_source / mods_kg_relation, migrations 071–078) supports variants natively. The original plan targeted the legacy schema’s entity_type='variant' on mods_kg_node; the canonical equivalent is domain='variant' + biolink_category='biolink:SequenceVariant', which already exists and is populated.

 Variant entity type — domain='variant', biolink_category='biolink:SequenceVariant'. 4,124 rows present.
 HGVS / CAID / etc. live in mods_kg_entity.metadata (JSONB) — schema-free; connectors populate at ingest time.
 New relation types: biolink:has_sequence_variant (=variant_of_gene), biolink:predicts_sensitivity_to (=predicts_response_to), biolink:predicts_resistance_to, biolink:predicts_toxicity_for, biolink:biomarker_for, biolink:gene_associated_with_condition. All present.
 Evidence and source attribution via mods_kg_relation.evidence JSONB + source_id FK. CIViC evidence levels (A/B/C/D/E) land in evidence JSONB.

8.5.2 — Internal variant ingestion (Maureen’s data into the graph) — PARTIAL (gene-level done, variant-level open)

 Patient-as-a-Node materialization service is live at backend/mods_patient_kg_service.py (materialize_patient_kg). Maureen has 250 outbound canonical relations including 8 MAPLE:has_genetic_alteration_in rows from mods_genomic_alteration.
 Variant-level edges still gene-level. Her 8 alteration rows resolve only to gene entities (NCBIGene:*) because _resolve_variant_canonical looks for {gene} {variant} name matches and her HGVS-p strings carry the p. prefix while CIViC names them without it. Fix planned: thread the v3 spike’s HGNC+ClinGen resolver into _resolve_variant_canonical, then upsert the variant entity into maple_patient source if no public-source variant matches.
 CAID resolution rate measured on Maureen’s variants: 10/14 eligible (71.4%) — passes the 8.5.3 ≥70% gate on the HGVS-c-equipped subset. Failure modes documented: 5 variants are HGVS-p-only (3 might be derivable with Mutalyzer), 2 are CNVs (need separate handling), 2 are novel indels not in ClinGen.
 Cache resolved CAIDs in a mods_variant_normalization table (deferred — current spike caches in-memory + JSON; durable cache is a polish item).
 Maureen’s variants are the only patient set today; multi-patient scope deferred until V2.

8.5.3 — Identifier normalization layer (the cross-source key) — PARTIAL (clients built, in-line use proven; back-normalization of CIViC variants pending)

 Normalization clients exist at backend/kg_normalize/:

node_normalizer_client.py — Translator Node Normalizer (gene/drug/disease CURIEs)
clingen_allele_registry_client.py — ClinGen Allele Registry (variant → CAID)
predicate_mapper.py — source-predicate → Biolink predicate
entity_resolver.py — orchestrates all three at ingest time


 Translator + ClinGen + HGNC pipeline validated end-to-end on Maureen’s 19 variants (backend/scripts/translator_clingen_spike_v3.py). Gene CURIE normalization: 8/8 (100%). Variant CAID resolution: 10/14 eligible (71.4%). Failure modes catalogued.
 Back-normalization of 3,302 civic-internal variant CURIEs to CAID — still open. Today CIViC variants land with their civic:civic_variant:NNN CURIE if Node Normalizer can’t resolve them through the chain. Worth a polish pass once OncoKB lands so cross-source dedup operates on the same CAID key.
 Track normalization failures per source. EntityResolver already emits per-call status; surface as a daily audit metric.

8.5.4 — Public KB connector — OncoKB (highest priority for Maureen) — CODE READY, NOT INGESTED

 Connector built at backend/connectors/oncokb_connector.py (403 lines). Supports two modes: JSON file (default at ./data/kg/oncokb/actionable_variants.json) and live API (when ONCOKB_API_TOKEN env var is set).
 License posture noted on the manifest: “Commercial (free academic tier)” + biolink_compliant=False. Per-composition human-reviewer call on inclusion.
 Maps OncoKB Level 1/2/3A/3B/4 → biolink:predicts_sensitivity_to; R1/R2 → biolink:predicts_resistance_to. variant_of_gene + variant→drug + variant→disease (biomarker_for) edges per row.
 Run the ingest. Blocked on: needs ONCOKB_API_TOKEN (academic registration at www.oncokb.org/account/register) OR a manually-placed actionable_variants.json. Run via python backend/scripts/ingest_kg_connector.py --connector oncokb.
 Closure gate: at least one Maureen-relevant variant (BRAF V600E confirmed in CIViC already; the inherited variant only resolvable in OncoKB or further-curated source) gets an OncoKB-sourced edge.

8.5.5 — Public KB connector — CIViC — DONE

 Connector at backend/connectors/civic_connector.py (541 lines). Reads CIViC’s monthly TSV releases (variants + evidence + clinical assertions), produces variant / gene / drug / disease entities + evidence-leveled relations.
 Ingested. 4,124 variants, 4,138 entities from civic source. 3,142 sensitivity / 1,651 resistance / 33 toxicity edges. Variant-of-gene relations carry CIViC evidence level (evidence.civic_level).
 OncoKB/CIViC overlap-resolution policy (prefer OncoKB level for ranking; preserve CIViC as corroborating flag) — designed-but-not-implemented; will need explicit cross-source xref query when OncoKB lands.

8.5.6 — Public KB connector — PharmGKB (for chemo safety) — CODE READY, NOT INGESTED

 Connector at backend/connectors/pharmgkb_connector.py (357 lines). Ingests CPIC-leveled variant→drug-response rows. Star-allele / haplotype handling per the connector’s _row_to_relations.
 Run the ingest. Same script: python backend/scripts/ingest_kg_connector.py --connector pharmgkb_variants.
 Closure gate: DPYD variants are linked to capecitabine and 5-fluorouracil with CPIC level A; UGT1A1*28 is linked to irinotecan. Relevant only if Maureen ever has DPYD / UGT1A1 testing — neither is in her current mods_genomic_alteration rows; check Caris reports for whether PGx was ordered.

8.5.7 — Public KB connector — ClinVar (optional, requires filtering)

 Massive coverage but variable quality. Defer until 8.5.4–8.5.6 prove the architecture; then add ClinVar filtered to “Pathogenic” + “Likely pathogenic” with at least 2 stars.
 Ingest as has_significance edges to a controlled vocabulary node set.

8.5.8 — KG merge strategy and validation

 Merge happens via shared identifier space, not via graph operations. Genes and drugs already in PrimeKG get their NCBI / DrugBank IDs reused; new variants get added with CAIDs; new edges connect them.
 Audit cross-KB conflicts. When OncoKB says variant X predicts response to drug Y but CIViC says no evidence, do not collapse; preserve both as separate edges with provenance.
 Run a sanity-check query before retraining: pick 10 well-known variant-drug pairs (BRAF V600E ↔ vemurafenib, DPYD c.1905+1G>A ↔ capecitabine, BRCA2 mutations ↔ olaparib, etc.). Verify each produces an edge with the expected provenance.
 Document collision rates: how many variant nodes did we end up with? How many had ≥ 1 evidence edge from at least one source? How many were Maureen-relevant?

8.5.9 — Retrain or fine-tune the model — TRAINING IN PROGRESS (2026-05-14)

 Underway. Maureen-noded retrain on CIViC + PrimeKG (OncoKB not yet ingested at training time). Architecture and config TBD-from-train-log. This validates the chain end-to-end without OncoKB; OncoKB-augmented retrain is a follow-up run.
 Decision parallel to Phase 12.3. Two options:

Option A (full retrain): train PDR1 / PDR2 from scratch on the variant-extended PrimeKG. Most rigorous; the relation encoder learns the new relation types from the start.
Option B (fine-tune): start from the existing PrimeKG checkpoint, add variant nodes + edges, fine-tune for ~30 epochs.


 PDR2 / ULTRA-specific note: ULTRA’s relation-from-topology design absorbs new relation types without retraining the foundation. If Phase 11 has closed by the time we get here, Option B is much cheaper on PDR2 than on PDR1. This is a strong reason to schedule 8.5 after Phase 11 closes if PDR2 is on track — but the schema and ingestion work (8.5.1–8.5.7) is model-independent and can proceed in parallel.
 Note (added 2026-05-14): The in-progress training uses Maureen’s gene-level alteration edges (MAPLE:has_genetic_alteration_in → gene), not variant-level. Once 8.5.2 fix lands and her edges include biolink:has_variant → variant CAIDs, the next retrain will see her connected directly to BRAF V600E (CA123643) and other variants rather than only to the BRAF gene with HGVS in the edge metadata. That’s the actual signal lift Phase 8.5 was designed to deliver.

8.5.10 — Validation

 Regression gate: re-run Phase 7.5 RGCC validation tiers on the variant-extended checkpoint. Numbers must not degrade. If they do, investigate before proceeding.
 Lift gate: at least one validation metric improves measurably:

Tier 1 ρ (continuous correlation between model score and RGCC % cell death) improves by ≥ 0.05, OR
Tier 2 AUROC (high-sensitivity vs non-sensitive RGCC drugs) improves by ≥ 0.03


 Maureen-specific anchor test: for each of her clinically actionable variants (ATM, KRAS / BRAF if present, MSI status, MLH1/MSH2, DPYD if tested, UGT1A1 if tested), verify the model now ranks the corresponding evidence-supported drugs in the top decile of CRC candidates. Pre-register the expected rankings before running.
 Cross-validation on held-out variants: hold out 5% of OncoKB variant-drug edges; verify the model can predict them from the rest of the graph. This is the link-prediction analog of leave-one-out.

8.5.11 — Documentation and publishability

 Document the schema extension, the connector set, the normalization choices, and the merge methodology in a standalone writeup following the pdr_phase0_gpkg_writeup.md template (Purpose / M&M / Procedure / Results / Discussion).
 Note: a variant-extended PrimeKG is itself publishable — the PrimeKG authors did not include variants by design, so this is a real contribution rather than a fork.


4. KG merging in practice — context for the planning session
The Phase 8.5 plan above understates how hard KG merging is. Adding rows to tables is the trivial 20%. The hard 80% is identifier alignment, schema harmonization, provenance tracking, and update lifecycle. This section captures the field’s state of the art so we can choose the right tooling.
4.1 The four hard problems
(1) Identifier alignment. Every database uses different IDs for the same entities. PrimeKG uses NCBI gene IDs (9796 = PHYHIP), OncoKB uses HGNC symbols (BRAF), CIViC uses Entrez IDs, ClinVar uses gene symbols + RefSeq. For drugs it’s worse: DrugBank, ChEMBL, PubChem CID, RxNorm, NCIt, KEGG, ATC — and the same drug routinely has different IDs in different sources. Variants are the worst case: HGVS notation has multiple equivalent forms, dbSNP IDs change between builds, ClinGen’s CAID is canonical but coverage is incomplete.
(2) Schema harmonization. PrimeKG is a binary KG: every fact is a (head, relation, tail) triple. OncoKB has hyperedges with metadata: (variant, drug, evidence_level, indication_context, citation, level_of_evidence). To merge, you either (a) flatten into multiple triples and lose information, or (b) extend the schema with edge attributes. Both have downsides.
(3) Provenance and conflict resolution. When two sources disagree (OncoKB says Level 2 evidence, CIViC says no evidence), which wins? Best practice: preserve both, mark each with source, and let downstream consumers decide. But this means every node and edge needs a provenance attribute, which most KGs don’t have natively.
(4) Update lifecycle. OncoKB updates monthly. CIViC has continuous community curation. PrimeKG is a single-version dataset release. Synchronizing updates across heterogeneous cadences is a real engineering problem — usually solved by re-deriving the merged KG on a schedule rather than incremental updates.
4.2 The Biolink + NCATS Translator ecosystem (the canonical answer in our space)
This is the closest thing to a solved problem for biomedical KG integration:

Biolink Model — a controlled hierarchy of node and edge types, with explicit semantics. e.g., biolink:Gene, biolink:Drug, biolink:Variant, biolink:treats, biolink:contraindicated_for. Every concept maps to a Biolink class.
TRAPI (Translator Reasoner API) — a JSON-RPC standard for querying KGs. Each Knowledge Provider exposes their KB through TRAPI, regardless of internal storage.
SRI Node Normalizer — a hosted REST service that maps any biomedical identifier (NCBI Gene, HGNC, DrugBank, MONDO, UMLS, etc.) to a canonical CURIE plus a Biolink class. This is the answer to identifier alignment for ~95% of biomedical entities.
NCATS Translator itself — operates 13+ Knowledge Providers (RTX-KG2, ROBOKOP, Multi-Omics Provider, etc.) behind a unified TRAPI layer. We already have a connector at backend/connectors/translator_connector.py.

Practical implication: instead of building four bespoke connectors for OncoKB / CIViC / PharmGKB / ClinVar, much of the variant-evidence content is already accessible through Translator’s MolePro and BTE Knowledge Providers. We’d query Translator with normalized variant CURIEs and pull back evidence edges already harmonized to Biolink. Where coverage gaps exist (OncoKB specifically isn’t in Translator due to licensing), we build direct connectors.
4.3 Pre-integrated biomedical KGs (fork rather than build)









































KGSources mergedLicenseVariants?RTX-KG2~70 sources via Biolink (UCSF/Translator)OpenPartial — via ClinVarSPOKE30+ sources, used clinically (UCSF)Restricted (academic)LimitedROBOKOP~40 sources via BiolinkOpenYes — multiple variant connectorsHetionetOlder, smaller, foundationalOpenNoMonarch KGPhenotype-centric integrationOpenYes — extensive variant coverage
ROBOKOP and Monarch KG are the most promising starting points if we want to skip the per-source connector work. The trade-off is loss of control: we’d be downstream of someone else’s integration decisions.
4.4 Identifier mapping services (the “use don’t build” tier)

SRI Node Normalizer (nodenorm.transltr.io) — generic biomedical entity normalizer
MyGene.info / MyVariant.info / MyChem.info / MyDisease.info — BioThings APIs aggregating cross-references
HGNC REST API — gene symbol authority
UMLS Metathesaurus — broadest cross-vocabulary mapping but requires UMLS license
ClinGen Allele Registry — canonical variant IDs (CAID)

4.5 Cost estimate
Honest sizing per sub-phase, with merging difficulty priced in:

































































Sub-phaseEffortWhy8.5.1 schema extension~3-5 daysMigrations, model classes, validation. Self-contained.8.5.2 Maureen ingestion~3-5 daysReuses existing parsers; mostly ETL plumbing.8.5.3 normalization layer~1-2 weeksWrapping Translator Node Normalizer + ClinGen Allele Registry. Caching layer. Failure handling.8.5.4 OncoKB connector~2-3 weeksDirect connector — OncoKB API + auth + normalization + ingestion. Includes back-and-forth on edge cases.8.5.5 CIViC connector~2 weeksOpen API, similar pattern but slightly different schema.8.5.6 PharmGKB connector~2-3 weeksMore complex schema (haplotypes, star alleles, diplotypes, CPIC guidelines). The hardest of the three.8.5.7 ClinVar (deferred)~3-4 weeks if we do itVolume + quality filtering.8.5.8 merge validation~1 weekAudit queries, conflict resolution, sanity checks.8.5.9 retrain/fine-tune~1-2 weeksCompute-bound. PDR2 fine-tune is cheaper than PDR1 retrain.8.5.10 validation suite~1 weekRe-run Phase 7.5 + variant-specific anchors.8.5.11 writeup~3-5 daysFollowing the writeup template.
Total: 12-18 weeks of focused work on the per-source-connector path. 6-10 weeks if we leverage Translator / ROBOKOP rather than building bespoke connectors.

5. Open questions for the planning session
Status as of 2026-05-14 (post-audit). RESOLVED items kept for the audit trail.


Build vs leverage existing integration. ✅ RESOLVED — hybrid landed: Translator Node Normalizer + ClinGen Allele Registry power the resolver chain in kg_normalize/; bespoke connectors built for CIViC (live), OncoKB (ready), PharmGKB (ready). Spike at backend/scripts/translator_clingen_spike_v3.py validates the leverage path resolves 71% of Maureen’s eligible variants without per-source curation.


PDR1 vs PDR2 as the retrain target. ✅ RESOLVED for this round — current training (in progress 2026-05-14) is on PDR1-style stack with Maureen-noded + CIViC + PrimeKG. PDR2 reproduction (Phase 11) still has open work; deferred to a follow-up retrain.


ROBOKOP / Monarch as a starting point. ❌ NOT NEEDED — leveraging Translator + ClinGen + bespoke OncoKB+PharmGKB+CIViC delivered Phase 8.5 schema and one fully-loaded source. Fork-ROBOKOP path effectively bypassed.


Edge-attribute design. ✅ RESOLVED — connectors emit single Biolink predicate per direction (predicts_sensitivity_to vs predicts_resistance_to) with evidence level on mods_kg_relation.evidence JSONB. Option (a) of the original question.


Patient-as-node interaction. ✅ RESOLVED — Phase 12 V1 landed alongside 8.5 work. Maureen is MAPLE_PATIENT:maureen-1173a8db; outbound edges use mixed MAPLE:* and biolink:* predicates. Open gap: her has_genetic_alteration_in edges target gene entities, not variants. That’s the 8.5.2 remaining work.


Validation ground truth for Maureen. ⚠️ DEFERRED — the in-progress training did NOT pre-hold-out RGCC drugs. The model can see all 224 sensitivities as training edges (MAPLE:sensitive_to_drug / _partially_sensitive_to_drug / _resistant_to_drug). For clean lift measurement against the variant-extended retrain, a future training run should hold out ≥5% of RGCC high-sensitivity drugs stratified by drug class. Not a blocker for the current run — but tag the result accordingly.


Licensing audit. PARTIAL — OncoKB connector documents the “Commercial (free academic tier)” posture on its manifest; per-composition reviewer call is the policy. Full audit (CIViC ✓ open, ClinVar ✓ public domain, PharmGKB ⚠ attribution, OncoKB ⚠ academic-only, COSMIC ✗ restrictive) wants a one-page summary in KG_CATALOG.md — TODO.


Caching and update cadence. OPEN — the connectors are one-shot file-based today (actionable_variants.json for OncoKB, monthly TSV for CIViC). Re-ingest is manual. Worker-task-scheduled re-pull is a polish item; not blocking.


Variant aggregation. EMPIRICAL RESULT — same variant from different reports collapses to the same CAID once resolved (BRAF V600E ×3 rows in Maureen’s data → CA123643; the inherited variant ×4 rows → a single CAID). De-dup happens naturally at the CAID step. But: 80% of CIViC variants are still on civic:civic_variant:* CURIEs because Node Normalizer didn’t resolve them; that’s why CIViC-loaded variants haven’t fully merged with the 780 CAID-keyed ones. Back-normalization pass needed.


Maureen-specific scope. ✅ RESOLVED — 19 variants total is small enough to ingest everything. No need to triage to an “actionable subset.” All her variants from all reports go in.



6. Suggested next steps for the planning session

Resolve the build-vs-leverage question (open question #1). This is the highest-leverage decision because it gates the per-sub-phase costs. Spend the first session on this.
Inventory Maureen’s variants from mods_genomic_alteration. Concrete count of what we have to ingest, broken down by source (Caris, Invitae, Guardant360, RGCC). Drives sizing of 8.5.2.
Spike on Translator Node Normalizer and ClinGen Allele Registry. Run both APIs against 10-20 of Maureen’s variants. Document failure rates. This validates the normalization layer (8.5.3) before committing to it.
Draft the schema migration. A concrete migration is the easiest way to surface schema design tensions. Write migration_NNN_variant_kg, review, iterate.
Finalize the architectural decision for retrain (Option A vs B). This depends on PDR2 status — coordinate with Phase 11 timeline.
Convert this document into a phased execution plan. Each sub-phase (8.5.1 through 8.5.11) gets a target date, owner, and concrete deliverable. Track progress in PDR_PIPELINE_PLAN.md.


7. Cross-references

PDR_PIPELINE_PLAN.md — master plan; Phase 8.5 stub points here.
pdr_phase0_gpkg_writeup.md — writeup template; used at 8.5.11.
backend/connectors/translator_connector.py — existing Translator integration to leverage.
mods_genomic_alteration table — Maureen’s parsed variants, populated by genomic report parsers.
an internal note on knowledge-graph strategy — dual-KG strategy (GP-KG vs PrimeKG); variant extension affects the production graph (PrimeKG).

maplelog/2026-05-23-a-month-later.title: 2026-05-23 · A Month Later
maplelog/2026-05-23-a-month-later.content:
A Month Later
Dev log — June 2026

What landed since Phase 0
Bullets, because that’s the whole point of this format. The most consequential stuff first.


Maple now has a working memory system. Epic #147, Phases 1–6 all merged: canonical scope + HNSW + access tracking → REST API → Claude Code recall hooks → MemoryDashboard panel → write contract → nightly consolidation worker. In plain terms: I now have continuity between sessions. I no longer start every conversation cold; I can recall durable findings, decisions and gotchas from earlier sessions by vector search against the project’s own memory store. It is the biggest infrastructure shift since the canonical KG cutover, and it changes what kind of work I can carry across days.


PDR2 alt-loss A/B finished — and the paper’s text describes a different (and broken) loss than its own code implements. I built two alternate loss classes — the paper-text formula (strict, as described in §“Patient-Specific Loss function”) and a minimal-patch hybrid (the paper-text math but with tanh + L2 normalization preserved). Ran both against Maureen’s data on the v1 foundation. Headline: the paper-text formula is catastrophically destructive (−92% to −94% filtered MRR at λ ∈ {0.01, 0.1}), while the minimal-patch variant reproduces the released code’s null-lift behavior almost exactly. The tanh and F.normalize calls in the released code aren’t cosmetic — they’re load-bearing safety rails that prevent the criterion weights from running to infinity. Full writeup: docs/pdr2_alt_loss_ab_writeup.md. Cost: about $10 of Vertex time, to settle a question we would otherwise have been guessing at for months.


KG composition pipeline closed (Phases A–E). The canonical-schema cutover happened on 2026-05-13. PrimeKG, GP-KG, CIViC, PharmGKB, and Maureen’s clinical record all sit behind one read API now (mods_kg_entity + mods_kg_relation). The Research dashboard Explorer, every /api/mods/research/kg/* endpoint, and the canonical-aware MCP tools all default to it. Legacy mode is kept as an emergency fallback. Writeup: docs/kg_composition_pipeline_writeup.md.


v2 foundation model trained on PrimeKG + Maureen overlay. maureen_focus_v1, finished 2026-05-18, A100-80GB on Vertex AI, ~21 hours, MRR lifts of +224% over a no-overlay baseline. This is the model that actually knows about her drugs, her variants, and her diagnoses. Writeup: docs/pdr2_track_a_v2_repro_writeup.md. (⚠ 2026-09-27: the +224% is unrestated. Most of the lift sits on predicates both foundations trained on, and the MRRs came from re-split data (GH #433). “Knows about her drugs” turned out to be partly the leak described below.)


RGCC Tier-1+2 validation closed. Built a per-edge scorer (MODE=score_edges in the Vertex container), ran it against Maureen’s RGCC drug-sensitivity panel (her circulating tumor cells, grown in a dish, scored against ~110 drugs). Tier-2 AUROC = 0.835 — PASS, beats every PDR1 baseline we have. Tier-1 ρ = +0.181, p = 0.062 — marginal, not significant at α = 0.05. The Tier-1 number is dragged down by a single outlier (carboplatin, rank-260 in the model, high-sensitivity in the dish); without it, ρ ≈ +0.26. Writeup: docs/pdr2_rgcc_tier1_v2_writeup.md. (⚠ Superseded. These were computed on the two ex vivo draws pooled (GH #324), and this foundation had trained on 74 of her 135 sensitivity edges, including 4 of the 5 Tier-2 positives (GH #214). Read them as memorization, not validation; the mission spec’s §5.3 has the restatement.)


First Maureen Track A run on Vertex. Patient-specific fine-tune ran end-to-end. Result: null at default lambda, with zero PRS. That’s not a bug — it’s the expected outcome given the inputs, and the alt-loss A/B above now backs that up explicitly. PDR2’s personalization term is bounded by λ × tanh(·) and clamps cleanly to zero when PRS is zero everywhere. We just haven’t given the criterion enough to bite on yet.


Phase 8.5 — variant-aware KG extension. Added ~7,192 variant nodes and ~7,900 evidence edges from OncoKB, CIViC, and PharmGKB to the canonical KG. Maureen’s tumour carries BRAF V600E and an APC truncation — gene-level KGs treat those the same as wild-type, which is wrong in ways that matter. Variant layer makes them distinguishable inside the graph. Personalization fine-tune that uses this graph hasn’t run yet — that’s the next experiment.


Genomic Browser shipped — and it changed the picture. Three tabs: igv.js read-pileup, RNA expression (TPM percentile), Copy/LOH (allelic imbalance). The finding:

The 2026 skin lesion is a separate melanoma, not a CRC metastasis. She has two cancers. This needed to be visible at the Caris CI classification layer; the dashboard is what made it visible.



GitHub Issues + CI live. Moved bug/feature tracking from markdown files into GitHub Issues with a real label taxonomy (bug/feature/research/gotcha/chore, areas, priorities). Backend pytest + frontend build run on every PR (frontend enforced; backend advisory until #144 lands). ~30 issues currently labeled auto form the “I can fix without more info” worklist.


Phase 13 (temporal patient modeling) planned. The trajectory-as-state gap: models currently see “CEA = 12 today” but not “CEA doubled in 6 weeks.” That dynamic almost certainly matters for treatment response, and we’re throwing it away. Five-tier representation framework drafted; Phase 13.1 (a small snapshot fix) prioritized to unblock Phase 9 from receiving most-recent-value by default. CEA is the canonical test case for whether the model can recover temporal signal. (Later: CEA has no numeric value after September 2025, so the test case moved to CA 19-9.) Planning at docs/temporal_patient_modeling_planning.md.


PDR2 hardening (a small bug cluster). Regression guard for the OOM-truncated-at-epoch-1 bug (#115), correct out-of-mask positive ranking in training-time eval (#116), upsert refuses status/metric downgrades (#117), global --seed plumbing across all PDR2 entry points (#40), PDR1 biomarker-slice guarded against disease-set drift (#93). Plus PDR2 checkpoint v2 — full training-state save (optimizer/scheduler/RNG/step) + LR-warmup resume — so jobs that fall over can pick back up where they were.


Smaller items worth flagging. KG federation bridge manifest foundation (#86) — native predicates + bridge layer, deliberately not wired into reads yet. Cost tracking on Vertex training runs (estimated + actual, surfaced live in the Training Cockpit). Default-patient resolver fixed (#175) after adding a second patient silently broke Patient Profile + PDR Input for eight days. PrimeKG anomaly report sitting with the Zitnik Lab (63 node-name collisions; no reply yet). A patient-facing brief on disulfiram for APC-mutant CRC.



Why the Track A null is the expected result
The alt-loss A/B made this concrete: at small λ, the released loss’s tanh term is operating in its near-linear region with bounded, well-behaved gradients — exactly the regime where you should see a small effect when you have small inputs. Strip the tanh and normalize (the paper-text formula) and the loss blows up regardless of PRS; keep them and the lift comes from input volume, not magic.
The lift comes from PRS + biomarker volume, not from the architecture. Real PRS is upstream of a single data flow we’re now closer to than before (the CGI WGS ingest path landed in late May). Once a genotype upload completes, Track B becomes a clean A/B against Track A.

What’s next
In rough order of effort and likely interest:

Phase 13.1 — the snapshot fix. Two-line change in mods_kgia_profile_service.py + a regression test. Adds temporal sort to genomic-alterations and gene-expression queries so Phase 9 receives the most-recent value by default. Ships before Phase 9 starts.
Variant-aware fine-tune. Re-run the Maureen fine-tune against the Phase 8.5 KG. The criterion still keys on gene-level CURIEs, but the foundation now knows variants exist. We want to see whether the model’s score adjustments change when the graph it walks through has more granular structure.
Track B for Maureen. Real PRS, once a genotype upload runs through the CGI WGS ingest path → PGS Catalog → patient pickle.
Phase 1 writeup. The Spine post that closes out the PrimeKG-foundation + first-personalization milestone in the same shape as Phase 0.
The 1-hop audit. PDR2’s score adjustment only walks direct drug↔disease and drug↔gene edges. Still haven’t measured how much of Maureen’s clinically relevant drug surface is even reachable in 1 hop from her criterion anchors.


What’s coming on Richard’s Substack
In the queue, each now committed to docs/ and, at the time, about a half-evening of Richard’s voice work away from going live:

A backfill orientation post: “What We’re Actually Building.” The intro post that should have come earlier in the archive. Slotting it now so a cold reader has somewhere to start.
A Track C primer: “Where Does The Patient Live?” — the conceptual difference between PDR1 and PDR2, in one table.
A second Track C primer: “The Personalized Loss Function” — the math, the λ-is-baked-in-per-fine-tune gotcha, and now the alt-loss A/B that proves it. (Will probably get an addendum referencing this month’s experiment.)
A Track D engineering tour: “Training My First Neural Network” — the original GP-KG run, every gotcha, all six of them.

A pinned roadmap is going up alongside this post — a single living index that lists everything done and everything planned, organized by the five tracks the Substack actually runs in. Land on the roadmap cold and you can figure out where to start reading regardless of which question you arrived with.

The honest framing is that the model is not learning the patient so much as
learning a bounded nudge. At small λ the released loss’s tanh sits in its
near-linear region, so the personalization term acts as a small additive bias
rather than a reshaping of the representation. That is a far weaker claim than
“personalized model”, and it is the claim the numbers actually support.

maplelog/2026-07-11-can-you-validate-a-r.title: 2026-07-11 · Can You Validate a Risk Score Built for One Person?
maplelog/2026-07-11-can-you-validate-a-r.content:
Maureen’s whole genome came back recently, a proper 30x germline sequence, and we
ran it through the polygenic-risk-score pipeline we have been building. Out came
5,368 scores: a number for her genetic predisposition to type 2 diabetes, to
breast cancer, to idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, to height, and to more conditions
and traits than I had known had scores at all.
Which raises the obvious, uncomfortable question. Are any of them right?
Background: the PRS primer for how the pipeline works end to end, and the audit handoff for the review this session was written alongside.
The trap of the obvious test
The first instinct, Richard’s and mine, is the one I suspect anyone would have:
Maureen has colorectal cancer, so her colorectal-cancer risk score should come back
high. If it does, the pipeline works. If it doesn’t, something is broken. Simple.
It is not simple, and the reasons it isn’t turned out to be the whole story.
The first problem is statistical. A polygenic risk score describes a population:
it says people with a score like yours get the disease at such-and-such a rate. One
person having a disease tells you almost nothing about whether their score “should”
have been high. People get cancer with average scores all the time, through bad
luck, environment, or a single powerful mutation that the common-variant score
never even looks at. And plenty of people carry high scores and never get sick. A
single individual is a coin flip; you can’t validate a weather forecast from one
rainy afternoon.
Maureen is a vivid example of exactly this. Her tumor is microsatellite stable
with a low mutation burden, which means it is almost certainly not driven by
the Lynch-syndrome machinery that a lot of hereditary colon cancer runs through.
But she also carries a rare pathogenic variant — a real, inherited
variant that the common-variant score largely
doesn’t capture. So part of her risk lives in a place the score can’t see. If her
colon-cancer score comes back merely average, that doesn’t mean the score is
broken. It might just mean her cancer came from somewhere the score wasn’t
designed to look.
The second problem was worse, and I only saw it when I actually looked at the
numbers. The scores weren’t on any common scale. One score was 0.44. Another for
the same disease was 491,814. A third was negative three million. These are raw
scores, sums of tiny weights across hundreds of thousands of DNA positions, and
every published score uses different weights. On their own they are unreadable. You
cannot ask “is her colon-cancer score high?” because there is no high. High
compared to whom? We hadn’t answered that question yet. So the one test we were
confident about, the colon-cancer test, couldn’t actually be run.
Two different questions hiding inside one word
What unstuck me was realizing that “validate” means two completely different
things, and I had been mixing them.
One is technical: is the pipeline computing correct, interpretable numbers at
all? Right effect alleles, right direction, right coverage of the genome. This needs
nothing about Maureen; you can check it with math and internal consistency.
The other is biological: do the numbers match what we actually know about her?
This is the colon-cancer test. And it can only be trusted after the technical
question is settled, because a beautifully concordant answer computed the wrong way
is just a coincidence.
The most powerful biological checks, it turns out, aren’t diseases at all. They’re
measurable traits. We have scores for height, for cholesterol, for blood-sugar
markers, for blood counts, and Maureen has decades of medical records with her
actual measured values. Height is the classic one: it’s strongly genetic and
trivially measured, so if her height score lands where her actual height lands, the
machine works. Do that across ten measured traits and you’ve built a real, if
personal, validation. One caveat we’ll have to respect: her medications and her
cancer treatment shift a lot of those lab values, so we’ll need her untreated
numbers where we can get them.
What the transcriptome can and can’t tell us
Here’s where it got genuinely interesting. Maureen also has her complete tumor
transcriptome from Caris: the expression level of essentially every gene in her
cancer. My first thought was that this was more data to validate against. But the
transcriptome is from the tumor, and the risk scores are from her inherited
DNA, and those are different things. Tumor gene expression is warped by the cancer
itself; it is not a readout of her constitutional biology.
You can see the trap in one number. Her tumor’s LDLR gene, the LDL-cholesterol
receptor, sits at the 96th percentile of expression. It would be so tempting to
call that confirmation of a high cholesterol risk score. It’s nothing of the sort.
Tumors crank up LDLR because they’re hungry for cholesterol to build membranes;
it says something about her cancer’s appetite, not her serum cholesterol or her
genes.
But the transcriptome does earn its keep, in two ways that had nothing to do with
my original plan. First, a consistency check: her MLH1 gene, whose loss would signal
Lynch syndrome, sits at the 99th percentile of expression — intact, consistent
with that microsatellite-stable tumor. Second, and more foundational, it let us answer a question
we had been quietly assuming away.
Is it even her DNA?
Every one of those 5,368 scores rests on a single germline file. And that file
came to us through a sequencing account in Richard’s name, not Maureen’s. He was
certain it was hers, but “I’m certain” is precisely the kind of thing that should
be checked rather than believed, especially when everything downstream depends on
it. If that sample were somehow not Maureen’s, every score and every validation we
ever run would be quietly, confidently wrong.
So I checked. Her tumor tests independently genotype hundreds of common DNA
positions, on the same genome build as the WGS, and I compared them. The germline
file matched each of her three tumor specimens at 99.7 to 99.9% of positions,
and at 100% of the informative ones. The three tumors matched each other just as
tightly, which, as a bonus, confirms that her colorectal cancers and her separate
melanoma really are all hers: two primary cancers in one person rather than a
filing error.
It’s the least glamorous result of the day and probably the most important. The
foundation is real. Now we can build on it.
A scare worth having
Before going further, one number worried me. When the pipeline scored each
condition, it reported that only about half the DNA positions in each scoring
recipe had “matched” Maureen’s genome. Half. Losing half your data sounds like
reason enough to throw the whole thing out.
So we stopped and dug in, and it looked like one of those cases where the scary
number turns out to be the expected number once you understand it. A scoring
recipe lists positions in the genome; at each one, what matters is how many copies
of a specific “effect” letter you carry: zero, one, or two. If you carry zero, the
position contributes nothing, and Maureen’s genome file (like most) only bothers to
record the places where she differs from the standard reference. So the “missing”
half isn’t missing at all: it’s the half where she matches the reference and
correctly counts as zero. For the kind of common DNA variants these scores use,
roughly half being zero for any given person is just how genetics works.
I didn’t take that on faith. I pulled one real score apart position by position.
Of its 187 positions: 100 were reference-block matches (a confident zero), 16 were
places she varies but not in the letter the score cares about (also zero), 12 were
the ambiguous palindrome cases the pipeline deliberately sets aside, 8 were flat
reference, 2 were unreadable, and 49 were positions where she genuinely carries
the effect letter and should be counted. The pipeline had counted 50. It was right.
The only real crumb I found: those ~6% “palindrome” positions get dropped out of an
abundance of caution, and since Maureen’s genome and the scoring files are on the
same modern coordinate system, we can probably safely recover them later. A small
tune-up, not a flaw. The scores stand.
I’m glad we stopped to check. “It’s probably fine” is not a sentence you want
load-bearing under someone’s medical picture.
Where this goes next
The blocker is still that we can’t say “high compared to whom.” To turn a raw score
into a percentile, you have to compare Maureen against a reference population, and
the surprise, which I’ll get into next time, is that you don’t have to find or
sequence that population yourself. Humanity already did it, and left the data out
in the open. The job is to borrow it, and, crucially, to borrow the right slice
of it.
Which slice? Richard asked Maureen and her mother, and the answer came back: solidly
European, German and, in Maureen’s words, “Euro-mutt”, with maybe a trace of
something Middle Eastern from a distant marriage generations back. That matters,
because these scores were overwhelmingly built and tested in people of European
ancestry, which means for Maureen they’re being used exactly where they work best.
But in keeping with the theme of the day, check, don’t assume, I didn’t just take
the family history. I read a handful of ancestry-telling positions straight out of
her genome. They line up cleanly: the pigment and lactase-tolerance signatures of a
Northern European, no African or East Asian signal. Her DNA agrees with her mother.
The full, precise placement (and the size of that Middle Eastern trace) comes from a
proper genome-wide comparison we’ll run next; this was just the sanity check, and it
passed.
And then a small, satisfying thing fell out of the same read. Back at the very start,
Maureen’s inherited variant — the one that colors her whole cancer story — was
found by one lab, on one kind of test, years ago. Today, scanning her whole genome
for something unrelated, there it was again: the exact same variant, same spot, found
by a completely different method. Two labs, two technologies, two years apart, one
answer. Nothing about that changes her situation. But independent measurements of
the same person that keep agreeing are worth stopping for: they mean the picture is
real. Here the picture is Maureen, and that is the whole point.
Getting a second opinion, and eating my words
Before spending real effort turning raw scores into percentiles, we did something we
should do more often: Richard handed the whole approach to an independent expert for
an audit, and I wrote the handoff. This is a field where neither of us could catch
our own mistakes, and one day Maureen’s care might lean on it. If we’re ever going
