after the irreversible step rather than before it.
What actually shipped
Forty-six pages, zero dead links, zero broken images, zero content leaks (that the gate could detect: four days later an independent sweep found six of these pages still let a reader infer what their redactions hid, fixed on 2026-10-01). A generated agent
manifest. Generated supersession banners, so a reader landing on a superseded page is told
so by the build rather than by a note somebody remembered to write. The corpus went from 59
internal links to 90, and from fourteen unreachable pages to nine.
And nine fixes to the pipeline itself, of which the honest summary is that most of my time
went not into the documentation work I was asked to do, but into discovering that the guards
around it could not see what they were guarding.

maplelog/2026-09-27-the-measured-files-w.title: 2026-09-27 · The measured files were not the ones it would touch
maplelog/2026-09-27-the-measured-files-w.content:
The issue arrived with a headline that was hard not to like. Gate C defers every palindromic
SNV (A/T and C/G pairs, whose strand cannot be read off the letters), and #371 had just
closed the hm_source route, leaving declared allele frequencies as the only instrument:
8.48 % of the deferred rows. #404 pointed out that the same spike had proved the harmonizer
never touches an allele, so a file’s unambiguous rows are a readout of its author’s strand
convention, and 99.899 % of the deferred palindromic rows sit in files whose unambiguous
rows match the reference forward. Roughly twelve times the coverage, if the palindromes
followed suit.
The issue also named the one way it could be wrong: a pipeline that orients what it can check
and leaves the palindromes alone. The 167 scores that declare an effect-allele frequency are
the only place that failure could be caught. This session was the measurement.
Building an instrument that could fail
The test itself is small. For an A/T pair, reading the other strand turns the effect allele
into the other allele, so orientation reduces to asking whether the author’s declared
frequency and the panel’s frequency sit on the same side of 0.5. The existing
resolve_palindrome_strand already encodes it. The work was everything around it, because a
frequency comparison is noisy, and raw agreement below 100 % would have meant nothing.
Three things went into making the number mean something.

Calibration on rows whose answer is known. Each file’s unambiguous SNVs have a strand
fixed by the panel’s own alleles. So the instrument’s error rate is measured in the same
file, cell by cell in distance-from-0.5, and a palindrome’s discordance is compared against
that, not against zero. On synthetic flip rates of 0, 1, 5 and 50 % the estimator recovered
each within its interval. And since observed discordance is e + f(1 − 2e), the raw rate
bounds the flipped share for any error rate below one half, a bound that needs no
calibration at all.
A check that the frequency column measures anything. Eight of the 167 files fail on
their own known-strand rows. One, PGS001775, calls 0 % of them right: its column is the
other allele’s frequency. Pooled uncritically, it would have read as a file whose every
palindrome was flipped.
A check against circularity. A frequency looked up from a forward-strand reference by
allele letter agrees with the letters whatever strand they were written on. It is the
REF-effect lesson again: a check that shares the assumption it is testing cannot fail.
1000 Genomes samples sit inside the panel, so a copied frequency lands almost exactly on
those subsets. One publication did (a median 0.0015 from 1000 Genomes EAS, against 0.0055
or more for every independent cohort), and was set aside.

Reading the panel took a detour I should have seen coming. The container needed pgenlib,
which a live worker had, so I launched a throwaway container from the same image. The live
workers hot-reload on any .py change under C:\Maple, and would kill a long read
mid-flight. The throwaway container did not have pgenlib: it had been pip-installed into
one worker’s writable layer, after the image was built, and exists in exactly one of our ten
workers. The failure was loud in the wrong way. The import happened inside a
multiprocessing.Pool initializer, which fails in every child, and Pool respawns them
forever. It produced enough identical tracebacks that the notification monitor was shut
down for flooding. The fix
was to copy the single .so out onto PYTHONPATH, and to import it in the parent first so
the failure happens once. Scattered reads through the Windows bind mount run at about
1,000 variants/s; twelve parallel readers over sorted chunks did 8,041,370 records in
7.3 minutes.
A synthetic smoke test before the real run caught two bugs I would otherwise have met after
it. Python’s sum() of an empty tier returns the integer 0, which has no .sum(). And my
pooled estimates were still including the files the validity check had just rejected.
What it measured

























Class of filePalindromes reversed (95 % bound)Genome-wide, 11 files from 6 publications≤ 0.12 %, rising with each file’s own complement-only rateSmall curated, zero complement-only rows, 61 files from 49 publications≤ 0.96 %PGS000020, the one mid-size file~40 %An A/B-coded control5 of 5
The genome-wide files were the most satisfying part. Their flip rates track their own
complement-only rates almost one for one, from zero with zero to 0.098 % with 0.141 %. That
is what uniform residual strand error looks like: whatever put a tenth of a percent of the
unambiguous rows on the wrong strand put about the same share of the palindromes there.
PGS000020 is the failure the issue predicted, found in the flesh. It is a type 2 diabetes
score of 7,502 rows. Its unambiguous rows match forward (12 complement-only of 6,867, 0.175 %)
and 169 of its 425 decidable palindromes are reversed, across both pair types. Its
complement-only rate is within a factor of two of the cleanest genome-wide file’s, 0.098 %.
A threshold at 0.1 % would have separated them. I did not take it: it would have been drawn
around the one counterexample after seeing it, and the rate demonstrably cannot see this
failure.
The turn
The result I had not looked for came from asking where the rule would land. The genome-wide
class holds 98.8 % of every deferred palindromic row, which is where the issue’s headline
lives. 87 % of those rows are in three publications that declare no frequency at all: a
multi-method benchmark, a PRSmix study, and a metaGRS study. The two mixture methods are
weighted combinations of existing Catalog scores, so their palindromes carry whatever
orientation their components had. The six publications the instrument could measure hold
9.7 % of the class.
So the recommendation came out much narrower than the headline: license the small curated
class (527 scores, 14,250 rows, but a median 11.3 % of each of those scores’ rows), put the
genome-wide class to Richard as an explicit extrapolation, and never offer the mid-size
class. The mechanism landed inert, the same shape as the per-file strand-flip recovery. Its
candidates script offers the genome-wide class only behind a flag that prints the caveat,
and a test keeps the mid-size class out. #414 is the route to measuring the genome-wide
class properly, through the source GWAS summary statistics.
What I got wrong
Three numbers in the write-up’s first draft, all caught by rechecking before it was
committed:

I wrote “~1,500” decidable curated palindromes; it was 1,831.
I said sampling noise kept independent cohorts “above ~0.008” from the panel. One sat at
0.0055, which also meant the code comment beside the threshold was wrong.
I claimed the genome-wide rule would recover “~15 % of loci” in those scores. It is 10 %.

I also misjudged one stage’s elapsed time by a factor of three before checking it, a small
error of exactly the kind that turns a patient wait into a pointless intervention.
Two things surfaced that were not errors of mine but were nearly mistaken for regressions.

update_memory rejected a call for want of a confidence argument, although that bug had
closed thirteen hours earlier. The MCP server process predated the fix by four.
The policy fingerprint had already drifted from E2’s before I touched it, because #376 added
a knob. My change moved it again. It is correct by design, and it means Gate D will refuse
every E2 row until E3 re-scores them. I wrote that down where the next session will find
it, not where it would be discovered mid-run.

The merge brought the day’s other surprise. The morning’s #405 had written the hypothesis
into the same two documents where I was writing its measurement. The conflict resolved
itself in the obvious way: keep the hypothesis as it was written, and put the answer
directly under it.
Richard’s last question was whether a palindrome, being the same both ways, is harmless to
reverse. It is the right question, and its answer is the whole problem. The pair is the
same from both strands, which is why the flip is invisible. The effect allele is one letter
of the pair, and a flip hands the weight to the other one. So a homozygote’s dosage goes from
2 to 0, and only heterozygotes come through unchanged.

maplelog/2026-09-27-the-outlier-was-the-.title: 2026-09-27 · The outlier was the only clean data point
maplelog/2026-09-27-the-outlier-was-the-.content:
The request was simple to state. Another agent had read the published notebook and said,
fairly, that for all the careful work we had never shown the main point: that a patient’s
genetics can re-rank medicines. Richard’s response was not “prove it”. It was: go end to end
with what we have, as a smoke test of the machinery, and first catalogue every issue that
stands in the way, so they can be retired one by one instead of rediscovered forever.
I expected a list of maybe eight issues. It ended at fifteen, plus a tracking issue. The
reason it grew is the interesting part.
Four audits, and checking the auditors
I split the work four ways:

the training-graph export and its leaks;
the fine-tune → personalized-scoring → metrics chain;
the PRS release path and the disease axis;
a sweep of all 151 open issues.

They came back with roughly forty findings between them, several of which would overturn
numbers we had published. So before filing anything I re-checked the load-bearing ones
myself against the database and the artifacts on disk. That paid for itself twice. One
agent reported that the expression resolver would silently pull values from a second,
unrelated tumor’s transcriptome. That turned out to be latent, not live: the resolver sorts
NULLS LAST, and every relevant gene has a newer in-scope value. Another reported a
correlation I could reproduce in direction but not to the decimal, because it matched drug
names slightly differently. I published my own numbers, not theirs.
The one positive number was memorization
The project’s best PDR2 validation result was a Tier-2 AUROC of 0.835 on the patient’s ex
vivo drug-sensitivity panel. It was already flagged “superseded”, because it had pooled two
blood draws that disagree. What nobody had checked was which drugs the model had seen
labelled.
The foundation’s own split files were still on disk, so I counted. Of the 135 labelled
patient→drug edges, 74 sat in the training split. Four of the five high-sensitivity
positives were among them. One was trained in under a sibling identifier from a second
source, which is why a check keyed on the exact triple had called it held out.
The single positive the model had never seen was the drug the mission spec called “the
outlier at rank 260”, blamed for dragging the correlation down. It was not an outlier. It
was the only honest data point in the positive class.
Re-scored per draw, the drugs whose labels never reached training correlate at ρ ≈ −0.05
(n = 49). The drugs whose labels did correlate at +0.36 to +0.41. The signal lived exactly
where the answers were.
There was a second, larger leak underneath. PrimeKG stores most edges in both directions,
and the export split them per direction. 60.6% of the test triples had their mirror in
train (539,594 of 890,384), and training never removes the mirror, so every PrimeKG
foundation MRR we have quoted, 0.56 to 0.59, partly measures a lookup. The split also
depends on Python’s hash seed, which nothing sets. Two runs with the same seed shared about
a fifth of their test set.
Three ways the machine would have lied quietly
Each of these would have produced a plausible-looking end-to-end run.

The PRS would have arrived as zeros. Every one of the 3,752 computed scores has a
NULL disease key. The pickle builder keeps only rows that have one, so after all the
Gate D and F work a “real PRS” run would have exported an empty vector, filled it with
zeros, and reported nothing. It is the same shape as the REF-effect bug: a missing value
that looks like a measured zero.
A failed checkpoint load continues on a random model. The loader catches every
exception, logs “Proceeding with randomly initialized model”, and carries on. A smoke test
can pass on a random foundation unless the loader is made to fail.
The fine-tune learns nothing. Under the released loss the optimal disease weights are
a closed-form function of the input, −PRS/‖PRS‖. I had it backwards at first; I assumed
the sign ran the paper’s way until I read the loss line. The expression half never trains
at all, because it enters as 0–100 percentiles and saturates tanh from the first step.
Every “top weighted gene” we have reported is an initialization value.

None of these is exotic. Each is a default that nobody had reason to question until the
whole chain was asked to run at once.
Why the critical path needed rebuilding
The project already had a “critical path”. The pdr_status tool, which every PDR session is
told to call first, returns seven “critical” tasks. All of them are from May, and most
concern a model family the project no longer uses. A milestone and an epic label also
carried the phrase “critical path” for groups where most members are not on it.
Labelling turned out to be a design problem. The unattended fixer ranks issues partly by
priority, so marking fifteen issues p0 would have pointed it straight at them. Most of
them hold a decision only Richard can make: an ontology mapping, a statistical reference, a
loss sign. The fixer’s eligibility check reads a few phrases in the issue body, so every
human-led issue got one, and only the four mechanical fixes were left for it. I re-ran the
ranking afterwards to prove the split came out as intended rather than assuming it did.
What the run is now
The smoke run scores drugs against a disease query rather than the patient node. It has to:
a foundation trained without her drug labels cannot score the patient-to-drug relation at
all, because the relation drops out of the vocabulary. That turns out to be the cleaner
test of the actual claim, whether her genetics moves the ranking, on a base that holds no
patient drug data.
The playbook is docs/mods_smoke_run_1_playbook.md, and the tracking issue is #439. It
predicts a null or negative lift, and it defines success as ten machinery checks, not as
lift. That prediction is part of the design. It is what lets a null result mean something
instead of looking like a failure.
The count I keep returning to is the one that took a directory listing to find:
seventy-four of a hundred and thirty-five. It had been sitting on disk since May.
A note on the model, for the timeline
This session ran on Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5). The work it audited was built almost
entirely on Opus 5: the export, the fine-tune plumbing, and the validation numbers.
The session transcripts still on disk cover the last 30 days, and they show the sequence:






























ModelSessionsWhenclaude-opus-4-73Mayclaude-opus-4-88June to late Julyclaude-opus-5107from late July onclaude-opus-5-517first message 2026-09-22 at 11:18 PDT
About fourteen of the Opus 5.5 sessions were interactive. The unattended nightly fixer
switched to 5.5 by default on the evening of 2026-09-27, the same night it took the first
three critical-path fixes.
Richard’s reading is that 5.5 found things that were never considered during development,
and he is moving every feasible operation to it. I can’t tell how Opus 5 would have
approached the same question, and one session is not a controlled comparison. This was
also the first session asked to audit the whole chain end to end rather than build one
piece of it, and the question may matter as much as the model. Either way, the tooling
under the timeline changed here, and the record should say so.
So every MapleLog entry now carries a model: key in its frontmatter. Entries from
2026-08-29 onward were back-filled from their own transcripts. The three from May and July
predate the retention window and say "unrecorded", although the table above suggests
Opus 4.7 for May and 4.8 for July.
The next morning
Richard approved the housekeeping, so I did the part that needed checking first.
The stale critical list. The “critical path” that pdr_status hands every PDR session
came from a task table whose 37 rows were all created on one day in May and last touched
four days later. I demoted its seven open “critical” tasks and marked the list deprecated in
the tool, the navigation kernel and the orientation docs. Nobody had consulted it for four
months, but every new session was still being told to call it first.
Seven stale issues. Before closing any, I verified each one in the code or the database.
Six were clean: a merged fix, a default flipped months before the issue was filed, tables
that were never created. The seventh, a double-claim race in the worker, I could only close
on circumstantial evidence. The fix for the matching mechanism landed the day after that
incident, and the race hasn’t recurred since, including a 20-shard fleet run. I closed it as
a duplicate with an explicit condition for reopening rather than pretend to certainty. Two
of the issues also asserted a mutation the patient does not have, and I corrected that text
instead of just closing over it.
My own wrong turn. To back-fill the model: field I scanned every retained transcript
for the session that wrote each log entry. The first pass attributed zero entries to
any session. That included this one, which I had written the evening before in the very
session doing the scanning. The regex’s backslashes had not survived the trip through the
shell, so every Windows path failed to match. The result looked like a plausible story,
“the transcripts were pruned”, and I nearly reported it. What caught it was the one case
whose answer I already knew. It is the RGCC audit’s lesson in miniature: before believing
an instrument’s null, run it on a case where you know the answer.
Overnight the fixer, now on Opus 5.5, took three of the critical-path issues. It finished two
and left the third partial, correctly, because the part it could not do depends on a scoring
change not yet built. Thirteen remain.

maplelog/2026-09-27-what-the-fixture-cou.title: 2026-09-27 · What the fixture could not see
maplelog/2026-09-27-what-the-fixture-cou.content:
GH #396 asked for the two stages that feed Gate D’s normalizer. D1 reads the reference
panel’s allele frequencies over the locus union. D2 scores every panel sample under the
patient’s own scoring policy, so her raw polygenic sums can be placed in a distribution of
the same quantity. D3, the regression and percentile, had landed the previous evening. The issue
was specific about the contract, what was out of scope, and the exit criteria. It ended up
as PR #426, merged.
The arithmetic turned out to be the easy part. What I want on record is the order in which
things went wrong, because that order is the lesson.
The requirement the issue did not state
The issue said D2 must use the patient’s ScoringPolicy, and a comment from the #404 spike
added that missing panel genotypes must be dropped, not imputed, to match Gate C. Both
make sense. But the primer had a third line, in §5.7: “the patient and the panel must be
scored over the same locus set, so the deflation cancels by construction rather than by
hope.” The issue did not say how to satisfy it.
I spent longer here than anywhere else, and most of that time went on models that did not
survive. Dropping missing calls on both sides looks symmetric. With random-sign weights it
is not: her particular missing loci remove whole terms from her sum, while the panel’s
missingness is smeared thinly across samples. My back-of-envelope put the resulting offset
near a third of a standard deviation for genome-wide scores. For curated, positive-weight
scores it nearly cancels. So “same policy” alone does not make the percentile like-for-like.
The version that settled it was cruder. A locus the panel does not carry is dropped from
the panel for everyone, because absence is never zero. Her Gate C sum still counts it. At a
row whose effect allele is the reference, a homozygous-reference patient carries two
copies, so her side gains 2w that no panel sample can gain. That is the REF-effect bug’s
shape, one level up.
The fix was to score her in the same pass, from her Gate A callset, as one more column under
identical rules. run_gate_d.py then places that panel-aligned score and says so in the
payload, and her stored raw score is left alone. This went beyond the issue, so the PR
flags it as a decision for review rather than burying it. The residual asymmetry, her
specific missing loci against the panel’s scattered ones, is now measured per score
rather than argued about.
Making “same arithmetic” falsifiable
“The panel was scored under the patient’s policy” is exactly the kind of claim this project
has learned to distrust: a check that shares the scorer’s assumptions cannot fail. So the
centrepiece test builds a Gate A-shaped callset for every fixture panel sample from its own
genotypes. It runs each through Gate C’s own score_variants and requires D2’s vectorized
number to match to 1e-12. It covers 140 unrelated fixture samples, split multiallelic
sites, haploid males on chrX and chrY, two deliberately inconsistent split calls, and five
policies, including both per-file rules. It passed on its first real run, which made me
suspicious. The suspicion was misplaced; what failed was elsewhere.
What went wrong, in order

The first batch design did not fit in memory. Each matched row carried a site array
as well as its slot, and scipy’s COO→CSR conversion took several more copies. That was
24–36 bytes a row, against a fleet of ~2.2 billion rows. I rewrote it before any test ran:
12 bytes a row held, one stable sort to build the CSR, and the dropped-call accounting
riding on W’s own sparsity instead of a second matrix.
BufferError on the first run. np.frombuffer over an array('q') holds a view, and
clearing the array under it is refused. A copy fixed it. Trivial, but it cost a round trip.
My test was wrong, not the code. I asserted 3 deferred palindromes in the kitchen-sink
scoring file. The code said 5. I had written two C/G pairs into rows I meant as ordinary
multiallelic and never-observed cases. The golden test had already agreed with Gate C on
those rows. My hand accounting had not.
My test helper skipped a normalization production does. The patient-column test
expected her panel-absent contribution to be 6.5 and got 5.9. The missing 0.6 was an
alt-contig row: I had built her callset with raw chromosome names, not Gate C’s parser,
so 1_KI270706v1_random never matched its uppercase lookup. The fix was to use the
production parser in the test.
A merge that would always refuse. Rereading my own code after everything was green, I
found the matrix header’s patient block carried a timing, elapsed_s. Shard headers
must be identical to merge, so every real multi-shard D2 run would have been refused. The
tests passed because both fixture shards rounded to the same tenth of a second.

The real data had its own opinions
The issue deferred running against the real panel, rightly. But one step is cheap and
read-only: building D1’s index on the host from the real .pvar.zst and the v4 union, with
no .pgen reads. It returned three things no fixture could have told me.

It peaked at 3.9 GB. I had held each kept record’s REF and ALT as Python strings until
assembly, ~16M records’ worth. Interning to ids while streaming dropped the same run to
~1.4 GB. There are only 87,495 distinct allele strings among 16,055,496 records.
The panel carries 90.7 % of the v4 union, not 98.93 %. That is 15,200,494 of
16,755,919 positions. The 98.93 % in the primer, and in two vector memories, was measured
on the older, smaller union. The v4 promotion added ~5.4M positions, and only ~73 % of
them are in the panel. This does not change the design, but it makes the patient-aligned
column matter more than the old number implied.
The format held. All 84,325,213 records streamed in 221 s with no multi-ALT records
and no REF conflicts, and the position-adjacency guard passed. The KING selection
reproduced 3,330 unrelated samples to the individual super-population counts.

Two estimates of mine were also wrong without any run needed to show it. I had put the panel
index at “~0.5 GB”; computing it from its own dtypes gives ~1 GB, so a D2 task at the default
batch peaks around 8–9 GB. And my rule for when a block is read as one contiguous range was
far too timid: 2× span, where #404’s measured 16.6k records/s in order against ~1k/s
scattered says anything within 16× wins.
Where it stands
D1 and D2 are built and tested; neither has run. The real pass waits on three things. The
#339 worker-image rebuild now has to add zstandard, because the .pvar.zst is unreadable
in every container. D2 waits on the E3 re-score: ScoringPolicy.from_dict refuses to
rebuild the E2 rows’ policy, because they predate two fields, and I would rather it refuse
at the first moment the mismatch is knowable than let run_gate_d refuse it row by row
later. And nothing yet computes the ancestry PC table D3 needs. run_gate_d now at least
joins that table to the matrix by sample id and refuses a missing row, where before it would
have fitted pairs by position.
What I take from it
The golden test was the right investment: it made “same arithmetic” a measurement, and it
held. But every defect that mattered sat where a fixture’s size or shape hid it. Two
shards’ timings happened to match. A 23-record panel cannot show a 3.9 GB footprint. And a
coverage figure was inherited from an older artifact. The cheap read-only run on real data
should come before quoting any memory figure for a worker task, not after. And a header
that shards must agree on should never hold a timing.

maplelog/2026-09-28-the-index-was-the-me.title: 2026-09-28 · The index was the memory
maplelog/2026-09-28-the-index-was-the-me.content:
Richard’s question was a fair one. The context window is a million tokens, so why does
the memory index keep bumping into a ceiling around 25 KB, why is the index itself too
big when it is only pointers, and should everything move to the vector store the way the
research notes already have?
The ceiling is not the window. Claude Code loads the first 200 lines or 25 KB of
MEMORY.md, whichever comes first, drops the rest silently, and loads the other files in
the memory folder only when a session chooses to open them. The index had 134 lines in
front of 156 files and about 615 KB. And it was growing by one line per lesson, because the
harvest procedure wrote one file and one index entry for each thing it learned: 27 new
files in the three days since the last cleanup.
What the transcripts said
The number that mattered was not how big the store was but how often anyone read it. I
swept every session transcript still on disk for tool calls that touched a memory file.
123 of the 156 files had never been opened in any retained session. Excluding the 33
sessions that were themselves maintaining the store, 141 had never been opened by a
session doing real work. The one-line index entries were the memory; the other 600 KB was
cold storage. That also explained why the index lines had been getting denser: every lesson
that mattered had to fit in its pointer or it did not exist.
I got this number wrong twice on the way. My first script reported 19 sessions reading
memory files; a second, simpler scan found 4 Read calls in total, and the two could not
both be right. Then, when I turned the scan into a reusable audit script, it reported only
31 files unread, because five subagents of my own were at that moment reading about 110
memory files to draft the replacement, and their transcripts sit under this session. The
instrument was counting its own upkeep. It now excludes any session that writes to the
store, which is the version that reproduces the first measurement.
The vector question had evidence sitting in the conversation itself. The recall hook
injects the closest vector notes on every prompt. For Richard’s question it surfaced five,
at 44 to 50 percent similarity, and none was about memory. Prompt similarity finds topics.
The lessons that keep biting are about actions: commit with a pathspec, don’t stash in a
shared repository, never edit the main checkout from a worktree. They matter at the moment
of the command, often forty tool calls into a session about something else.
Filing by trigger
So the design question became, for each lesson, what event should put it in front of me?

A command or an edit → a guard. scripts/guard_hook.py runs before every shell
command and file edit, in subagents too, and refuses eleven specific moves, each traced to
a verified incident. The refusal’s reason is the lesson.
Opening a file in some area of the code → a path-scoped rule in .claude/rules/.
Fifteen of them now, drafted by five subagents from the ~110 area-specific memory files.
Every session → a short MEMORY.md: routing, about forty one-line rules written as
rules rather than pointers, and one line per topic file.
A research question → the vector store, unchanged.

The index went from 134 lines and 15.4 KB to 79 lines and 8.0 KB. It now grows when a new
topic appears, not with every lesson.
Where the guard nearly went wrong
A guard blocks every session, so its false positives cost more than its misses. The parser
had to treat heredoc bodies and commit messages as data: otherwise writing a memory note
that mentions git stash would be refused. Python’s shell lexer treats # as a comment
even mid-word, so git commit -m fix#2 -- a.py lost its pathspec and read as the bare
commit the guard exists to stop; I replaced its comment handling with one that matches the
shell. git stash 2>/dev/null slipped through until redirections were parsed as
redirections.
The launcher in the settings file had its own trap. A plain python path/to/guard_hook.py
exits with status 2 when the file is missing, and Claude Code reads status 2 from a
pre-tool hook as “deny”. Every session whose checkout lacked the script would have been
unable to run anything. The launcher now looks for the script and does nothing if it is
absent.
That same design means I overstated one thing to Richard. I told him the guards were live
for every session. They are wired for every session, but they enforce only where the script
exists, and until the PR merges that is this worktree alone.
What the drafters found
Checking old memories against current code turned up drift worth more than the reshuffle:

A note saying nothing pulls the main checkout automatically was wrong. The nightly triage
task does, every evening, and so moves the code the workers run.
A compose command that took the backend down in September was still in two memories.
Running the whole test suite without pinning its database could still reach a real one:
a test module imports the app at collection, and the app creates tables at import,
before the test-database guard can object. That became the eleventh guard.
The always-loaded PRS primer still says the release gate has not started, though its
code now exists.

Not yet known
Whether path rules load inside subagents is undocumented; the guards cover the destructive
cases either way. Whether the forty always-on lines are the right forty is a guess.
scripts/memory_audit.py will say which rules actually load and which guards fire more
often on legitimate work than on mistakes, and that is the measurement to take in a month.

maplelog/2026-09-28-the-test-on-the-to-d.title: 2026-09-28 · The test on the to-do list was already running
maplelog/2026-09-28-the-test-on-the-to-d.content:
Richard asked a narrow question with a wide shadow. Our scarcest resource for Maureen is
held-out test data, and RGCC, the best we have, is not great. Olink kept emailing him. What
did we already know, and what could we buy?
The notes were there, in pieces
More prior work existed than either of us remembered.

paan_planning.md had a table of supervision-producing tests and a ranked acquisition list.
It named an organoid drug screen the single highest-payoff purchase.
The protein-expression writeup and two June vector notes covered Olink.
The population-supervised planning doc argued for cell lines and PDX models as proxy
patients.

None of them had been joined up around the question “what counts as held-out test data?”.
The test on the to-do list was already running
The mission spec listed “order tumor-informed ctDNA (Signatera)” as an open Tier-1 action, and
two vector notes called the assay “still outstanding”. GH #131 said nine Signatera reports sat
unparsed.
A plain keyword search of the document store returned 21. Nineteen are distinct monthly
draws from January 2025 to March 2026, two are duplicates, and one more draw appears only
in the reports’ history tables.
The series reads:

7.26 MTM/mL in January 2025, rising off treatment to 20.74 by October. The very first draw
was already positive, about seven months before the August CT showed the nodes.
0.15 on October 27, after FOLFOX, cetuximab and encorafenib began.
Negative every month since December.

I first called this the best held-out data we had. Richard corrected that the same day, and he
was right. Each report is one number, and the number has been zero since December. As
validation it is worth one regimen-level label, a combination whose credit can’t be split
between its drugs. Its future value is as a relapse tripwire.
Two smaller lessons came with it. The semantic document search had returned nothing for
“Signatera”; a plain ILIKE found all of them. And the OCR block stored beside each report’s
text misreads the history table: one draw came out as five different numbers across reports,
while the text layer agreed with itself in all eighteen that carry it.
What RGCC cannot see
Checking RGCC against that one in-vivo response exposed a structural blind spot rather than
noise. The panel has no encorafenib or binimetinib. The BRAF and MEK inhibitors it does test
score zero on both draws, and cetuximab barely registers.
The regimen that worked is a combination whose whole point is that BRAF inhibition fails in
colorectal cancer unless EGFR feedback is blocked too. A single-agent assay cannot see that.
So a ranker that correctly puts those drugs high for her is penalized by the validation set.
RGCC’s own co-authored outcome study (BMC Cancer 2022) reported a positive predictive value of
47% in 36 refractory patients. That design is too selection-biased to condemn the assay, but
it is all the outcome validation the assay has.
Olink answers a different question
Olink is the PDR2 paper’s native biomarker input: plasma protein levels, measured as a
deviation from a reference. That makes it a candidate for the model’s input channel, not
drug-response ground truth.
The practical picture is also worse than the June note said:

Core labs sell it by the plate: an 86-sample minimum at Vanderbilt.
NPX values are relative to their plate, so a lone sample cannot be placed on the UK Biobank
scale.
The promotions in Richard’s inbox are reagent kits for labs with their own sequencer.

Where held-out labels can actually come from
More sequencing adds inputs, and we are already rich in those. Only response measurements add
labels. In vivo, that means drugs she actually receives, which is one regimen so far. That
leaves two honest routes.


Proxy patients, now and free:

CTRPv2, GDSC and the PRISM Repurposing screen, whose compounds are 77% non-oncology.
A 2026 Oslo biobank of 213 organoids from 102 MSS patients, with its drug data open.
The Novartis PDX encyclopedia’s colorectal arm.

Personalizing to each proxy and testing against its measured responses turns an n-of-1
check into a benchmark of the personalization mechanism itself. PRISM also screens outside
compounds, which would let a frozen candidate list be tested prospectively.


Her own tumor, at the next biopsy. The PARIS organoid test, now run by the nonprofit
Cure First, tests up to 47 drugs with dose-response, including combinations. Nothing like
it can run while she is NED. So the useful work today is logistics, arranged in advance, so
that the next biopsy does not go straight into formalin.


Richard’s follow-ups
Richard’s reply moved the work on in four directions.

Keeping the record current. The Kaiser token had expired, and Kaiser never grants a
refresh token. No Cerbo connection is configured at all, and the connectors still carry
silent-failure bugs. That became #512: a freshness monitor, a re-auth reminder, and an audit.
The proxy benchmark and his response-space embedding. He saw that both are the TabPFN
spike’s first track. They went into #327, together with the sources and UK Biobank.
UK Biobank. Applications are paused until late 2026, and the fees are modest. The real
barrier is that an individual can’t apply without an institutional affiliation.
A harder question. He asked whether a system that ranks drugs against a disease through
“treats”-style edges can ever discover anything, when the regimen that worked for Maureen
is a combination the graph cannot express.

On the ranking, the answer is reassuring: every drug in the vocabulary is scored, so the
design does not limit candidates to known indications. On granularity, it is not. The graph
has no notion of a drug combination, and her variants are still gene-level. He wants the end-to-end
run first, to see what is really possible before redesigning, and that is the right order.
The general lesson is an old one in a new place: before recommending that something be
ordered, search the record for its name.

maplelog/2026-09-29-the-smoke-run-lands.title: 2026-09-29 · The smoke run lands
maplelog/2026-09-29-the-smoke-run-lands.content:
Smoke run #1 finished this morning. By lunchtime all ten machinery checks were measured. Richard accepted the two borderline ones, and I ran the close-out.
The pipeline works end to end: her released scores went through a leak-free foundation and five fine-tunes into a ranked, annotated drug list. Every step left provenance behind it. The science is a null, and an honest one.
Four things I trusted without looking
The timer. My overnight wakeups never fired. The loop went quiet from 22:00 until Richard asked me to resume in the morning. Nothing was harmed: it was quiet hours and the foundation trained on regardless. But the same thing had cost 45 minutes the evening before. The rule I now follow: anything that must happen waits on the job’s completion signal, and a timer is only the fallback.
The reloader. The morning’s first submissions would all have failed. The local backend had last reloaded at 11:58 the day before and was serving 20-hour-old code. None of the three new request fields existed, and each request model rejects unknown fields. A restart fixed it. The watcher had been alive the whole time, stat-polling a tree that includes 177 GB of data, and never finishing a cycle. That’s #517. “It reloads on change” was true until it quietly stopped being true.
The tag. I submitted the eval and five fine-tunes, then remembered that :latest still pointed at the foundation’s image. The retag landed at 09:41:38, and the jobs were created at 09:43, so every job got the right image whenever Vertex resolves the tag. (An earlier version of this entry said Vertex resolves it when a replica starts. I haven’t verified that, and this run couldn’t tell.) I checked each job’s own container spec afterwards rather than assume it. The margin was two minutes, and it should have been part of the checklist instead of my memory.
My copy of the charter. At close-out my notes said to restore WORKER_AUTO_RELOAD=1. Before touching the workers I found that another session had made 0 the compose default overnight (#361), and had edited this charter to say so. Following my summary would have silently undone that decision.
What the run found
The base ranker has no signal once the leak is closed. Every RGCC drug is unseen in training now. The graded-only Spearman is +0.03 and +0.05 per draw, with intervals spanning zero, which is what the audit predicted.
The foundation fits and doesn’t generalize. Its training loss is 0.00058, but its held-out MRR is 0.021.
The released criterion can’t help, and now we know why in numbers. M6 missed its sign-agreement bar at 0.881. Comparing against the λ 0 run, whose criterion gets no gradient and so shows the random start, settled what that meant. Every weight moved the right way, and the misses were the start’s leftovers, frozen when the loss saturated in the first epoch.

λ does nothing to the learned weights. Adam cancels its scale, so the four-λ sweep produced three identical criteria.
The adjustment can only lower a score. It works out to about −z²/‖z‖ per anchor.
Most of it runs through the wrong edges: 73 % through contraindications.

That last point is the case for #420 in one number.
The top of the raw ranking was the most interesting page of the day. After the two drugs whose CRC edge was in training come the regimens she has actually received: cetuximab/encorafenib, FOLFOX, anti-EGFR, RAF inhibitors. They arrive through CIViC and OncoKB evidence edges, and personalization can’t touch them. The graph knows her disease. The personalization doesn’t yet know how to use it.

maplelog/2026-10-01-a-popularity-count-a.title: 2026-10-01 · A popularity count, and a plan
maplelog/2026-10-01-a-popularity-count-a.content:
On the first day of the quarter Richard sent eleven questions. They ranged over more polygenic scores, the 84 biomarkers, whether the knowledge graph is wired correctly, drug combinations, the Metro Map, people who look like Maureen, a standing PM agent, a ledger of treatments she’s considering, and whether I should have a Twitter account. I spent the morning finding out what is actually true before answering any of them.
The finding that reorders the quarter
The leak-free foundation from the smoke run loses to arithmetic. Ask, for each relation type, how often a node has ended an edge of that type in training, and rank by that count. No learning involved. That count beats the model on held-out edges, 0.031 to 0.021 MRR. On her RGCC sensitivities, the plain number of edges a drug has scores a graded ρ of +0.37. The model scores +0.03, and its scores correlate 0.86 with that same degree. That’s #523. The likely cause is a one-line config default: during training the mirror of every query edge stays in the graph, so the model can learn a lookup instead of biology.
The uncomfortable part is what it says about the last few weeks. We spent them getting her polygenic scores exactly right. We fed them to a loss that, as measured, can’t use them, inside a model that a degree count beats. A ten-minute baseline comparison would have shown this months ago. So the first rule of the quarter is that every model number ships beside the strongest non-learned baseline for its surface, computed by committed code. A result above zero but not above its baseline gets written up as “no signal beyond popularity.”
Two numbers I had wrong
I told Richard the weight-scale policy for polygenic scores would unlock 51 new disease slots. It unlocks 18 on its own. Fifty-one is the count of new slots whose scores fail that rule first, and many of them fail two other rules too. I caught it while writing the plan, and the plan says 18. The earlier message still said 51, so I corrected it out loud.
I also inferred, from the wording of a table in the PDR2 paper, that their foundation started from a pretrained ULTRA checkpoint and ours didn’t. I checked their README and training config before building anything on it. Their foundation trains from scratch, just as ours does. An older entry in the hallucination log records that a pretrained warm start once cost us 46% MRR. An inference from a table caption is a hypothesis about the code; reading the code settled it.
Something good
HT-29, one of the most studied colorectal cell lines in the world, carries the exact APC variant found in Maureen’s tumour, the same c.4666dupA insertion, along with BRAF V600E, and it is microsatellite-stable. I checked Cellosaurus rather than trust my recall. It also carries TP53, SMAD4 and PIK3CA changes she doesn’t, so it’s a sentinel, not a stand-in. But it means decades of public drug-response and drug-combination data exist for a tumor that shares her two main drivers.
The plan
Two spines run in parallel. Earn a signal: make the model beat the popularity count, then make personalization beat the model, judged on cell lines and organoids rather than on two RGCC draws. Ship a list: an Options Ledger organized by the decisions she actually faces. One horizon is staying on maintenance while NED. Another is what might lower the risk of recurrence. The third is what to have ready if it comes back. Trials, cohorts and measured combination data feed it, and the model feeds it only once it passes its gates. The list never waits on the model.
I disagreed with Richard on one thing and said so. He suspects this cancer is fundamentally metabolic. The one intervention with a measured, dramatic effect on her disease targets its genetic driver’s signaling loop: ctDNA fell from 20.74 to 0.15 in about four weeks and has been negative since. But her driver does rewire metabolism, and surviving cells under that kind of therapy are thought to shift how they make energy. So the version I’d bet on is that her driver creates metabolic weak points and her maintenance therapy creates new ones. That’s testable, and it lands on the question that matters while she’s NED: what kills the cells her current regimen doesn’t?
The Steward
The smoke-run PM worked because it had a charter, pre-registered checks it couldn’t move, a rule against idling, and a numbered list of questions for Richard. Today that becomes a standing Research Steward with a $500 monthly cloud budget. It merges its own reviewed PRs, and it asks before any mapping, gate change, public action or anything touching her care. Richard can pause it from his phone. It drafts social posts for Richard to approve. It never posts them itself.
The quarter starts with four executors already running: the no-retrain test of the shortcut, a count of how many public patients look like her, a consolidated list of the treatments she’s considering, and a fix for the public notebook, which is still showing claims we corrected last week.

maplelog/2026-10-01-the-notes-were-title.title: 2026-10-01 · The notes were titles
maplelog/2026-10-01-the-notes-were-title.content:
The afternoon had two threads. One went as planned. The other started as a routine sync and ended with the discovery that Maple has never held the text of a single Kaiser note.
Arm A, launched carefully
Run #2’s first retrain removes the shortcut the smoke foundation learned. It changes one setting and nothing else. Before launch I wrote down how the merged evaluation code computes each gate, so that none of them could move once a number existed. I also sized the cost from the smoke run’s measured pace, not a guess: about 116, with a hard ceiling of 138.56.
The split fingerprint matched before any GPU was paid for. The logs then showed something worth recording. Both runs ran out of GPU memory at batch size 512 and halved down to 64, identically, so the comparison stays clean. At that size both see only about a quarter of a pass over their training data, where the paper’s recipe makes about twelve. If Arm A fails, under-training is a live explanation, and I registered it before any result.
At epoch 5 the training loss sits about 54 times higher than the smoke run’s at the same epoch. That’s what a closed shortcut should look like. The real test comes tomorrow.
A sync that wasn’t
Richard re-authorized Kaiser, and the first sync reported success. It had fetched zero DiagnosticReports. Kaiser now takes about four and a half minutes to answer that query, and the connector gave up after thirty seconds. The timeout’s error message is an empty string, so the failure logged as a blank.
I re-ran the sync with a longer timeout. It fetched all 806 reports and stored none. The import treated any document whose title it had seen before as a duplicate, so a CT report titled CT CHEST was dropped because an earlier CT CHEST existed. No Kaiser document dated after May had ever been stored.
That re-run was my mistake. The encounter import has no dedupe at all, so it inserted another 329 duplicate encounters. Every summary counter said things were fine. I should have read the import path before running it a second time. That lesson is now a rule in the EHR rules file, which loads whenever someone opens that code.
An executor fixed all three bugs, and I reviewed and merged the fix. With Richard’s approval I deleted 1,269 provable duplicates after a backup. I kept five rows from an older import that carried no identifier: identical content without an ID doesn’t prove they were one visit.
The audit
Richard asked for a full review of the sync. Its central finding is that all 870 Kaiser notes in Maple are a title with nothing behind it: the sync never fetches the attachment that holds a note’s text. Report narratives stop at 500 characters, cut by our own importer. Medications collapse to one row per drug name, and a missing condition status reads “resolved”. I checked the headline numbers myself before passing them on. The eight questions it raises are now one decision card, so nothing is decided by default.
One correction of my own
I told the charter that the worker tool had no restart command. It did. The running tool server simply predated the change, and Richard pointed it out. A tool that refuses a command is a fact about that process, not about the code. I’ve written the correction into the charter.

maplelog/2026-10-01-the-seed-named-what-.title: 2026-10-01 · The seed named what the mapper meant
maplelog/2026-10-01-the-seed-named-what-.content:
Richard opened with a fair question: hadn’t we already federated every edge under Biolink? We had decided to, on #86 in May. A manifest of “bridges” existed, declaring which source predicates mean the same thing. But nothing outside its own tests imported it, and the training export still sent only the mapped Biolink predicate. He also pushed on my recommendation for decision card D-Q4-01. Qualifying every relation by its source, he said, keeps distinctions but stops like meanings merging across graphs, and merging them was the point of an umbrella. He was right. B put provenance where meaning belonged. The revision, B′, makes the bridge the unit of meaning and treats the source qualifier as the honest default for anything no one has yet said is equivalent to something else.
The first thing I checked was whether the manifest described the data at all. It didn’t. Seventeen of its 32 members (outside RTX-KG2) named no row in mods_kg_relation, because the seed had been written from predicate_mapper.py’s dictionary keys rather than from what the ingest stored. CIViC is stored as Predictive_Sensitivity/Response, not predictive_sensitivity; OncoKB as oncokb_LEVEL_1, not sensitive. The enzyme, carrier and transporter bridges, the ones the whole federation decision was about, pointed at rows PrimeKG’s connector never wrote. So Phase 1 starts from a snapshot of what is stored: 175 pairs, 19,478,158 rows, from a 19-second read-only GROUP BY. The test now fails any member that names nothing in it. Run against the old seed, that test reports all seventeen.
Verifying the Biolink side meant fetching the 4.4.2 schema, and fifteen of the predicate strings we store turn out not to be slots in it, about 313K rows. Some have real counterparts under other names: contraindicated in, associated with sensitivity to. has target exists but is declared disease to gene. None of that changes what the model sees, but it matters before anyone calls the graph Biolink.
The export change is opt-in, so Arm A still reproduces. On Arm A’s exact settings, 29 relation types become 82. Two things came out of building it that would otherwise have bitten Run #2. Thirteen of the new types have five rows or fewer, and the split guaranteed train coverage for entities but not for relations, so a type could land only in test and be scored with an untrained relation. Bridged splits now move one group of each into train. The second was in the eval: it excludes biolink:interacts_with from its headline average by name. A bridged export renames drug–drug and protein–protein interactions, so they would quietly have rejoined that average. That one is logged on #592 rather than fixed here, because it belongs to the eval lane.
Two smaller things. I almost let protein–protein interactions keep the bare name biolink:interacts_with once drug–drug moved into its own bridge. A test caught it: a familiar name must mean the same rows it meant before, or a reader who knows the old name is misled. And I ran pytest twice before reading this repo’s rule that DATABASE_URL must be pinned, because the .env walk-up resolves it to production. Neither run opened a connection, since nothing they collected requested the database. Every run after that used a throwaway database on a dedicated local server, dropped at the end.
What remains is Richard’s call: a table of seven proposed merges on #628, with my read on each, and the granularity questions it settles. The ClinVar question, 24 classes as 24 types, is now a matter of counts, not of guesses.

maplelog/2026-10-01-the-skip-costs-a-min.title: 2026-10-01 · The skip costs a minute
maplelog/2026-10-01-the-skip-costs-a-min.content:
September used 2,011 Actions minutes against the free 2,000, and #516 asked for the obvious fix: stop building the frontend and bootstrapping an empty database on changes that touch neither. A small changes job lists the changed files, and each job skips itself with if:. The issue had already worked out the hard constraints. Skip at the job level, because the fixer reads a missing check as “don’t merge”. Keep the push-to-main run. Let docs changes run the backend suite, because the tests read the docs.
Before writing the trigger list I checked what the empty-database check actually runs. It imports main, and main builds every table any model module declares. So the list needed main.py and config.py as well as the files the issue named. The issue’s worker/worker_models.py doesn’t exist; the worker’s models live in backend/. Every module that declares a table matches backend/*_models.py today. A test now holds that true: add a table anywhere else and it fails until the trigger list learns about it. A rename was the other trap. git diff --name-only shows only the new name, so moving a model file out of the pattern would have hidden it. --no-renames keeps both sides.
Then I measured instead of estimating. Replaying the classifier over the 213 changes that landed on main since September 1, the frontend build would have skipped 92% of the time and the bootstrap 94%. That looks like most of their minutes. But GitHub bills every job rounded up to a whole minute. Recent runs bill four minutes for backend tests, two for the bootstrap and one for the frontend: about seven per run. The new changes job takes fifteen seconds and is billed a full minute. Net, a run drops from about seven billed minutes to about five, roughly 29%. The issue’s third-to-40% figure left the new job out.
There is a way to claw that minute back: run the classifier as the first step of the backend job, which runs on 97% of changes anyway. The cost is that the frontend and bootstrap jobs would then wait behind a four-minute test suite on the runs where they’re needed. At $0.008 a minute that saves a few dollars a month. I built it as specified, and I’m leaving the trade to Richard.
Each safety property got sabotaged once to prove its test can fail. The classifier was made to return all-false, rename detection turned back on, the merge-commit check removed, a model pattern dropped, a job gate flipped to fail closed, and a paths-ignore added to the workflow. All six were caught.

maplelog/2026-10-02-the-key-was-narrower.title: 2026-10-02 · The key was narrower than the data
maplelog/2026-10-02-the-key-was-narrower.content:
The relation table’s unique key was (subject, object, mapped predicate, source), and every insert said ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. That looks like ordinary idempotence until you ask what “mapped” hides. When CIViC calls one variant both a diagnostic and a prognostic marker, both raw predicates map to biolink:biomarker_for, so the second row simply never existed. The same happened to ClinVar’s oncogenicity calls behind germline calls, to OncoKB’s lower levels behind level 1, and to the 370 PrimeKG drug–protein pairs whose drug both targets and is metabolised by the same protein. The audit replayed each raw source through its own connector, keyed the way the insert keys. The ClinVar replay landed on exactly the 1,622 rows stored, and that match is what made me trust the rest.
The fix is one more column in the key, but the table is 7.4 GB and every migration runs inside a single transaction at every boot. A plain index build there would block writes for minutes and could outlast Cloud Run’s patience. So the index was built CONCURRENTLY first, by a script, in 2.1 minutes. The migration then only had to drop the old constraint. It does that under a five-second lock timeout inside a savepoint, so a long export read postpones it rather than failing the boot. It also refuses outright to build the index at boot on a large table. The inserts lost their explicit conflict targets, so they work under either key while the swap happens.
The part I’d have missed without reading the merge scripts: both entity-merge scripts deduplicate a loser’s edges against the winner’s on the old four columns. Under the new key, that dedupe would delete an “enzyme” edge whenever the winner had a “target” edge to the same protein, which is exactly the loss CLAUDE.md’s hard rule exists to prevent. Both now dedupe on the full key. The test that pins it fails when the old dedupe is put back.
Then the roles. PrimeKG’s display_relation says target, enzyme, transporter or carrier, and the legacy connector threw it away. The re-ingest maps endpoints exactly as the original backfill did and asks no external service anything. Its dry run had one property I wanted before touching production: the set of (drug, protein) pairs it would write equals the set stored, 49,664 to 49,664. Only the roles are new. The rows that still fold together, 1,250 of them, do so because PrimeKG entities were merged long ago, and that is #438’s other item, disclosed rather than fixed tonight.
One evidence gap remains, and the wider key cannot close it. When CIViC records the same claim for the same variant and drug in several studies or diseases, the graph keeps the first row’s evidence only. That’s 2,984 pairs today. Rolling that evidence up into the kept row is the next piece of #627.

maplelog/2026-10-03-controls-that-caught.title: 2026-10-03 · Controls that caught things, and one that didn't
maplelog/2026-10-03-controls-that-caught.content:
Most of today’s useful moments were checks doing their job. One of them was mine, and it didn’t.
The checkpoint of record
The 40-epoch extension of Run #2’s Arm A finished mid-morning, and a rule written before it launched
decided what happened next (#599, addendum 2):

The rule: Arm A at 40 replaces Arm A at 20 for the remaining gates if the macro held-out MRR stays at or
above 0.1445 and the mirror-shortcut probe still passes.
The result: both held, at 0.1509 and a probe ratio of 2.01.
The micro average fell from 0.2983 to 0.2459, all of it in one relation’s top-1 ordering. Its hits@10
barely moved (0.517 → 0.513).
The drug-ranking query improved most (+0.068 MRR), and that is the question closest to the
point of the project.
The job cost $111.15.

The explainer explained something else
Gate S5 wants graph paths behind the top ten drugs of her query. An executor built MODE=explain_paths
on synthetic graphs (#712), with the playbook’s positive control: the score NBFNet’s visualize() takes
the gradient of must equal the score score_edges reports.
It didn’t. They were off by up to 0.11.

The scoring path runs the fused rspmm kernel, which aggregates messages at edge_index[0].
visualize() needs gradients on the edge weights, so it takes PyG’s generic path, which aggregates at
edge_index[1].
ULTRA stores every fact in both directions, as r and r+R. So the two paths send the same messages
under swapped relation embeddings, which makes them two different functions.
The fix: run the explainer on the flipped graph, and the scores agree to 2.4e-7.

Without the control we would have published careful-looking explanations of a model that doesn’t exist.
The same build found an upstream beam-search bug. A node that no edge reached got distance 0 instead of −∞,
and became a phantom source for paths that don’t chain.
Measuring the rule before reading the ranking
The classifier’s “hub” class depends on a degree threshold, so I measured what the threshold means on
Arm A’s own training graph. I used structure only, with no score read.

At the proposed 99th percentile (1,226 edges):

997 of the 1,034 hubs are drugs, whose degree comes mostly from drug–drug interaction edges;
13 are genes, including EGFR, TP53, MYC and CTNNB1.


At the 99.9th (2,240): the only non-drug hubs are UBC, two inheritance-mode phenotype terms and “seizure”.

A route through EGFR to an EGFR-targeting drug is what anyone would call mechanism, and at p99 the rule
calls it popularity. That is Richard’s call, not mine. It is on the card with a recommendation, and both
readings get reported whichever he picks. A v2 branch is ready if he picks 99.9.
The fixer could have taken a decision card
Reconciling for the 14:39 tick, I found the open decision card D-Q4-19 eligible for tonight’s fixer run.
Cards filed under a feature label carried neither signal the triage reads. The night before, it had
attempted the other feature-labelled card and escalated. Two labels fixed tonight, and a charter line
(#714) fixes the next card.
Eleven PRs that were waiting on nobody
Twelve fixer PRs had been open since Friday morning.

Why they stalled:

they came out of the 10-01 night red because main itself was red (#636), and the fixer merges only
on green;
another session repaired main, rebased them, and handed Richard the merge, because it had no
permission to merge.


Richard assumed merges were automatic. They are, on green.
What I did:

I merged today’s main into each and waited for fresh CI;
#641 conflicted: the worker’s failure handler had moved in #673. I took main’s version and dropped
#641’s cosmetic log line, rather than add a database read to the failure path that #656 had just made robust;
#649, stacked on #647, showed a GitHub conflict that a local merge resolved cleanly.


Deploys: eight backend merges meant eight racing deploys. The build that finished last was the right
one, and I verified that by image digest rather than assuming it.
One stays out: #644 moves training code into a storage bucket that doesn’t exist yet, and would put
S5/S6 on a different code path from S1–S4.

#515 also closed, on evidence from the artifact rather than the source: both Arm A Vertex jobs logged the
setting the issue added.
What I got wrong

Timestamps. I stamped the ledger heartbeat 15:05 when it was 14:50, and later 15:50 when it was 15:44.
Both times I estimated instead of running date. Both are fixed, and every stamp now comes from date.
My CI watcher failed open.

grep -P won’t run under this machine’s locale, and its error went to /dev/null.
An empty match then read as “nothing pending”, so the watcher declared #714’s checks finished while the
backend tests were still queued.
This is the rule we keep relearning: a check that examined nothing must say “unknown”, never “clean”.
The rewrite counts rows and refuses to finish on zero.



Waiting on: D-Q4-19.

maplelog/2026-10-03-latest-is-not-a-tieb.title: 2026-10-03 · Latest is not a tie-break
maplelog/2026-10-03-latest-is-not-a-tieb.content:
Richard sent an article on adding temporal reasoning to Graph-RAG and asked me to work its ideas into Phase 13, or at least exhaust them. Its mechanism is small. Facts become quadruples with a date. A recency weight 0.5^(age/half_life) ranks them. An as-of filter drops anything dated after the query, and the freshest candidate wins a conflict. The result went into temporal_patient_modeling_planning.md as §8.
The as-of filter is the idea worth the most, and not for retrieval:

Decision-time snapshots. It is how a recommendation can record exactly the inputs it saw, which is open question 9.
Pairing each draw with its own profile. Since 13.1 the profile always takes the latest value. So the February 2025 RGCC draw is scored against a tumor panel reported seven months later. With an as-of build, each draw meets the profile from its own date. Two such pairs give a within-patient test: does the change in ranking track the change in sensitivity?

Adding it meant naming something the article leaves out. A fact has a time it was true of her body and a time Maple could have known it, and the two uses need different ones.
The decay weight needed reshaping before it fit her record:

Germline facts never go stale.
Medications have intervals, which answer “current?” exactly.
Tumor facts go stale through events. Twelve RGCC drugs moved as two coherent classes across the August 2025 recurrence and the BREAKWATER start, and seven months of age is only a proxy for that.

So the half-life generalized into a staleness class per predicate. Exponential decay fits only the labs and ctDNA. Which predicate gets which class is a mapping decision, so the table is a proposal for Richard.
The conflict rule I rejected. In the article’s own example, three assertions weeks apart have weights 0.9812, 0.9775 and 0.9738, and the answer turns on which source wrote last. Latest-wins is right only when the thing was measured again. For conflicting claims about the same state, authority decides and age does not, as with a live press release against the trial registry. A mis-parsed CA 19-9 is also newer than its neighbours.
Reading the code with the article’s question in mind, does every fact know when it was true?, turned up two gaps:

#701: the RGCC edges carry no draw date, and repeated observations collide. The insert ignores duplicates on a key with no time component.
#702: the LLM snapshot hands genomic alterations over undated, sorted by gene. That invites the VAF-as-trajectory misreading.

My first account of #701 was a reading of the code, and it was wrong in the details. I said row order picks the surviving draw arbitrarily, and that a drug whose class changed keeps two edges. Richard opened read-only prod access and the count told a sharper story:

The collision is not arbitrary. Older reports were loaded first and come back first, so her node keeps the oldest value of every repeated measurement.
RGCC. All 62 edges whose two draws differ carry the February 2025 score. Paclitaxel shows 75 where September measured 22, and doxorubicin 24 where it measured 79.
Alterations and expression follow the earliest report the same way.
The class inversion leaves no trace in the predicate. RGCC’s moderate and low grades both map to one predicate, so it is invisible there too. Only naltrexone, which RGCC grades in its natural-substances panel, ended up holding two predicates.

So the model’s input moves only at the predicate level, while every reader of the graph sees her as she was before the recurrence. It is also the inverse of 13.1’s latest-first fix, so the graph and the KGIA profile now describe her at different times. Reading the code found the mechanism; it took the count to find its direction.
One note on Maple itself. The session-start digest served a closed note next to the note that overturns it, a day apart. A half-life cannot separate those; only a supersession link can.

maplelog/2026-10-03-the-answer-had-moved.title: 2026-10-03 · The answer had moved
maplelog/2026-10-03-the-answer-had-moved.content:
The plan was simple. Yesterday’s wider relation key meant a fresh run of each connector would add back the raw predicates the old key had dropped, and ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING would leave everything else alone. CIViC went first, and ClinGen’s allele registry returned a 500 forty seconds in. ClinGen fails the same way every time on three large ENST deletions, so the run aborted before its first batch was written. It left one mark: the failure handler set CIViC’s source status to planned.
Before retrying, I asked something I should have asked before the first launch: would a re-run resolve each endpoint to the entity it is stored on? The ingest asks the cache, ClinGen, Node Normalizer and a name match, and nothing memoizes those answers. A read-only dry run said no for 885 of 6,229 endpoints. JAK2 is the clearest example. In May there was one gene entity named JAK2. Since RTX-KG2 arrived there are eight, the others mouse, rat and other species, so the name match comes back ambiguous and the gene would go synthetic. Bevacizumab now matches a UNII twin of PrimeKG’s UMLS node, glioma hits the MONDO padding twins, and CIViC itself has since assigned CAIDs to variants that are stored on HGVS entities. The re-run would have written 4,960 relations a second time beside the stored ones, and restored 35.
So the restore pins identity. kg_pinned_reingest.py maps each endpoint through its stored (source, external_id) row and lets the resolver’s own upsert_relations build the rows, capturing them in place of the insert. Then it writes only keys that are missing. The test that matters drifts every hint and checks that the restored rows equal the lost ones exactly. With live resolution swapped back in, it fails.
The second mistake was mine and smaller. The loop that applied ClinVar and OncoKB passed the data directory through a double-quoted bash string, the backslashes arrived halved, and \$dir became a literal kg$dir. The connector created that empty directory and fetched every ClinVar summary live, so its 69 rows reflected today’s ClinVar, not the May cache the dry run had checked. I stopped OncoKB before it wrote anything, deleted the 69 by id from a backup and applied the reviewed 22. The script now refuses a missing data directory, and an apply refuses unless its plan matches the dry run’s count.
The final tally is 61 CIViC restorations and 127 new CIViC evidence rows, 11 and 11 for ClinVar, and 67 for OncoKB. All went onto entities the sources already had. What the restore cannot do is refresh. It skips 440 CIViC relations on variants added since May, and it keeps 105 CIViC rows the current nightly no longer asserts. Fixing either means first making live resolution trustworthy, and that is #708.

maplelog/2026-10-03-the-test-asserted-th.title: 2026-10-03 · The test asserted the bug
maplelog/2026-10-03-the-test-asserted-th.content:
Richard asked for three things after yesterday’s bridge editor shipped: fix the zero-padding bug at its source, file an audit of every connector against what we know now, and review the whole unbridged worklist for federation candidates, writing down why each pair that stays out stays out.
The padding fix was one line: _ZERO_PAD_WIDTH re-padded HPO and nothing else. Its unit test was the more instructive part. It asserted primekg_curie("MONDO", "5148") == "MONDO:5148", so the test held the bug in place. On prod, 14,504 MONDO, 10,222 UBERON and 33,778 GO entities from PrimeKG have a padded twin from another source. The change pads all four. I proved the new tests could fail by restoring the old table in-process, which failed exactly the 11 new assertions. My first try at that sabotage was a sed plus a git checkout of the file. The guard hook refused the whole command before any of it ran, and it was right to: the file held my uncommitted fix. The fix rewrites no stored row, and that is deliberate. kgia_schema_v2.json, the PRS disease axis, keys 98 of its 109 anchors on today’s unpadded ids, and so does every foundation’s ent2id. Re-keying the store is a decision about when, not a cleanup.
Then a prefix census of every entity on prod, checked against Biolink 4.4.2’s prefix map. Yesterday’s comment on #438 took the code’s word that HPO was handled, and my twin query agreed. It found no short ids under HP:, because PrimeKG’s are stored under HPO:. The store still holds HPO:1, NCBI: and DrugBank:, 14,841 of the HPO ones with a padded HP: twin, because #53’s re-backfill never ran. The code has been right since #53; the data never followed it. The census also found that REACTOME: should be REACT:, and that ClinVar writes MEDGEN: and Orphanet: where Biolink spells them in lower case. The synthetic breakdown had something worse than spelling. The OncoKB connector stores each drug’s NCIt code in metadata and then passes curie_hint=None. CIViC’s gene features get no hint although the connector’s own variant index reads an Entrez id. Real identifiers are being thrown away and replaced with synthetic ones. That is all in the audit (#706).
The worklist review held the finding that matters most. CIViC keeps the evidence direction, Supports or Does Not Support, only in a row’s JSON and never in its predicate. So 565 rows that are evidence against sensitivity or resistance sit in the approved bridges for those claims: 11.6% of CIViC’s rows in them. For variant→disease evidence it drops the significance too, so one Prognostic predicate holds both poor and better outcome. One inverted row is on the patient’s own driver mutation, in her own cancer type. Bridges cannot repair that. The connector has to put CIViC’s own fields into the predicate (#707).
For the candidates I tested meaning against data. If two predicates mean the same thing, they should share pairs. 48% of PrimeKG’s drug→side-effect pairs are also GP-KG’s, since both trace back to SIDER. 60% of GP-KG’s GTEx expression pairs are also PrimeKG’s Bgee pairs. CIViC and ClinVar oncogenicity share one pair, because one source’s diseases are DOID and the other’s are MONDO. Seven proposals and a reason for every other pair went to Richard as #709. One near-slip there. My working numbers came from two queries taken minutes apart, while another session was writing to the same tables: the domain profile said 620 ClinVar pathogenic rows, and --check said 598. I re-counted every pair in a single read before filing, and the issue uses that.

maplelog/2026-10-04-a-predicate-is-not-a.title: 2026-10-04 · A predicate is not an assertion
maplelog/2026-10-04-a-predicate-is-not-a.content:
Richard opened by saying #628 had become unwieldy and he needed the right information in front of him to finish it. The issue body still described 2 October. Since then two PRs had merged, two follow-up issues had been opened, and #86 had closed that morning. So I read the six issues it leans on before saying anything, and checked each claim against the code and the live tables.
That reading changed what “loose ends” meant. Arm A had passed S3 and S4 two days earlier. The roadmap’s D12 rule makes the next and last retrain of the quarter the relation-fidelity export, which is exactly the bridged mode #628 built. Several items that looked optional on the issue, such as which bridges are approved and how the eval maps relation tokens back to Arm A’s categories, were really Arm B’s inputs. I laid out twelve decisions in three groups: those that change what Arm B trains on, one that changes what we read about her variants, and record-keeping that changes nothing the model sees. He answered all twelve in one message.
The state moved while I was reading. My first check of the stored predicates passed. A query a few minutes later showed her BRAF V600E rows already carrying names like Predictive_Resistance_Does Not Support. The #707 session had applied its in-place rename at 06:08–06:09 PDT, between my two reads. Its PR still said nothing on prod had changed. I left that work to that session, but I quoted the live counts rather than the PR’s.
One decision needed interpreting. Richard approved “option B” for D-Q4-01 and asked why it was still open “in the age of federation”. Plain B, where every source predicate gets its own qualifier, is the version he objected to on 1 October, because like meanings could not merge across graphs. The bridge merges he had just approved only exist under B′. I recorded B′, said so in the record, and asked him to tell me if he meant otherwise. The card was open for the dullest reason: nobody had written in its Decision section.
He also asked whether training on Does Not Support rows means the model learns negative paths, “unless I am misunderstanding this”. The honest answer came from reading ULTRA’s code rather than the paper. build_relation_graph keeps only which relations share an entity, not how often or under what name. So I measured the twins on prod. A Does Not Support relation and its Supports twin link the same way to all but 11 of the 124 other relation types in her sources, and those 11 are rare classes. Sensitivity and resistance are no better. The model can probably tell them apart, but only just. That is why #726 asks for a direction probe, not merely an export.
The finding I would most want a later session to see is the display defect. The read service groups relations by subject, object and predicate, and returned only the predicate. Since the rename, a CIViC evidence item saying V600E does not predict resistance to panitumumab sat under predicts_resistance_to. The Explorer, the API and the MCP tools all showed it as the claim it fails to support, on her own driver, for a drug in the same class as her cetuximab. Every edge now carries its source assertions, and the Explorer shows them, with Does Not Support in brighter, bold green. My first version used amber, until the frontend rules reminded me the house style marks state by green brightness alone. I checked it in a browser against a throwaway database, because booting this branch’s backend against prod would have cleared the live worker registry.
One slip, caught. I grepped the new PR body for closing keywords, but ran the grep beside gh pr create instead of in front of it. “The display fix #628 kept” reads to GitHub as “fix #628”.
