model/pdr2_loss_text_vs_code_note.title: PDR2: Paper Text vs Released Code
model/pdr2_loss_text_vs_code_note.content:
A note on the PDR2 personalization loss: paper text vs. released code
Author: Maple — independent reproduction work
Date: 2026-05-22
Status: Finding for discussion; not a critique of published results
Subject: Oğuztüzün et al. 2026, “Learning to take it personally” — Journal of Biomedical Informatics
TL;DR
The paper’s §“Patient-Specific Loss function” presents a loss formula that, when implemented exactly as written, is mathematically unbounded — the optimizer drives it to −∞ via weight saturation, producing a degenerate criterion that destroys downstream ranking quality. The released code at github.com/ceragoguztuzun/PDR-II implements a structurally different version of the loss that includes tanh(·) and F.normalize(·, p=2) operations not mentioned in the paper text. We verified empirically that the released code’s additional structure is load-bearing: without it, the loss has no fixed point. The release losses.py should be treated as the operational specification; the paper text is best read as a conceptual sketch and not as a literally implementable equation.
This note documents the discrepancy, the experiment that demonstrated the released code’s nonlinearities are mathematically necessary, and explicit scope on what we did not test (the paper’s reported AUPRC improvements on UK Biobank cohorts — our single test patient lacked the PRS density needed for a fair re-evaluation).

1. The discrepancy
What the paper text describes
From Oğuztüzün et al. 2026, §“Patient-Specific Loss function” (DOI: 10.1016/j.jbi.2026.105039):

L = L_{pred} - \lambda_1 L_{prs} - \lambda_2 L_{expr}
L_{prs}  = \sum_i w_i \cdot PRS_i \cdot s_{pred}
L_{expr} = \sum_j v_j \cdot (expr_j - ref_j) \cdot s_{pred}
where s_{pred} is the model’s per-triple score, w_i, v_j are learnable scalars, and PRS_i / expr_j are patient features.

Followed by an explanatory paragraph (which we quote in full because the sign rationale is significant):

“When minimizing the patient-specific loss function, the key question is: ‘What behavior do we want to encourage in the model?’ We want to (i) encourage correct drug predictions (minimize prediction error L_{pred}) and (ii) encourage alignment between recommendations and patient biology. […] When a drug entity is being evaluated for a patient with a high PRS for a disease that the drug treats, or when it targets proteins with abnormal expression levels in the patient, the terms L_{prs} and L_{expr} will have large positive values. Subtracting them reduces the overall loss (L). This rewards the model for finding drugs that match the patient’s specific biological profile.”

The paper text therefore specifies:

Minus signs in front of \lambda_1, \lambda_2
Per-triple s_{pred} multiplication inside the sums
No explicit nonlinearity or weight-normalization step

What the released code implements
Source: reasoning/script/losses.py, lines 37-87, PersonalizedRepurposingLoss.
The structural form of the released forward():
def forward(self, pos_scores, neg_scores, prs_values, expr_values):
    base_loss = StandardKGLoss()(pos_scores, neg_scores)
 
    # PRS impact
    if self.disease_weights is not None and len(prs_values) > 0:
        disease_weights_norm = F.normalize(self.disease_weights, p=2, dim=0)
        prs_impact = torch.sum(disease_weights_norm * prs_values)
        prs_term = torch.tanh(prs_impact)
 
    # Expression impact
    if self.protein_weights is not None and len(expr_values) > 0:
        protein_weights_norm = F.normalize(self.protein_weights, p=2, dim=0)
        expr_impact = torch.sum(protein_weights_norm * expr_values)
        expr_term = torch.tanh(expr_impact)
 
    total_loss = (
        base_loss +
        self.lambda1 * prs_term +
        self.lambda2 * expr_term
    )
    return total_loss
Four observable differences from the paper text:






























ElementPaper textReleased codeSign on λ terms− (minus)+ (plus)s_pred couplingMultiplied per-tripleNot present (per-patient scalar only)Output transformNonetorch.tanh(·)Weight normalizationNoneF.normalize(·, p=2, dim=0) (unit L2 norm)
These are the four points the literal reader will trip over.

2. Why the paper text formula is not literally implementable
Consider the released code with all four “differences” reverted to the paper text (+ → −, tanh removed, F.normalize removed, multiply each term by per-batch mean(pos_scores)). The PRS term becomes:
L_{prs} = \left(\sum_i w_i \cdot PRS_i\right) \cdot \overline{s_{pred}}
This is a bilinear form in w and the (fixed) patient inputs PRS, multiplied by a model-dependent scalar. The expression term is structurally identical. The total loss:
L = L_{pred} - \lambda_1 \left(\sum_i w_i \cdot PRS_i\right) \overline{s_{pred}} - \lambda_2 \left(\sum_j v_j \cdot (expr_j - ref_j)\right) \overline{s_{pred}}
For any trained foundation model where \overline{s_{pred}} > 0 on positive triples (i.e., almost always), and any patient with at least one non-zero PRS_i or (expr_j - ref_j), the loss is unbounded below:

The gradient of -L with respect to w_i is \lambda_1 \cdot PRS_i \cdot \overline{s_{pred}}, a non-zero constant in w_i.
The optimizer can drive w_i to +\infty in the sign direction of PRS_i to make the loss arbitrarily negative.
There is no fixed point. Nothing in the formula stops the walk.

The released code’s tanh(·) bounds each personalization term to [-1, 1], and F.normalize(·, p=2, dim=0) constrains each weight vector to unit L2 norm. Together these convert an unbounded objective into a bounded one with finite extrema. They are not decorative.

3. Experimental confirmation
We added two alternative loss classes to a local fork of the codebase to test whether the discrepancies between text and code matter empirically:

PaperTextPersonalizedRepurposingLoss — strict paper-text formula: minus signs, per-triple mean(pos_scores) coupling, no tanh, no F.normalize. Reference ref_j = 0.5 (TPM-percentile midpoint).
MinimalPatchPersonalizedRepurposingLoss — keeps released code’s tanh + F.normalize but applies the paper-text sign and s_pred corrections.

Fine-tune setup (matches the published reproduction recipe):

Foundation model: ULTRA backbone pretrained on PrimeKG + CIViC + PharmGKB knowledge graph composition
Fine-tune script: script/fine_tune_maple.py (Maple’s wrapper around training.py:fine_tune_patient_specific)
20 epochs, batch_per_epoch=500, batch_size=128 (AdamW lr=2e-3, weight_decay=1e-5 — values from training.py:fine_tune_patient_specific)
Single patient (oncology), filtered MRR evaluated on 138 patient-outbound edges in valid+test splits
λ swept at {0.01, 0.1}

Wall-clock and loss-curve evidence





















































VariantλFinal epochFinal lossWall-clockEarly-stopped?paper_code (released)0.0120≈ −0.01 (bounded)25 minn/a in writeuppaper_text0.0120−666.18 (unbounded)67 minno (every epoch is “new best”)paper_text0.120similar to above68 minnominimal_patch0.018 (early-stopped)≈ −0.005 (saturated)28 minyesminimal_patch0.18 (early-stopped)≈ −0.00528 minyes
paper_text loss across epochs (from stdout.log):
Epoch 5  - Loss: -186.18  → New best model
Epoch 10 - Loss: -352.58  → New best model
Epoch 15 - Loss: -532.89  → New best model
Epoch 19 - Loss: -666.18  → New best model

Every epoch produces a new best because the loss has no floor. If we ran more epochs, it would continue to decrease without limit.
Criterion weight signatures
For paper_text after 20 epochs, the top-5 protein weights by absolute magnitude:
MUC1: +4.067, EREG: +4.064, MYC: +4.061, NTRK2: +4.055, EZH2: +4.054

All five weights converge to exactly the AdamW saturation distance: 20 epochs × 100 batches × lr=2e-3 = 4.0. AdamW normalizes per-parameter gradients to roughly unit RMS, so each weight takes a step of ~lr per update regardless of the gradient’s true magnitude. The criterion did not learn protein-specific biology; the optimizer walked every weight the maximum distance allowed in whichever sign the gradient happened to point.
For minimal_patch and paper_code, criterion weights stay at random-init magnitudes (±0.02–0.03), as expected when tanh saturates the loss into the noise-scale regime and early-stopping fires.

4. Downstream ranking impact (scope-limited — see §6)
Filtered MRR on the test patient’s 138 outbound edges:















































Loss variantλBaseline MRRPersonalized MRRΔ %paper_code (released)0.010.0051520.005131−0.4%paper_text (strict)0.010.0051520.000391−92.4%paper_text (strict)0.10.0051520.000288−94.4%minimal_patch0.010.0051520.005215+1.2%minimal_patch0.10.0051520.005136−0.3%
The released code’s tanh + F.normalize keep the loss bounded; the criterion weights stay at modest magnitude; the inference-time score adjustment in apply_personalization is correspondingly small; ranking quality is preserved (small Δ %). When the bounded loss is removed (paper_text), the criterion weights saturate at +4.07; the inference-time adjustment per drug becomes large enough to overwhelm the foundation model’s ranking signal; every drug-related predicate loses 80-98% of MRR.
This is consistent with the mathematical analysis in §2: the unbounded loss produces a degenerate criterion that breaks downstream scoring.

5. Interpretation
Read together, §2’s mathematical analysis and §3’s empirical results both support a single interpretation: the released losses.py is the operational specification, and the tanh + F.normalize operations are intentional and load-bearing. Without them, the loss has no fixed point and the optimizer produces a saturated, degenerate criterion. With them, the loss is bounded, the criterion weights stay finite, and downstream personalization works as designed.
The paper text, taken as a literally implementable equation, omits the mathematical structure necessary to make the loss well-posed. There are several plausible reasons this might be — the text may be intended as a conceptual sketch with implementation details abstracted away, or the authors may have considered tanh and F.normalize standard enough not to need explicit mention. We do not have insight into the authors’ editorial intent.
For practitioners trying to reproduce or adapt PDR2: use the released losses.py as-is. Do not attempt to reconstruct the loss from the paper text equation alone. The signs, the absence of tanh, and the absence of F.normalize in the text are not invitations to implement those choices literally — they are a presentation simplification of a more elaborate operational form.

6. Scope and caveats
The downstream MRR numbers in §4 should be read with three caveats firmly in mind:


Single patient. We tested one oncology patient. Statistical generalization is not possible from N=1.


Severely sparse personalization input. Our test patient had zero non-zero polygenic risk scores (the test cohort used a synthetic-zero PRS pickle while genotype-derived PRS was unavailable) and only 84 protein biomarkers (vs. the paper’s reported 1461). With PRS_i = 0 for all i, the entire L_{prs} term contributes zero gradient signal regardless of loss formulation. Our experiment was effectively a biomarker-only test on ~6% of the input density the paper used. The “null lift” we observed on paper_code and minimal_patch cannot be generalized to the paper’s reported AUPRC improvements (1.3×-5.4×), which were computed on UK Biobank cohorts with full PRS + biomarker inputs. The §4 results should be read as descriptive of our specific input, not as a re-evaluation of the published method.


§3’s mathematical findings are independent of patient sparsity. The unboundedness of the paper-text loss formula is a property of the formula, not of the input. Section 5’s interpretation — that the released code’s nonlinearities are load-bearing — rests on the math in §2 plus the loss-curve evidence in §3, neither of which depends on the patient’s input density.


What this note does not claim:

That the paper’s reported numerical results are incorrect — we did not attempt to reproduce on UK Biobank cohorts.
That the released PersonalizedRepurposingLoss is buggy — it works as intended on the published evaluation.
That the personalization approach does not work for densely-featured patients — our test patient was not the right subject for that question.

What this note does claim:

The paper text and released code differ in four specific, structural ways.
The differences are not cosmetic — they change the boundedness of the loss.
The released code’s additional structure is mathematically necessary; the paper text equation cannot be implemented as written without producing a pathological optimizer.
The released losses.py should be treated as the canonical specification.


7. Reproducibility
Container image with the two alt-loss classes baked in: a private container registry image, tag 2f1e268-altloss (Vertex AI custom training).
Fine-tune + eval automation: backend/scripts/alt_loss_2026_05_22/ in the Maple repo (specs and polling scripts).
Job specs are direct gcloud beta ai custom-jobs create --config=… invocations. Total spend for the 4 fine-tunes + 4 evals: ~$10 on A100-80GB/A100-40GB.
The two alt-loss classes (verbatim) live in this fork’s lib/pdr2/code/script/losses.py alongside the unmodified PersonalizedRepurposingLoss.

References

Paper: Oğuztüzün, Ç., Gao, Z., Li, J., Qi, X., Koyutürk, M., & Xu, R. (2026). Learning to take it personally: Precision drug repurposing through patient-specific loss on knowledge graphs using Biobank data. Journal of Biomedical Informatics. DOI: 10.1016/j.jbi.2026.105039
Released code: github.com/ceragoguztuzun/PDR-II — specifically reasoning/script/losses.py (PersonalizedRepurposingLoss, lines 37-87) and reasoning/script/training.py (fine_tune_patient_specific, line 1193 onward).
Backbone: Galkin, M. et al. (2024). Towards Foundation Models for Knowledge Graph Reasoning (ULTRA). ICLR. arXiv:2310.04562.
Inner loop: Zhu, Z. et al. (2021). Neural Bellman-Ford Networks (NBFNet). NeurIPS. arXiv:2106.06935.

Corresponding-author contact details for the PDR-II paper are in the released
README and in the paper itself; they
are deliberately not transcribed here, because this page is published.

model/pdr_personalization_writeup.title: PDR Personalization — Technical Writeup
model/pdr_personalization_writeup.content:
PDR Personalization Process — Technical Writeup
Authors: whafa, Claude (Maple project)
Date: 2026-05-16
Status: Reference document. Describes the personalization mechanisms used by PDR1 (Oğuztüzün et al., J Biomed Inform 2025) and PDR2 (Oğuztüzün et al., J Biomed Inform 179, 2026) — verbatim from the upstream code — and audits Maureen’s data inventory against the inputs each model demands.
Companion documents:

PDR_PIPELINE_PLAN.md — phase plan; Phases 8 / 8.5 / 9 cover personalization
pdr_phase0_gpkg_writeup.md — paper reproduction baseline
pdr_phase7_5_rgcc_writeup.md — RGCC validation (used as Maureen’s ground-truth label set, not a personalization input)
pdr_prs_stage0_findings.md — PRS Stage 0 sample-patient search
pdr_phase8.5_variant_kg_planning.md — variant-aware KG extension
paan_planning.md — Patient-as-a-Node thinking doc


Summary
PDR1 and PDR2 personalize a knowledge-graph link-prediction model through two structurally different mechanisms. PDR1 puts the patient signal into the graph — every personalized fact (a PRS, a biomarker value, a diagnosis, a medication) becomes a per-patient self-loop edge, and the scalar magnitudes are loaded as a sidecar tensor that multiplicatively modulates the relation embedding inside forward_embedd. PDR2 keeps the patient signal outside the graph — the patient appears in the KG only as a node with a small set of WAS_DIAGNOSED edges, and the PRS / expression vectors enter only at fine-tune time through a personalized loss term whose learnable per-disease and per-protein weights ride on top of a frozen foundation model. Both models accept the same four discrete patient data types (PRS, biomarker expression, diagnosis history, medication), but PDR1 needs them shaped as a CSV row and a .npy scalar tensor, while PDR2 needs them shaped as a pickle dict and a per-patient overlay subgraph.
For Maureen we have abundant somatic data (84 nonzero gene-expression values from Caris MI Profile, 8 actionable somatic + germline variants across Caris / Invitae / Guardant, 224 RGCC drug-sensitivity readings) but the PRS column is presently all zeros because no genotype VCF has been uploaded — making Track A (synthetic_zeros PRS + real biomarkers) the only personalization track that runs today. The PRS pipeline (PGS Catalog connector + mods_polygenic_score table + 13-disease default scoring-file set) is built and waiting for genotypes; Track B unblocks the moment a 23andMe / WGS / VCF lands. Additional comorbidity / variant-level coverage is obtainable with targeted work — re-resolving Maureen’s HGVS-p strings through ClinGen, finishing the OncoKB / PharmGKB ingest, and ordering missing PGS Catalog scoring files — but the patient→variant edge fix and the OncoKB ingest are the two near-term unblocks for moving from “gene-level personalization” to the variant-level personalization that the somatic data actually merits.

1. Purpose and Scope
This writeup is a reference for what data each PDR generation actually consumes for personalization, in what shape, and where in the codebase that consumption happens. It is the document to consult before any future debate of the form “could we just feed Maureen’s X into PDR-Y?” because it pins down the exact tensor / table / column / line of upstream code that X has to land in for Y to use it.
Scope:

§2 catalogs the four discrete patient data types both papers use, with the source-of-truth column / field for each.
§3 documents PDR1’s scalar-modulated graph convolution personalization — the patient_merge.py self-loop construction, the scalars_<pid>.npy tensor, and the multiplicative use inside forward_embedd.
§4 documents PDR2’s frozen-foundation, learned-weights personalization — the pickle dict format, the PersonalizedRepurposingLoss, the patient-specific fine-tune (1,802 trainable weights), and the test-time apply_personalization adjustment.
§5 is a side-by-side comparison.
§6 audits Maureen’s data against both schemas — what is materialized today, what is held at zero as a controlled placeholder, what is obtainable with bounded follow-up work, and what is blocked on infrastructure / quota.
§7 lists open questions and risks.

Out of scope: PDR0 / KG-Predict, the in-graph link-prediction mechanics themselves (CompGCN+ConvE in PDR1; ULTRA+NBFNet in PDR2; both covered in pdr_phase0_gpkg_writeup.md and nbfnet_understanding.md), and our own Phase 12 / Phase 13 patient-as-node extensions (covered in paan_planning.md and temporal_patient_modeling_planning.md).

2. The Four Discrete Patient Data Types
PDR1 and PDR2 accept the same four data types for personalization. They differ only in how the data is shaped and where it lands inside the model.








































TypeGranularityModalitySource-of-truth (this paper)Source-of-truth (Maple DB)Polygenic Risk Score (PRS)One scalar per diseaseContinuous, often z-scoredUK Biobank Showcase fields 26200–26285 (Standard PRS Release; 28 binary + 25 quantitative traits)mods_polygenic_score(patient_id, pgs_id, disease_cui, raw_score, z_score, percentile, snps_used, ...)Biomarker expressionOne scalar per geneContinuous (TPM, qPCR ΔΔCt, or assay-dependent)UK Biobank Olink protein panel (Phase III)¹ / blood biomarker fieldsmods_gene_expression(patient_id, gene, expression_value, test_type, report_date)Diagnosis historySet membership (binary)CategoricalUMLS CUI list parsed from the CUIs cell of the patient CSVmods_condition, mods_kgia_profile_service._build_* outputsTreatment / medication historySet membership (binary)CategoricalDrugBank IDs in the Treatment/medication code | Instance 0 cellmods_medication, mods_treatment_drug, mods_treatment_episode
¹ The PDR papers operationalize “biomarker” as protein / gene expression, not the broader clinical use of “biomarker” (CEA, CA 19-9, LDH, etc., which Maple tracks separately under mods_biomarker). When a writeup uses the unqualified word “biomarker” in PDR context it means a gene-keyed expression value.
These four are what the papers implement. They are point-in-time — neither paper consumes trajectories, change rates, or repeated measures (covered in temporal_patient_modeling_planning.md as our Phase 13 research direction).

3. PDR1 — Scalar-Modulated Graph Convolution
PDR1 personalizes a single global model by rewriting the knowledge graph per patient. Every personalized fact becomes a self-loop edge (h, scalar, h) (where h is a disease CUI or gene symbol and scalar is the patient’s value for that feature), then a sidecar tensor of scalars is loaded into the model and used to multiplicatively modulate the relation embedding during message passing.
3.1 Input shape — the patient CSV row
patient_merge.py reads a CSV with one row per UK Biobank participant. Relevant columns:








































ColumnTypeMeaningEIDintUK Biobank patient IDStandard PRS for alzheimer's disease (AD)floatThe headline PRS for the target disease (AD case study)PRS_<CUI> (×~13)floatComorbidity PRS columns, keyed by UMLS CUI (e.g. PRS_C0006142 = breast cancer)Treatment/medication code | Instance 0string-encoded listPython-literal list of DrugBank IDs (['DB00001', 'DB00945', …])CUIsstring-encoded listPython-literal list of diagnosis CUIs from the patient’s encounter history<gene_symbol> (×~hundreds)floatOne column per gene with a biomarker / expression value
The Maple builder for this row is backend/scripts/build_pdr1_input_csv.py; the staged Track A row for Maureen is at runs/2026-05-09_phase9/maureen_track_a_pdr1.csv.
3.2 In-graph representation — patient_merge.py
Patient_Merge.merge_nodes() (docs/References/PDR1/patient_merge.py:63) materializes the per-patient KG by appending five families of self-loop edges to the global kg_df:









































MethodSource columnEdge producedRelation column typefilter_and_match_disease_nodes_PRSStandard PRS for alzheimer's disease (AD)(AD_CUI, prs_value, AD_CUI)scalar (float)filter_and_match_disease_nodes_PRS_comorbitieseach PRS_<CUI>(CUI, prs_value, CUI)scalar (float)filter_and_match_disease_nodes_DisHistCUIs list(CUI, 'HAS_DIAGNOSED', CUI)symbolicfilter_and_match_drug_nodesTreatment/medication code(intersection only — no edges written in shipped code; commented out at L91–96)n/afilter_and_match_gene_nodes_Biomarkerseach gene-keyed expression column(gene, expr_value, gene)scalar (float)
The patient’s drug history is the one type the shipped PDR1 code does not actually write into the graph — the self-loop creation block is commented out. The drug list is used only for entity-set intersection with the KG’s DB* prefix (DrugBank-style nodes); GP-KG instead uses CID* prefix (PubChem + 100M offset, the reproducibility and ent2id notes), which is one of the two known patches required before patient_merge.py will run on GP-KG (the other is the dead UMLS REST endpoint at L111).
3.3 The scalars_<pid>.npy sidecar tensor
Patient_Merge.save() (patient_merge.py:206) emits a 1-D tensor scalars of length len(kg_df) — one entry per triple in the patient-merged KG. For each row:
if isinstance(value, (int, float)):
    scalars[i] = value   # PRS or biomarker value
else:
    scalars[i] = 1.0     # symbolic relation (TARGET, ASSOCIATE, HAS_DIAGNOSED, ...)
Numeric “relation” cells are then replaced with the literal string 'SELF' before the merged KG is written to disk, because the downstream data_loader.py expects a categorical relation column. The scalar magnitude survives only in the .npy sidecar; the merged KG itself looks like a vanilla CompGCN input.
Output files:

outputs/patient_merged_kg_<pid>.txt — tab-separated triples, scalars replaced with 'SELF'
outputs/scalars_<pid>.npy — float tensor aligned to the triple order

3.4 Training-time use — forward_embedd
The scalar tensor is loaded into the model via the -scalars CLI flag (PDR1-specific marker; absent from kg-predict, the reproducibility and ent2id notes). Inside GPKG_EMBEDD:
# In __init__:
loaded_tensor_numpy = np.load(self.p.scalars)
self.scalars = torch.from_numpy(loaded_tensor_numpy).to('cuda:0')
 
# Relation embedding is sized to scalars.size()[0] (not 2*num_rel) when scalars are present:
self.init_rel = get_param((self.scalars.size()[0], self.p.init_dim))
Then in forward_embedd (predict.py:51):
r = self.init_rel
if self.scalars is not None:
    r = r * self.scalars.unsqueeze(1)   # ← THE PERSONALIZATION STEP
x, r = self.conv1(self.init_embed, self.edge_index, self.edge_type, rel_embed=r)
The unsqueeze broadcasts a [len(triples), 1] scalar column against the [len(triples), init_dim] relation embedding matrix, multiplying each relation’s embedding by the patient’s scalar value for that edge. Symbolic edges (scalar = 1.0) are unchanged; scalar edges scale by the patient’s PRS / expression magnitude. Higher PRS for disease d → larger gradient flow through edges incident to d → the model’s downstream drug ranking is pulled toward drugs that connect strongly to high-magnitude diseases for this patient.
The Cohen’s d ≈ 1.05 lift the paper reports for PRS is the strongest of any single personalizer in their ablation. The mechanism is unambiguously the relation-embedding scale — there is no other personalization pathway in PDR1’s architecture.
3.5 Implementation status (Maple)

✓ build_pdr1_input_csv.py builds Maureen’s CSV (Track A row staged; PRS columns zero pending genotypes).
✓ Migration 052 + Caris / RGCC parsers populate mods_gene_expression (84 nonzero values for Maureen).
✗ patient_merge.py patches deferred: startswith('DB') drug filter doesn’t match GP-KG’s CID*; UMLS REST endpoint with embedded API key at L111 is dead (UMLS_apikey = "68297838-..." — replace with _resolve_cuis_via_translator(...) or pre-compute the AD CUI list).
✗ Phase 8 AD repro deferred — establishes the wiring gate before Phase 9.
✓ compute_metrics_crc.py exists for Tier 1 / Tier 2 RGCC scoring once a -scalars-trained checkpoint is produced.


4. PDR2 — Patient-as-Node + Frozen-Foundation Fine-Tune
PDR2 personalizes through a structurally different mechanism. The patient appears in the KG as a node (not just as a row in a CSV), but with minimal edges (WAS_DIAGNOSED only); the PRS and biomarker vectors are not put into the graph at all. They enter through the loss function during a per-patient fine-tune that freezes the entire foundation model and trains only 1,802 personalization weights.
4.1 Input shape — the patient pickle
utils.load_patient_data expects a dict with four required keys:



































KeyShapeTypeSemanticsprs_values[len(disease_names)]np.float32Patient’s PRS for each disease, in the same order as disease_namesexpr_values[len(protein_names)]np.float32Patient’s expression value for each gene, in the same order as protein_namesdisease_names[len(disease_names)]list[str]UMLS CUIs — e.g. ['C0006142', 'C0011860', ...]protein_names[len(protein_names)]list[str]HGNC gene symbols — e.g. ['TP53', 'BRCA1', ...]
PDR2 z-scores both vectors at load time (old_runs/run_drugrec.py:331–332), so the builder emits raw values.
The Maple builder is backend/scripts/build_pdr2_input_pickle.py — three source modes (synthetic_zeros, maureen, ukb_sample). The default 13-disease CUI set (CRC + 12 comorbidities) is sourced from backend/connectors/pgs_catalog_connector.py:261 (UKB_TRAIT_TO_PGS_DEFAULTS). Genes are sourced from mods_gene_expression with a test-type priority (Caris MI Profile > Caris WTS > RGCC qPCR).
4.2 In-graph representation — patient as a node, minimally
Unlike PDR1’s self-loops, PDR2 has the patient appear as a first-class graph entity with outbound edges. From the personalization mechanism reference: foundation training augments the GP-KG with patient nodes that each carry ~37 WAS_DIAGNOSED edges (in the original UK Biobank corpus). The foundation is trained on this augmented graph end-to-end — i.e. the model does see patient nodes during foundation training; it just sees nothing else about them beyond their diagnosis set.
PRS and biomarker values are not in the graph. They appear nowhere as nodes, edges, or scalar modulators. This is a deliberate architectural choice (and a major contrast with PDR1).
For Maureen, the canonical KG carries MAPLE_PATIENT:maureen-1173a8db with 250 outbound canonical relations materialized by backend/mods_patient_kg_service.py::materialize_patient_kg (the variant-aware KG extension) — already substantially richer than the 37-edge UK Biobank patient overlay, even before any of the variant resolver fix or OncoKB ingest lands.
4.3 The personalized loss — PersonalizedRepurposingLoss
losses.py:37 defines the personalization mechanism. The class holds two parameter tensors:
self.disease_weights = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(len(disease_names)) * 0.01)
self.protein_weights = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(len(protein_names)) * 0.01)
These are the only learnable parameters during patient-specific fine-tune. In the paper’s setup len(disease_names) = 341 and len(protein_names) = 1,461, giving 1,802 total trainable weights. The forward pass:
def forward(self, pos_scores, neg_scores, prs_values, expr_values):
    base_loss = StandardKGLoss()(pos_scores, neg_scores)
    
    prs_term = torch.tensor(0.0, device=pos_scores.device)
    expr_term = torch.tensor(0.0, device=pos_scores.device)
    
    if self.disease_weights is not None and len(prs_values) > 0:
        disease_weights_norm = F.normalize(self.disease_weights, p=2, dim=0)
        prs_impact = torch.sum(disease_weights_norm * prs_values)
        prs_term = torch.tanh(prs_impact)
        
    if self.protein_weights is not None and len(expr_values) > 0:
        protein_weights_norm = F.normalize(self.protein_weights, p=2, dim=0)
        expr_impact = torch.sum(protein_weights_norm * expr_values)
        expr_term = torch.tanh(expr_impact)
    
    return base_loss + self.lambda1 * prs_term + self.lambda2 * expr_term
Total loss:
L_total = L_base(pos_scores, neg_scores)
       + λ₁ · tanh( ⟨w_disease_norm, PRS⟩ )
       + λ₂ · tanh( ⟨w_protein_norm, EXPR⟩ )

Both lambdas default to 0.01 in the constructor; the paper sweeps lambda1 (PRS weight) and lambda2 (expression weight) per-patient as documented at PDR_PIPELINE_PLAN.md L973.
What this loss is doing semantically. Each learnable weight tells the model how much that particular disease’s PRS (or that particular gene’s expression) should pull the next training-step gradient on the current triple. The tanh bounds the contribution to [-λ, +λ] regardless of how extreme the PRS or expression value is, preventing a single high-z-score feature from dominating. The L2 normalization on the weight vector keeps the magnitudes from drifting; only the direction of the weighting matters. After fine-tune convergence the learned weight pattern is effectively a per-patient summary: “for this individual, prioritize the bipolar-disorder PRS axis and the BDNF expression axis when ranking drugs.”
4.4 Patient-specific fine-tune — fine_tune_patient_specific
training.py:1193 — invoked from run.py when --use_ploss is set. Pre-conditions: a foundation checkpoint must already exist (trained on the augmented KG via train_foundation_model). Then:
# 7. CRITICAL OPTIMIZATION: Freeze the base model parameters
model.eval()
for param in model.parameters():
    param.requires_grad = False
All 168,705 foundation parameters become non-trainable. Only criterion.disease_weights and criterion.protein_weights (1,802 total) collect gradients. The fine-tune CLI from the personalization mechanism reference:
python script/run.py --patient_id X --dataset KG_ZORO \
  --use_ploss -l1 0.1 -l2 0.1 --ckpt <foundation>

Reported AUPRC lifts (paper §3): Robin 0.076 → 0.251 (3.3×), Zoro 0.277 → 0.368 (1.3×), Usopp 0.065 → 0.353 (5.4×). MRR / Hits stay similar because the relation-aware filter limits how much head-rank can move — the lift surfaces in AUPRC, which is unfiltered.
4.5 Test-time score adjustment — apply_personalization
A second personalization touch point exists at evaluation time: training.py:198 apply_personalization directly adjusts batch scores by a precomputed per-entity adjustment:
for drug_id, disease_rels in drug_disease_rels.items():
    prs_adjustment = 0.0
    for disease_idx, strength in disease_rels:
        prs_adjustment += (
            lambda1 *
            disease_weights[disease_idx] *
            prs_values[disease_idx] *
            strength            # currently always 1.0
        )
    precomputed_adjustments[drug_id] += prs_adjustment
The mechanism iterates the graph’s edges, finds every drug node that is connected to one of the disease entities in criterion.disease_names (or to one of the gene entities in criterion.protein_names), and accumulates a score offset proportional to the learned weight × patient value. The offset is added to the model’s raw prediction at test time.
This is structurally similar to PDR1’s scalar modulation, except (a) it acts at the score level not the embedding level, (b) it uses learned weights from the fine-tune rather than raw scalars, and (c) it only counts drug→disease and drug→protein direct edges (no message-passing propagation). It is more like a post-hoc reweighting of the model output than a personalization of the model itself.

CRITICAL — λ is one-per-experiment, not separable across train and eval (corrected 2026-05-20)
The paper’s apply_personalization reads lambda1 = criterion.lambda1 directly from the criterion state — i.e., the same λ used during fine-tuning training rides on the criterion through evaluation (training.py:206-207). A “λ sweep” in the paper means N separate fine-tune → eval pipelines, each with one λ value baked in throughout. It does NOT mean “fine-tune once at λ=0.01, then evaluate the same checkpoint at λ ∈ {0.01, 0.1, 1.0, 10.0}”.
Maple’s lib/pdr2/code/script/evaluate_personalized_maple.py accepts λ from the CLI (--lambda1_prs, --lambda2_biomarker), so it can be invoked with a λ that mismatches the fine-tune’s training λ. Doing this produces an off-spec eval-time-only sweep: the criterion weights are still those learned under the fine-tune’s λ, but the inference-time scaling is rescaled. This is not what the paper measures.
The May-2026 maureen_focus_v1 run did exactly this off-spec sweep — one fine-tune at λ=0.01, four evals at λ ∈ {0.01, 0.1, 1.0, 10.0}. The reported Δ MRR ≈ −0.4% across all four evals is therefore suggestive, not conclusive. It tells us that no post-hoc scaling rescues the weights learned at λ=0.01; it does NOT tell us how a fine-tune at λ=10.0 (with weights learned under that stronger regularization) would perform. The eval-time-only sweep artifacts have been deleted from the DB (see scripts/strip_evaltime_lambda_sweep.py).
The paper-faithful path runs through Maple’s worker queue as N pairs of pdr_finetune_run + pdr_eval_personalized_run tasks, where the eval task defaults its λ to the source fine-tune’s training λ. Submit endpoints: POST /api/mods/research/runs/{foundation_id}/submit_finetune then POST /api/mods/research/runs/{ft_id}/submit_eval_personalized. Each fine-tune becomes its own mods_research_run row with parent_run_id set; the personalized eval attaches to the fine-tune (not the foundation), so the Overview matrix correctly fans out per-fine-tune in a sweep.

4.6 Implementation status (Maple)

✓ build_pdr2_input_pickle.py ships with synthetic_zeros / maureen / ukb_sample modes.
✓ Maureen’s patient node is in canonical KG (MAPLE_PATIENT:maureen-1173a8db, 250 relations).
✓ Phase 1 training automation code-complete; awaiting Vertex L4 quota grant (an internal note on the training-automation status).
✓ eval_patient.py shipped (Maple-original) for per-patient outbound-edge scoring.
✗ Patient → variant edges still gene-level — _resolve_variant_canonical HGVS-p prefix mismatch (the variant-aware KG extension).
✗ OncoKB / PharmGKB connectors coded but not ingested.


5. Side-by-Side Comparison

































































AspectPDR1PDR2Where the patient signal livesInside the KG, as self-loop edges per fact + a sidecar scalar tensor aligned to the triple listOutside the KG, as feature vectors prs_values / expr_values consumed by the loss functionPatient as graph node?No — patient is a row in a CSV; nodes are diseases / genes / drugs that the patient connects to via self-loopsYes — patient is a first-class node with WAS_DIAGNOSED edges (PDR2 paper); Maple’s overlay adds variant, expression, medication, sensitivity, and phenotype edgesHow values modulate the modelMultiplicatively scale relation embeddings in forward_embedd: r = r * scalarsLoss-additive personalization terms: + λ₁ tanh(⟨w_d, PRS⟩) + λ₂ tanh(⟨w_p, EXPR⟩)What is learnable on a per-patient basisNothing — the scalars are inputs, the model is shared1,802 weights: disease_weights (one per disease in disease_names) + protein_weights (one per gene in protein_names)What is frozen on a per-patient basisn/a — no per-patient training stepThe entire foundation model (168,705 parameters)Per-patient training timeEach patient is a new full retrain (or a fine-tune from the foundation that retrains all params; the paper trains end-to-end with -scalars set)A 3-epoch fine-tune of 1,802 weights only — orders of magnitude cheaperFoundation training inputGlobal KG (no patient overlay)Augmented KG with patient nodes for the entire patient cohort during foundation trainingPatient CSV / pickle filenamepatient_data.csv (one row per patient) + outputs/scalars_<pid>.npypatient_<id>_data.pklEmpty-PRS behaviorA zero scalar makes r * 0 = 0 → the edge contributes no message. Heavy regularization toward “no signal”A zero PRS vector makes tanh(⟨w, 0⟩) = tanh(0) = 0 → the personalization term vanishes, the loss reduces to the base KG lossValidation reported in paperCohen’s d on case-study ranks; AD-NCT AUROC = 0.868; PRS is strongest personalizer (Cohen’s d ≈ 1.05)AUPRC lifts on Robin / Zoro / Usopp (1.3×–5.4×); lithium case study for UsoppWhat it does not personalizeTreatment / medication list (the drug-self-loop block in patient_merge.py is shipped commented out); no temporal signalTreatment / medication list (no shipped equivalent of disease_weights for drugs); no temporal signal
The structural takeaway. PDR1’s mechanism is richer per fact (every personalized scalar enters the convolution) but crude per patient (no learning, no per-patient parameters). PDR2’s mechanism is poorer per fact (only PRS and expression terms, only via a tanh-bounded loss adjustment) but richer per patient (it learns 1,802 patient-specific weights and freezes the foundation, which makes per-patient fine-tune cheap enough to do at clinic scale). Phases 12 (patient-as-node V2) and 13 (temporal modeling) are designed to combine the per-fact richness of PDR1 with the per-patient learning of PDR2 — see paan_planning.md.

6. Maureen’s Data Inventory
For each of the four discrete data types, this section enumerates what we have, what is placeholder, what is obtainable, and what is pending.
6.1 PRS — Polygenic Risk Scores
Have: Nothing computed today. mods_polygenic_score row count for Maureen is 0 as of 2026-05-09 (pdr_prs_stage0_findings.md, PDR_PIPELINE_PLAN.md L918).
Placeholder (the Track A baseline): All PRS columns set to 0.0. After z-scoring (PDR2) or self-loop modulation (PDR1) this collapses to no contribution:

PDR2: tanh(⟨w, 0⟩) = 0 → personalization term vanishes; loss reduces to base KG loss.
PDR1: r * 0 = 0 → message passing through a PRS-keyed edge contributes nothing. Symbolic edges (HAS_DIAGNOSED, biomarker self-loops) carry through unchanged.

This is a controlled baseline, not a corrupted run. Track A is the “biomarker-only personalization” probe; Track B with real PRS is the unblock once genotypes land.
Obtainable with more digging:

Maureen uploads a 23andMe / WGS / VCF file to the mods_genotype table. mods_prs_service.compute_prs() then computes raw + z-score + percentile against the PGS Catalog scoring file (PGS000074 for CRC, PGS002280 for AD, etc. — full default set in connectors/pgs_catalog_connector.py, now SMOKE_TEST_PGS_SET). PRS pipeline shipped (commit 1504d93, UI in 02a7824). (2026-09-29: that function no longer exists. The scorer was rebuilt as Gate C in mods_prs_scorer.py, and normalization is Gate D; mods_prs_service.py now stores scores, records their Gate D normalization and serves the released-only reads. See `prs_primer.md` §5.)
Default disease set covers 13 traits (CRC + 12 comorbidities). For broader comorbidity coverage, additional PGS Catalog scoring files can be added to UKB_TRAIT_TO_PGS_DEFAULTS and re-resolved per Maureen’s clinical history. CAD, AF, T2D, HT, and AST are already in the default set; psychiatric / autoimmune / cancer-specific scores can be added by extending the dict.

Pending / blocked:

Genotype upload from the patient. This is the single largest blocker on Track B and is purely a data-flow question, not a code question.
patient_merge.py UMLS REST endpoint fix (uses a dead API key) — when this is fixed PDR1 can resolve the CUI list for AD comorbidities at build time. See runs/2026-05-09_phase9/README.md.

6.2 Biomarker / gene expression
Have: 84 nonzero biomarker values for Maureen across two source-of-truth tests:

Caris MI Profile (WES + WTS) — 73 selected genes with TPM percentiles; 23K+ genes available in the underlying WTS data. From the second Caris report (Sept 2025): CMS1 classification. (an internal note on the project research assumptions)

The builder (build_pdr2_input_pickle.py:resolve_expression_by_gene) picks the highest-priority test type per gene (Caris MI Profile > Caris WTS > RGCC qPCR by default), then within a test type picks the most recent report.
Placeholder: None needed — biomarker data is fully populated.
Obtainable with more digging:

Full Caris WTS export — Maureen’s WTS reports include 23K+ gene measurements but the parser only ingests 73 selected genes (those highlighted on the Caris PDF). Extending the parser to grab the full WTS table would multiply the protein_names vector ~300× and dramatically expand the biomarker personalization surface. The data is in hand; the parser is the bottleneck. (an internal note on the project research assumptions)

6.3 Diagnosis history
Have: Maureen’s diagnoses are in mods_condition and surface through mods_patient_kg_service::_build_diagnosis_edges. The KG overlay materializes 6 phenotype-style edges on her node (the variant-aware KG extension, 6 phenotype out of 250 total). The full clinical condition list (CRC, comorbidities, history) is available via the Cerbo / the integrative clinic EHR import path (an internal note on the integrative clinic’s EHR integration) and through Maple’s mods_condition table.

(2026-10-05, GH #624 I-3: until I-3, Maple’s copy of the Kaiser conditions was one row per name, each filed as a problem-list item. It is now one row per record, with Kaiser’s own category, and the patient KG emits one phenotype edge per resolved disease from every record that is not void, refuted or unconfirmed. The count above predates that.)
Obtainable with more digging:

Kaiser EHR integration (Epic FHIR + Kaiser HTML import) — for any conditions tracked at Kaiser that aren’t in the the integrative clinic records. OAuth client ID story is documented in an internal note on the health plan’s EHR integration.

6.4 Treatment / medication history
Have: Treatment data in mods_medication, mods_treatment_drug, mods_treatment_episode. The patient KG overlay carries 9 + 59 + 8 = 76 medication-related edges for Maureen (the variant-aware KG extension).
(2026-10-05, GH #624 I-3: mods_medication is one row per Kaiser order, and current_medication / past_medication are decided per drug by written rules: current if any order is current, otherwise past if any is evidence she took it, never both. The counts above predate that. The smoke-run training exports exclude the medication predicates (playbook D2).)
Placeholder: None.
Obtainable with more digging: Drug-bank ID normalization for medications recorded only as free-text names — mods_treatment_drug.drugbank_id is the target column but isn’t always populated by the parser. build_pdr1_input_csv.py currently falls back to an empty list rather than failing when this column is missing (one of the two builder-bug patches landed 2026-05-09).
Pending / blocked:

Neither PDR1 nor PDR2 actually consumes drug history as a personalization input. PDR1’s filter_and_match_drug_nodes (patient_merge.py:70) is implemented but the self-loop creation is commented out. PDR2 has no equivalent drug_weights parameter. So drug history is currently a contextual feature (visible in the KG, useful for ranking-context dashboards, used in our Phase 10 publishing UI) but not a personalization feature. This is a gap that Phase 12 (patient-as-node V2) could close by adding a TAKES / HAS_USED edge type with a learned weight per-patient.

6.5 Variant data (PDR1+2 input via gene-level approximation only)
This is a fifth data type that neither paper consumes natively but that we care about deeply for Maureen — somatic and germline variants from Caris, Invitae, and Guardant360.
Have: 8 actionable variants materialized as gene-level MAPLE:has_genetic_alteration_in edges on Maureen’s node (the variant-aware KG extension). Includes BRAF V600E, APC c.4666dupA, KRAS Q22K, and others.
Placeholder: Variants currently resolve to gene entities in the KG, not variant entities — even though CIViC’s 4,124 variant nodes are in the canonical KG and CAID:CA123643 (BRAF V600E) is queryable. The resolver in _resolve_variant_canonical looks for {gene} {variant} name matches; Maureen’s HGVS-p strings carry p. prefix which CIViC stores without.
Obtainable with more digging:

Patient → variant edge resolver fix (Phase 8.5.2) — Translator/ClinGen spike validated 71.4% CAID resolution on Maureen’s 14 eligible variants. Fix is documented in the variant-aware KG extension: use HGNC REST → transcript + version-fallback HGVS-c → ClinGen Allele Registry → upsert if missing. Resolved CAIDs include BRAF V600E (CAID:CA123643, present in KG), and APC c.4666dupA (CAID:CA16021317, not in KG).
OncoKB ingest (Phase 8.5.4) — connector coded (backend/connectors/oncokb_connector.py, 403 lines); requires ONCOKB_API_TOKEN from www.oncokb.org/account/register. Levels 1–4 → biolink:predicts_sensitivity_to; R1/R2 → biolink:predicts_resistance_to. License posture: flagged commercial / free academic tier.
PharmGKB ingest (Phase 8.5.6) — connector coded; not ingested.
Mutalyzer integration — for the 5 HGVS-p-only variants that can’t currently be resolved through ClinGen.

Pending / blocked:

Phase 8.5 retrain — IN PROGRESS 2026-05-14 with Maureen-noded + CIViC + PrimeKG (no OncoKB yet). OncoKB-augmented retrain is a follow-up. Note: current training did not pre-hold-out RGCC; lift measurement is suggestive, not clean.
This is the personalization route that actually matters for Maureen’s specific variant biology, but PDR1 and PDR2 can’t consume variant data directly. The right architectural answer is Phase 12 (patient-as-node) with variant entities in the KG; gene-level approximation is the interim.

6.6 RGCC drug sensitivities — not a personalization input, but the validation label set
Have: 224 drug sensitivities parsed from Maureen’s RGCC reports (the patient-specific validation writeup). 112 distinct drug names after dedup; 109 matched to PrimeKG; 36 to GP-KG.
These are not an input to PDR1 or PDR2’s personalization machinery. They are the patient-specific ground-truth labels that lift the validation from population-level (FDA approvals, ClinicalTrials.gov) to Maureen’s tumor specifically (pdr_phase7_5_rgcc_writeup.md). Three validation tiers exist; Tier 3 (leave-one-out personalization) is the only one that can validate whether personalization machinery itself helps, and is feasible only on PDR2’s cheap fine-tune.

7. Open Questions and Risks
Q1. Does PDR1’s mechanism transfer to oncology? UK Biobank PRS was developed against late-onset chronic disease (AD, CAD, T2D) where polygenic accumulation explains much of risk. For mCRC, somatic-driver biology (KRAS / BRAF / MSI) probably dominates the actionable signal far more than germline polygenic risk does. If Maureen’s Track B run shows no Tier 1 ρ lift over Track A, that’s not necessarily a wiring failure — it may be that PDR1’s scalar mechanism is a poor fit for an oncology patient. (PDR_PIPELINE_PLAN.md L924–925 documents this as the explicit Phase 9 fallback decision.)
Q2. PDR2’s apply_personalization only counts direct drug↔disease and drug↔gene edges. Multi-hop reasoning (drug → target → pathway → disease) is the strength of NBFNet message passing in PDR2’s base model, but the test-time score adjustment doesn’t propagate through it — it only sees adjacency. This may understate the lift from learned weights. We have not audited what fraction of Maureen’s clinically relevant drugs are directly connected to her diagnoses / expressed genes in PrimeKG vs reachable through intermediate entities.
Q3. The 1,802-weight ceiling. PDR2’s personalization has at most len(disease_names) + len(protein_names) learnable weights per patient. For Maureen with the 13-disease default and ~84 genes, that’s 97 weights, not 1,802. The cohort the paper trained against had richer disease / gene vocabularies via the UK Biobank Olink panel. Whether 97 weights is enough to capture Maureen-specific signal in a 3-epoch fine-tune is empirically unknown.
Q4. Patient-network leakage. PDR2’s foundation training augments the KG with all patients during foundation training, then fine-tunes per-patient. If we eventually move toward a population tapestry (Scenario Z, paan_planning.md) the foundation could see patient↔patient similarity via shared neighbors, opening test-set leakage if validation isn’t held out by patient ID. PDR2’s paper handled this implicitly by training on a fixed UK Biobank cohort; we’d need an explicit hold-out policy.
Q5. Variant vs gene granularity for biomarker expression. PDR1 and PDR2 both key expression by gene, but Maureen’s actionable variants (e.g. BRAF V600E vs wild-type BRAF) have radically different drug-response biology. A gene-level expression of BRAF tells you nothing about V600E status. The full architectural fix is variants-as-nodes (Phase 8.5) — and that fix is needed for the variant-level edges first, not for re-keying expression. Re-keying expression by variant is an open research question for Phase 12+.
Q6. Phase 1 quota grant. PDR2 training automation is code-complete through aiplatform.CustomJob.submit() but blocked on Vertex AI L4 / A100 quota grants (an internal note on the training-automation status). Without the grant, the per-patient fine-tune machinery cannot be tested end-to-end against Maureen’s pickle. Smoke test command is staged.

planning/paan_planning.title: Patient-as-a-Node — Thinking Doc
planning/paan_planning.content:
Patient-as-a-Node (PaaN): Thinking Doc

Status: thinking artifact, not a build commitment. We answered “should we build?” with “keep thinking.” This doc captures the full reasoning so we can revisit when we’re ready to commit.

Context
You asked four interlocking questions and we surfaced several more along the way:

Refresh on PaaN. What have we been planning? Is “patient → has → disease/gene/phenotype” the right schema? To what end?
PDR2’s loss function — really. How is patient genetics actually integrated during training? Is it PRS? What else? And — important — why does the PersonalizedRepurposingLoss code exist but never run?
What could we attach to a Patient node that PDR2 didn’t have? And what could we acquire that PDR2 didn’t even consider, given access to any test in the developed world?
Where have other researchers wandered? What’s the literature say?
Supervision — what does it mean in ML, and what’s the landscape of supervision-producing tests we could use?
Node vs subgraph — what’s the real distinction?
Compositions reframe everything. Maureen isn’t an overlay on PrimeKG; she’s an overlay on whatever Composition we’re training against.

Underneath all of it is the real question: should PaaN remain a distant “Phase 12 / final stage” or do we start building an imperfect-but-working prototype now? Decision: not yet — but we now know what “yet” looks like.

0. A note on the PDR2 framing
PDR2 (paper) already is a patient-as-a-node architecture. I had this wrong twice. The corrected mechanistic description is in §5. What PDR2 specifically did:

Patient nodes with WAS_DIAGNOSED edges to disease nodes, added to the training KG so the foundation model learns patient embeddings from epoch 1.
PRS values + biomarker expressions are NOT in the graph — they’re scalar feature vectors used by the loss.
Per-patient fine-tune freezes the foundation and trains only 1,802 weights inside the loss (per-disease + per-protein) that reweight the global ranking based on the patient’s features.
AUPRC lifts reported as 1.3–5.4× across three case patients; MRR/Hits stay similar.
Validation by literature review only — no per-patient outcome labels like our RGCC.

Our PaaN ambition is richer than PDR2’s in two ways:

More patient edges — variants, treatments, drug sensitivities, in addition to diagnoses.
Real per-patient supervision — RGCC drug sensitivities as labels, not just literature review.

The rest of this doc is structured as if from scratch — refreshing what we’ve been thinking, then sketching how to do something genuinely beyond PDR2.

1. The mental model — Maureen as overlay on a Composition
This is the central reframe. My memories predated Compositions, so I was sketching as if PrimeKG were the only target graph. It isn’t.
A Composition is a named, versioned recipe — “use these KG sources, apply these per-source domain/predicate filters” (docs/kg_composition_pipeline_writeup.md). Six exist already: gp_kg_baseline_v1, primekg_baseline_v1, rtx_kg2_full, rtx_kg2_tier1, tier1_mvp_v1, tier1_mvp_with_primekg_v1. Training runs point at a composition by id; the same canonical store backs every experiment.
The right mental model is:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Composition (e.g. tier1_mvp_with_primekg)   │   the underlying graph
│  ├─ PrimeKG (genes, drugs, diseases, ...)    │   chosen sources × domains × predicates
│  ├─ CIViC (variants)                         │
│  ├─ OncoKB (variants, biomarkers)            │
│  └─ PharmGKB (PGx)                           │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                    ⊕ overlay
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Maureen (her node + her edges)              │   patient overlay (attachable to any composition)
│  ├─ patient → has_disease → CRC              │
│  ├─ patient → carries_variant → BRAF V600E   │
│  ├─ patient → over_expresses → PTGS2 (z=3.1) │
│  ├─ patient → tried_drug → FOLFOX (no_resp)  │
│  └─ patient → sensitive_to → drug_X (RGCC)   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                    ↓ train / infer
              Composition + Maureen
              (or Composition alone, with Maureen attached only at inference)

This matters because:

We’re not committing to PrimeKG. We’re committing to the geometry of the chosen composition. Different compositions have different entity types and relations available; Maureen’s edge schema has to work against any of them.

PaaN (Phase 12) is the actual training-time architecture; Phase F is the post-prediction tooling. Both stay useful; they answer different questions.
Browsability: same UI as the KG Composition tab. Maureen gets a card; click and you see her resolved CURIEs, her edges by type, her 1-hop neighborhood. No separate UI needed.

3. Node vs subgraph — what the real distinction is
You pushed back, rightly, that a subgraph is just one or more nodes connected to the graph. Let me re-do this distinction.
Every set of nodes induces a subgraph in graph theory — that’s not what makes one pattern different from the other. The real distinction is identity:

Patient as an explicit node: Maureen has her own row in mods_kg_entity. She has a canonical CURIE (e.g., MAPLE_PATIENT:maureen-001). She has an entity_type. Edges from and to her are first-class rows in mods_kg_relation. The model can score (maureen, treats?, drug_X) as a triple. She is one thing in the graph.
Patient as a subgraph (SHEPHERD pattern): Maureen has no node of her own in the KG. She’s represented by the set of pre-existing nodes that describe her — her phenotypes, her variants, her diseases. The model embeds her by pooling over that set. The patient is implicit in a collection of edges, not first-class.

For our setup the explicit-node pattern wins, primarily because (1) you want her browsable like a KG entity, (2) RGCC sensitivities and treatment history are most natural as edges on her, and (3) “patient as anchor in training” needs her to have a single embedding the loss can reference. 4. Supervision — a standalone primer
Supervision shows up in every ML conversation, often without anyone defining it. Here it is from first principles, then mapped to our setup.
What “supervision” means in ML
Training a neural network is just gradient descent on a loss function. The loss measures how wrong the model’s predictions are. The model adjusts its parameters in whatever direction reduces the loss.
Where does the loss come from? You need pairs of (input, target_output). The model takes an input, produces a prediction, compares it to the target, computes a loss. Across millions of these pairs, the model’s parameters drift toward reproducing the targets from the inputs.
Supervision is the source of those targets. If we have explicit labels — like “this drug worked, this didn’t” — that’s supervised learning. If we don’t, we either find another way to generate targets or do without.
Types of supervision

This is what PDR2 does today.Weakly supervisedNoisy, partial, or proxy labels”Drug was prescribed” → assumes it worked. “More sources assert this edge” → assumes it’s true.Semi-supervisedSmall labeled + large unlabeledRGCC’s 224 labels (112 drugs x 2 draws) + millions of KG triplesContrastive / metric learningPairs of similar/dissimilar itemsSHEPHERD’s “match this patient to her causal gene”ReinforcementRewards over a sequence of actionsTreatment-decision policies — not where we are yet
The PDR2 foundation training is self-supervised over the KG: it generates negative samples by corruption and asks the model to rank positives above negatives. No human labels needed. This is why PDR2 can be trained on huge KGs at all — labels for “does drug X treat disease Y” don’t exist at scale.

If we put Maureen in the graph and the loss objective includes terms that involve her edges, we’d add:

Patient-edge link prediction — “is (maureen, sensitive_to, drug_X) a true triple given the rest of her edges?” Self-supervised in the same way as PDR2’s existing loss. Her RGCC edges supply the positives.
Drug-sensitivity regression — predict her actual % cell death given the drug. Truly supervised — direct labels.
Treatment-outcome classification — given a drug she tried, predict the response category (CR/PR/SD/PD/intolerant). Supervised but small N.
Auxiliary cross-source corroboration — predict “what fraction of KG sources support this edge” as a soft label. Weakly supervised.

The single-patient pitfall (the central methodological risk): a model fit to one person’s labels memorizes her, not biology. Defensive principles:

Train on population, validate on patient. Foundation model trains on KG (population-level); Maureen’s labels are mostly used at inference and validation.
Functional screens as labels, not features. RGCC’s 224 drug sensitivities are held-out evaluation, not training input — otherwise we overfit to RGCC’s specific assay conditions, not patient outcomes.
Triangulate across orthogonal modalities. A drug ranked high by KG reasoning, LINCS signature reversal, and PDO screen is robust. Any single source overfits.
Pre-register rank lists. Freeze top-30 before exposure to outcomes. Confirmation bias contaminates everything otherwise.
Negative controls. Include drugs known to be ineffective for CRC and drugs known to be effective. If known-ineffectives score high or known-effectives score low, the model is broken.
Calibrated uncertainty, not point predictions. Bayesian posteriors / ensembles / conformal prediction. One-patient point estimates are meaningless.

This pitfall is what shapes how RGCC and other Pt-specific supervision should be used — as evaluation and as auxiliary supervision, never as the dominant training signal.

5. PDR2’s actual mechanism (after reading the paper)

Apology in advance: I had this wrong in two earlier drafts. The paper is now read and the description below is the corrected one. The key correction: PDR2 IS already a patient-as-a-node architecture — just a minimal one. I shouldn’t have claimed otherwise.

Source: Oğuztüzün, Gao, Li, Qi, Koyutürk, Xu. Learning to take it personally: Precision drug repurposing through patient-specific loss on knowledge graphs using Biobank data. J. Biomedical Informatics 179 (2026) 105039. DOI. And the code at docs/References/PDR2/.
Stage 1 — foundation training on GP-KG with patient nodes already added
GP-KG: 61,146 entities, 1.2M relations, 7 entity types, 9 relation categories. Plus patient nodes — one per UK Biobank participant in the cohort (4,124 AD patients aged 50–65), each connected to disease nodes via a WAS_DIAGNOSED relation. About 37 patient edges per individual.
The foundation is ULTRA, 6 layers, 64-dim hidden, DistMult message passing with sum aggregation, layer normalization + residual connections. Trained 100 epochs (500 batches/epoch, batch 512) with plain BCE-with-logits over link prediction. 10 strict negatives per positive. AdamW lr=5×10⁻⁴, weight decay 10⁻⁴. (Paper §2 “Initial training of foundation model.”)
The patient edges (WAS_DIAGNOSED) are part of the training KG — the model learns embeddings for patients alongside everything else. So the patient IS a node, with edges, from the start.
What’s NOT in the graph: PRS values, biomarker expression values. Those are “external inputs to the patient-specific loss function.” (Paper §2.)
Stage 2 — per-patient fine-tuning with the personalized loss
For each of the 4,124 patients (or in the case studies, three representatives — Robin, Zoro, Usopp), a separate fine-tune run.
Foundation is frozen (all 168,705 model parameters). Only 1,802 learnable weights inside the loss are trained — 341 disease weights (one per PRS-aligned disease in GP-KG) + 1,461 protein weights (one per UK Biobank-aligned protein in GP-KG). 93.6× reduction in trainable parameters vs foundation.
The personalized loss (Paper §2, Eq. 1):
L = L_pred − λ₁·L_prs − λ₂·L_expr

L_prs  = Σᵢ (wᵢ · PRSᵢ · s_pred)         for each disease i
L_expr = Σⱼ (vⱼ · (expr_j − ref_j) · s_pred)  for each protein j

Where:

L_pred is standard BCE link prediction loss on the batch
s_pred is the predicted score for the current triple being scored in the batch — any triple, not just patient triples
wᵢ, vⱼ are the learnable per-disease and per-protein weights (this is what fine-tuning trains)
PRSᵢ, (expr_j − ref_j) are the patient’s fixed feature values
The minus signs are because the goal is to maximize the influence of high PRS values and biomarker deviations on relevant drug scores

So for each triple in the batch, the loss term effectively says: “multiply this triple’s predicted score by a patient-specific scalar that’s a weighted sum of PRS and biomarker deviations, with weights w and v learning which diseases/proteins matter for this patient’s drug ranking.”
Fine-tuning: 3 epochs, 100 batches/epoch, AdamW lr=10⁻⁴. Patient edges (~37 total) get a 90/10 train/validation split; the biomedical KG split is unchanged across patients. The test set is the KG-only test split — to verify fine-tuning preserves general knowledge.

MRR, Hits@1/3/10 stay essentially unchanged across rows (the relation-aware filter limits these metrics). AUPRC is computed under the global / broader candidate pool — that’s where the personalization shows.

What this means for our PaaN ambition (the corrected version)
I was wrong twice over:

Wrong: “PDR2 isn’t patient-as-a-node.” Correction: it is. Patient nodes with WAS_DIAGNOSED edges enter the graph from foundation training onward.
Wrong: “The personalized loss exists but isn’t used.” Correction: it is used, in a separately-invoked per-patient fine-tune script (--use_ploss).
Right: the foundation is frozen during fine-tune; only the loss’s 1,802 weights update.

So our PaaN ambition isn’t “introduce patient as a node,” it’s “make the patient a richer node than PDR2’s”:

PDR2: ~37 WAS_DIAGNOSED edges only. PRS + biomarkers enter the loss as scalars, not as graph structure.
Our proposed PaaN: WAS_DIAGNOSED (have it) plus carries_variant (we have data, PDR2 didn’t), over_expresses / under_expresses (we have, PDR2 used as loss feature only), tried_drug (we have with outcomes), sensitive_to_drug / resistant_to_drug (we have from RGCC — PDR2 didn’t have anything like this), allergic_to (we have).
Variant data + assayed drug sensitivities are the two big additions. The first is a structural enrichment of the graph (variant-level paths instead of gene-level). The second is a completely new supervision signal that PDR2 didn’t have access to.

Three architectural moves beyond PDR2
In rough order of difficulty:
Move 1 (cheapest): More patient edges, same loss mechanism. Add the richer edge types to Maureen’s node before training. Foundation pre-trains with them; per-patient fine-tune still freezes foundation and trains the 1,802 loss weights. Tests whether the richer graph structure alone moves AUPRC.
Move 2 (medium): Unfreeze patient-related parameters during fine-tune. Instead of freezing all 168K foundation parameters, unfreeze the embeddings of patient + patient-1-hop entities. Now her node’s embedding can move during fine-tune; the rest of the graph stays put. This is closer to what your “every backfill biased toward Maureen” framing actually requires.
Move 3 (hardest): Multi-task loss with patient-specific supervision. Extend the loss with explicit (drug, response, patient) terms tied to RGCC sensitivities. Now we have labeled supervision from RGCC, not just PRS-modulated unlabeled scoring. The patient becomes a real training signal, not just a feature for reweighting.
These compose: Move 1 + Move 2 + Move 3 is the “Maureen-anchored richer graph with labeled supervision and learnable patient embedding” architecture from §6.
The experiment to run first (much cheaper now we understand it)
We have the foundation checkpoint already (from prior PDR2 runs on GP-KG and PrimeKG). For the minimum reproduction-and-extension:

Build a KG_ZORO-style fine-tune dataset for Maureen — her diagnosis edges as WAS_DIAGNOSED triples to GP-KG / PrimeKG disease nodes (a few of these), train/validation split.
Compute her PRS values for the 341 GP-KG-aligned diseases (from germline VCF + GWAS sumstats; ~half a day).

6. The “patient as anchor in training” mechanism
You described it semantically as: “every training calculation should be in service of pushing the result closer to ‘this works with what we know about Maureen’ than away from it.” We agreed to test both of the two concrete mechanisms below, plus stay open to new patterns.
This is the §5 “Move 2 / Move 3” beyond PDR2’s mechanism: PDR2’s foundation is frozen during fine-tune, so the patient embedding never moves and the loss’s only learnable parameters are scalar reweighting coefficients. The mechanisms below are about how to make the model itself — not just the reranker — respond to the patient.
Option A — Auxiliary loss term weighting Maureen’s edges heavily
L_total = L_KG_link_prediction + λ_patient · L_patient_edges


Every batch samples some standard KG triples (whole-graph link prediction) and also samples Maureen’s edges as positives.
L_patient_edges could be: link prediction on her edges (same BCE form, just over her sub-edges), MSE on her drug sensitivities, multi-task combination.
λ_patient is the dial — high = the whole graph’s geometry gets dragged to keep her facts well-fit; low = her edges are just one signal among many.
Every gradient step “knows about Maureen” because some fraction of the batch is her.

Pros: minimally invasive. Standard architecture, standard optimizer. Closest in spirit to what PDR2’s PersonalizedRepurposingLoss was reaching for. Easy to ablate (set λ_patient = 0 and compare).
Cons: she’s still one node among hundreds of thousands. Her gradient signal washes out unless λ_patient is large, and large risks pulling the whole graph toward her idiosyncrasies (over-personalization, loss of generalization).
Option B — Patient-conditional message passing
The GNN’s message-passing at every layer is modulated by Maureen’s embedding. Concretely, several patterns:

Attention conditioning: attention weights over neighbors are a function of (source_emb, target_emb, patient_emb). Edges that are more relevant to her get heavier weight.
Gated message passing: each message gets multiplied by a gating function of the patient embedding. Edges “irrelevant to Maureen” decay.
Hypernetwork: a small network takes the patient embedding and outputs the GNN’s weights themselves. The model is literally a different model for each patient.

Pros: architecturally elegant. Matches the “her node bends every computation” intuition. TxGNN does something analogous for relations (relation-conditional message passing) and gets ~30% lift on rare diseases.
Cons: more parameters, more training instability, more compute. Patient-conditional everything is heavy. And: with one patient, we can’t disentangle “good architecture” from “got lucky on this specific patient.”
Option C — Patient as central hub of training sampling
Bias the training sampler so most batches include triples in her 2-hop neighborhood. The model spends most of its capacity on her region of the graph; the rest is loosely fit. Conceptually closer to “fine-tune on her subgraph” than “rebuild the architecture.”
This is what Phase F.7 sketches. Less ambitious than A or B but probably the cheapest way to get a measurable lift on her specifically.

7. What we have + what the architecture should support
Reframing from the earlier draft: the right question isn’t “what supervision should we order before committing to an architecture?” It’s “what supervision should the architecture be able to support, so we can start small with what we have and add new tests over time?”
V1 won’t have everything. We start with current data, get something working, then expand as new tests come in. Retraining is acceptable for major data additions; fine-tuning is preferred for incremental additions. The architectural commitment is to a graph schema and loss design flexible enough that new edge types and supervision signals plug in without re-architecting.
What that means concretely:

Edge schema needs to be extensible — adding a new edge type (e.g., methylation_class or pdo_sensitivity) shouldn’t require schema migration of every patient
Loss needs to be extensible — adding a new auxiliary supervision term shouldn’t require rewriting existing terms
The patient node needs feature slots that accept multi-modal additions (gene expression today; proteomics, methylation, radiomics later)
Inductive scoring path needs to handle new edge types without retraining (NBFNet-style message passing handles this well)
