RGCN-with-literals for temporal patient pathways (arXiv:2502.21138, 2025) — literal patient nodes with literal-valued features.

Cluster B — KG drug repurposing without the patient
TxGNN (Nat Med 2024), DREAMwalk (Nat Comm 2023), Decagon, BioPathNet, K-Paths, MLAN, GDRnet — all population-level. None model the patient. This is the cleanest gap.
Cluster C — Adjacent fields

Causal ITE on graphs (TARNet+CGC, CauGramer, DCHGNN, van der Schaar lab) — graph-structured covariates for treatment effects, doesn’t ingest biomedical KGs.
EHR-KG (Frontiers PCKG survey 2024, MedGCN, Mendel.ai) — patient-centric KGs for clinical outcome prediction, not repurposing.
Rare disease subgraph methods (PhenoKG, RareNet, RareAgent — all 2025) — diagnostic reasoning, not therapy ranking.
Patient digital twins (Nat Rev Cancer 2025) — mechanistic ODE/PDE, not graph-based.

White space
No published paper combines all of:

Patient as a node in a PrimeKG-class biomedical KG
Multi-omic patient edges (variants + expression + treatment + functional sensitivities)
Patient-specific supervision (assayed drug response as labels)
KG link-prediction backbone for repurposing

That’s our specific differentiator. SHEPHERD has 1 (phenotype-only); the bioRxiv mutation paper has 2+3 (no phenotype/treatment integration, no inductive reasoner); none combine all four.
8a. SHEPHERD deep-read
Sources: npj Digital Medicine 2025, Zitnik Lab project page, GitHub: mims-harvard/SHEPHERD, medRxiv preprint. The Nature link returned a 303 from WebFetch — mechanistic details below come from the project page, GitHub README, and search snippets. Read the PDF before basing any architecture decision on these claims.
What it is. SHEPHERD is diagnostic, not therapeutic. Three tasks, all phenotype-driven:

Causal gene discovery — given patient phenotypes + candidate genes, rank genes (true causal gene at avg rank 3.52 across 465 real UDN patients).
Patients-like-me retrieval.
Novel disease characterization.

It does not model drug repurposing. There are no drug nodes in its KG and no therapy-ranking objective.
Architecture.

Backbone: geometric deep learning over a rare-disease KG (“knowledge-grounded metric learning”). PyTorch + PyTorch Geometric. The README doesn’t specify which GNN flavor; the paper’s methods section would.
Patient encoding: each patient = a set of HPO terms + optional candidate Ensembl gene IDs. The phenotypes define a subgraph in the KG; the model embeds the patient by aggregating over that subgraph. This is patient-as-subgraph, not patient-as-explicit-node.
KG: a custom rare-disease KG hosted on Harvard Dataverse, smaller than PrimeKG.
Training: ~40K simulated patients across 2,134 diseases. Evaluated on 465 real UDN patients.
Loss: metric learning framing — pull matched (patient embedding, causal gene embedding) together, push non-matches apart. Likely contrastive/triplet.
Inductive over patients: trained on simulated, deployed on real. A new patient is scored at inference without retraining.

What’s transferable to a PaaN-for-repurposing design

A patient is meaningfully embedded into a biomedical KG, and that embedding drives ranking — same general shape as ours.
Inductive scoring on novel patients — exactly the capability we’d need if we don’t want to retrain when Maureen’s data updates.
Same KG family as TxGNN/PrimeKG — tooling is compatible.

What doesn’t transfer

Diagnostic, not therapeutic. No drug-repurposing supervision signal.
Phenotype-only patient. Our patient has variants, expression, treatments, CTC profiles, drug sensitivities — none of which SHEPHERD shows how to combine.
Simulated-patient training. SHEPHERD scales by training on 40K synthetic patients. We have one real patient and no way to simulate “Maureen-like” synthetic patients without losing what makes her useful as a single instance. We have to find a different way to inject patient-specific supervision.
Metric learning vs link prediction. SHEPHERD’s contrastive objective fits retrieval; ours fits ranking. Different loss surface.

Net. SHEPHERD validates the idea that patients can be embedded into a biomedical KG and the embedding can drive useful downstream tasks. It does not give us the exact mechanism. The Maureen-anchored architectures in §6 are what we need to design, and they look more like PDR2 + patient edges + patient loss than like SHEPHERD.

9. If we wanted to build — the staged path (revised, not yet committed)
Three scenarios, in order of ambition. We’re not committing to any of them yet, but here’s what each would entail given the constraints you’ve added.
Scenario X (cheapest, do-anytime): direct PDR2 reproduction on Maureen
After reading the paper (§5), this is well-specified. PDR2 already exposes a CLI flag (--use_ploss) for the per-patient fine-tune. The foundation model is frozen; only 1,802 weights inside the loss train.
Steps:

Add Maureen as a patient node in the chosen Composition’s training graph, with WAS_DIAGNOSED edges to her diseases (~5–10 edges; far fewer than PDR2’s UK Biobank average of 37 because she’s one patient with limited diagnosis breadth).
Re-run foundation training on (Composition + Maureen’s diagnosis edges) — this is needed because PDR2’s foundation included patient nodes from epoch 1. If we already have a foundation trained without Maureen’s node, we can skip this and just attempt fine-tune on the frozen one (the patient embedding will be random, which is the closest PDR2 analog).
Compute PRS for Maureen from her germline VCF + public GWAS sumstats (~half a day if Invitae export available). Filter to PRSs whose disease CURIE is in the Composition.
Pull her expression deviations for the proteins/genes in the Composition from ModsGeneExpression (already structured; ~176 values).
Run python script/run.py -c config/transductive/inference.yaml --patient_id maureen --dataset <maureen-zoro> --use_ploss -l1 0.1 -l2 0.1 --ckpt <foundation_ckpt> (using PDR2’s reported optimum (0.1, 0.1) for the case patient with lowest baseline AUPRC).
Measure: AUPRC on KG link prediction; Spearman ρ between the model’s drug ranking for her CRC and her RGCC drug sensitivities; convergence of the 1,802 weights to see which diseases/proteins are upweighted.
~1 day setup + a few hours of fine-tune compute.

Tells us whether PDR2’s exact mechanism transfers to Maureen and what the AUPRC and RGCC-ρ baseline numbers are. Any architecture in §6 that goes beyond PDR2’s mechanism (Move 2 or 3) needs to clear those bars. Useful baseline to publish against either way.
Scenario Y (MVP, if we decide to build): “Maureen as a node, attached to current Composition”
Bundled scope:

Phase 8.5 (variant nodes) — CIViC/OncoKB/PharmGKB ingest, since you noted variants are critical for MVP.
Phase F.1–F.2 (anchor resolver + storage) — needed to translate her medical record into canonical CURIEs.
Phase 13 Tier 1 (trajectory features as static attributes on her node).
Phase 12.0 (the actual node + edges):

Add patient to mods_kg_entity (just an entity_type — no separate table, no join). Maureen gets a row keyed by canonical CURIE.
Materialize her edges: has_disease, carries_variant (after 8.5), over/under_expresses_gene, tried_drug (with outcome attribute), sensitive_to_drug / resistant_to_drug (from RGCC), allergic_to, plus Tier 1 trajectory features as node attributes.
Store her mods_kg_entity.id on ModsPatient for the back-pointer (no join table).
Browsable in the KG Composition tab next to compositions — same UI, same interaction patterns.


Foundation training is back on the table. Two training architectures to test:

Option A: standard ULTRA + auxiliary loss term weighting her edges
Option B: patient-conditional message passing (relation- and patient-conditional)


Validate against RGCC ρ (held-out), held-out-recent-months trajectory, clinician sanity-check on top-10 drugs.

Time estimate revised. With Phase 8.5 bundled (~3 weeks based on Phase F doc + connector ingest), Phase F.1–F.2 (~1.5 days), Phase 13 Tier 1 (~2 days), Phase 12.0 schema + ETL (~1 week), Option A foundation retrain (~1 week) — realistically 5–7 weeks, not 1–2. The 1–2-week framing in the earlier draft assumed no retraining and no variants; with both included, it’s bigger.
Scenario Z (full ambition): co-developed patient + KG geometry, with population tapestry

The Composition includes population sources (§5a): GDSC, CCLE, DepMap, LINCS, TCGA, PDXNet, GENIE — each ingested as a mods_kg_source. Each contributes thousands of patient/cell-line nodes with genome_alteration, sensitive_to, resistant_to, treated_with → outcome edges.
Maureen’s node and her edges are added to the same graph; she’s one node among thousands of “patient-like” entities.
The foundation model trains on the population-tapestry composition from epoch 1. The §6 anchor-loss patterns (A/B/C) determine how the patient-edge supervision enters the loss — per-batch sampling can rotate which patient is “anchored” to prevent overfit to any one.
Both auxiliary-loss (Option A) and patient-conditional message passing (Option B) are tested; whichever wins is expanded on.
Phase 13 Tier 4 (temporal encoder) feeds Maureen’s node feature vector — her node updates as her trajectory evolves.
New patients can be added by adding new rows to mods_kg_entity with their edges; inductive scoring via NBFNet handles them at inference without retraining.
Supervision sources expand per §7: PGx, PRS, possibly PDO/Olink/Methylation added as additional edges and auxiliary loss terms.

This is the “data structure that understands Maureen’s disease in the most granular way possible, attachable to new data sources as we find them” you described. The population tapestry is what gives it enough signal to be more than a one-patient overfit. It’s a real research project — months to years, with substantial risk of dead ends.
What “imperfect but working prototype” means under each scenario

Scenario X is the imperfect prototype for whether PDR2’s loss buys anything. Doesn’t depend on PaaN at all. Cheapest learning per day.
Scenario Y is the imperfect prototype for PaaN as an architecture — proves the schema, the loss patterns, the validation pipeline, and gives us a measurement.
Scenario Z is the production target. Not an MVP.

If we ever commit to building, my recommendation would be X first, then Y if X is encouraging, then Z if Y validates. Each scenario’s failure pattern teaches us something different.

10. Open questions (updated)

Composition target. Which Composition is the right one to attach Maureen to? tier1_mvp_with_primekg_v1 after variant connectors ingest is the obvious candidate, but primekg_baseline_v1 (already ingested) lets us measure earlier. Trade-off: latest-and-greatest vs measurable-now.
Foundation retraining cost. Each training run is ~1 H100-day. Five runs (§6’s test plan) = 5 H100-days = real money. Worth it once the architecture is locked, premature before.
PRS computation pipeline. Needs her germline VCF (Invitae provides this; need to confirm export availability) + a GWAS sumstats source + PRS tool. Not blocked by anything except the work itself. Probably half a day.
PDO acquisition. Highest-payoff data acquisition (§7 item 4), but logistics (vendor selection, biopsy timing, insurance) are real. Worth scoping before relying on it.
Multi-patient generalization design. “I’d like to be able to browse Maureen’s node the same way we browse our KGs” implies a generalized UI pattern. Already supported by the existing KG Composition tab if Maureen is just another entity. But if we ever add a second patient, do we want a mods_patient_set that groups them, or are they just entity_type='patient' rows?
PDR2 paper — now read. Resolved. §5 is corrected. Key findings: patient IS already a node (WAS_DIAGNOSED edges); fine-tune freezes foundation and trains only 1,802 loss weights; reported AUPRC lift 1.3–5.4× across the three case patients; validation by literature only (no patient-level gold standard like our RGCC). Limitations they note: cohort of 3 patients for case studies (4,124 in principle); single disease (AD); no automated per-patient λ adaptation; multi-modal extensions and longitudinal data are future work.
Does the population-tapestry direction (§5a) shift priorities in §7? If we go Scenario Z (population tapestry), the priority for ordering Maureen-specific tests changes — the highest-value acquisitions become ones that integrate with the public population data (e.g., Tempus xT uses the same genome reference as TCGA; methylation EPIC v2 aligns with TCGA methylation). Worth thinking about acquisition order in light of which other patient data we’d be training against.
Closure criterion for MVP — you said “net positive energy output,” i.e., any measurable improvement counts. ρ improvement on RGCC is the cleanest single signal. Worth pinning down whether we need just RGCC improvement, or also concordance with clinician-curated top-10, or also held-out-recent-months.


TL;DR

Important correction: PDR2 IS already a patient-as-a-node architecture. I had this wrong in earlier drafts. Each UK Biobank patient enters the graph as a node with ~37 WAS_DIAGNOSED edges. The foundation model trains on the augmented graph. Then for each patient, fine-tune freezes the foundation and trains only 1,802 weights inside the loss (341 per-disease + 1,461 per-protein) — these weights learn which diseases/proteins matter for the patient’s drug ranking. AUPRC lifts 1.3–5.4× across the three reported case patients (Robin, Zoro, Usopp); MRR stays unchanged. Validation is literature-review only. Lithium prediction for Usopp was independently validated by a Nature 2025 paper after PDR2’s experiments completed — a real “predicted before the field knew” win.
Our white space isn’t “introduce a patient node” — PDR2 already does that. Our white space is richer patient edges (variants, gene expression as graph structure not just loss features, treatment outcomes, drug sensitivities) + labeled per-patient supervision from RGCC and similar functional assays. PDR2 has zero patient-level outcome labels; we have 224.
Three architectural moves beyond PDR2 (§5, end): (1) richer patient edges, same frozen-foundation loss mechanism; (2) unfreeze patient-1-hop embeddings during fine-tune so her node embedding actually moves; (3) multi-task loss with RGCC sensitivities as labeled supervision. They compose; we should test the cheapest one first.
The first experiment to run is direct PDR2 reproduction on Maureen (§9 Scenario X): build a KG_ZORO-style fine-tune dataset, compute her PRS, run --use_ploss. Establishes the PDR2-mechanism baseline on her data. ~1 day setup. Doesn’t require any architectural innovation.
Population tapestry (§5a) is a meaningfully different direction. Train the foundation on granular per-patient outcomes from many patients/cell lines (GDSC, CCLE, DepMap, LINCS, TCGA, PDXNet, GENIE, PDO consortia) — Maureen becomes one query point in a learned geometry, not the sole anchor. Composes with the Maureen-anchored architecture, doesn’t replace it.
Compositions reframe the design. Maureen is an overlay attachable to any Composition (current options: GP-KG, PrimeKG, future ones include CIViC/OncoKB/PharmGKB after Phase 8.5 ingest). She becomes a first-class entity (entity_type='patient') browsable next to compositions. Schema: simple — node ID on ModsPatient, no join table.
Variants mandatory for MVP (Phase 8.5 bundled). Tier 1 trajectory features bundled too.
Supervision matters more than the architecture until we have orthogonal sources. RGCC is the floor (and confirmed-continuous-1%-granularity, not 20% bands — your concern was reasonable but the data is finer-grained than that). PGx, PRS, CMap/LINCS reversal, methylation, PDO, Olink — every additional source closes a different supervision gap.
Recommended next concrete step: spawn a new planning session for “Create Maureen’s Patient Entity node + edges, expose in KG browser.” This is Scenario Y’s first deliverable, stripped of any training-architecture commitment. It gives us a browsable patient subgraph in the existing KG Composition tab UI, forces us to make the schema decisions in §10 Q1–Q2, and produces an artifact that’s immediately useful for inspection. The training-architecture question (X → Y → Z, in that order) follows after we have a stable patient-node data substrate. The new planning session should reference this thinking doc and pick up from §9 Scenario Y’s schema and ETL details.


Parallelization Analysis (if we ever execute)
Surfaces touched per scenario:


















































SurfaceScenario XScenario YBackend APINoYes (Maureen as KG entity in browsing API)Frontend componentNoYes (new “Patient” card in KG Composition tab, or extension of existing)Worker handlerMaybe (training run dispatch)Yes (training run, anchor resolution, possibly PRS compute)Migration (backend/migrations.py)NoYes (Phase 8.5 + Phase F.2 + nodeID column on ModsPatient)MCP toolMaybeYes (mods_kg_get_patient_node, etc.)DB-stored configNoNoDocsBrief writeupPhase 12.0 writeupTestsYes (run-level integration)Yes (schema + materialization + training-run integration)
Parallel split (Scenario Y):

Phase 8.5 variant ingest, Phase F.1–F.2 anchor service, and Phase 13 Tier 1 trajectory features can all happen in parallel — they touch different services and tables.
The Phase 12.0 schema (entity_type=‘patient’, new edges) must land before the training-architecture experiments — serial dependency.
Within training, Options A/B/C runs are fully parallel (each is an independent H100 job).
Frontend KG Composition tab update for “patient as browsable entity” can run in parallel with backend schema once API contract is defined.

Collision hotspots:

backend/migrations.py — Phase 8.5 + Phase F.2 + Phase 12.0 schema each add a migration. Coordinate migration numbers; batch the work to one session if possible.
backend/mcp_servers/mods_server.py — both Phase F and Phase 12.0 add MCP tools. Single-session preferred to avoid merge drift.
frontend/src/components/ModsKGCompositionTab.jsx — Phase F.4 (anchor inspection sub-tab) and Phase 12.0 (patient as entity card) both touch this file. Sequence them.
Cloud SQL load — variant connectors ingest is multi-GB; coordinate timing with any other large migrations.

Verify-how per surface:

Schema migration: column_exists / table_exists guards verified by running migration twice; final psql count audit.
Backend API: pytest with a fixture patient (Maureen-like synthetic).
Frontend: preview_* walkthrough of the KG Composition tab with Maureen visible as a card; click to expand should show resolved CURIEs, edge breakdown, 1-hop neighborhood.
MCP tool: invoke from a claude terminal session, verify output shape.
Training run: Spearman ρ on RGCC against the existing Phase 7.5 validation harness (Run B baseline = ρ 0.351 on PrimeKG — ⚠ superseded pending restatement, GH #324; re-run per timepoint before using as a comparator).
Personalized-loss experiment: side-by-side MRR + ρ comparison against the current PDR2 baseline.

planning/population_supervised_outcome_p.title: Population-Supervised Outcome Prediction
planning/population_supervised_outcome_p.content:
Population-Supervised Outcome Prediction: A Planning Doc
Context
This doc started as paan_planning §5a — a short section sketching a reframe: instead of building a KG that fits Maureen and using her labels for validation, build a KG trained on thousands of (genome, drug, outcome) triples from diverse populations, and let Maureen’s predictions emerge from where her genome lands in that learned geometry.
It got promoted to its own doc because you flagged the underlying prompt as “one of the most important… may be our greatest project”, and because the prompt actually contains three intertwined threads that all need real space to breathe:

The SHEPHERD lift. SHEPHERD is the closest prior art we found (paan_planning §8a), but it’s diagnostic, phenotype-only, and trained on 40,000 synthetic patients. What does it look like to lift the general shape of the idea into therapeutic repurposing? And specifically: why did SHEPHERD need synthetic patients in the first place?
Patient cohorts as training data. The user’s framing: “real patients resembling Maureen, with data we can also get about Maureen, trained on that to predict what an arbitrary example would generate.” This is standard supervised ML — train/val/test, batched, loss-on-outcome. It feels surprising that nobody’s done this cleanly for individual repurposing.
Architecture and unification. Are NBFNet/ULTRA still right? Now that the supervision isn’t “is this KG triple true” but “did drug Y produce outcome Z in subject X” — should the fundamental neural net architecture change? And across the many data sources we’ve identified, what’s the common pattern, and how do we handle the calibration/scale mess?

Three threads, one underlying question: how do we scale training signal beyond Maureen’s own labels to predict her outcomes?
This doc is exploratory — it walks the paths honestly before recommending a starting point in §7.

1. Lifting SHEPHERD — what synthetic patients gave them, and the analog that fits us
1.1 Why SHEPHERD needed synthetic patients
SHEPHERD (Zitnik lab, npj Digital Medicine 2025) trained on ~40,000 simulated rare-disease patients and evaluated on 465 real UDN patients. Why simulate?
Two reasons, in order of importance:
Reason A — Scale for metric learning. SHEPHERD’s loss is contrastive: pull (patient embedding, true causal gene embedding) together; push non-matches apart. Contrastive losses need many examples to populate the metric space meaningfully. 465 patients is not enough; 40,000 is. Real UDN patients are bottlenecked by the rate of clinical enrollment plus the rarity of definitive causal-gene diagnosis — they couldn’t get to 40K with real patients even in principle on a publication timeline.
Reason B — Supervision target is exactly known from the generator. This is the load-bearing observation. In SHEPHERD’s domain:

Sample a disease D (one of 2,134 rare-disease nodes).
Sample HPO phenotype terms for D using the known disease→phenotype edges, with some noise/dropout.
Sample candidate Ensembl genes including the actual causal gene for D plus distractors.

The “causal gene” label for each synthetic patient is known by construction, not estimated. There’s no measurement noise; the supervision signal is exact. Synthetic patients work because the simulator produces labeled training examples without ambiguity.
The key generalization: synthetic supervision is well-defined for problems where the simulator dictates the label. Diagnosis from phenotypes is one such problem. Many others — especially most therapeutic ones — are not.
1.2 Why the synthetic-patient trick doesn’t lift to drug repurposing
Try to imagine what “synthetic patient with synthetic drug response” would look like.

Sample a patient genome G.
Sample a drug D.
Generate an outcome label O.

What’s O? If O is “the response a real patient with genome G would have to drug D,” that’s the function we’re trying to learn. We can’t synthesize it; we’d need a calibrated mechanistic simulator from (G, D) to O, and that doesn’t exist at the scale or breadth we need. If such a simulator existed, we’d already have solved the problem and wouldn’t need ML.
So the SHEPHERD playbook doesn’t extend cleanly. Synthetic patients buy you scale only when the label comes free.
1.3 The right analog: proxy patients, not synthetic ones
What SHEPHERD solved with simulation, we solve with proxies. Cell lines, patient-derived xenografts (PDX), organoids, TCGA patients on standard-of-care, GENIE patients on named regimens — these are real biological entities with real measurements that produce real labels. They’re not the target patient (Maureen), but they’re not synthetic either.
Scale comparison:






























WhatSHEPHERD analogUsTargetone real UDN patient at inference timeone real patient (Maureen) at inference timeTraining scale40,000 synthetic patients~1,000 cell lines (GDSC, CCLE) + ~1,000 cell lines × CRISPR (DepMap) + ~11,000 TCGA patients + ~5,500 CRC patients in MSK-CHORD and ~1,500-3,000 in GENIE BPC (not the ~100K main GENIE registry — see §4.5) + hundreds of PDX/organoidsLabel qualityexact (by construction)real measurements, but with assay noise + biological gapsLabel semanticscausal gene rankIC50 / AUC / % cell death / RECIST / OS / TGI — heterogeneous
We get more training data than SHEPHERD did, and it’s real biology, not simulated. The cost: heterogeneous label scales, distribution shift from cell line to patient, and identifier-reconciliation overhead. Those costs are addressable. The benefit is the supervision is grounded in measurement.
1.4 What does actually transfer from SHEPHERD
Three pieces survive the lift:

A patient can be meaningfully embedded into a biomedical KG, and the embedding can drive useful ranking. SHEPHERD shows this empirically for diagnostic ranking; the inductive bias is preserved across diagnostic and therapeutic tasks.
Inductive scoring on novel patients without retraining. Critical for clinical workflows — when Maureen’s data updates (new RGCC test, new lab value), we don’t want to retrain.
Patient-as-subgraph is a real architectural option. PDR2 (and our current direction) makes patient an explicit node. SHEPHERD makes patient = a set of phenotype terms that induce a subgraph. The patient gets no learned embedding of their own — their representation is constructed at inference by aggregating over the induced subgraph. This option is worth seriously considering — see §5.

1.5 The architectural choice this forces
Patient-as-subgraph vs patient-as-explicit-node:



































Patient-as-subgraphPatient-as-explicit-nodeInference flexibilityExcellent — new patient = new subgraph, no retrainingLimited — need the patient in the training graphLearned representationNone of their own; built from subgraph at inferenceEach patient gets a learned embeddingPDR2 trickDoesn’t applyFoundation frozen + small learnable loss weights (1,802 of them) → exactly worksMaureen-specific overfittingLowHigh if not carefulGeneralization to a brand-new patientFreeRequires graph augmentation + (per PDR2) fine-tune the loss weights
PDR2 picks the second column because its trick — freezing the foundation and only training the loss — lets the patient’s edges influence the model without learning a patient-specific embedding that wouldn’t generalize.
We could pick either. We could pick both: subgraph-style at inference, explicit-node-style at training for the cohort of proxies. The recommendation lands in §7.

2. Patient cohorts as training data — the standard ML framing
2.1 The framing in one paragraph
Input: (subject_features, drug_features). Output: response_label. Train on many (subject, drug) pairs from many subjects; validate on held-out (subject, drug) pairs; test on a held-out cohort or a strictly held-out drug list. Loss is regression on response, or pairwise/listwise ranking, or survival, depending on the response type. At inference, encode Maureen → predict her response → rank drugs by predicted response.
This is the standard cancer drug response prediction (CDRP) setup. The user’s framing is correct.
2.2 What the user thinks vs what the field has actually done
The user wrote: “It’s hard to believe nobody else has thought about doing this for drug repurposing to the individual.”
The honest answer: many people have thought about it, just not exactly this. The cancer drug response prediction literature is large. Representative papers:

PaccMann (Manica et al., Mol. Pharm. 2019; arXiv:1811.05741) — attention over gene expression + drug SMILES → IC50.
DeepDR (Chiu et al., BMC Med. Genomics 2019) — autoencoder for mutation + expression → drug response.
MOLI (Sharifi-Noghabi et al., Bioinformatics 2019) — multi-omics late-integration network for drug response.
DeepCDR (Liu et al., Bioinformatics 2020) — drug molecular graph + omics + ConvNet → drug response.
CDRscan, tCNNs, CaDRReS-Sc, scDEAL, scPDS — variations on the same theme.

What’s actually under-served — and where our setup is unusually well-positioned — is the intersection of:

Drug repurposing. Existing approved or already-in-trial drugs, not de novo discovery.
Individual patient resolution. Not “what works for KRAS-mutant CRC” but “what works for this CRC patient with this expression profile and this germline.”
Outcome-supervised ranking, not IC50 regression in cell lines. The deliverable is “rank these 500 drugs for this patient by expected effect,” not “predict log(IC50) accurately across the GDSC test set.”
A patient with our depth of supervision. Maureen has RGCC (224 drug x % cell death labels over 112 drugs), Caris WTS (whole-transcriptome), Caris WES (somatic + germline variants), Invitae germline, treatment history with response, longitudinal labs. Most patients in any cohort lack one or more of these. The user’s “real patients resembling Maureen, with data we can also get about Maureen” criterion is genuinely restrictive — and is the empirical reason nobody’s done this cleanly. There aren’t many Maureens.

So: the field has done the encoder + drug-feature + response-head architecture many times. What we’d add is (a) the repurposing framing, (b) the individual focus driven by an unusually-instrumented anchor patient, and (c) outcome-ranking rather than IC50-regression objectives.
2.3 What does the loss function look like?
Several options, and the right one depends on what we want to deliver:

MSE / Huber regression on response. Standard. Works when the response is on a single scale (e.g., log(IC50) within GDSC). Breaks across sources with different scales unless we calibrate first.
Pairwise ranking (BPR, RankNet). Each training example is a triplet (subject, drug_a, drug_b) where drug_a was better. The loss pushes the model to score drug_a higher than drug_b for that subject. Robust to scale differences — only the order matters. This is probably the right primary loss for individual repurposing: we don’t actually care about predicted IC50; we care about ranking the candidate drugs.
Listwise (NDCG-based). Generalizes pairwise to “for this subject, the top-K drugs should be these.” Good if we have many drugs tested in each subject, which we do in RGCC and GDSC.
Survival losses (Cox, DeepSurv, DeepHit). Needed if we use TCGA or GENIE OS/PFS as labels. Handles censoring.
PDR2-style composite. L = L_base − λ₁·L_prs − λ₂·L_expr where L_base is any of the above and the patient-prior terms modulate scores based on PRS and biomarker deviations. Compatible with the above as a wrapper.

If we had to pick one for v0: pairwise BPR within source. Rank-based, scale-robust, well-understood, and aligned with the actual deliverable (drug ranking for a patient).
2.4 Validation, in layers
The whole point of the population-tapestry approach is that we have thousands of proxy subjects (cell lines, PDX, organoids, TCGA patients), so the standard held-out-test-set move is available and used. The reason validation in this setup still deserves its own section is that there are at least four distinct layers of validation, each progressively harder, and it’s easy to conflate them. The patient-of-1 framing only bites at the last layer.


Layer 1 — Standard held-out within the training source. Train on 80% of GDSC, validate on 10%, test on 10%. Standard ML practice. This is exactly the same proxy-patient data used for training, partitioned. There is no problem here — it’s the cleanest validation we have, and it’s what we’d report as the primary internal metric for the trained model.


Layer 2 — Cross-source generalization. Train on GDSC, validate on CCLE over the shared cell-line subset. Tests whether the model generalized or just learned GDSC’s idiosyncrasies. Harder because of the Haibe-Kains 2013 receipt — measurements disagree across panels even on the same cell lines. Per-source decoder heads (Path B in §3.3) keep this layer from becoming an architectural problem.


Layer 3 — Cell-line → patient transfer. Train on cell lines, evaluate on TCGA real-patient outcomes (OS, PFS) under the corresponding regimens where known. This is the field’s central hard problem (gotcha #2 in §6). Many published cell-line-trained models look great on Layers 1–2 and fail Layer 3 badly. It’s why the PDX and organoid consortia exist.
Data source for this layer (added 2026-09-24). Layer 3 was specified here without a
dataset attached to it. The candidates are MSK-CHORD (5,543 CRC patients) and GENIE
BPC CRC (1,485→3,000+, curated line-of-therapy). Note this is not in tension with §9’s
exclusion of EHR mining: that exclusion is about using real-world cohorts as training
labels, where line-of-therapy confounding is fatal. Using them to check whether a
cell-line-trained ranker holds up against real outcomes is a weaker claim that tolerates
confounding far better — and it is the only way to measure Layer 3 at all. PDX
(Novartis PDXE: ~1,000 models, 62 treatments, mRECIST incl. CRC) and the CRC organoid
studies (OPTIC: PPV 0.78 / NPV 0.80 / AUC 0.78–0.88 vs patient response) sit between
Layers 2 and 3 and are the cleanest bridge, because they carry molecular depth and
per-drug response.


Layer 4 — Population → this specific patient. Predict Maureen’s RGCC drug rankings; predict her future RECIST outcomes from pre-treatment features. This is the layer where “patient-of-1” actually bites: RGCC gives us 224 labels for Maureen — meaningful internal signal — but there is only one Maureen. We can’t validate “did the model learn precision medicine for her” the way we’d validate a normal model, because there’s no cohort of comparably-instrumented patients to test against.


Layers 1–3 are standard machine learning territory and don’t require any special framing. Layer 4 is where the discomfort lives. Realistic moves for Layer 4:

Drug-held-out within Maureen. Train on 80% of her RGCC drugs (and on all the proxy cohort data); test on the held-out 20%. Tests whether the model generalizes across drugs for the same patient.
Time-held-out. Use Maureen’s pre-2026 data to predict her 2026 RECIST outcomes. Strict but low-resolution (few clinical episodes).
Held-out variant signature. Hold out all proxy subjects sharing a Maureen-defining variant or signature from training; test on Maureen. Tests variant-specific generalization vs cohort averages.
RGCC-as-proxy-for-clinical-outcome. Even Maureen’s RGCC isn’t the actual deliverable (clinical response is). The ex-vivo CTC assay → in-vivo response gap (gotcha #8) is part of the Layer 4 validation budget, not separate from it.

The point of separating these layers: don’t muddle them. Standard supervised ML on proxy patients gives us Layer 1 cleanly. The further you climb, the more uncomfortable validation becomes, but each layer is a separately reportable signal — and Layer 4 being hard is not a reason to skip Layers 1–3.
2.5 The intended-output problem (the deeper one)
Layer 4 above actually understates what’s happening. The model’s drug ranking for Maureen is the intended output of the system. Validating it the standard ML way would require a ground-truth label for “the best drug for Maureen.” That label doesn’t exist — if it did, we wouldn’t need the model. This isn’t a defect in our setup; it’s the same problem all of personalized medicine prediction faces. We never observe the counterfactual outcomes of what would have happened to her on the drugs she didn’t take. The standard ML loop (train → predict → check) breaks because the “check” step has no ground-truth target.
Terminology note. This is, technically, zero-shot per-subject inference: Maureen wasn’t in training; we encode her features and produce a ranking without ever having seen labels for her. ULTRA and PDR2 already use “zero-shot” for the KG-level analog (apply a pre-trained model to a never-seen KG); the subject-level version is the same idea, one rung down. What separates our setup from standard zero-shot ML benchmarks is that those benchmarks do have ground truth on held-out classes — zero-shot CUB-200 birds, you know what species the test image actually is. We don’t. So we’re doing zero-shot inference in a regime where standard zero-shot evaluation doesn’t apply. The one validation path the zero-shot literature does offer that survives this gap is reasoning-chain / attribute-attribution validation — validate the reasoning even when you can’t validate the answer (“the model ranks drug X high because Maureen has biomarker Y, and drug X is known to act on the Y pathway; is that chain biologically plausible?”). That’s what the four shifted answers below are circling.
So what does validation mean here? Four shifted answers:

Validate the learning, not the answer. Layers 1–3 show the model captures (subject, drug) → response patterns where we have labels. That’s necessary for trusting its Maureen prediction, not sufficient. The right analog is a clinical trial: we don’t validate “this drug works for patient X”; we validate “this drug works in a population that includes patient X,” and then trust the inference one step further.
Validate against the imperfect proxy we do have. RGCC gives 224 labels for Maureen. Drug-held-out within her tests whether the model can recover the rest. This validates against an ex-vivo CTC assay whose own concordance with in-vivo clinical outcome is an open empirical question (gotcha #8). Useful, partial, not definitive.
Reframe to decision-support validation. The deliverable isn’t “the right drug.” It’s “candidates worth investigating, with reasoning a clinician/patient can evaluate.” Validation under this framing is downstream: does the recommendation change action and improve outcomes vs. the alternative process (SOC, intuition, a coin flip)? Different statistics, different cadence — the framing used for clinical decision support systems, not pure prediction models.
Eventually, prospective outcomes — slowly. Predictions made at time T checked against what was tried and how Maureen responded. One patient is statistically thin, but a pattern accumulates over years of decisions. The counterfactual outcomes (what the other drugs would have done) remain unobserved.

The right mental model: this is a decision support tool whose final output is itself the deliverable. The model surfaces a best guess from population evidence. Validation of the learning process is necessary and reportable (Layers 1–3). Full validation of the specific prediction for Maureen is partial at best — and that’s not a defect, it’s the epistemology of the problem. Anyone who claims they can fully validate a personalized prediction without observing counterfactuals is selling something.
2.6 The structural consequence — PDR2’s paths are not optional
The framing above has a sharp architectural implication that’s worth naming directly. If the system’s job is to surface recommendations that we’d only act on if they look like good ideas, and the way they “look like good ideas” is by being defensible through inspectable reasoning a domain expert can evaluate, then the reasoning surface is structurally necessary — not a nice-to-have, not interpretability theatre, but the actual mechanism of validation.
Put plainly: by definition, the validation of any personalized recommendation we’d ever act on is validation of the logical path that produced it. If the path looks like a good idea, we try it. If it doesn’t, we don’t. There is no other operating mode.
This makes PDR2/ULTRA’s KG-completion track (Track 1 in §5.4) load-bearing in a way that wasn’t obvious before. NBFNet-style path-based models don’t just produce a score for (Maureen, treats, drug_X) — they produce one or more paths through the KG that justify the score:

Maureen → has_variant → BRAF_V600E → activates → MAPK_pathway → inhibited_by → BRAF_inhibitors → drug_X

A clinician (or the user, or Maureen herself) reads that path and either says “yes, this is biologically defensible” or “no, that path goes through a known-spurious edge, skip this drug.” The path is the unit of validation. The score, on its own, is unactionable.
Track 2 (cell-line bi-encoder, §5.4) does not have this property. It produces an opaque score from a learned (subject, drug) → response function. Without Track 1, we’d have a number with no reasoning behind it — and a number without reasoning is not something we’d act on.
This refines the two-track architecture recommendation:

Track 1 is not replaceable by Track 2. Even if Track 2 had higher Layer 1–3 accuracy, removing Track 1 would remove the reasoning surface — and the reasoning surface is the validation mechanism.
The combiner at inference must preserve at least one Track 1 path for every top candidate, not just rank by combined score.
Track 2’s scores are supplementary confidence; Track 1’s paths are the validation surface. A drug that Track 2 ranks high but for which Track 1 produces no defensible path is a flagged candidate worth investigating further, not an actionable recommendation.
Layers 1–3 (§2.4) remain necessary in this picture, but for a narrower reason than before: they validate that the model’s learning process generalized, so that the paths it produces aren’t memorized noise. Without that prior, even a beautiful-looking path is suspect.

This also gives a structural answer to a question we hadn’t quite asked directly: why a KG at all? The KG isn’t here because graphs are trendy or because PrimeKG was available. It’s here because the KG is the substrate on which reasoning paths exist, and reasoning paths are the only thing that survives as a validation mechanism when the intended output has no ground truth.

3. The data sources, examined — what’s the common pattern?
Don’t re-list every source — KG_CATALOG.md and the memory entries already do that. Here we focus on the unification question.
3.1 A common schema across all sources
Every patient-outcome data source can be cast as:

3.2 Two architectural paths through unification
Path A — Unify into a single response target. Force everything to a common abstraction. Example: convert all responses to “is this drug in the top-20% of effective drugs for this subject?” — a binary label that’s defined regardless of whether the underlying scale was IC50, AUC, RECIST, or OS. Trainable end-to-end with a single loss. Lossy: we throw away absolute response magnitude. Hard: the threshold (top-20%) is arbitrary and may not transfer biological meaning across sources.
Path B — Per-source decoder heads with shared encoder. Each source keeps its own scale. The (subject, drug) encoder is shared across sources — that’s where the generalization comes from. The response head is per-source: one head emits log(IC50), another emits RECIST probability, another emits hazard ratio. At training time, each batch goes through the appropriate head. At inference, we either pick one source’s head (the closest match to our deliverable) or combine multiple via meta-model.
Recommendation: Path B for MVP, Path A as a stretch goal. Path B is what the multi-task literature recommends when scales differ. It also makes the calibration question (§4) optional rather than required.

4. Calibration and scale — the genuinely hard problem
The user asked specifically: “Isn’t this what z-scaling is for? If that doesn’t get us all the way there, what do other people do?”
The honest answer is that z-scaling is necessary but nowhere near sufficient, and there’s a famous receipt for why.
4.1 What z-scaling does and doesn’t
Z-scaling centers and rescales a vector to mean 0, std 1. It’s the right answer when you want to compare two things on different scales but with the same meaning. It does nothing to fix two sources that disagree on the same measurement.
Concretely: if GDSC says paclitaxel has IC50 = 5 nM in cell line X and CCLE says paclitaxel has IC50 = 50 nM in the same cell line X, z-scaling each panel within itself doesn’t reconcile them — z(GDSC X) and z(CCLE X) come out at different points relative to their own panels’ distributions.
4.2 The Haibe-Kains receipt
Haibe-Kains et al. (Nature 2013, “Inconsistency in large pharmacogenomic studies”) showed exactly this empirically: GDSC and CCLE drug responses disagree on the same cell lines for many drugs, with Spearman correlations on shared subset ranging from near-zero to modest. The paper kicked off a multi-year reconciliation effort and motivated PharmacoDB and similar harmonization projects.
This isn’t a “we need better z-scoring” problem. It’s “the underlying assays disagree because of differences in concentration ranges tested, exposure duration, viability readout (CellTiter-Glo vs SRB vs syto60), and analysis pipeline.” Calibration in this space is genuinely hard, and people who say “just z-score” have not actually tried to do it across panels.
4.3 Quantile normalization
Force the marginal distributions to match. Preserve ranks within each panel, destroy the absolute scale. This is OK if downstream is rank-based (BPR/NDCG). It’s not OK if downstream needs to predict an absolute IC50 because the absolute information is gone.
This pairs well with Path B + pairwise ranking loss. We don’t need absolute scale to rank drugs for a patient.
4.4 Linker drugs (empirical calibration)
Pick drugs that were tested in multiple panels. For GDSC ↔ CCLE there are ~250 shared drugs. Fit a regression (linear, monotonic, or isotonic) for each shared drug mapping source A’s response to source B’s response on shared subjects. Apply the regression to unshared drugs as a calibration prior.
This is analogous to ComBat batch correction in genomics or ratio normalization in cross-platform proteomics. It’s the empirical answer to the user’s question “can we calibrate things empirically somehow?” — yes, and there’s a literature on it.
4.5 Start with the biggest, cleanest single source
The user explicitly asked: “What if we started with the biggest / best / richest data set, and used only that?”
This is the right MVP move. Single-source training side-steps the calibration nightmare entirely. The candidate sources, ranked by suitability for our purpose:

GDSC v2 — ~1,000 cell lines × ~500 drugs, well-curated, open license, log(IC50) is a single coherent scale, and a substantial subset of the RGCC drug list (estimate ≥60 drugs; verify against actual RGCC panel before committing). Recommended starting point.
CCLE — ~1,000 cell lines, narrower drug panel than GDSC v2 but richer multi-omics on the cell lines. Strong second option, especially if we want to leverage transcriptome features the same way Caris WTS gives us them for Maureen.
DepMap — gene-knockout viability, not drug response. Different question. Useful for target-relevance reasoning, not direct drug-response prediction.
TCGA — real patients, outcome labels. Confounded by line-of-therapy + supportive care; mostly first-line outcomes; censoring; selection effects.
AACR GENIE (main registry) — 100K+ patient genomes, but essentially no treatment or
outcome data at all: it is genomics plus minimal clinical. Not a supervised training source.
(Corrected 2026-09-24 — an earlier revision of this doc counted these 100K as labelled
proxies and separately dismissed the labels as “inconsistent”. Both were wrong.)
GENIE BPC — the curated subset that does carry outcomes, via PRISSMM: treatment
histories with timing, imaging-based disease status, PFS, plus MSI/MMR/PD-L1. The CRC cohort
is released (BPC CRC v2.0-public, 1,485 patients; phase II expanded past 3,000). Free via
Synapse. Labels are deliberately curated, not inconsistent. Good v2 source.
MSK-CHORD — 5,543 CRC patients, MSK-IMPACT + NLP-derived outcomes, treatments and
timelines; public via cBioPortal, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (Nature 2024). Largest free CRC
clinicogenomic cohort. Panel sequencing only, so no transcriptome — which matters, because
Maureen’s strongest feature is her full WTS. Best used for Layer 3 (§2.4), not as a training
source.
Project Data Sphere — patient-level control-arm data from phase III oncology trials
including CRC, free and with no research proposal required. RECIST response + regimen,
usually no genomics.

Recommendation: GDSC v2 alone, train bi-encoder regression on log(IC50), validate on cell-line held-out, test on Maureen RGCC. If signal looks good, add CCLE next via linker-drug calibration or per-source decoder heads.
4.6 Could ensembles avoid the calibration problem?
The user asked: “Maybe an ensemble of models, each trained on its own data set, could avoid calibration issues?”
Yes — this is a real strategy. Train one model per source (GDSC model, CCLE model, TCGA model, …) and combine at inference time via mean rank, learned meta-model, or voting. No cross-source calibration is required at training time; each model only sees its own coherent scale.
The cost is that we lose cross-source generalization at training time. A drug tested only in CCLE doesn’t get the benefit of GDSC patterns. But for MVP, this loss is acceptable — and the ensemble is a defensible final architecture regardless. Many production recommender systems work this way.
4.7 Recommended calibration approach

Start single-source (GDSC v2). No calibration.
Add a second source (CCLE) via per-source decoder heads. Shared encoder, separate heads. No calibration between heads.
Add TCGA via survival head. Still no cross-source calibration; just another decoder head.
At inference, combine via rank fusion or learned meta-model. Don’t try to force calibration earlier than necessary.
Only attempt unified scaling (Path A) if rank-fusion is empirically worse than a unified target. Let empirics decide.


5. Architecture — is NBFNet/ULTRA still the right primitive?
The user asked: “Now that we aren’t exactly talking about predicting paths through graphs (or are we?), should we be rethinking the fundamental neural net architecture?”
The honest answer: NBFNet/ULTRA is right for one of the two things we want to do, and wrong for the other. The doc should be honest that we need both.
5.1 What NBFNet/ULTRA is good at

Path reasoning over a discrete KG: “drug treats disease that has gene that interacts with gene that has variant in patient.”
Compositional inductive bias — the same path patterns generalize to new entities.
Inductive in the new-entity sense — ULTRA generalizes to KGs it’s never seen.
Mature, runnable, already integrated (PDR2 foundation training is operational per memory).

For the KG-completion side of the problem — “given this KG, what drugs should rank highly for this disease?” — NBFNet/ULTRA is the right tool. PDR2 has shown it can be personalized with the patient-specific loss.
5.2 What NBFNet/ULTRA is bad at

Continuous-valued tabular regression. The output is a triple-existence probability, not a calibrated drug-response prediction.
Scaling to millions of labeled (subject, drug, response) triples where the labels are continuous and the subjects don’t have a natural KG-node representation. Cell lines aren’t really “in the KG” in a useful sense — they’re tabular objects with omics vectors.
Multi-modal fusion at the node level. A patient with gene expression, variants, methylation, and treatment history isn’t a single KG node — it’s a structured object with several modalities.

For the cell-line-to-patient supervised-learning side — “I have GDSC, learn (cell_line_features, drug_features) → log(IC50)” — NBFNet/ULTRA is not the natural primitive.
5.3 Alternatives, briefly

Bi-encoder regression. Industry-standard recommender pattern. Subject encoder (MLP or transformer over omics + variants) + drug encoder (MLP or GNN over molecular graph) + scalar head (dot product or MLP). Cheap to train. Scales to millions of pairs. The right primitive for the cell-line track.
Multi-modal fusion transformer. Token streams from each modality (genome tokens, expression tokens, drug structure tokens) + self-attention + head. PaccMann and DeepCDR are in this family. More expressive, more data-hungry, harder to debug.
Pretrained omics foundation models. scGPT (single-cell transcriptome, Cui et al. Nature Methods 2024), Geneformer (bulk transcriptome from large public corpora, Theodoris et al. Nature 2023). Use them as the subject encoder. Particularly relevant because Maureen’s WTS is one sample — having a pretrained encoder that’s seen millions of transcriptomes is a meaningful inductive bias.
Hybrid KG + tabular. Use KG embeddings (ULTRA over PrimeKG) as features for a tabular learner (transformer or gradient-boosting) on the (subject, drug, response) data. Two-stage but lets us reuse what we’ve already built and lets each piece do what it’s good at.
Equivariant / geometric (EquiBind, DiffDock). Operates on 3D molecular structure for binding-pose prediction. Tangential to our question — we’re predicting outcomes, not binding poses. Mention and move on.

5.4 Recommendation — a two-track architecture
The right move is not to pick one. It’s to run two tracks and combine at inference time. Note that §2.6 sharpens the role of Track 1: it’s not “the KG track we happen to have running” — it’s the load-bearing source of reasoning paths, which are the system’s actual validation surface. Track 2 cannot stand alone.


Track 1 — KG (PDR2 / ULTRA, existing). Patient-as-node + patient-specific loss. Optimized for KG-completion-style ranking. Foundation training is already operational. Outputs a relevance score and at least one explanatory path per (patient, drug, treats-relation). The path is the surface a clinician inspects to judge whether the recommendation is defensible.


Track 2 — Cell-line bi-encoder (new). Subject encoder over Caris-aligned expression features + variant features + (optional) pretrained scGPT/Geneformer embedding. Drug encoder over SMILES → Morgan fingerprint (v0) or learned drug graph embedding (v1). Output: predicted log(IC50) or pairwise rank. Trained on GDSC v2 first. Scores are supplementary confidence; this track does not produce paths and so cannot stand alone as a recommendation source.


Combiner at inference. Take Track 1 score, Track 1 path(s), and Track 2 score per drug. Fuse the scores via simple averaging or a learned meta-model, but require at least one Track 1 path per candidate that’s surfaced as actionable. Drugs that Track 2 ranks high but for which Track 1 has no defensible path are surfaced as a separate “flagged candidates worth investigating further” list, not as actionable recommendations.


This is the cell-line-to-patient transfer pattern used in scDEAL/scPDS/CaDRReS-Sc — pretrain on cell lines, condition on patient. The PaaN architecture is the unification of that with KG-based reasoning, with the KG-based reasoning playing the dominant role for validation reasons (§2.6).
The two-track approach has another property: each track can be debugged, validated, and ablated independently. If Track 1’s paths are biologically implausible, we can see it. If Track 2 has poor cell-line-to-patient transfer (the field’s central problem), we can see that too.

6. Critical gotchas — surface honestly, don’t bury

Haibe-Kains 2013 is real. Drug response measurements disagree across panels. Don’t assume calibration is solvable with z-scoring; it isn’t.
Cell-line → patient distribution shift is the field’s central problem. Many CDRP models look great on cell-line held-out and degrade sharply when moved to patient outcomes. Anything we build must take this seriously. The PDX consortia exist because of this.
The CDRP literature is large. Push back on “nobody’s done this.” The novelty is in the intersection (repurposing + individual + RGCC-anchored), not in the bi-encoder + drug-response framing per se.
Patient-of-1 only bites at Layer 4 of validation. Standard held-out test sets on proxy patients (cell lines, TCGA, etc.) work normally — that’s Layers 1–3 in §2.4. Layer 4 — does the proxy-trained model actually help this patient — is the uncomfortable one, because we have one Maureen.
Outcome semantics are heterogeneous. IC50, AUC, % cell death, RECIST, OS, TGI — different scales, different biological meaning. Path B (per-source heads) is the safe move.
NBFNet vs regression mismatch. Link prediction is not outcome regression. Architecture must match the task, not the comfort zone.
Maureen’s variants are rare in cell lines. Her inherited variant, her exact tumor profile, her CMS subtype — no cell line is a clean match. The model has to learn at a functional level (pathway, expression, signature), not at variant-identity level.
RGCC ≠ in vivo response. It’s an ex-vivo CTC assay. Concordance with clinical outcome is itself an open empirical question. Phase 7.5 has begun characterizing this (pdr_phase7_5_rgcc_writeup.md).
Identifier reconciliation is real work. Cell lines (CCLE/COSMIC/DepMap), drugs (DrugBank/ChEMBL/PubChem/NCIt), genes (Ensembl/HGNC/Entrez). The Composition primitive helps but isn’t free.
Ensemble combination is hard. Combining an IC50 prediction + a survival hazard + a KG-completion score into a single rank requires care. Rank-fusion is the cheap first move; learned combiners come later.
SHEPHERD’s synthetic-patient trick does not lift. Therapeutic supervision isn’t simulatable. Real proxies (cell lines, PDX, organoids, real cohorts) are the answer.
TCGA outcomes are mostly first-line. Most drug × patient combinations are unobserved. Causal-inference territory if we lean on TCGA seriously.
AACR GENIE’s main registry has no outcome labels at all — it is genomics plus minimal clinical, so it is not a training set on any day. The outcomes live in GENIE BPC, a separately curated subset whose CRC cohort is released and is consistent. Corrected 2026-09-24; the earlier “inconsistent labels” framing was wrong in both directions.
Patient-as-node requires the patient in the training graph. PDR2’s trick (foundation frozen, 1,802 learnable loss weights) is what makes this actually work without overfitting. If we switch backbones (bi-encoder, transformer), we lose this architecture and need to redesign personalization. Worth knowing before we commit.
Removing the KG-path track removes the system’s validation surface. Track 1 (PDR2/ULTRA) is not replaceable by Track 2 (bi-encoder regression) alone — see §2.6. A black-box regressor produces opaque scores that no domain expert can sanity-check, and we will not act on un-reasoned scores. Don’t optimize Track 1 away in pursuit of Track 2 accuracy, and don’t replace path-based KG models with non-explanatory KG models (plain DistMult/ComplEx without path tracing) for the same reason.


7. Recommended minimum viable experiment
Cheap, falsifiable, runs in days.

Source: GDSC v2 only. Single source first. No calibration. ~1,000 cell lines × ~500 drugs.
Subject features: gene expression vector (CCLE-aligned where overlap exists) + variant burden. For Maureen: Caris WTS-aligned expression + Caris/Invitae variant calls. Compute the feature vector once; cache.
Drug features: SMILES → 1024-bit Morgan fingerprint. Simple, fast, no model needed. Upgrade to learned drug graph embedding in v1.
Architecture: bi-encoder regression. Two small MLPs (subject encoder: 512 → 256 → 128; drug encoder: 1024 → 256 → 128). Head: concatenate + 2-layer MLP → predict log(IC50). Total params well under 1M.
Loss: MSE on log(IC50) for v0. Pairwise BPR on (subject, drug_better, drug_worse) for v1.
Train/val/test: blind on both subjects and drugs — strictly held-out cell lines AND strictly held-out drugs. Hardest split. Reports true generalization.
Maureen evaluation: encode her via Caris WTS-aligned features. Predict log(IC50) for the drug overlap with her RGCC panel. Compute Spearman ρ between predicted log(IC50) and her RGCC % cell death. Positive ρ with reasonable confidence = the approach is alive.
Compare to: PDR2 foundation Track-A baseline (Phase 7.5 ρ = +0.351 on PrimeKG) — ⚠ that comparator is superseded pending restatement (GH #324): it was computed on RGCC labels averaged across her two draws, which flattened the 12 drugs that inverted by class. Restate it per timepoint before using it as the bar. If the bi-encoder is competitive or complementary, the two-track combination is worth pursuing.
Cost: a few days for v0. Roughly one foundation-training-equivalent in compute. Cheap relative to the foundation work already running.

Decision gate: if ρ on Maureen is meaningfully positive (say > +0.15) with the cell-line-only model, the cell-line → patient transfer works for our setup and the two-track architecture is worth building out. If ρ is near zero or negative, the transfer doesn’t work for Maureen and we need to think harder (organoid data, PDX, cohort matching, or restricting the model to a Caris-similarity-weighted subset).

8. Open questions, consolidated
Not pre-decided. These survive into the next round of thinking.

Patient-as-node (PDR2-style) vs patient-as-subgraph (SHEPHERD-style) at inference? Recommendation defaulted to PDR2-style for Track 1 because it’s running, but the subgraph approach may matter when we add new patients.
Path A (unified target) vs Path B (per-source heads)? Recommendation defaulted to Path B; revisit if signal is strong enough that calibration would unlock more.
Cell lines first, or jump to PDX/organoids? Cell-line first for scale; PDX/organoid as v2 when we’ve learned what the cell-line-only model can’t do.
Maureen’s RGCC: train on it (drug-held-out) or strictly validate-only? v0 keeps RGCC strictly held-out so we know the cell-line model alone can transfer; v1 may use drug-held-out RGCC for fine-tuning.
TCGA outcomes useful or hopelessly confounded? Worth a separate explore — survival head trained on TCGA could complement IC50 head; the confounding is real but maybe addressable with line-of-therapy stratification.
How aggressively to lean on omics foundation models (scGPT, Geneformer) for the subject encoder? Worth a single-sweep comparison early; if pretrained encoders dominate, the architecture pivots toward foundation-model-fine-tuning.
Does the two-track architecture stay two tracks, or do we eventually fuse into a single unified model? Probably stays two tracks for a long time — each is debuggable on its own.


9. What we are explicitly not proposing
To prevent scope creep and to be honest about what we ruled out:

Synthetic patients à la SHEPHERD. The supervision target isn’t simulatable for therapy. Proxy patients (cell lines, PDX, organoids, real cohorts) replace this role.
A pivot away from PDR2. PDR2 stays as Track 1. We run a parallel Track 2 (bi-encoder regression on cell lines) and combine at inference. Both contribute; neither is sacrificed.
Mining EHR for “patients like Maureen” who got drug X and predicting OS — as a training signal. Too confounded by line-of-therapy, supportive care, selection effects, and lack of matched-control patients. Refined 2026-09-24: this exclusion is about training. The same cohorts (MSK-CHORD, GENIE BPC) are legitimate for Layer 3 validation (§2.4), where the claim is weaker and confounding is tolerable. Do not conflate the two uses.
A unified single-loss model spanning all sources. Calibration is too hard for MVP. Per-source decoder heads with shared encoder is the safer move.
Equivariant / geometric models (DiffDock, EquiBind). Wrong task — they’re for binding pose prediction, not outcome prediction.


TL;DR

The SHEPHERD lift exists, but the synthetic-patient piece doesn’t transfer. The analog for us is proxy patients (cell lines / PDX / organoids / TCGA / GENIE), which are real biology with real labels at population scale.
Patient cohorts as training data is the standard cancer drug response prediction (CDRP) setup, and the literature is large (PaccMann, DeepDR, MOLI, DeepCDR, …). What’s novel about our setup is the intersection: repurposing + individual + RGCC-anchored + outcome-ranking objective.
The right loss is probably pairwise ranking (rank drug A > drug B for this patient), not absolute response regression. Rank-based losses sidestep the calibration nightmare.
Calibration is genuinely hard — z-scoring is necessary but nowhere near sufficient (Haibe-Kains 2013). Best practical answer: single-source first (GDSC v2); add sources via per-source decoder heads + rank-fusion at inference; only attempt unified calibration via linker drugs if rank-fusion empirically underperforms.
NBFNet/ULTRA is right for Track 1 (KG path reasoning) and wrong for Track 2 (cell-line tabular regression). Use a bi-encoder for Track 2 and combine at inference. Don’t make one architecture do both jobs.
Validation is layered (§2.4) and bounded by an epistemic ceiling (§2.5). Layers 1–3 work the standard way on proxy patients (held-out from training source, cross-source, cell-line→patient). The model’s prediction for Maureen IS the intended output — there’s no ground-truth label for “her best drug” to check against. The right framing is decision support, not closed-loop prediction.
The validation surface is the reasoning, not the answer (§2.6). Because we’d only act on a recommendation that looks defensible by inspectable reasoning, validation is — by definition — validation of the logical path. This makes PDR2/ULTRA’s KG paths structurally non-negotiable. Track 2’s scores are supplementary confidence; Track 1’s paths are the validation surface. A black-box regressor without paths is unactionable regardless of accuracy. This also answers “why a KG at all?”: the KG is the substrate on which reasoning paths exist.
MVP: GDSC v2 + bi-encoder regression + Maureen RGCC as held-out validation. A few days of compute. If Spearman ρ > +0.15, the approach is alive.

planning/temporal_patient_modeling_plann.title: Temporal Patient State Modeling — Planning
planning/temporal_patient_modeling_plann.content:
Phase 13 — Temporal Patient State Modeling — Planning Document
Status: PLANNING (not yet started)
Created: 2026-05-07
Owner: whafa
Master plan reference: PDR_PIPELINE_PLAN.md § Phase 13
Companion writeup template: pdr_phase0_gpkg_writeup.md
Adjacent planning doc: pdr_phase8.5_variant_kg_planning.md — variant-aware KG; complementary not overlapping.

Seed for a dedicated planning session on representing temporal change in Maureen’s biomarker, genomic-test, and clinical data — both as immediate snapshot-policy fixes and as deeper temporal-graph architecture work.


1. Problem statement
Maureen’s health record changes daily. New labs come in (CEA, LDH, albumin, lymphocytes). Imaging gets re-read. RGCC and Caris panels can be repeated. Symptoms progress and regress. Treatments start and stop. Each of these is a trajectory of a patient parameter, not a static fact — and the trajectory is often clinically more informative than any single point on it. CEA doubling time predicts CRC recurrence months before imaging shows it. A falling albumin trajectory during chemo signals failure-to-thrive even when the absolute value is in range.
Our current MODS architecture treats patient state as a snapshot. Two distinct concerns hide inside that:
(1) The snapshot policy bug. When the same parameter has multiple values across time (e.g., re-tested gene expression, repeated blood panels), our consumer code currently picks the earliest available value rather than the most recent. This is a near-term fix that can be done independently. Findings from a code audit (2026-05-07):

mods_kgia_profile_service.py::_build_biomarker_series (line 389) is correct — uses ORDER BY v.ts DESC LIMIT 1 via LATERAL join to take the latest value, with prior-value capture for trend computation.
mods_kgia_profile_service.py::_build_genomic_alterations (line 236) is the bug. Orders rows by gene only — no temporal sort. When Maureen has multiple genomic test reports (e.g., 2024 Caris + 2025 Caris re-test) covering the same gene, all rows are returned in alphabetical-by-gene order. Whatever consumer dedupes by gene picks the first row encountered — typically the earliest report by insertion order.
mods_kgia_profile_service.py::_build_gene_expression (line 265) has the same bug — ordered by regulation and expression_value, never by report_date.
mods_snapshot_service.py::_build_biomarkers_section (line 189) is correct in intent — returns the full trajectory, not a single value. Whether the LLM downstream picks the right value is a separate question.

Recommended fix for (1): add ModsGenomicTestReport.reported_date.desc().nullslast() as the primary sort key in _build_genomic_alterations and _build_gene_expression, then dedupe by gene at the consumer level taking the first row per gene (which will now be the most recent). Two-line code change in each method.
(2026-10-03: shipped. Both methods now sort on report_date DESC NULLS LAST (the column on the alteration and expression rows, not the report table). The date gaps still open are in §8.2.)
(2) Representing trajectory itself. This is the deeper concern. Currently we have no way to feed change into the link-prediction model — only state. The CEA trajectory over the last six months is invisible to the GNN unless we encode it as features somewhere. This requires architectural decisions, not just a code fix.
What the papers do (and don’t)
Audited 2026-05-07 for temporal handling in PDR1 and PDR2:

PDR1 (Oğuztüzün 2025) uses patient_merge.py to ingest UK Biobank patient data. Features used: PRS for AD, PRS for comorbidities, and protein biomarker expression values. Each is a single scalar per patient. No temporal modeling.
PDR2 (Oğuztüzün 2026) uses ULTRA + KGIA loss with --lambda1 for genetic risk and --lambda2 for biomarker influence. Same shape: per-patient scalars at fine-tune time. No temporal modeling.

Conclusion: neither paper provides a precedent for temporal patient modeling in this drug-repurposing-by-KG-completion lineage. If we want trajectory-aware ranking, we are operating beyond the published architecture. This is a research direction, not a reproduction task. Two implications:

No paper-target benchmark for closure. Phase 0 closes against KG-Predict’s published metrics; Phase 13 doesn’t have an equivalent. We need to design our own validation criteria (see § 5 closure criteria).
Literature search is part of the work. Outside the PDR lineage, temporal KG completion is a real research subfield (TKG models like TNTComplEx, RE-NET; clinical-AI temporal patient models; multimodal architectures combining time-series with KGs). We need to map this landscape before architectural commitment.

Why this matters specifically for Maureen
CRC has one of the strongest “trajectory-matters-more-than-state” stories in oncology:

CEA can be normal at diagnosis even with metastatic disease. Doubling time predicts recurrence with a months-long lead vs imaging.
Tumor markers and inflammatory markers (LDH, albumin, neutrophil-lymphocyte ratio) have prognostic value as trajectories that single values lack.
Caris re-tests (if ordered) would let us see actual biological evolution of the tumor — which genes turn on/off under treatment pressure. That signal is invisible if we only carry the most recent test.
RGCC re-tests show whether her tumor’s drug sensitivity profile is shifting. Critical for adaptive therapy decisions.

For Phase 9 (current personalization plan) operating on a single snapshot, we lose all of this.

2. The five-tier framework
Approaches to representing temporal data in graphs, ordered from “easiest to ship” to “research project.”
Tier 1 — Trajectory features as static node attributes
Compute summary statistics from the time series and encode them as attributes on a single (current) node. The graph stays static. Per biomarker: most recent value, slope (regression of value vs time, last 3-6 months), variance / coefficient of variation, ratio to baseline, days since last out-of-range crossing, count of threshold crossings.
Pros: No model architecture changes. Fits any static GNN (PDR1, PDR2, anything). Keeps the KG human-auditable. Schema work is straightforward.
Cons: Loses interaction effects between biomarker trajectories. Requires manual feature engineering per biomarker. Limited to features humans think to compute.
Tier 2 — Multi-snapshot training
Build the KG at multiple time points (Maureen-as-of-2025-01-01, Maureen-as-of-2025-04-01, etc.) and train the model on the sequence.
Pros: Captures evolution. Lets the model learn to recognize concerning trajectories rather than relying on hand-crafted features.
Cons: Storage and compute cost balloons. The model still treats each snapshot as static unless we add temporal edges (which moves to Tier 3-4). Snapshot intervals are arbitrary given uneven sampling rates (genomic tests rare, labs frequent).
Tier 3 — Time-stamped edges (Temporal Knowledge Graph)
Every edge gets valid_from / valid_to timestamps. Add edges like (Maureen, had_value, CEA=8.2, 2025-03-15) and (Maureen, had_value, CEA=12.1, 2025-04-15). Query the graph “as of date X” to recover historical state.
Pros: Preserves full history. Standardized — TKG completion is a research subfield with established models (TNTComplEx, TeMP, RE-NET, ULTRA-Time variants).
Cons: Most TKG models are tested on event data (news, social), not clinical data — generalization is uncertain. Graph size balloons (every lab result becomes an edge). Most TKG models predict “what edge will exist at time T+1” rather than “given this trajectory, what drug ranks highest” — there’s a translation layer needed.
Tier 4 — Patient-as-node with trajectory-encoded embedding (recommended target)
The patient is a node (per Phase 12). Her embedding is computed by a small temporal encoder (1-D CNN or Transformer over her time series), and that embedding feeds into the graph as her node features. The graph model itself stays static; the temporal complexity is absorbed into a separate sub-model that produces her node representation.
Time series of labs / imaging / symptoms / genomic re-tests
    ↓
Temporal encoder (Transformer or LSTM)
    ↓
Patient embedding vector (e.g., 256-d)
    ↓
GNN (CompGCN / ULTRA) — Maureen is a node with this embedding as features
    ↓
Drug ranking

Pros: Cleanest separation of concerns. The temporal encoder can be small and trained on whatever per-patient data we have, while the GNN keeps its static-KG advantages. Captures interaction effects natively (Transformer self-attention over multivariate biomarker series). Ships in a reasonable time frame. Aligns naturally with Phase 12’s patient-as-node architecture.
Cons: Embedding becomes a learned summary — less human-auditable than Tier 1. Training requires patient outcome labels, of which we have one patient. Multi-patient generalization is unclear until we have a cohort. Encoder overfit risk on a single patient is real.
Tier 5 — Full continuous-time dynamic graph
Each edge appears and disappears as events occur. The model maintains time-varying embeddings via methods like TGN (Temporal Graph Networks) or DyRep. Most sophisticated, most expensive, most research-grade.
Pros: State of the art in temporal graph modeling.
Cons: Production-ready clinical implementations are rare. Probably overkill for our use case. Defer indefinitely.

3. Recommendation
A phased approach within Phase 13:
13.1 — Snapshot policy fix (immediate, in service of Phase 9). Fix the genomic-alteration and gene-expression dedup bugs documented in §1. Take most recent value per gene as the default, with a configurable “freshness window” (default: prefer values within 12 months over older ones). Should ship before Phase 9 starts.
13.2 — Tier 1 trajectory features (Phase 9 / 12 alignment). Add trajectory features as node attributes on the patient (Phase 12) or as patient-feature scalars (Phase 9 PDR1 path). Per biomarker: latest value, slope over 90 days, ratio to baseline, days since out-of-range crossing. CEA as the first test case. Cheap, well-scoped, captures most of the clinical signal.
13.3 — Tier 4 trajectory-encoded patient embedding (research project). Build the temporal encoder for the patient node. Genuinely a research project — needs validation against alternative architectures, needs an outcome labeling strategy, may benefit from a small cohort (even 2-3 patients) to validate the temporal encoder rather than overfitting Maureen.
Skip Tiers 2, 3, 5 unless we hit a specific blocker. Tier 1 + Tier 4 cover the practical clinical-AI space well. The other tiers are research artifacts that haven’t broken into clinical production.

4. Why CEA is the concrete first test case
For CRC specifically, CEA trajectory is THE textbook example of why temporal matters:

CEA can be normal at diagnosis even with metastatic disease.
Doubling time predicts recurrence months before imaging shows it.
Absolute value matters less than trend.
Threshold crossings (5 ng/mL conventional cutoff, 25%-rise-over-baseline) trigger clinical action.

If we get any temporal modeling in, CEA should be the test case. Maureen’s record likely has CEA values across her treatment history — there’s enough signal to validate that trajectory features improve drug ranking vs current-value-alone.
(2026-10-03: stale. CEA has no numeric value after 2025-09-16. Kaiser appears to have moved her surveillance marker to CA 19-9, so a CEA series flatlines to null. CA 19-9 should be the first series, then ctDNA MTM/mL once GH #131 parses the Signatera reports. See the mission spec §2.3 and §2.6.)
Concrete validation hypothesis: patient features that include CEA slope over 90 days produce different drug rankings than features using only the most recent CEA value, AND those rankings agree better with clinical guidelines for CRC progression (escalation to next-line therapy when CEA is rising).

5. Closure criteria
Phase 13 is unusual because no published paper provides a comparator. Closure criteria are internal:
13.1 (snapshot fix) is closed when:

For each parameter with multiple values per patient, the most recent value is selected by default.
A regression test against Maureen’s known data confirms specific known-correct values are now selected (e.g., 2025 Caris values not 2024).
No degradation in any existing Phase 7.5 RGCC validation metric.

13.2 (Tier 1 trajectory features) is closed when:

Trajectory features (slope, baseline ratio, crossings) are computed and stored for at least 5 prioritized biomarkers per patient.
CEA-trajectory feature improves Phase 7.5 RGCC validation by at least one of: ≥ 0.03 AUROC, ≥ 0.05 Spearman ρ.
Feature definitions are documented and reproducible.

(2026-10-03: the Phase 7.5 RGCC figures these criteria compare against are superseded. They pooled the two draws (GH #324), and the PDR2 v2 numbers were leak-driven (GH #214). A criterion now needs a clean, per-draw baseline. §8.4 proposes a within-patient alternative.)
13.3 (Tier 4 temporal encoder) is closed when:

A temporal encoder (LSTM or Transformer) is trained on Maureen’s biomarker history and produces a fixed-dim patient embedding.
The embedding is consumable by the Phase 12 patient-as-node architecture.
Compared to Tier 1 baseline: at least one validation metric improves by ≥ 0.02 AUROC or ≥ 0.03 ρ. Meaningful improvement is hard to define on a single patient — see open question 6.
Cohort generalization: when a second patient is added, the encoder produces meaningfully different embeddings without retraining.


6. Open questions


Biomarker priority list. Which parameters get trajectory features first? CEA is obvious. After that: LDH, albumin, neutrophil-lymphocyte ratio, platelet count, CA 19-9. What’s the cutoff?


Trajectory feature set per biomarker. Slope over what window? Baseline defined how (first value? rolling 6-month median?)? Threshold crossings against clinical reference range or per-patient personalized range?
