Uneven sampling rates. Genomic tests are sparse (months/years apart), labs are dense (days/weeks). Imaging is intermediate. Some biomarkers are sampled regularly during chemo cycles, irregularly otherwise. How does the temporal encoder handle this? Options: time-aware Transformer, irregular-interval RNN (e.g., GRU-D), interpolation to regular grid.


Missing data handling. Some biomarkers are tested rarely or only when specific treatments are considered. How do we represent “we just don’t have this for Maureen”? Mask the feature? Imputation? Treat absence as informative?


Outcome labeling strategy. What’s the supervision signal for training a temporal encoder? Options: treatment response (RECIST), tumor marker change as proxy, RGCC re-test changes, survival, hand-labeled clinical milestones. Each has issues.


Validating temporal modeling with one patient. Single-patient temporal encoders overfit easily. How do we validate? Options: hold out the most recent N months (predict her current state from past); leave-one-biomarker-out (train without CEA, predict CEA trajectory); sensitivity analysis (how much does ranking shift for plausible feature perturbations).


Imaging-derived features. RECIST measurements, tumor size, location. Are these biomarkers in the same model, or a separate modality? If separate, how do they integrate with the temporal encoder?


Genomic test repeat handling. When Caris is re-run, do we add a new variant edge with timestamp, or overwrite the old one? This intersects with Phase 8.5 (variant nodes). If a known variant is no longer detected on re-test, what does that mean — biological loss, or sampling difference?


Snapshot freeze for reporting. When a clinical recommendation is generated, we need to commit to a “decision time” snapshot for reproducibility. How do we represent that snapshot in the data model? Materialized snapshot table? Reconstruct on demand from time-stamped raw data?


Cohort dependency. Tier 4 generalization requires multiple patients. Maple is currently single-patient (Maureen). When does multi-patient become realistic, and does that change Phase 13 sequencing?



7. Suggested next steps for the planning session

Ship 13.1 (snapshot fix) immediately. It’s a two-line change in mods_kgia_profile_service.py plus a test. Don’t wait for the full Phase 13 plan.
Inventory available biomarker history for Maureen. Concrete count per parameter, with date range and sampling cadence. Drives prioritization in open question 1.
Literature spike on temporal patient modeling in clinical AI. Survey of Tier 1-4 approaches in clinical applications. Particular attention to: time-aware Transformers, irregular-interval RNNs, multimodal architectures combining time-series with KGs. Output: a one-page recommendation memo for the Tier 1 vs Tier 4 sequencing.
Design CEA as the validation anchor. Pre-register what improvement we expect from CEA trajectory features over CEA-current-value features in Phase 7.5 RGCC validation.
Schema sketch for Tier 1. Where do trajectory features live? On ModsBiomarkerSeries as computed attributes? In a new mods_biomarker_trajectory_features table? Ties into Phase 12 schema.
Coordinate with Phase 8.5 and Phase 12. Variant-as-graph-node and patient-as-graph-node are both upstream design decisions that interact with Phase 13. Ideally the schema for all three settles together rather than retrofitting later.


8. Temporal Graph-RAG ideas, evaluated one by one (2026-10-03)
Source: Adding Temporal Reasoning to Graph RAG: Tracking Fact Freshness and Staleness (MachineLearningMastery, read 2026-10-03). The article’s whole mechanism is below, so each verdict can be checked against it:

Dated facts. Subject → predicate → list of (object, date). A triple becomes a quadruple.
Recency weight. weight = 0.5 ^ (age_in_days / half_life), default half-life 365 days. A fact dated after the query date gets 1.0.
As-of query. Only facts with fact_date ≤ query_date come back.
Conflict resolution. All candidates for one (subject, predicate) are ranked by weight, freshest first.
Per-domain half-life. 365 days is too slow for volatile facts; the article’s example drops to 7.
Prompt assembly. The retriever passes the top-weighted fact, or a short ranked list with dates and weights, into the LLM’s context.

In short:

The as-of query is the article’s most valuable idea for MODS, though not for retrieval. It is the missing piece for decision-time snapshots (§6 Q9) and for validating against Maureen’s own timeline (§6 Q6).
Dated facts and dated prompts are worth adopting. The code mostly has them already; checking it found two gaps (§8.2).
The decay weight needs reshaping first. Most of her data goes stale through events, not elapsed days.
Recency-ranked conflict resolution should be rejected as a general rule. It is tie-breaking by date.

8.1 Verdicts





















































#IdeaVerdictWhere it lands1Dated factsAdopt. Mostly in place§8.2; new 13.1b2Recency weightAdapt. A staleness class per predicate, of which exponential decay is one§8.3; 13.2 features3As-of queryAdopt. Highest value§8.4; new 13.1c4Freshest wins a conflictReject, except for state that was measured again§8.55Per-domain half-lifeAdopt, generalized into the staleness table§8.36Dated facts in the promptAdopt. Never pass a lone winner§8.2, §8.6—Future-dated facts weigh 1.0Reject. A future date is a parse error or a scheduled event, never an observation13.1b ingest check
The article’s storage layer (nested in-memory dicts) has nothing to offer a Postgres schema with JSONB metadata, and is not considered further.
8.2 Dated facts: what the code already does, and two gaps
Most patient edges built by mods_patient_kg_service.py already carry their date in metadata:

expression and resistance factors: report_date;
medications and treatment episodes: start_date, end_date;
conditions: onset_date, abatement_date.

The LLM snapshot (mods_snapshot_service.py) dates biomarker values (ts) and RGCC tests (collected_date, reported_date). And 13.1 has shipped (§1).
Reading the code with the article’s question in mind, does every fact know when it was true?, found two gaps:


Her patient node shows the oldest value of every repeated measurement (GH #701). The edge builders query with no ORDER BY, and the insert is ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING on a relation key with no time component. In practice the oldest report was loaded first and comes back first, so it is the one kept. That is the opposite of 13.1’s latest-first rule for the KGIA profile, so the graph the foundation trains on and the profile the criterion reads describe her at different times. Counted on prod, read-only, on 2026-10-03, against a node last materialized 2026-05-18:


RGCC. Her two draws (reported 2025-02-15 and 2025-09-19, with no collection date recorded) hold 165 results each and became 135 undated edges. All 62 edges whose two draws scored differently carry the February score. That includes all eight graph-resolved drugs from the 12 that moved at least 25 points:

paclitaxel shows 75 (22 in September), docetaxel 70 (20) and cabazitaxel 70 (14);
doxorubicin shows 24 (79) and etoposide 22 (71);
daunorubicin, idarubicin and epirubicin show 20 (67).

The predicate hides the inversion too, because RGCC’s moderate and low grades both map to partially_sensitive_to_drug. Only 15 agents changed predicate between draws, all natural substances without numeric scores. Of those, only naltrexone resolves to a graph entity, and it now holds both partially_sensitive_to_drug and resistant_to_drug. The other four movers do not resolve at all (Abraxane, liposomal doxorubicin, amrubicin, and mitoxantrone, which RGCC spells “Mitoxandrone”), nor do 65 of the 164 agents overall.


Alterations. Five variants appear on more than one report with differing VAFs. Five of their edges carry the earliest report’s VAF and one matches neither. No alteration edge carries a date.


Expression. Expression edges are dated. Of 13 genes with a regulation call on more than one report, 12 carry the earliest report’s date. And because every report contributes edges, three genes called regulated in January 2024 but normal in September 2025 still carry the regulation edge.


So the model’s input changes only at the predicate level: naltrexone’s double edge and the three stale regulation calls. What a person or the LLM reads off her node, the scores, VAFs and dates, is the February 2025 and January 2024 picture. Validation is unaffected: compute_metrics_crc.py reads per draw from the functional-test tables. The fix is a representation choice, so the issue waits on a decision. The same question is §6 Q8 for repeat Caris panels, and both should get one answer.
(2026-10-04: decided and implemented for RGCC, alterations, expression and resistance factors (GH #701). The rules:

Each measurement becomes one edge. Its predicate and headline values come from the latest report, and every report is listed in metadata.observations.
A property the reports state differently, such as a variant’s origin, is left unstated and named in disagreeing_fields. Date does not decide it.
When the latest reports disagree on the predicate, there is no edge, and the measurement is reported as a conflict.
A latest expression call of normal retires an earlier regulation call. Assays never decide for each other.
Two measurements that land on one (target, predicate) are merged, with the rest kept under also_from.

That answers Q8 for repeat panels. What a variant missing from a later report means is still open: an alteration has no “not detected” call, so its edge stays.)


The LLM snapshot’s genomics section is undated (GH #702). _build_genomics_section sorts by gene and emits the variant, VAF and source report, but not report_date. A model reading one variant at two VAFs cannot tell which came first. It is invited into the trap the mission spec’s §7.1 names: VAF across specimens tracks purity, so it is not a trajectory.


8.3 Staleness classes, not one half-life
The article’s single decay curve fits a lab value and little else in Maureen’s record. What makes a tumor fact stale is usually an event: a recurrence or a new treatment line. The RGCC draws show it. Twelve drugs moved at least 25 points between February and September 2025, as two coherent classes: taxanes down, topoisomerase-II agents up. That interval straddles the August 2025 recurrence and the BREAKWATER start. Seven months of age is a proxy; the regime change is the cause.
So “half-life per domain” generalizes to a staleness class per predicate:



































ClassA fact is current while…Examples in her recordArticle’s decay?Never stalealwaysgermline genotypes, polygenic scoresNo. Decay here would be an errorIntervalstart ≤ as_of ≤ endmedications, treatment episodes, conditions with an abatement dateNo. The interval answers “current?” exactly; decay blurs itEpochno treatment-line change or progression event since it was observedsomatic alterations, tumor expression, RGCC sensitivity, imaging readsNo. After the next event it is prior-epoch: flagged, not fractionally weightedDecayingweight 0.5 ^ (age / h), with h set per markerCA 19-9, ctDNA MTM/mL, albumin, LDH, blood countsYes. This is the article’s case
Epoch boundaries come from treatment-episode start dates plus dated progression events. Two cautions:

Assigning a predicate to a class encodes meaning. Under CLAUDE.md’s rule on vocabulary mappings, that is a judgement call. The table above is a proposal for sign-off, not a decision.
Weights are computed on read and never stored. They depend on the as-of date, which is the same reason Gate C stores counts rather than ratios.

Where a weight could enter the model. Three slots, in the order to try them:

Use staleness to decide which edges exist, not how heavy they are. Materialize current-epoch somatic edges, and leave prior-epoch facts out or under a distinct predicate. No model change, fully auditable, fails closed. Try this first.
Phase 12’s strength(f, c), constant 1.0 today, could become s_r · ω(e). But Phase 12’s defect is sign, not magnitude (its planning doc, pdr2_phase12_per_relation_criterion_planning.md), so ω waits until a signed s_r works.
ULTRA message passing. GeneralizedRelationalConv.forward accepts an edge_weight (default ones), but BaseNBFNet.bellmanford never passes one, so this needs plumbing. A foundation trained on all-ones weights would see fractional weights only on her edges, at inference. Whether that behaves is untested; this is an inference, not a result. Try it last.

For 13.2’s trajectory features, decay belongs inside the feature, not on the fact. Replace “slope over 90 days” with an exponentially weighted least-squares slope, weighting each point by 0.5 ^ (age / h). A hard 90-day window over monthly draws holds about three points and jumps when one ages out; a soft window changes smoothly. That also answers part of §6 Q3 (uneven sampling).
8.4 As-of builds: the idea worth the most
An as_of date on the KGIA profile build and on materialize_patient_kg would hide everything observed after it. The raw rows are already dated (biomarker ts, report_date, collected_date, episode dates), so a profile can be rebuilt for any date on demand.
Two timelines, which the article does not distinguish. A fact has a valid time, when it was true of her body (the specimen collection date). It also has a knowledge time, when Maple could have known it (the report or ingest date). A tumor panel is typically reported weeks after its specimen was taken, and it can describe tissue from much earlier. The Altera panel, for example, was reported 2025-02-25, ten days after the 2025-02-15 RGCC date on file. Each use below needs a different timeline. Genomic rows carry only a report date, so valid time for them means adding the collection date, which is printed on each report.
Three uses:


Decision-time snapshots (§6 Q9), on knowledge time. A recommendation records its as_of, and anyone can rebuild exactly the inputs it saw. That answers Q9 without a materialized snapshot table.


Feature–label alignment, on valid time. Since 13.1, the profile always takes the latest value; the patient graph keeps the oldest (§8.2), so neither is aligned with both draws. And the February 2025 RGCC draw is scored against a profile containing the tumor panel reported in September 2025, seven months after that draw. The draws are evaluated separately; their features are not. With as_of, each draw pairs with the profile as of its own date:

February 2025 with the January 2024 tumor profile and the February 2025 panels;
September 2025 with the panel reported 2025-09-13, six days before the 2025-09-19 draw, and most likely run on tissue from the 2025-08-25 excision (to confirm from the report).



A within-patient longitudinal test. Two as-of profiles give two rankings, and two draws give two label sets. The test asks whether the change in ranking tracks the change in measured sensitivity: taxanes down, topoisomerase-II agents up. It is patient-specific, needs no second patient, and the 12 drugs that moved ≥25 points give it a sharp contrast. Its limits:

n is small;
only the somatic channels differ between the two profiles, since the polygenic scores are constant;
RGCC measures circulating tumor cells, while the profile describes tissue;
it is premature until the base ranker shows a clean signal, and smoke run #1’s clean holdout showed none.

The design costs nothing to keep ready, and it is a candidate closure criterion for §5.


As-of filtering is necessary, not sufficient. The profile must also be scoped to the colorectal primary, because her separate melanoma primary has its own specimens and dates. A date filter alone cannot tell two cancers apart. The expression builder already scopes to the index cancer (ExpressionScope, GH #212), and an as-of build has to keep that scope, not replace it.
The same idea applied to the graph. PrimeKG is a 2023 snapshot whose edges carry no dates. A time-split evaluation would hold out indications approved after the snapshot as positives and ask whether the foundation ranks them high. That needs a dated approvals list from outside the graph, such as FDA approval dates. It tests the base ranker, not personalization, but at population scale rather than on her 112 drugs. mods_kg_source records a version and an ingested_at, but no upstream release date. Recording one would also let the Explorer and the LLM say “per PrimeKG (2023)” instead of stating a fact undated.
8.5 Conflicts: the latest wins only when the thing was measured again
The article’s own example shows the hazard. Three assertions about one fact within a few weeks get weights 0.9812, 0.9775 and 0.9738. The “answer” turns on a 0.4% difference, that is, on which source wrote last. That is tie-breaking by date, which Maple refuses for anything feeding the model or a clinical view. Two cases have to be kept apart:


State measured again. A later lab, ctDNA draw, RGCC draw or re-biopsy describes a later state. Taking the latest as of a date is the definition of “current”, not a tie-break. 13.1 does this.


Conflicting assertions about the same state. Here recency is not evidence:

the duplicate Signatera documents (21 documents, 19 draws);
the CA 19-9 of 78 on 2026-03-16, between 23 and 22, with null rows the same day. It is a probable mis-parse, and a freshness ranker would promote it.
trial status: the BATTMAN enrollment press releases are still live, so a retriever dating them by fetch time would rank them fresh, while ClinicalTrials.gov says terminated. Authority decides, not age.
VAFs across specimens: a later one supersedes nothing.

Resolve by source authority, then by agreement between sources. If neither settles it, show both and refuse to pick.


8.6 Dated facts in the prompt
The article’s last step is the one Maple’s clinical LLM path can use directly:

Every fact the LLM sees should carry its observation date, and the snapshot its as-of date.
Facts that are prior-epoch or decaying should say so.

The article’s alternative, passing only the top-weighted fact, is the wrong half of its advice for clinical use. Hiding the prior value hides the trajectory, which §1 argues is often the signal. Pass the latest value with its predecessors, dated. Apart from the genomics gap in §8.2, mods_snapshot_service already does this.
8.7 Beyond Phase 13: Maple’s own memory
The article is about retrieval, and Maple’s vector memory is a retrieval system. It already has recency ranking, salience decay and a superseded_by stamp from consolidation merges. Migration 095 dropped its valid_from/valid_to columns as unused. Its decay is keyed on last access (by default ×0.9 per 30 days unread, floor 0.1), not on the age of the assertion.
The gap the article exposes is supersession, not decay. On 2026-10-03 the session-start digest served two notes side by side: “CLOSED (GH #371): … frequency route yields 8.48%”, and the note that overturns that conclusion (GH #404). Both sit in the pinned/high-salience set, written a day apart. No half-life can separate notes a day apart; only an explicit link can. The older note is still partly right (hm_source still cannot orient palindromes), so the link has to be per-claim, or at least visible in the digest. This belongs in memory_architecture.md, not in Phase 13.
8.8 Changes to the Phase 13 plan













































ItemChangeStatus13.1Snapshot sort fixShipped (checked in code 2026-10-03)13.1b (new)Date every patient edge, and stop keeping the oldest. RGCC, alteration and expression edges get their observation date and report id, with repeat observations kept rather than colliding (GH #701). Prod shows the oldest observation winning today (§8.2). The LLM genomics section gets report_date (GH #702). An ingest check flags any observation dated after its own ingestpatient edges fixed (GH #701, 2026-10-04); #702 and the ingest check open13.1c (new)as_of on profile build and patient-KG materialization, on both timelines (§8.4). Recommendations record the as_of they usednot started13.2Exponentially weighted trajectory features, with h per marker. CA 19-9 replaces CEA as the first series. ctDNA MTM/mL follows once GH #131 lands. The staleness table (§8.3) defines “current”design; table needs sign-off§5Within-patient longitudinal test (§8.4, use 3) as a closure-criterion candidate, gated on a clean base signaldesign—Time-split evaluation of the graph; upstream release date on mods_kg_sourceoption, not scheduled—One shared RGCC reader (Richard, 2026-10-04: “a centralized place to publish the RGCC data, so the logic is only in one place”). A small module returning dated per-draw rows, a latest-draw view, same-date conflicts refused, and one name-alias map. Each reader (patient graph, scoring, metro #750, embedding, calibration, viz) adopts it when next touched; no big-bang refactorwishlist
None of this is on the current critical path (GH #599: earn a signal, ship a list):

The two date gaps and the as_of parameter are the cheapest items with direct value.
The within-patient test is the item that could help earn a signal, once there is one to earn.

Parallelization analysis

Surfaces touched.

Yes: backend services (mods_patient_kg_service.py, mods_snapshot_service.py, mods_kgia_profile_service.py), tests, docs.
Only if an option is taken: a migration (an upstream release date on mods_kg_source, unless it goes in metadata); the MCP tools (only if as_of is exposed there).
No: frontend, worker handlers, DB-stored config.


Parallel split.

The two 13.1b issues are independent of each other and of 13.1c.
13.2 waits on the staleness-table sign-off.
The longitudinal test waits on 13.1c and on a base signal.


Collision hotspots. backend/migrations.py, and only if the release date becomes a column. Nothing else on the list.
How to verify each surface.

RGCC edges: a unit test with two draws of one drug, in the same class and in a changed class, asserting both observations survive with their dates. Then count her sensitivity edges per drug on prod.
Snapshot: a unit test that report_date is emitted, newest first.
as_of: a unit test that a row dated after as_of is excluded, and a rebuild as of 2025-03-01 that contains no September 2025 tumor data.




9. Cross-references

PDR_PIPELINE_PLAN.md — master plan; Phase 13 stub points here.
pdr_phase8.5_variant_kg_planning.md — variant-aware KG; complementary.
pdr_phase0_gpkg_writeup.md — writeup template for Phase 13 closure documentation.
backend/mods_kgia_profile_service.py — site of the snapshot policy bug for 13.1.
backend/mods_snapshot_service.py — patient snapshot builder; preserves full trajectory (correctly).
docs/References/PDR1/patient_merge.py — paper precedent (PRS + biomarker scalars, no temporal).
docs/References/PDR2/ — paper precedent (KGIA loss with genetic + biomarker scalars, no temporal).

prs/audit_handoff_2026-07-12.title: PRS Validation — Audit Handoff
prs/audit_handoff_2026-07-12.content:
PRS Validation — Audit Handoff
Date: 2026-07-12
Subject: Validation of 5,368 polygenic risk scores (PRS) computed for the patient “Maureen” from her germline whole-genome sequence.
Purpose of this doc: Independent review. Please challenge methods, numbers, assumptions, and the plan. Author is a non-specialist; explicitly assume nothing is obviously correct.

1. Context & objective

Patient: Maureen. Stage IV colorectal adenocarcinoma, microsatellite-stable (MSS), TMB 3 (low). One pathogenic inherited variant on file (gene, variant and genotype withheld).
Input genome: 30x germline WGS, GRCh38.p13, from sequencing.com (kit id withheld). File: a 30x WGS VCF under backend/data/genomes/, named for the ordering account rather than the patient. Note it arrived under her husband’s account, hence the provenance concern below.
PRS output: 5,368 scores, one per PGS Catalog scoring file, in DB table ModsPolygenicScore. Computed by backend/mods_prs_service.py (compute_prs_pure), genotypes imported by backend/connectors/genotype_importer.py. Genotype store = 4,419,571 variants.
Objective: determine whether these scores are trustworthy, and validate them against what is independently known about Maureen.

2. Key artifacts (for reproduction)





































ItemPath / handleGermline WGS (GRCh38)a 30x WGS VCF under backend/data/genomes/Tumor DNA+RNA BAMs/VCFs (hg38)backend/data/caris/{the 2024 colorectal specimen, the 2025 colorectal specimen [colorectal], the melanoma specimen [melanoma]}/Tumor transcriptome (percentile TSV)backend/data/caris/WTS_tab/the 2025 colorectal specimen_allgenes_percentile.tsvPGS scoring files (cache)worker/data/pgs_catalog/<PGSID>/<PGSID>_hmPOS_GRCh38.txt.gzPRS compute + matching logicbackend/mods_prs_service.py, backend/connectors/genotype_importer.pyIdentity-check script + result<scratchpad>/idcheck/concordance.py, concordance_results.jsonPRS status snapshot (5,368 scores)via MCP mods_prs_status
3. Validation steps completed this session
3.1 Inventory of the PRS output — found the core blocker

All 5,368 scores have z_score = null and ukb_trait_code = null. → No normalization/percentiles exist; scores are raw only.
raw_score ranges −3.2M to +837K; 40 of 5,368 have |raw| > 1,000. Different PGS use different weight conventions, so raw scores are not comparable across PGS and not interpretable individually. A per-PGS reference distribution is a hard precondition for any interpretation (including the “is her colorectal score high?” question).

3.2 Clinical grounding (shapes what validation is even possible)

n=1 disease status is a weak PRS validator (population-level tool, individual outcome).
MSS/TMB-low ⇒ not Lynch-driven ⇒ a common-variant colorectal PRS is more relevant for her, but her inherited variant is a monogenic contributor common-variant PRS does not capture ⇒ a merely-average colorectal PRS would NOT falsify the pipeline.

3.3 Multi-omic sample-identity check (provenance) — PASSED

Why: all 5,368 scores derive from one germline file that arrived under a different-named account; the link to Maureen must be verified, not assumed.
Method (pure Python, no external tools; concordance.py): built a shared common-SNP panel of 923 biallelic-SNV rsID sites from the three Caris tumor DNA VCFs (all hg38, matching the germline build), streamed the germline gVCF once, extracted genotypes at those sites (888 had germline genotypes), computed pairwise genotype concordance. Logic mirrors somalier/NGSCheckMate.
Result: germline WGS vs each tumor = 99.7–99.9% exact GT concordance, 100% allele-share at identity-informative (non-ref) sites; tumor-vs-tumor = 99.9–100%. ⇒ The germline is Maureen’s; all three specimens (2 colorectal + 1 melanoma) are the same individual.
Independent corroboration: the germline WGS independently carries the same pathogenic variant the clinical panel found, on a different platform.
Caveats: panel is ~888 common SNPs from Caris panel regions (unrelated individuals would score near chance, so this margin is unambiguous). The “100% het retention” LOH readout is only over these panel sites, not a genome-wide LOH claim.

3.4 Coverage (“~50% of scoring SNPs matched”) — diagnosed as BENIGN

Concern: snps_used / snps_in_scoring_file ≈ 50% looked like half the data missing.
Evidence it is expected, not a bug:

Code. mods_prs_service.py (~L102-107): an unmatched scoring SNP is missing += 1; continue (skipped), which is numerically identical to dosage 0 (score = Σ dosage·weight). Matching is rsID → (chrom,pos) fallback with strand-flip and palindrome handling. genotype_importer.py (~L175) skips gVCF reference blocks (<NON_REF>), storing only ALT-bearing sites ⇒ store is variant-only (explains the 4.4M count) ⇒ a truly hom-ref scoring SNP is legitimately absent ⇒ correctly contributes 0.
Distribution. Coverage mean 44.9%, median 48.8%, unimodal, no near-zero spike (a build/identifier bug would spike near 0). Large PGS (≥100k SNPs) median 48.3% ≈ small PGS (<1k) median 47.4% ⇒ coverage is independent of file size = a population constant (“fraction of common SNPs where a person is non-reference”), not an artifact. The only <5%-coverage cases (60 PGS) are 1–2 SNP scores (granularity).
Single-SNP reconstruction (PGS000019, 192-SNP CAD score, 187 with GRCh38 positions). Classified every scoring SNP against her WGS: 49 carry the effect allele (should be scored); pipeline reported snps_used = 50 — match. Full decomposition: 100 hom-ref in reference block, 16 variant-but-for-the-other-allele (dosage 0), 12 palindromic (skipped), 8 explicit 0/0, 2 no-call, 49 scored.


Conclusion: raw scores are not invalidated by ~50% coverage.
One real (minor, unbiased) finding: ~6% palindromic (A/T, C/G) SNPs are conservatively dropped; recoverable since her WGS and the scoring files are both GRCh38/forward-strand.
Caveat: the per-SNP proof is n=1 PGS; the code + distribution generalize it, but the definitive fleet-wide confirmation is the pgsc_calc cross-check (still pending, see §5).

3.5 Ancestry — self-report EUROPEAN, genetically corroborated (spot-check only)

Self-report (patient + mother): solidly European (German/“Euro-mutt”), possible trace Middle Eastern from a distant relative.
Genetic spot-check (6 loci read from WGS): SLC45A2 rs16891982 G/G, LCT rs4988235 A/A (Northern-European lactase persistence), SLC24A5 / EDAR / DARC all hom-reference (= European pigment allele / non-East-Asian / non-African). ⇒ Consistent with European; rules out substantial African or East Asian ancestry. Cannot resolve the trace Middle Eastern component (pigment loci are shared across West Eurasia).
Consequence: reference panel = 1000G EUR / continuous-PCA; PRS portability is best-case for a European individual (most PGS were trained/validated in Europeans), so no per-score portability flagging is needed.
Caveat: this is a crude few-SNP sanity check, not a formal ancestry estimate. Genome-wide PCA is still required (see §5) for precise placement and to quantify admixture.

3.6 Transcriptome usage boundary (important scope limit)

The Caris WTS is tumor RNA, not germline. It validates identity, genotyping QC, and single-variant mechanism — NOT germline quantitative-trait risk.
Consistency signals observed: MLH1 at 99th (MMR intact ⇒ consistent with MSS).
Explicit trap to avoid: tumor LDLR at 96th percentile does NOT validate an LDL PRS (tumor cholesterol-uptake demand, not serum LDL or germline lipid genetics).

3.7 Normalization feasibility — both shortcuts ruled out

No reference panel on disk (only the PGP hu52B7E5 sample).
Only 7% (17/250 sampled) of scoring files embed allelefrequency_effect ⇒ the analytic route needs external European allele frequencies (gnomAD NFE or 1000G EUR).

4. Interim conclusions (what we believe is now established)

The germline substrate is Maureen’s DNA (99.7–100% concordance).
The ~50% coverage is expected/benign; raw scores are not corrupted by it.
Her ancestry is European (spot-check; formal PCA pending) ⇒ EUR reference, best-case portability.
The only blocker to interpretation is the absence of percentiles (no reference distribution yet).

5. What is still needed (gaps)

Percentiles (the deliverable). Convert raw → z/percentile against an ancestry-matched reference. Blocks ALL biological validation, including the original colorectal question.
Formal ancestry placement. Genome-wide PCA vs 1000G+HGDP (not the 6-SNP sanity check) to confirm/place precisely and quantify the trace, and to drive continuous ancestry adjustment.
Fleet-wide coverage/matching audit. Reproduce our raw scores with an independent implementation (pgsc_calc) across all 5,368 to confirm matching/dosage beyond the single-PGS proof; recover palindromes.
Quantitative-trait biological validation (Tier 2, strongest). Compare her PRS percentiles for measurable traits (height [sentinel], LDL/HDL/triglycerides, fasting glucose/HbA1c, BMI, blood pressure, CBC indices) against her actual medical-record values. Requires percentiles (#1) + sourcing measured values. Blocker: two MODS tools are currently broken — trt_list_bloodwork (BloodworkResult has no attribute 'test_type') and mods_search_documents (SQL parameter-binding error) — and must be fixed or bypassed to reach lab values. Control for treatment confounders (e.g., statins→LDL, cancer therapy→CBC): use untreated values where possible.
Disease-concordance checks (Tier 3, weak). Colorectal, ATM-linked breast/pancreatic, once percentiles exist. Frame as consistency, not confirmation.
Label normalization. 1,760 disease_label values with fragmentation (e.g., “Breast cancer” vs “Breast cancer (female)”; three T2D labels). Normalize to EFO/MONDO before internal-consistency grouping.

6. Plan

Task 1 — Ancestry PCA. 1000G+HGDP reference; project her WGS. Output: ancestry coordinates + trace quantification. Async/worker.
Task 2 — Empirical percentiles (gold standard). Run pgsc_calc (PGS Catalog’s official Nextflow calculator) scoring Maureen + the 1000G EUR reference, with continuous PCA ancestry adjustment. Output: ancestry-adjusted percentiles for the PGS set; also serves as the fleet-wide coverage/matching audit (#5.3) and recovers palindromes. Async/cloud/worker (multi-GB reference + Nextflow).
Task 3 — Analytic first-pass. gnomAD non-Finnish-European allele frequencies → per-PGS μ = Σ 2·p·w, σ² = Σ 2·p·(1−p)·w²; z = (raw − μ)/σ → percentile across all 5,368. Fast rough numbers + independent cross-check on Task 2. Caveats: ignores LD (σ approximate), μ/σ over all scoring SNPs vs raw over used-only (small inconsistency), uses training-population AF.
Order: Task 3 (analytic) first for speed (rough percentiles on all 5,368, incl. colorectal, ~1 day), then Task 2 (empirical) to confirm/adjust. Task 1 feeds both.
Then: Tier 2 quantitative validation and Tier 3 disease concordance once percentiles land.
Execution: async cloud/worker jobs (not local Windows Docker), consistent with project infra.

7. Questions we specifically want the auditor to scrutinize

Identity check rigor: is a 888-common-SNP pure-Python concordance sufficient, or should we re-run with a standard tool (somalier / NGSCheckMate) for defensibility?
Palindromic SNPs: is dropping ~6% acceptable, or should we recover them (both sides GRCh38/forward)? Any risk in recovering?
Analytic μ/σ approximation: is the HWE + no-LD + all-SNPs-vs-used approximation acceptable for a first pass, or misleading enough to skip? Should σ include an LD correction?
Ancestry adjustment specification: is continuous PCA adjustment (regress PRS mean and variance on PCs, then standardize) the right method vs a EUR-bucket? Are we handling the trace admixture correctly?
Coverage proof generality: the per-SNP reconstruction is n=1 PGS. Is that acceptable pending pgsc_calc, or should we reconstruct several PGS (incl. a large genome-wide one) now?
Build consistency: confirm no GRCh37 leakage anywhere (germline GRCh38.p13; scoring files hmPOS_GRCh38; tumor VCFs hg38). Any silent liftover risk?
PRS best-practices we may be missing: duplicate/overlapping PGS per trait, effect-allele orientation edge cases, indel handling, multi-allelic sites, and whether to weight by PGS Catalog per-ancestry performance metrics.
Reference choice: 1000G EUR (~500 samples) vs 1000G+HGDP combined vs gnomAD — which for the empirical distribution, and does N matter for tail percentiles?

8. Known limitations / what we did NOT do

Did not compute any percentiles yet (no reference distribution).
Did not run formal genome-wide ancestry PCA (only a 6-SNP sanity check).
Coverage correctness proven on one small PGS only.
Did not verify the genotype importer captured all true variant sites (only that used≈effect-allele-carrying for one PGS); pgsc_calc cross-check is intended to close this.
Did not yet source any measured clinical lab values (tooling broken).

prs/compatibility_classification.title: PRS Compatibility Classification
prs/compatibility_classification.content:
PGS Score Compatibility Classification
How MODS decides, for each published polygenic score, whether it can compute that score
for a patient — and if not, exactly why.
This document describes the compatibility classifier (backend/mods_prs_compat.py,
“Gate B” of the PRS rebuild). It is written to be read on its own: the first half is
concepts and rationale; the second half is the precise rules and worked examples.

1. The problem it solves
A polygenic score (PGS, also “PRS” for
polygenic risk score) estimates a person’s genetic predisposition to a trait by adding up
the effects of many genetic variants. Each variant contributes dosage × weight, where the
dosage is how many copies of the trait-associated allele the person carries (0, 1, or 2),
and the weight comes from a genome-wide association study.
The PGS Catalog publishes ~5,000+ such scores as
downloadable scoring files — each a table of variants, alleles, and weights.
Here is the catch: not every published score can be computed the same way, and some
cannot be computed responsibly at all. A score might rely on complex biology (a whole
haplotype, an interaction
between variants, a copy-number change)
that a simple additive sum gets wrong. Or it might use a variant whose position we cannot
place on the genome, or an allele pair that is ambiguous about which DNA
strand it refers to.
If we blindly computed every score, some numbers would be quietly, confidently wrong —
the most dangerous kind of error in a clinical-decision context. So before computing
anything, MODS classifies every scoring file into one of four compatibility classes and
records why. The classifier is deliberately conservative: when a score’s format is
unusual, it would rather defer the score than compute it as if it were simple.
A little vocabulary

Effect allele / other allele. Each variant row names two alleles
(versions of the DNA at that spot): the effect allele (whose count drives the score) and
the other allele. Cf. the reference genome,
the standard “consensus” sequence every allele is compared against.
Dosage is the person’s genotype expressed as
a count of effect alleles: 0, 1, or 2 (see zygosity).
Harmonization is the PGS Catalog’s process of mapping every variant to genomic
coordinates on a common build (here GRCh38)
so scores from different studies line up. Harmonized columns are prefixed hm_.


2. The four classes






























ClassMeaningOutcomeAClean: additive, biallelic, autosomal SNVs, position-resolvable, explicit alleles, no complex rules.Computed in production.BConditionally supported: computable with care (indels, strand-ambiguous SNVs, X-chromosome, inferred alleles, …).Computed only if every one of its complications is on the approved list (“promotion”, §5); otherwise deferred.CNeeds a dedicated calculator: the biology is not a simple additive sum (haplotypes, interactions, dosage-specific weights, APOE / HLA / CYP star-alleles).Deferred — returns “not calculated” with a reason, never a partial number.DUnavailable: cannot be placed on the genome at all.”Not calculated.”
The guiding rule for C and D is the same: a missing score is honest; a wrong score is
not. We never emit a partial or approximate number for a score we cannot compute
correctly.

3. The signals the classifier reads
The classifier looks only at the structure of the scoring file — never at a patient. For
each file it computes a small set of feature counts and inspects which columns the file
contains.























































SignalWhat it isWhy it matters for scoringUnplaceable rowsVariant has no chromosome/position (hm_chr/hm_pos blank).Our genotype pipeline is position-keyed; an unplaceable variant cannot be looked up.IndelAn insertion or deletion — alleles longer than one base (A → ATTCT).Indels need careful left-alignment and reference verification; the anchor base is shared between the two alleles, so naïve matching is wrong.Palindromic SNVA biallelic SNV whose two alleles are DNA complements: A/T or C/G.Because A pairs with T and C with G, you cannot tell from the alleles alone which strand the study meant — a “strand flip” would silently invert the dosage. Resolvable only via allele frequency.Multiallelic siteOne genomic position carrying more than two alleles across the score.Ordinary SNP scoring assumes two alleles per site; more than two needs special handling to match the right one.X-chromosome variantVariant on chromosome X.Dosage on X depends on sex (dosage compensation): a person with one X is hemizygous (0/1), not 0/1/2.Inferred other-alleleThe “other” allele was guessed by the harmonizer (hm_inferOtherAllele), not stated by the study.An inferred allele is not authoritative; trusting it like a stated one can misassign the reference vs. alternate and thus the dosage.Missing other-alleleNo other allele at all — not even an inferred one.Without both alleles we cannot orient the variant against the reference to know a wild-type person’s dosage.Dedicated-calculator columnsColumns like is_interaction, is_haplotype, is_diplotype, dosage_0/1/2_weight.Their presence means the score is not a simple additive sum — it encodes interactions, haplotypes, or per-genotype weights.Inheritance-model columnsis_dominant / is_recessive.The dosage → contribution mapping is non-additive (dominant/recessive), not the standard 0/1/2 × weight.

Conservative-by-presence. For the complex-format and inheritance columns the classifier
flags on the presence of the column, not on confirming every row uses it. This can
over-defer a score that carries an unused column, but that is the safe direction — we would
rather review a deferred score than silently compute a complex one. Row-level refinement is
a planned hardening step.


4. How a class is chosen
The classifier assigns exactly one class, checked in this precedence (first match wins):

D — if no variant in the file is position-resolvable.
C — else if any dedicated-calculator column is present.
B — else if any Class-B signal is present (indel, multiallelic, palindromic, X, inferred-other, missing-other, inheritance model, or some unplaceable rows).
A — otherwise: a clean additive, biallelic, autosomal, position-resolvable SNV score.

Every result records the specific reasons behind it, so a score is never a bare label — it is
a label plus the evidence. The assignment is a pure function of the scoring file, so it is
deterministic and reproducible from the file’s checksum.

5. Class-B promotion (which “computable-with-care” scores we actually compute)
Class B is the interesting middle. Its scores can be computed, but each complication needs
handling that must be validated before we trust it. So Class B carries a second decision —
promotion — that is a signed-off policy, not an automatic judgement.
A Class-B score is production-eligible only if every one of its complications is on the
promoted list. One un-promoted signal defers the whole score (the strict-AND rule keeps a
mostly-simple score from sneaking through on the strength of its simple parts).
Current promoted set (approved 2026-07-14; ambiguous_other added deferred 2026-09-22):























































Class-B signalPromoted?RationaleIndels✅The genotype builder emits normalized, reference-verified indel alleles; the reference scorer matches them.X chromosome✅The current patient has two X chromosomes, so X dosage behaves like an autosome (0/1/2). A single-X patient would need hemizygous handling.Inferred other-allele✅Every allele is verified against the reference genome, so an inferred allele that matches the genome is safe to use.Palindromic SNV✅ (resolvable subset)Standard tooling resolves strand by allele frequency; genuinely ambiguous ones stay deferred at compute time.Unresolvable allele (ambiguous_other)❌ deferThe allele names no single sequence — a harmonizer candidate set (A/T, C/G/T), an unknown base (N), presence/absence notation (-, P), or a star-allele name. Added in classifier v3 (GH #273): these rows used to be counted as indels, which are promoted, so they could qualify a score for production on an allele we cannot even orient.Multiallelic site❌ deferDuplicate-position handling and allele matching need golden tests first.Missing other-allele❌ deferCannot orient a wild-type dosage with no other allele.Inheritance model (dom/rec)❌ deferNon-additive dosage mapping, out of scope for the additive scorer.Unplaceable rows❌ deferPartial coverage — handled by the coverage gate later, not promoted here.
Promotion sets policy; nothing is actually computed until a later release step, and only
after golden tests.

6. Theoretical bounds — a free sanity check
For any additive score, the raw total S = Σ dosageᵢ · weightᵢ with each dosage in {0,1,2}
is mathematically bounded:
L = Σ min(0, 2·weightᵢ)      (all effect alleles absent or present, whichever is lower)
U = Σ max(0, 2·weightᵢ)

Every computed score must satisfy L ≤ S ≤ U. A value outside that interval is not a
biological finding — it is a bug in the scorer, and downstream code asserts the bound per
score. It costs nothing and catches whole classes of arithmetic and allele-orientation
errors. (Note: a score whose weights are odds ratios
rather than log-effects must be transformed before summing — a separate biological check, not
this bound.)

7. Worked examples (real PGS Catalog scores)
Run on four actual scoring files (harmonized to GRCh38):








































ScoreVariantsClassEligibleWhyPGS0000272,100,302A✅Entirely clean additive SNVs — and the classifier handled a 2.1-million-variant file without trouble.PGS000004313B✅Has indels and palindromic SNVs — both promoted — so eligible.PGS00011829B✅Indels + palindromic + inferred-other — all promoted.PGS000019192B❌168 of 192 rows rely on an inferred other-allele, plus it has missing-other and unplaceable rows. Two of those (missing-other, unplaceable) are not promoted, so the whole score is correctly deferred.
PGS000019 is instructive: it was the score used in the original audit that exposed the
underlying dosage bug, and here the classifier independently flags it as not-yet-trustworthy
for exactly the right reasons.

8. The fleet run (2026-07-21)
The classifier was run across the entire cached GRCh38 catalog: 5,377 scoring files,
~59 GB, 3.45 billion variant rows examined. Every score is now classified, on one
classifier version, with reasons and a scoring-file checksum.















































ClassScoresShareProduction-eligibleVariant rowsA1,99737.1%1,9971,424,367,610B2,95054.9%1,8662,007,436,633C4267.9%020,736,700D40.1%017Total5,3773,863 (71.8%)3,452,540,960
So roughly seven in ten published scores are computable under the current promotion
policy, and the eligible set carries ~1.88 billion variant rows — the real size of the
job facing the later gates.
What blocks the other 1,084
Of the deferred Class-B scores, the table below counts how many carry each
not-yet-promoted category, and — more usefully — how many would become eligible if that
category alone were promoted (a score with two deferred categories needs both, so it
counts toward neither).






























Deferred categoryAppears inSole blockerMultiallelic site588588Missing other-allele47794Unplaceable rows39918Inheritance model31
Multiallelic handling is by far the highest-leverage open decision: it is the only
thing standing between 588 scores and production, and promoting it alone would lift
eligibility from 3,863 to 4,451 (+15%). By contrast unplaceable_rows appears in 399
deferred scores but is almost never the lone blocker — those scores have other problems
too, so work there buys little.
Notes from the run

Five cached scoring files were truncated (interrupted downloads from an earlier
sweep). Every one failed loudly on its gzip checksum rather than being parsed as far
as the truncation and classified on partial data. All five were re-downloaded — each
25–62% larger than the truncated copy — and classified cleanly.
Fifteen scores parse to zero variant rows, because they carry their weights in
dosage_0/1/2_weight instead of effect_weight. These are correctly Class C
(dedicated calculator), not Class D — the zero-row result is a fact about this parser,
not about the file. §4’s ordering exists to preserve that distinction.
weight_type is not clean catalog-wide and will need attention at the biological
checks: 3,250 beta, 1,390 NR (not reported), plus BETA/Beta case variants,
199 log(OR), and a long tail of free-text values. A score whose weights are odds
ratios must not be summed as if they were log-effects.
Classifying at this scale needs the streaming reader (open_scoring_file), not
parse_scoring_file: the largest single score carries 10,318,272 variants
(PGS003162), and the largest file is PGS005197 at 9,503,677 variants and 185.8 MB
compressed. Five scores exceed 10 million variants.

Reproduce with backend/scripts/prs/build_prs_manifest.py; verify with
check_manifest_invariants.py; summarize with manifest_report.py.

9. Where this sits in the pipeline
The classifier populates a score manifest (mods_prs_score_manifest, one row per PGS
score) with the class, eligibility, reasons, feature counts, and theoretical bounds. Nothing
downstream computes a score that the manifest has not marked production-eligible. In the full
PRS rebuild this is Gate B: it decides which scores to compute; a later gate makes the
computation itself correct, and a final gate applies coverage and biological checks before any
score is released.
Source: backend/mods_prs_compat.py · Manifest schema: migration 104
(mods_prs_score_manifest) · Tests: backend/tests/test_mods_prs_compat.py.

prs/frontend_requirements.title: PRS Read-Layer Requirements
prs/frontend_requirements.content:
PRS Frontend — requirements sketch
Input for a dedicated planning session. Written 2026-07-21, immediately after Gate B
completed, to preserve decisions made while the data was in front of us. Not a design —
a brief plus the constraints a design has to satisfy.

1. Why this needs its own session
The PRS pipeline rebuild has produced two substantial data structures that nothing can
see:

mods_prs_run (Gate A) — dense-callset provenance: caller, callability policy, FASTA
checksum, autosomal median depth, four-outcome reconciliation counts.
mods_prs_score_manifest (Gate B) — 5,377 rows, one per published score:
compatibility class, production-eligibility, reasons, structural feature counts,
theoretical bounds, scoring-file checksum.

Grepping both frontend/src/components/PRSVectorBody.jsx and backend/mods_prs_api.py
for compat_class, production_eligible, score_manifest, prs_run, dense_callset,
validity returns zero matches in either file. There is no API surface and no UI.
Meanwhile Gates C–E will add computed scores with coverage, missingness and percentile
semantics that are easy to display wrongly. Deciding the API contract now, before Gate C
writes its first score, avoids retrofitting.

2. What exists today (all legacy)






























SurfaceFileCoversPatient Profile PRS slotfrontend/src/components/PRSVectorBody.jsxgenotype summary, per-disease score table, upload, compute, PDR exportTerminal commandfrontend/src/components/Terminal.jsx (~1502)prs status | compute | export | openDownstream consumersPDRInputInspector.jsx, PatientWeightsPanel.jsxPDR input displayAPIbackend/mods_prs_api.py/genotype/upload|summary|concordance, /prs/compute|scores|export/*|preview/pdr-input
Released-only filtering does exist, but in mods_prs_service.py
(all_scores_for / latest_score_for, .where(validity == "released")), so the API
inherits it. mods_polygenic_score is currently empty, so the UI correctly shows nothing.

3. Hard constraints (things a design must not get wrong)
3.1 Retire the “Cov.” column — do not port it
PRSVectorBody.jsx renders a colour-coded coverage column computing
snps_used / snps_in_scoring_file, painting <50% red as “unreliable”.
That ratio is the REF-effect bug’s signature, not a property of the score. Across all
40 legacy outlier scores it clusters at 42–52% — the ~49% of loci the old scorer silently
dropped. The UI presents a symptom of our own defect as a data-quality verdict about a
published score. It must be removed, not carried forward under a new name.
3.2 Three coverage quantities, never conflated
Each is a distinct number and must be labelled distinctly:

Structural overlap — % of scoring rows matched to target/reference alleles.
Genotype callability — % of matched loci with a confident patient genotype.
Effective score-information coverage — Σ_retained 2p(1-p)w² / Σ_all 2p(1-p)w²
(variance-weighted; the one that actually matters).

A single “coverage %” chip is exactly the mistake §3.1 describes.
3.3 Deferred means deferred
A score that is not production_eligible shows “not calculated — ”. Never a
partial number, never a greyed-out estimate, never an em-dash that could read as zero. The
reasons are already stored per row and are human-readable.
3.4 Percentiles: rank + N + interval, no decorative precision
Show “1 of 930” or “above ~99.9th in this panel”. Never “98.1376th”. A parametric
percentile is a secondary field, valid only when the gates pass — never for
few-variant, haplotype, skewed or multimodal scores.
3.5 Nothing unreleased may reach a display or an export
validity='released' gates the score readers today. Any new endpoint must inherit that,
and the PDR export path must never ingest a non-released row.

4. What the manifest makes newly displayable
Real numbers, already in prod, that have no home yet:

Fleet composition — A 1,997 / B 2,950 / C 426 / D 4; 3,863 production-eligible
(71.8%); 3.45B variant rows examined.
Sole-blocker analysis — the decision-driving view: multiallelic is the only thing
deferring 588 scores; unplaceable_rows appears in 399 but blocks alone in 18.
Report “appears in” and “sole blocker” as separate columns (they rank oppositely).
Per-score detail — class, eligibility, reasons, feature counts (indel, palindromic,
multiallelic, chrX, inferred/missing other-allele, unplaceable), theoretical [L, U],
scoring-file checksum, trait, weight_type.
Gate A provenance — reconciliation counts proving zero residual implicit-zero,
callability policy, reference-FASTA checksum, median depth.
weight_type distribution — messy catalog-wide (3,250 beta, 1,390 NR,
BETA/Beta case variants, 199 log(OR), free-text tail). Worth surfacing, since it
affects whether a score’s scale is interpretable.


5. Open questions for the session

Where does this live? A new tab on the Research dashboard, an extension of the
Patient Profile PRS slot, or a distinct “PRS pipeline” panel? The manifest is
catalog-scoped (not patient-scoped), unlike everything currently in the PRS slot —
that may argue for separating “which scores can we compute” from “this patient’s
scores”.
Does the manifest need a browsable 5,377-row table, or only aggregates plus lookup
by PGS ID? Pagination/filtering cost vs. actual use.
API shape — extend mods_prs_api.py or a new mods_prs_manifest_api.py Endpoints
for fleet summary, per-score detail, sole-blocker analysis, run provenance.
Terminal vs GUI split — the existing prs command is genuinely useful; how much of
this is better as prs manifest / prs runs subcommands rather than pixels?
Does the promotion policy get a UI? Promoting multiallelic is a signed-off human
decision worth 588 scores; showing its impact before approval may be valuable, but the
decision must not become a casual toggle.
Mobile — per CLAUDE.md all frontend work must be mobile-compatible; a 5,377-row
table is not, so decide the mobile view deliberately.


6. Sequencing note
Gate C (now built as backend/mods_prs_scorer.py) produces the first correct scores and
emits the three coverage quantities as a coverage_v1 metadata payload, which
mods_prs_pipeline_service.coverage_block re-validates on read. The frontend needs that
API contract to be settled anyway, so either do this planning first and build against
an agreed contract, or accept one revision after Gate C. Deciding §3.2’s three
quantities up front is the part that matters most, because that is what the legacy UI got
wrong.
Reference: docs/prs_validation/compatibility_classification.md (the classifier +
fleet results), the rebuild plan at
an internal agent path, and
GH #237 (classifier cross-validation).

prs/palindrome_forward_rule.title: Can a file's own unambiguous SNVs orient its palindromes?
prs/palindrome_forward_rule.content:
Can a file’s own unambiguous SNVs orient its palindromes?
GH #404, the successor to
#371. The short answer is: for most files, yes, with a
measured error under 1 %. The rule cannot tell which files are the exceptions, though, and
the exceptions are real. So it is licensed per class of file, and the class that holds most
of the rows cannot be measured with the data we have.

0. Why this was asked
Gate C defers palindromic SNVs
(A/T and C/G pairs, whose strand complement
is the pair itself). A wrong strand guess inverts the dosage silently. At E2 scope that
deferral costs 64,834,179 rows across 1,687 production-eligible scores.
#371 closed the hm_source route and proved something
more useful along the way: the PGS Catalog’s harmonizer never touches an allele. So
every scoring file’s alleles are its author’s, verbatim, and its unambiguous rows (which
Gate C checks against the pinned GRCh38 reference) are a direct readout of the author’s
strand convention. #404 proposed to lean on that corollary: if a file’s unambiguous rows
all match forward, read its palindromes forward too.
The issue named the risk precisely. A pipeline that orients the variants it can check and
leaves the palindromes alone produces a file that looks forward everywhere we can look and
is unoriented exactly where we cannot. The complement-only rate is blind to that by
construction. Only ground truth can price it, and the 167 scores that declare an
effect-allele frequency (EAF) are the only ground truth there is.

1. The answer






























Class of fileWhat the frequency test foundMeasured flipped share (95 % bound)Genome-wide (≥ 100k rows), complement-only ≤ 0.1 %11 files, 6 publications, 5,353,342 decidable palindromes≤ 0.12 %, and it tracks each file’s own complement-only rateSmall curated (< 1k rows), zero complement-only rows61 files, 49 publications, 953 decidable palindromes≤ 0.96 %Mid-size (1k–100k rows)one file, PGS000020: unambiguous rows forward, ~40 % of palindromes reversedrefutedStrand-mixed, A/B-coded (the control)PGS000714: 5 of 5 palindromes reversedas expected
So the forward rule is right almost everywhere it was measured. Three things stop that from
becoming a fleet-wide licence:

The counterexample exists. PGS000020 has a complement-only rate of 0.175 %, the
same order as the clean genome-wide files (up to 0.098 %). No threshold separates them
except a post hoc one.
The measured genome-wide files are not the ones the rule would mostly touch. They hold
9.7 % of the genome-wide class’s palindromic rows. 87 % sit in three publications that
declare no frequency: Ma 2022, Truong 2024 (PRSmix) and Bakker 2023 (metaGRS). Nothing
we hold can test them.
The EAF-carrying set under-samples mid-size files. It has one, and it fails; the
fleet has 535.

The recommendation (§7) is to license the small-curated class, which the measurement
covers well, and to put the genome-wide class to Richard as an explicit extrapolation. That
class is 98.8 % of the rows, so its answer decides the arithmetic.

2. The instrument, and why agreement alone is not the answer
The test. For an A/T pair, reading the effect allele on the other strand turns it into
the other allele, so the reverse reading’s panel frequency is exactly 1 − p. Comparing
the author’s declared EAF with the panel’s
allele frequency for the effect base read
forward is therefore a sign test. Same side of 0.5 is forward, opposite sides is
flipped, decisive only when both frequencies are clear of 0.5 by a margin (0.08 here, the
usual MAF < 0.42 convention). This is exactly the rule
mods_prs_normalization.resolve_palindrome_strand implements for Gate D, so this spike also
validates the code D1 will run.
The panel. HGDP+1kGP (pgsc_HGDP+1kGP_v1), read from its .pgen with pgenlib: allele
counts over the 3,330 unrelated samples, overall and per super-population. Each file’s
frequencies are compared with the population that sits closest to its EAF on its own
unambiguous rows (European for 114 of 167 files).
Why agreement is not the answer. A cohort frequency and a panel frequency can straddle
0.5 for reasons that have nothing to do with strand: ancestry mismatch, sampling noise, an
EAF column that means something else. So raw agreement sits below 100 % even if every
palindrome is forward. The same file’s unambiguous SNVs calibrate the instrument: their
strand is known from the panel’s own alleles, so its error rate on them is measured. Under
“every palindrome is forward” the palindromic discordance should equal that error rate, cell
for cell in (|EAF − 0.5|, |p − 0.5|). Each flipped palindrome raises its cell from e to
1 − e, so
f_hat = (observed discordant palindromes − expected) / (n − 2·expected)

estimates the flipped share. On synthetic data with known flip rates of 0, 1 %, 5 % and
50 % it recovers each within its interval.
The bound that needs no calibration. Observed discordance is r = e + f(1 − 2e). For
any instrument error e below 0.5, f ≤ r. So the raw discordance
upper-bounds the
flipped share without trusting the calibration at all. §5 leads with these bounds wherever
the calibration is shaky.

3. Three ways the ground truth could lie, and the check for each
A population mismatch. An East Asian cohort’s EAF compared with a European panel
frequency straddles 0.5 far more often, which would inflate discordance. Check: each file
is compared with its closest population (above). The calibration then absorbs whatever
mismatch remains, cell by cell.
An EAF column that is not an effect-allele frequency. Some files report a minor-allele
frequency, a constant, or the other allele’s frequency. Such a column would read as a
wholesale “flip”. Check: a file’s instrument must call ≥ 80 % of its own known-strand SNVs
correctly before its palindromes count. 8 files fail, set aside rather than pooled.
PGS001775 calls 0 % of them right: its column is the other allele’s frequency, which
without this check would have counted as 100 % flipped palindromes.
A frequency that was looked up, not measured. This is the circularity threat, and the
reason it matters is structural. An EAF copied from a forward-strand reference by allele
letter reports the forward frequency of whatever letter the file wrote. It therefore calls
every palindrome forward whether it is or not: a check that shares the assumption it is
checking, the lesson of the REF-effect bug.
Check: the commonest such reference is 1000 Genomes, whose samples are inside the panel.
So a copied EAF sits almost exactly on those subsets’ frequencies, far closer than an
independent cohort can (every publication judged independent here sits at a median of
0.0055 or more from the nearest 1000 Genomes subset).
One publication fails: PGP000324 (PGS002294) sits a median 0.0015 from 1000 Genomes EAS
against 0.0095 from the full EAS group. Every genome-wide file is measured (medians
0.0065–0.0125, no closer to 1000 Genomes than to the full group).

4. The ground-truth set
167 EAF-carrying scores from 103 publications, streamed through the connector’s own row
parser and classified by the same branch order Gate B uses. The palindromic counts reconcile
file by file against the manifest. 6,180,181 palindromic and 35,688,115 unambiguous rows
carry a frequency and a position, and 99.31 % of their positions are present in the panel.
The set is two populations wearing one label, and every result is reported in that shape:























FilesPublicationsDecidable palindromes (margin 0.08)Genome-wide (≥ 10k palindromic EAF rows)1165,353,342Curated156 (118 with a verified instrument)971,831
A pooled row rate over all 167 would be a statement about 6 pipelines. This is the
row-aggregate-versus-per-score trap of `prs_primer.md` §5.4, arriving
again.
The reconciliation that anchors everything: the complement-only bands recomputed here match
the issue’s table exactly (784 / 298 / 325 / 81 / 9 / 190 scores; 64,834,179 palindromic
rows).

5. Results
5.1 The instrument, on rows whose strand is known




















RowsGenome-wideCuratedForward unambiguous SNVs, called forward99.982 % of 30,997,61297.735 % of 17,261Complement-only SNVs, called reversed99.905 % of 23,10385.3 % of 68
The second row is the positive control. Complement-only rows are genuinely written on the
reverse strand, and the frequency test sees them as reversed. So it has the power to see a
real flip, on real data, at the rate that matters.
5.2 Genome-wide files






















































































ScorePublicationComplement-only rateDecidable palindromesAgreementCeilingFlipped sharePGS003576–85 (×4)Dahl 20220.098 %756,112 each99.817 %99.958 %0.141 %PGS005349Tanha 2026~0721,60099.998 %99.998 %0.001 %PGS005241Tanha 2025~0528,01899.999 %99.999 %0.000 %PGS000909Campos 20210.055 %367,89399.924 %99.998 %0.075 %PGS000908Campos 20210.056 %350,18699.925 %99.998 %0.073 %PGS000907Campos 20210.009 %218,45299.962 %99.998 %0.036 %PGS000882Revez 20200.057 %71,59799.950 %99.999 %0.050 %PGS004926Tsepilov 20230.057 %71,14899.949 %99.999 %0.050 %
Pooled: agreement 99.883 % against a ceiling of 99.976 %. The calibration-free bound is
6,258 / 5,353,342 = 0.117 %, ≤ 0.119 %.
The column worth reading is the complement-only rate beside the flipped share: they move
together, from ~0 with ~0 up to 0.098 % with 0.141 %. That is what uniform residual
strand error looks like: whatever put 0.1 % of the unambiguous rows on the wrong strand put
about the same share of the palindromes there, where no allele check can see them. It is also
flat across the margin. The flipped share is 0.090 % at a margin of 0.20 and 0.104 % at
0.02, with no sign of a pipeline that aligned the easy palindromes by frequency and left the
near-0.5 ones unaligned.
5.3 Curated files





























SetFilesDiscordant / decidableFlipped share, 95 % boundRate = 062 (61 with a decidable palindrome)4 / 953 = 0.420 %≤ 0.958 %Rate ≤ 1 %, excluding the two outliers of §5.4664 / 1,068 = 0.375 %≤ 0.855 %Fewer than 20 orientable rows242 / 36≤ 16.5 % (too small to judge)
For curated files the calibration runs slightly pessimistic: the rate-0 band’s f_hat is
−1.4 %, meaning palindromes agree better than the files’ unambiguous rows predict. So the
calibration-free bounds are the numbers to use here. Of the curated files with any discordant
palindrome, 9 were observed against 21.5 expected from instrument noise alone.
5.4 The counterexample: PGS000020
PGS000020 is a type 2 diabetes score (Läll et al., Genet Med 2016; pruning and
thresholding on external GWAS summary statistics). It has 7,502 rows. Its unambiguous rows
match GRCh38 forward: 12 complement-only of 6,867, 0.175 %, with a balanced allele
profile (top_fraction 0.483, so not an A/B convention). Its instrument calls its own
unambiguous SNVs almost perfectly (expected palindromic discordance 0.10). Its palindromes:
169 of 425 decidable are reversed, across both pair types (A/T 75 of 169, C/G 94 of 256).
The examples are unambiguous: 10:112989181 A declared at 2 % where the panel has A at 97 %.
That is the failure mode the issue described, observed. The forward rule would have silently
inverted roughly 40 % of this score’s palindromes. Nothing in the file’s unambiguous
behaviour warns of it, and its complement-only rate is within a factor of two of the cleanest
genome-wide files’. A clean complement-only rate is necessary and not sufficient.
It matters beyond its own rows because of what it is. It is the only mid-size (1k–100k
rows) file in the ground truth, and the fleet has 535 of them.
5.5 The control
The issue asked for the comparison to be run on files that fail the complement-rate gate,
expecting no better than chance. The one genuinely strand-mixed EAF file, PGS000714
(Sipeky 2020, all-A/x allele convention, 47.8 % complement-only), has 5 of 5 decidable
palindromes reversed (binomial p ≈ 4 × 10⁻⁸ against its calibration). The gate is measuring
what we think. The band-level “gate-failing” pool (302 decidable, 6 discordant) is mostly
small files in the 1–5 % band, where one or two complement-only rows out of fifty is not
strand-mixing. Their palindromes are fine, which is itself a finding about how coarse the
rate is for small files.

6. Where the rule would land
The fleet’s deferred palindromic rows by size of file and complement-only band, beside the
ground truth covering each cell:





























































































File sizeBandScoresPalindromic rowsShareGround truth< 1krate = 052714,2500.022 %62 files → ≤ 0.96 %< 1k0.1–1 %1567,7390.012 %4 files → ≤ 2.6 %< 1k1–5 %812,2790.004 %24 files → ≤ 1.7 %< 1k> 5 %946—the control< 1k< 20 orientable1903940.001 %too small to judge1k–100krate = 0182277,0320.43 %none1k–100k0–0.1 %184399,5630.62 %none1k–100k0.1–1 %16955,0920.09 %PGS000020 → ~40 % reversed≥ 100krate = 07512,412,32719.1 %none≥ 100k0–0.1 %11451,665,45779.7 %11 files → ≤ 0.12 %
And the genome-wide class (≥ 100k rows, ≤ 0.1 %) by publication, since a pipeline’s strand
handling belongs to its publication:





















































PublicationFilesPalindromic rowsShareMethod (PGS Catalog)EAF?Ma et al. 2022, AJHG7437,998,11859.3 %DBSLMM, lassosum, P+T and othersnoTruong et al. 2024, Cell Genom6412,057,35218.8 %PRSmixnoBakker et al. 2023, Stroke65,696,4548.9 %elastic-net metaGRSnothe 6 measured publications116,184,0269.7 %PRSice-2, SBayesR(C), SCTyes10 others342,141,8343.3 %mixedno
Two of the three dominant pipelines deserve a sentence each, labelled as inference from the
method rather than measurement. PRSmix and metaGRS files are weighted mixtures of existing
PGS Catalog scores, so their palindromes carry whatever orientation their components had.
If any component was a PGS000020, the mixture inherited it. Ma 2022 is a multi-method
benchmark built on external summary statistics. The measured set does include external
consortium pipelines (Tanha on BCAC; Campos), which is some comfort, but it is not these.

7. Recommendation








































OptionScopeScoresPalindromic rowsMeasured flipped shareA. Refusenothing00n/aB. Small curated (recommended)< 1k rows, zero complement-only over ≥ 20 orientable52714,250≤ 0.96 %, 61 files from 49 publicationsC. B + genome-wideadds ≥ 100k rows at ≤ 0.1 % complement-only71664,092,034≤ 0.12 % on 9.7 % of the added rows; unmeasured on the restnever1k–100k rows535731,687counterexample
Recommended rule (B). Read a file’s palindromic SNVs on the forward strand when it has
fewer than 1,000 rows, zero complement-only rows over at least 20 orientable rows, and is
not strand-mixed by the two-signal test. Measured error: ≤ 0.96 % of palindromes reversed
(95 %), point estimate 0.42 % raw, indistinguishable from zero after calibration.
It is small in rows and large where it counts. The primer’s §1.4 point is that these scores
are ML features, consumed one score at a time. For the 527 scores in B, palindromes are a
median 11.3 % of each score’s rows (IQR 8.0–14.3 %), the curated, interpretable scores
where the deferral hurts most per score.
C is Richard’s call, and it is a real one. For the pipelines measured, the genome-wide
rule is excellent: ≤ 0.12 %, error tracking each file’s own complement-only rate. The case
for C is that it recovers ~10 % of the loci (median 10.1 % per score) in 189 genome-wide
scores, at a probable error that small. The case against is that 87 % of those rows are in pipelines built differently
from anything measured. Two of them mix existing scores and inherit their components’
orientation, and PGS000020 shows the unseen failure is not hypothetical. My lean is to hold C
until one of the two routes in §8 can measure the dominant publications. For a genome-wide
score, the deferral mostly costs variance that Gate D’s normalization carries, while a
systematic inversion is exactly what §1.4
calls “a confident, learnable lie”.
What landed, inert until someone chooses:

ScoringPolicy.palindrome_forward_scores has the shape of strand_flip_recovery_scores:
a set of ids, empty by default, named in the run’s provenance. Each score records
palindrome_forward_rule and n_palindromic_read_forward in its gate_c payload, so
Gate F can gate on them and a reader can see how much of a score rests on the rule.
scripts/prs/palindrome_forward_candidates.py derives the set per class. B is the
default; C only with --include-genome-wide, which prints the caveat. The mid-size class
is not offered at all, and tests/test_palindrome_forward_candidates.py keeps it that way.
Like the strand-recovery script, it exits non-zero while any manifest row is on an older
classifier.
Populating the set changes the policy fingerprint, so it rides E3 with the patient and
D2 with the panel, never a pass of its own (GH #360).


8. What this does not settle
The genome-wide class, and two ways to measure it. Both are feasible and neither was in
scope.

The source GWAS as the second frequency. #371 §5.1
argued that a bigger panel cannot help, because orientation needs the author’s
frequency and a file without EAF has none. The source summary statistics do have one. The
Catalog records the GWAS accession (Ma 2022’s scores cite GCST sources), and most
harmonized summary statistics carry effect-allele frequencies and β signs. Joining a
scoring file to its source by position recovers the author-side frequency, and comparing
weight sign with β sign on unambiguous rows calibrates the join. That would measure
Ma 2022 directly.
Mixtures through their components. A PRSmix or metaGRS file’s palindromes come from
named component scores. Where a component is EAF-carrying or already measured, its
verdict transfers.

The weight-sign mode. A pipeline can relabel a palindrome’s letters to its reference and
attach the other allele’s β. The letters then look perfect and the contribution is inverted
anyway. The frequency test catches this only when the EAF travels with the β, i.e. when it
was measured in the author’s cohort, which is what §3’s provenance check establishes. Letter
checks, including the REF/ALT convention of a file’s unambiguous rows (strict in Truong,
Bakker, Tanha and Revez), cannot catch it. So they are not offered as evidence here.
The last 0.02. Palindromes within 0.02 of 0.5 are invisible to any frequency test.
§5.2’s flat margin curve says the genome-wide flip rate does not climb toward 0.5 through
0.02. Below that it is unmeasurable, and the rule reads those palindromes forward on the
strength of the neighbouring bins.
The EAF route and the forward rule, together. 73 of the 527 scores in B also carry an
EAF, so D1’s frequency route could orient their palindromes row by row. The frequency route
is the better instrument where it is decisive. When both are implemented, it should take
precedence per row and the forward rule should cover what it leaves undecided. That wiring
belongs to D1.
A trap in the fingerprint, noted rather than fixed. Today’s default policy fingerprint
(b96ec1786f6f19b4) already differs from E2’s (c6a513393403a5cb), because #376 added a
field after E2 ran. This change adds another. That is by design: a new knob must move the
fingerprint. But it means a D2 panel scored with current code will refuse every E2 row,
which is right, since E3 is planned before normalization anyway, and it would be confusing
to discover mid-run.

9. Reproducing it
backend/scripts/prs/spike_palindrome_forward_rule.py. Four stages, each resumable. The
module docstring carries the exact commands, including the throwaway-container step that
reads the .pgen (pgenlib has no Windows wheel and lives only in the live worker’s writable
layer, not in the maple-worker image). The stages were measured at 102 s, 175 s, 7.3 min
over 8,041,370 panel records, and ~4 min. The report prints the reconciliation first: if the
recomputed bands do not match the issue’s table, every number under it is void. Outputs land
in backend/data/prs_palindrome_404/ (host-only): report.txt, results.json, and the
per-file target rows.
Further reading: `palindrome_orientation_spike.md`
(#371, the harmonizer and the EAF ceiling) · `prs_primer.md` §5.4 and
§5.7b (why Gate C defers, and the road to release) ·
`compatibility_classification.md` (how a palindromic row
is counted in the first place).

prs/palindrome_orientation_spike.title: Can hm_source orient a palindromic SNV?
prs/palindrome_orientation_spike.content:
Can hm_source orient a palindromic SNV?
GH #371. The short answer is no, for every
value of hm_source, and the reason is structural rather than statistical: the
harmonization stage that writes hm_source never looks at an allele.

0. Why this was asked
Gate C defers palindromic SNVs — A/T and C/G pairs, whose strand complement is the
pair itself — because nothing in the alleles says which strand they were written on, and
guessing wrong inverts the dosage silently. It is the one failure mode where being
wrong is both undetectable downstream and maximally harmful. At the Gate E2 scope that
deferral costs 64,810,321 rows, 2.99 % of the fleet, concentrated in the small curated
pre-2015 scores: 1,687 production-eligible scores carry at least one palindromic row, and
among those the median score loses 10.41 % of its rows.
The assumed way out is a frequency comparison — the scoring file’s declared
allelefrequency_effect against a reference panel’s frequency at that locus. Concordant
means same strand, complementary means flipped. But only 167 of the 1,687 affected
scores declare an effect-allele frequency at all, capping that route at 9.5 % of the
deferred rows.
GH #371 proposed a second route. Harmonized files carry an hm_source column, and a
150-file sample found 44.2 % of palindromic rows carrying hm_source = ENSEMBL. If
ENSEMBL meant “this variant was matched to an Ensembl/dbSNP record”, and dbSNP records
are strand-defined, then those rows would already be forward-strand and would need no
frequency at all — lifting the recoverable share from ~9.5 % to ~45 %.
That hypothesis is false. This document says why, on four independent lines of evidence,
and prices what is left.

1. The answer






























hm_sourceWhat it actually meansCan it orient a palindrome?ENSEMBLThe variant’s position was looked up from its rsID in the Catalog’s Ensembl coordinate map.No.liftoverThe position was converted from the author’s build with pyliftover.No.Author-reportedThe author’s own coordinates were kept, because the file was already on the target build.No.UnknownNo position could be resolved at all. Emitted by the harmonizer but absent from the published column documentation.No — such a row is unplaceable anyway.
The verdict is the same for every value for one reason: hm_source is the provenance of
the coordinate, not of the alleles. The PGS Catalog’s own column definition says so in
as many words — “Data source of the variant position” — and the harmonization stage that
writes it does not read, write, or check effect_allele or other_allele.
