There is therefore no hm_source-based route, and no partial one. H1, H2 and H3 from the
issue are all answered “no”, and H1 is answered “no” for a different reason than the issue
supposed — not because ENSEMBL matching is unreliable, but because ENSEMBL never
claimed anything about alleles in the first place.
§2 is the mechanism. §4.1 is the measurement that would have settled it without reading a
line of the harmonizer: in one scoring file, hm_source = ENSEMBL labels 26,901
forward-strand rows and 26,801 reverse-complemented ones.

2. The evidence
2.1 The harmonizer has two stages, and only the second one touches strand
PGScatalog/pgs-harmonizer runs in two
passes, and the distinction between them is the whole answer:




















StageWhat it doesWhat it writesHmPOSResolves each variant’s coordinate on the target build, by rsID lookup, by liftover, or by keeping the author’s.hm_source, hm_rsID, hm_chr, hm_pos, hm_inferOtherAlleleHmVCFLooks the variant up in a reference VCF and checks the alleles against it: matches, palindromic, reverse-complement.hm_code, hm_vid, and on a correction hm_fixedStrandFlip + hm_reported_effect_allele
variant_HmPOS() returns exactly five values — hm_source, hm_rsID, hm_chr,
hm_pos, hm_inferOtherAllele — and effect_allele is not among them. It is passed
through untouched. hm_source = 'ENSEMBL' is set on the single condition that the row’s
rsID was found in the coordinate map; the alleles are never compared to the Ensembl
record’s.
Strand lives entirely in HmVCF. DetermineHarmonizationCode() maps the triple
(matches-VCF, is-palindromic, is-flipped) to an hm_code, and FixStrandFlips() rewrites
alleles only where hm_code == -4, preserving the original in
hm_reported_effect_allele. The codes that matter here:

























hm_codeMeaning5Variant matches the reference VCF3Matched, but with ambiguous orientation (A/T, C/G)-4Strand flip suspected; corrected by default-5Not present in the reference VCF
So the Catalog does identify palindromes — it just labels them and moves on. Its own
source carries the unimplemented intent beside that code: a ToDo to use allele frequency
to resolve the hm_code=3 variants. The frequency route is an open item in the
Catalog’s harmonizer too, which is a useful calibration on how tractable it is.
One corollary worth stating, because it closes a tempting side door:
hm_inferOtherAllele carries no strand information either. infer_OtherAllele() requires
the author’s effect allele to appear verbatim in the Ensembl record’s allele list, with
no complement check. For a palindromic A/T variant the author’s A matches whichever
strand it came from, and T comes back either way.
2.2 The files we hold never went through HmVCF
That is the mechanism; here is our data. Scanning every cached scoring file’s header and
column names (spike_palindrome_hm_source.py headers):

























filescached GRCh38 scoring files scanned5,377carrying hm_source5,377carrying HmPOS_build / HmPOS_date header keys5,377carrying any HmVCF artifact — hm_code, hm_vid, hm_info, hm_fixedStrandFlip, hm_reported_effect_allele, hm_reported_other_allele, or an HmVCF_* header key0
Not one file in the catalog we hold has been through the stage that checks alleles. The
hm_code column that would flag a palindrome, and the strand correction that would fix a
flip, are both absent from every row we have ever scored.
This is not a gap in our mirror. The Catalog’s FTP publishes exactly two harmonized
flavours per score — PGS######_hmPOS_GRCh37.txt.gz and PGS######_hmPOS_GRCh38.txt.gz
— and no hmVCF flavour at all. hm_code is not available to any consumer of the PGS
Catalog, so there is nothing to fetch and no version of this route that works by
downloading a better file.
2.3 Harmonization does not change alleles — measured, not inferred
The two arguments above are a code reading. This one is our data. For nine scores chosen
to span all three hm_source values, the author-submitted scoring file was downloaded
from the Catalog’s FTP and joined to our harmonized copy row by row:

















scoresrows joinedeffect_allele differsother_allele differs9 (3 ENSEMBL, 3 liftover, 3 Author-reported)40100
Harmonization moved coordinates — in the liftover files by up to megabases — and left
every allele exactly as the author wrote it. Whatever strand a scoring file arrived on is
the strand we score it on.
2.4 What the witness does
pgsc_calc — the Catalog’s own calculator, and our reconciliation witness (see
`prs_primer.md` §5.4) — labels A/T and C/G SNPs ambiguous in its
match step and excludes them by default (keep_ambiguous = false). It has no
frequency-based resolution path anywhere; the only alternative it offers is to keep them
as written, and its own parameter documentation describes that as assuming the scoring
file and the target data are on the same strand.
Its match code is blunter still: even on the same build, it notes, data can arrive
improperly strand-oriented.
So Gate C’s deferral is not a conservative deviation from the field. It is the field’s
default, arrived at independently, and the one opt-out that exists is documented as an
assumption rather than a resolution.

3. The fleet-wide distribution
The issue’s table was a 150-file sample. This is the full measurement over all 1,687
production-eligible scores carrying a palindromic row — every row of every one of them,
645,528,195 rows in total, of which 64,834,179 are palindromic.








































hm_source on a palindromic rowrowssharedominant inof those rows, carrying an EAFliftover38,674,47659.65 %616 files1,076ENSEMBL14,072,76021.71 %984 files6,179,102Author-reported12,078,16918.63 %87 files20Unknown8,7740.01 %0 files6,266
and over the same files’ 577,298,945 non-palindromic biallelic SNV rows, for contrast:
Author-reported 43.88 %, liftover 38.58 %, ENSEMBL 17.54 %, Unknown 0.00 %.
The measured palindromic total reconciles exactly against the manifest’s
sum(n_palindromic) over the same scores — 64,834,179 both ways — which is what
establishes that this scan’s allele-pair classification is the same one Gate B and Gate C
use rather than a re-implementation that drifted.
Two things worth reading off that table.
The issue’s sample was right about files and wrong about rows, and the discrepancy is
instructive. It reported ENSEMBL at 44.2 % of palindromic rows against the fleet’s
21.71 %. But it capped each file at 300 palindromic rows, which makes it a file-weighted
measure wearing a row-weighted label — and on the file measure it was nearly exact:
84 of 150 files (56 %) ENSEMBL-dominant against the fleet’s 984 of 1,687 (58.3 %).
Row-weighted, liftover dominates because the multi-million-row genome-wide scores were
harmonized that way; file-weighted, ENSEMBL dominates because most files are small.
This is the same row-aggregate-versus-per-score trap the primer flags at §5.4, arriving
from a third direction.
Essentially every EAF-carrying palindromic row is ENSEMBL-sourced — 6,179,102 of the
6,186,464 in §5. So the one route that does work and the hm_source value the hypothesis
singled out are almost perfectly correlated, which is exactly the coincidence that makes a
spurious hypothesis look promising. The correlation is real; the causal claim behind it is
not.

4. The counterexample: strand-discordant files are real
Everything above says hm_source cannot certify forward strand. A separate question is
whether the catalog’s palindromes happen to be forward-strand anyway, which would make
“assume forward” empirically safe even though it is formally unjustified.
It is not safe, and the demonstration is cheap.
The detector. On the forward strand, A/G and C/T are the same transition seen from
the two strands and occur about equally often; likewise the A/C / G/T transversions.
So for any file, top_fraction — the share of its unambiguous SNVs written as A/C or
A/G — should sit at ~0.5. On three normal files measured here it lands at 0.4991,
0.5017, 0.5018, with the paired counts agreeing to within 1 %.
A value near 1.0 means something else entirely: every row was written in Illumina’s TOP
allele convention, where the reported pair is always A/x. TOP is assigned per variant
from the surrounding sequence, so roughly half of those rows are reverse-complemented
relative to GRCh38 — and nothing in the scoring file records which.
It happens. Auditing the allele pairs of the outliers directly against the pinned
GRCh38 FASTA:









































scoretraitsingle-base rowsallele pairs presentforward-matchcomplement-onlypalindromicPGS005393post-traumatic stress disorder53,705A/G, A/C only50.1 %49.9 %0PGS000741prostate cancer46A/G, A/C only41.3 %45.7 %6PGS004237coronary artery disease200,000all four99.9 %0.1 %0
PGS005393 does not contain a single C/T or G/T row out of 53,705. That is not a
statistical tendency, it is a coding convention, and half its rows are on the opposite
strand from the genome. PGS000741 shows the same signature — and it carries six
palindromic rows (three A/T, three C/G) that a forward-strand assumption would resolve
by coin flip.
top_fraction alone is not enough, and checking that mattered. Three files —
PGS005087, PGS005088, PGS005089 — are top_fraction = 1.000 and yet 0 % of their
orientable rows are complement-only. Audited against the FASTA, other_allele == REF at
5,326 of 5,326 checkable loci in PGS005087: its alleles genuinely are the
forward-strand pair, so the all-A/x shape describes its variant set rather than a
relabelling of it, and its palindromes are no worse off than anyone’s. The detector
therefore requires both signals — an A/B-shaped allele convention and rows that only
match complemented. The first names the convention; only the second proves the file is
strand-mixed. Shipping top_fraction alone would have refused three innocent files.
How much is actually at stake — the honest number. Under the two-signal rule, of the
1,687 palindrome-carrying eligible scores, 3 are strand-mixed (PGS000714, PGS000741,
PGS000733), carrying 21 deferred palindromic rows between them. Relaxing to “any
complement-only rate above 5 %, whatever the convention” gives 18 scores and 62 rows;
above 1 %, 99 scores and 2,341 rows — 0.0036 % of the fleet’s 64.8 M. Fleet-wide the
complement-only rate is 490,602 of 2,037,784,515 orientable rows = 0.0241 % (the
primer’s 0.0226 % is the same numerator over all 2.166 B scoring rows).
So this finding changes the arithmetic of the palindrome question by essentially nothing.
What it changes is the warrant. “Assume forward strand” cannot be defended as
empirically safe, because the exceptions exist, are identifiable in advance, and fail in
the one mode — silent dosage inversion — that nothing downstream catches. A policy that is
right 99.996 % of the time and unfalsifiable on the remainder is not the same object as a
policy that is right.
There is also a reason the exposure is small, and it is not luck: the large A/B-coded
files carry no palindromes at all. PGS005393, the cleanest case in the catalog at 53,705
rows and 50.8 % complement-only, has zero. A submitter who knows their data is in A/B
coding generally also knows the ambiguous SNPs are unrecoverable and drops them. The files
that kept theirs are the ones that did not know — which is precisely why their palindromes
should not be trusted.
4.1 And these files are hm_source = ENSEMBL
The same audit, split by hm_source, is the direct empirical refutation of H1 — not an
argument from the harmonizer’s source, but a measurement on rows we hold:



































scoreENSEMBL rows that are forwardENSEMBL rows that are reverse-complementedpalindromic rows, all ENSEMBL-sourcedPGS00539326,90126,8010PGS00074119216PGS00071424229PGS00004726213
In PGS005393, hm_source = ENSEMBL labels 26,901 forward-strand rows and 26,801
reverse-strand rows in the same file. The label takes the same value on both halves of
a file split down the middle by strand, which is what “carries no strand information”
looks like when you measure it rather than reason about it.
And the rows H1 would have licensed us to orient — the ENSEMBL-sourced palindromes of
PGS000741, PGS000714 and PGS000047 — sit in files that are 45–48 % reverse-strand. They
are not merely un-certified by hm_source; they are among the most dangerous rows in the
fleet, and H1 would have singled them out as safe.
(PGS000047 sits at top_fraction 0.875, just under the A/B gate, with a 44.7 %
complement-only rate — a file that is strand-mixed without being cleanly A/B-shaped. It is
in this table as evidence about hm_source, not as one of the three the two-signal rule
flags.)

5. What is left of the frequency route
The 9.5 % ceiling is a count of rows that have a declared frequency. It is not a count
of rows a panel could orient, because a frequency near 0.5 is as consistent with one
strand as the other — that is the same ambiguity one level up.
Measured over all 167 EAF-carrying scores (spike_palindrome_hm_source.py eaf):

















rowspalindromic rows in those 167 scores6,186,687…declaring a parseable effect-allele frequency6,186,464 (223 rows carry an unusable value)
and of those, the share a panel comparison could actually separate, by the margin from
0.5 required to call it:















































required |EAF − 0.5|rows orientableof EAF-carrying palindromic rowsof the fleet’s 64.8M deferred> 0.026,014,18597.22 %9.28 %> 0.055,753,39593.00 %8.88 %> 0.085,495,35688.83 %8.48 %> 0.105,318,59885.97 %8.21 %> 0.154,861,47878.58 %7.50 %> 0.204,389,81270.96 %6.77 %
The curve is gentle, which is the good news: the EAF-carrying scores are not clustered at
0.5, so the margin can be set conservatively without losing much. At a margin of 0.08 —
equivalent to requiring a minor allele frequency below 0.42, a common convention in GWAS
harmonization — the route delivers 8.48 % of the fleet’s deferred palindromic rows
rather than 9.5 %.
This is an upper bound in one further respect that only D1 can close: it counts rows whose
declared frequency is far enough from 0.5 to be decisive, and assumes the panel agrees
with the author’s cohort closely enough to call the side. Where a score was trained in a
cohort whose allele frequencies differ materially from HGDP+1kGP, a row can clear the
margin and still not be callable. That measurement needs the panel and belongs to D1.
Note what the margin does not interact with: a file being Illumina A/B-coded (§4) does
not spoil the frequency route. A/B coding is a per-variant strand assignment, and a
per-row frequency comparison resolves it per row, which is precisely the case it is for.
What A/B coding rules out is assuming forward strand — §6 item 4.
5.1 Why a bigger frequency source would not raise the ceiling
The obvious objection is that 1,520 scores lack a frequency only because the file lacks
one, and frequencies are freely available — dbSNP, gnomAD, ALFA, and the HGDP+1kGP panel
already staged for Gate D all carry them. Why not look the locus up?
Because orientation needs two frequencies, not one. The test is whether the value the
author attached to their effect allele matches the panel’s frequency for the same allele
read forward, or its complement. A panel frequency on its own says how common each base is
at that locus; it says nothing about which of them the author meant by “effect”. Swapping
in a larger panel replaces one side of a comparison whose other side does not exist.
The same answer disposes of “look the rsID up in dbSNP, which is strand-defined.” dbSNP
reports an A/T variant as A/T — the allele set is anchored to the forward strand, but
a palindromic set is its own complement, so the file’s A still matches under either
reading. That is the definition of the problem, not a way around it. It is also exactly
what our own reference check already does against the pinned FASTA, and why the scorer
defers instead of resolving.

6. Recommended policy


Keep deferring palindromic SNVs, and stop treating hm_source as a possible
reprieve. There is no partial credit here: the column is positional provenance and
promoting any of its values would be exactly the “decide an ambiguous mapping that
isn’t crystal clear” that CLAUDE.md forbids — with dosage inversion as the failure.


Do not run the Catalog’s HmVCF stage ourselves to get hm_code. It would tell us
which rows are palindromic — which Gate B already computes — and its answer for those
rows is 3, meaning unresolved. The one thing it adds, hm_code = -4 strand-flip
detection, we already measure ourselves as n_complement_only_match, against a pinned
reference rather than against Ensembl’s VCF.


Resolve palindromes in D1 only for the EAF-carrying subset, and only above a stated
margin from 0.5. §5 prices it: 8.48 % of the fleet’s deferred rows at a margin of
0.08, against the 9.5 % headline. Everything else becomes a Gate F coverage gate, not a
pending decision — there is no instrument that would settle it later.


Gate any assumption-based orientation on the per-score complement-only rate, which
we already store. Gate C writes n_complement_only_match on every score; a rate
above ~5 % of orientable rows means the file is strand-mixed and no forward-strand
assumption may be applied to it — including the TOP/BOT reconstruction in §7. No new
manifest column is needed for the guard, because the scorer computes the signal
anyway. top_fraction is worth adding to Gate B only to explain which convention
caused it, and §4 is the reason it cannot stand alone as the guard.
Landed (GH #377): classifier v5
counts n_snv_pair_top / n_snv_pair_bot (migration 108), strand_profile() joins them
to Gate C’s measured complement-only rate and returns strand_mixed — null, not
false, when either signal is unmeasured — and the Manifest tab renders both signals
side by side rather than collapsing them into a verdict.
This does not gate the frequency route. A frequency comparison resolves strand per
row and is precisely the right tool for an A/B-coded file.


Separately, the strand-mixed files are losing rows. In an A/B-coded file about half
the non-palindromic rows fail the reference check and are dropped as
ref_allele_mismatch — which reads as “the score and the genome describe different
variants” when the real cause is a known, correctable convention. A per-file,
evidence-gated flip would recover 26,885 rows across 5 scores, without weakening the
global check that allow_strand_flip=True would destroy.
(An earlier revision said 56,411 rows in 37 scores. That was the complement-rate cut
alone, before the two-signal rule existed. Requiring the allele convention too removes
PGS005285 — 29,389 rows at a 5.8 % rate but a balanced allele profile, so its mismatches
are not an A/B convention and a flip there would be a guess, not a repair. The rule
halving its own headline number is the rule working.)
Landed (GH #376):
ScoringPolicy.strand_flip_recovery_scores is a set of pgs_ids, not a second boolean —
the global flag is an assumption about the catalog, this is a finding about named files,
and the run’s provenance records the ids so the difference is auditable.
scripts/prs/strand_recovery_candidates.py derives the set from the two signals and
exits non-zero while any manifest row is still at an older classifier, so a provisional
answer cannot be piped into a scoring policy by accident. Empty by default: turning
it on obliges a re-score of the affected scores, which is Gate F’s call and can ride E3.
It does not block Gate D, it cannot touch a palindromic row, and it is coverage rather
than correctness.



7. What this does not settle

Added 2026-09-27 — this section originally read as though the frequency route were the
only one left. It is not, and this document’s own §2 is what makes the other one
legitimate. Because HmPOS never touches alleles, a scoring file’s alleles are the
author’s, verbatim and uniformly — so its non-palindromic rows are a direct readout of
that author’s strand convention, measured against the pinned reference on thousands of
rows per file. §6 item 4 uses that signal as a guard; its positive side is a licence,
and I wrote the first without drawing the second.
Banded over all 1,687 palindrome-carrying eligible scores: 99.899 % of the 64,834,179
deferred palindromic rows sit in files whose non-palindromic rows match the reference
forward at ≥ 99.9 %. Forty-six rows are in strand-suspect files. Against the declared-EAF
ceiling of 8.48 % in §5, that is roughly 12× the coverage, and it needs no scoring file
to have volunteered a frequency.
It is a hypothesis with one named failure mode — a pipeline that orients non-palindromic
variants and leaves palindromes alone, which the GWAS Catalog and OpenTargets sumstats
harmonisers genuinely do — and the 167 EAF-carrying scores are the instrument that decides
it. GH #404 specifies the experiment.
Measured the same day (`palindrome_forward_rule.md`): the
licence holds per class of file, not for the 99.899 %. The failure mode is real —
PGS000020 has ~40 % of its palindromes reversed at a 0.175 % complement-only rate — and
87 % of the genome-wide rows sit in pipelines with no frequency to test.

Whether a TOP-coded file’s palindromes could be oriented by reconstructing Illumina’s
TOP/BOT rule. The designation for an ambiguous SNP is decided by walking outward through
the flanking sequence — which we have, in the pinned FASTA. So in principle, a file known
to be TOP-coded could have its A/T and C/G rows oriented by computing what TOP would
have meant at that locus.
This is not recommended, for two reasons. The first is that any convention reporting the
A-bearing strand produces A/C and A/G pairs on unambiguous SNVs, so
top_fraction ≈ 1 identifies the family of conventions, not Illumina’s specifically —
and only Illumina’s full rule defines a designation for the ambiguous pairs. Assuming
the submitter implemented the flanking-sequence walk rather than a naive “A-first”
relabelling is exactly the judgement call that must be tested before it ships, not shipped
because it is plausible.
The second is that it cannot be tested on what we hold. Validating it needs a file
that is both A/B-shaped and EAF-carrying, so the reconstruction can be scored against a
frequency comparison. Of the 15 A/B-shaped scores in the palindrome-carrying set, two
declare a frequency, and one of those has three unambiguous SNVs — its top_fraction is
noise. The single usable candidate, PGS000714, carries 9 palindromic rows. That is not
a ground-truth set; it is an anecdote. The hypothesis stays unproven and unprovable here,
which is the strongest available reason to leave those rows deferred rather than the
weakest.
The EAF route’s actual yield against a real panel. This spike measures how many rows
could be oriented if a panel frequency were available. Whether the declared frequency
and the panel’s agree — and how often a score’s declared cohort frequency is simply too
far from HGDP+1kGP to be usable — is a D1 measurement, not a spike one.

Measured since, by GH #404 (`palindrome_forward_rule.md`),
against the panel’s per-super-population frequencies. On unambiguous rows, where strand is
known, the declared frequency and the panel agree in 99.982 % of decisive cases in
genome-wide files and 97.7 % in curated ones. 8 of the 167 files carry a frequency
column that fails that test, one because it reports the other allele’s frequency, and
one publication’s frequencies were copied from 1000 Genomes rather than measured. #404
also tested §6 item 4’s inversion, reading palindromes forward where a file’s unambiguous
rows match. That is licensed for small curated files and refuted by one mid-size file.


8. Reproducing it
backend/scripts/prs/spike_palindrome_hm_source.py, which needs DATABASE_URL (a git
worktree has no .env; export the canonical checkout’s value):
python backend/scripts/prs/spike_palindrome_hm_source.py headers --out headers.json
python backend/scripts/prs/spike_palindrome_hm_source.py rows --shards 6 --shard N --out-dir out/
python backend/scripts/prs/spike_palindrome_hm_source.py eaf --out eaf.json
python backend/scripts/prs/spike_palindrome_hm_source.py report --in-dir out/ --with-e2
rows reads 10.7 GB of gzip; six shards, longest-processing-time-first on n_variants,
balance to 1.00×. report prints the reconciliation first — if the measured palindromic
total does not equal the manifest’s, every number under it is void.
Further reading: `prs_primer.md` §5.4 (why Gate C defers rather
than guesses) and §5.7b (the staged road to release) ·
`compatibility_classification.md` (how a palindromic
row is counted in the first place).

PRS Pipeline — Stage 0 Findings
Date: 2026-05-07
Status: Stage 0 complete; falling back to zero-PRS for Track A.
Question being answered
Can we obtain a UKB-shaped sample patient (CSV row + biomarker values + comorbidity PRS scalars) to use as the Track A pipeline burn-in input for build_pdr1_input_csv.py and build_pdr2_input_pickle.py, before Maureen’s genome-wide genotype data arrives?
Sources checked
Local snapshots

Live GitHub

The same is true for the PDR2 paper’s repo (it’s the ULTRA fork — code only, no patient pickles).

UK Biobank

Resource 5202 readme PDF confirms 28 binary disease traits + 25 quantitative traits in the Standard PRS Release, Field IDs in 26200-26285. Pre-computed scoring is not publicly downloadable — the PRS values themselves are access-controlled UKB data. Only trait definitions are public.
Genomicsplc/ukb-pret/src/ukb_pret/data/traits.yaml — full trait code list. No Field-ID mapping in this YAML; it’s just (code, full_name, sex, scale, follow_up_months). The exact code→Field-ID mapping is in UKB Showcase per-trait pages and is not trivially extractable in batch.
The 28 binary disease trait codes (relevant subset for PDR’s PRS slot): AD, AF, AMD, AST, BC, BD, CAD, CD, CED, CRC, CVD, EOC, HT, ISS, MEL, MS, OP, PC, PD, POAG, PSO, RA, SCZ, SLE, T1D, T2D, UC, VTE. (CRC = “Bowel cancer”; relevant for Maureen.)

Email path (deferred)
The PDR paper authors were already contacted previously, per an internal memory note, re: the original split files. We could append a request for a sample patient pickle to that thread, but per user policy emails require explicit approval — flagged as a follow-up the user can choose to send.
Conclusion
No usable sample patient data is obtainable through automated channels. Falling back to the planned zero-PRS placeholder for Track A:

This makes Track A a controlled baseline: the zero-PRS run is the foundation-model-with-expression-only baseline, against which Track B’s real-PRS run can be A/B’d to measure PRS contribution.

Implications for downstream stages

prs/prs_primer.title: Polygenic Risk Scores - a primer
prs/prs_primer.content:
Polygenic Risk Scores — a primer, and how Maple computes them
What a polygenic score is, where the idea came from, what a scoring file actually
contains, and the machinery MODS uses to turn one genome plus five thousand published
scores into numbers we are willing to stand behind.
Status as of 2026-09-26: Gates A, B, C, E1 and E2 are done; D is part-staged and F
is not started. (2026-09-29: stale on D and F. Both have now run for the v0 set, and the Gate F v0
release writer is built: backend/mods_prs_release.py, driven by
backend/scripts/prs/release_gate_f.py (GH #296); see §5.5.) (2026-09-27: all three Gate D stages are now built — D3 in PR #386, D1 and D2
in GH #396 — and none has run against the real panel; §5.7.) The scorer has now been run over the whole v4 eligible set: 3,752 of
3,753 scores computed against a 16,964,243-record callset (19,215,298-locus union), every
one reconciling and every one inside its theoretical bounds, with the fleet’s outcome
counts summing to the manifest’s eligible row total exactly (§5.8). No released
patient scores exist — Gate C writes at validity='quarantined' and only Gate F
promotes, so every reader still correctly returns nothing (§5.5). (2026-09-28: superseded by the first release of her PRS: a v0 smoke release of 590 scores over 109 disease anchors (tag smoke_v0, release run c3be9df0), normalized against the 667-sample EUR reference, after D1–D3 ran on the 594 v0 candidates. The final Gate F is still ahead; §5.5.)
E1 was a measurement run by design, and it paid for itself the same day. Its histograms
closed the largest open policy question (unplaceable_rows, §3.5) and corrected this
document’s palindrome figures by 4× (§5.4), so classifier v4 promoted unplaceable_rows
at a coverage threshold and the eligible set went 2,322 → 3,753 scores, 894.5M → 2.166B
variant rows. Every “2,322” below is a statement about the E1 run, which is history and
correct as written; the forward-looking number is 3,753.

Read “E2” carefully: the running order changed, and the name did not. The plan below
was E1 → settle policy → D → E2, where E2 meant “the re-run under the final policy —
the one that can be released.” That is not what E2 was. Gate D has never run
(mods_prs_run holds zero gate_d rows), so E2 is better understood as E1 repeated at
the corrected v4 scope — a second measurement run, not the post-D final one.
This was not drift for its own sake. E1’s histograms settled unplaceable_rows from E1’s
own data, needing nothing from the panel, and that alone moved eligibility 2,322 → 3,753
— which invalidated the union and the callset. Since D1 extracts frequencies over the
union, the union had to be rebuilt at final scope before D or it would be built twice.
Rebuilding it was therefore correct and necessary; re-scoring the patient against it was
the optional part, and it bought the measurements that close out the remaining policy
questions (§5.8) plus a clean baseline to diff against later.
So E2 is final with respect to eligibility, and not final with respect to
palindromic SNVs, which Gate C still defers — 64,810,321 rows, 2.99 % of the fleet.
Decided (Richard, 2026-09-26): no release candidate is declared until the palindrome
question is settled, and an E3 follows D1. So E2 is explicitly not the release
candidate. Note what “settled” can mean, because it is narrower than it sounds: only
167 of the 1,687 affected scores carry the effect-allele frequency that orientation
needs, so D1 can recover at most 9.5 % of the deferred rows and the rest become a
Gate F coverage gate rather than a pending decision. The staged plan, with what each
stage is for, is §5.7b. Nothing else is outstanding except the NR weight-type call,
which is Gate F’s and does not require re-scoring.

Companion documents. `genomics_glossary.md` defines the
vocabulary for readers who want the terms first — allele, dosage, strand flip, gVCF, plus
what “calling” means (§2.1, with GQ/DP/MIN_DP/FILTER), contig, and FASTA
vs FASTQ including the provenance of our pinned reference (§4.1).
`prs_validation/compatibility_classification.md`
is the standalone explainer for the classifier in §4.5–4.6. This primer is the wider arc
that connects them.

1. What a polygenic score is
1.1 The arithmetic
A polygenic score is a weighted sum, and that is genuinely all it is:
PRS = Σ  dosageᵢ × weightᵢ

For each of a set of positions in the genome, dosage is how many copies of the
trait-associated allele this person carries — 0, 1, or 2, because we have two copies of
each autosome — and weight is how much that allele shifted the trait in a large
association study. Multiply, add, done. A thousand multiplications and one sum.
The entire difficulty of the field lives in three places, none of which is the
arithmetic:

Getting the weights. That is the GWAS
literature’s job, and it is upstream of us.
Lining the two sides up. Deciding that this row in a scoring file and this
position in this person’s genome refer to the same thing, on the same strand, with
the same allele playing the same role. This is where essentially every bug we have
hit actually lived.
Interpreting the total. A raw sum is a number with no units and no meaning until
it is placed against a reference distribution of people (§1.4).

1.2 A short history






































































WhenWhat happenedWhy it matters here1918R. A. Fisher shows that many small Mendelian effects, added up, produce the smooth bell-curve inheritance seen in traits like height — the infinitesimal model.This is the theoretical licence for adding thousands of tiny effects together. The additive sum in §1.1 is Fisher’s model, unchanged.1965Falconer’s liability-threshold model: a yes/no disease is modelled as a continuous underlying liability with a cutoff.Why it is coherent to give someone a continuous “risk score” for a binary outcome like colorectal cancer.2002–2005The HapMap project maps linkage disequilibrium — which variants travel together — making cheap tag-SNP genotyping arrays viable.Made large-scale association studies economically possible. Also the reason scores can use proxy variants rather than causal ones.2005Klein et al. link complement factor H to age-related macular degeneration: the first widely accepted GWAS hit.Proof the approach finds real biology.2007The Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium publishes 7 diseases × ~14,000 cases.The GWAS era starts in earnest; effect sizes turn out to be tiny, which kills the one-gene-one-disease hope and makes aggregation mandatory.2009The International Schizophrenia Consortium (Purcell et al.) takes thousands of SNPs that individually failed significance, weights them by effect size, sums them, and shows the aggregate predicts schizophrenia in an independent cohort.This is the birth of the modern polygenic score. The key insight: signal too weak to be individually credible is still real in aggregate.2015–2019Method generation: LDpred, LDpred2, lassosum, PRS-CS, SBayesR, MegaPRS. Instead of picking significant SNPs, these re-weight every variant using an LD reference panel.This is why the modern catalog contains scores with millions of variants and no rsIDs (§3.3) — they are genome-wide posterior weights, not curated hit lists.2018Khera et al. publish genome-wide scores for five common diseases and argue that the top few percent carry risk comparable to a monogenic mutation.The paper that pushed PRS toward clinical translation — and toward controversy.2017–2019Martin et al. quantify the portability problem: scores trained in European-ancestry cohorts lose much of their accuracy in other ancestries.A first-order limitation, not a footnote. It determines how we normalize (§1.4) and is why ancestry is a pipeline input, not a nicety.2021The PGS Catalog launches (Lambert et al.) with a standardized scoring-file format, harmonized coordinates, and a reference calculator (pgsc_calc).The entire supply side of our pipeline. Without a common file format, §3 does not exist.2022T2T-CHM13: the first gapless human genome.Not yet our reference (§2.2) — but it is where the field is going.nowProspective clinical trials (eMERGE, GenoVA, WISDOM), regulatory caution, and a large direct-to-consumer market of varying rigour.The reason a pipeline like ours has to be able to say “not calculated, and here is why” out loud.
The through-line: the idea (Fisher) is a century old, the data (GWAS) is twenty years
old, the practical method (ISC) is fifteen, and the standardized plumbing (PGS
Catalog) is five. We are working entirely in that last layer.
1.3 What a polygenic score is not
Worth stating plainly, because the failure modes of this pipeline are mostly failures of
interpretation rather than of code:

Not a diagnosis, and not a probability. A raw PRS is an unnormalized sum. On its
own it is meaningless — it only acquires meaning relative to a population.
Not portable across ancestries without care. See 2017–2019 above.
Not the whole genetic story. A PRS captures common, additive liability. It says
nothing about a rare high-penetrance variant. A rare high-penetrance germline
variant is exactly the kind of thing a PRS structurally cannot see — which is why the
variant-level pipeline and the PRS pipeline are separate inputs to the same model.
Not causal. Weights sit on tag variants in LD with whatever is actually doing the
work.
Not comparable between scores. Two scores for the same trait, from different
studies with different weight conventions, produce numbers on different scales.

1.4 Why Maple computes them
This matters for design, because our use is not the usual one. MODS does not compute
PRS in order to hand somebody a clinical risk report. It computes them as a broad,
patient-specific genetic feature vector that feeds the PDR2 personalized loss:
L = L_pred − λ₁·L_prs − λ₂·L_expr

where L_prs aggregates, over diseases i, a learnable weight wᵢ times the patient’s
PRSᵢ times the model’s per-triple score. The polygenic score for each trait becomes a
signed, learnable nudge on drug–disease edges incident to that disease node — the patient
enters the objective, not just the inputs.

Take the shape, not the algebra. The paper’s literal formula
(L_prs = Σᵢ wᵢ·PRSᵢ·s_pred) is unbounded as written, and the released code adds
tanh(·) and L2 weight normalization that the text omits. We verified those
nonlinearities are load-bearing. losses.py is the operational specification — see
`pdr2_loss_text_vs_code_note.md` and
`pdr_personalization_writeup.md`.

Three consequences follow, and they explain choices that would otherwise look strange:


Breadth beats depth. We want as many scores as the genome supports, not a
curated clinical shortlist. A wide feature vector is the point. This is why the
target is the ~5,377-score catalog and not thirteen diseases.

The trap this is guarding against, stated bluntly (Richard, 2026-09-23, after
a session report led with “44 colorectal scores are eligible”): counting
disease-relevant scores is not a result. We already know she has colorectal
cancer, and we know a great deal about it. A colorectal PRS can, at best, tell us
whether she was unlucky in getting it — which changes no decision. No individual
score and no individual disease is the object of interest. These are ML inputs.
The goal is to maximise the number of usable data points without regard to what
they predict; anything that refines that data is a direction to move toward, and
anything that degrades it a direction to move away from. When tempted to report
“N scores for disease X”, report the size and quality of the feature vector
instead.



The relative ordering across a cohort matters more than any absolute number — but
we have a cohort of one, so a reference distribution is required to make the value
mean anything at all. That is Gate D.


A wrong number is worse than a missing number. A missing feature is a zero the
loss ignores. A wrong feature is a confident, learnable lie. Every “we defer this
rather than approximate it” decision below traces back to this line.


A corollary that changes how the partial-coverage decision should be made — and a
correction to how this document used to justify it. A score computed on only part of its
loci is not simply “wrong” the way it would be clinically, so the coverage bar for “usable
as an ML feature” sits genuinely lower than for “usable as a clinical risk estimate.” That
conclusion stands. The reason previously given for it did not.

Superseded (2026-09-23). This section used to argue that a roughly constant deflation
is “largely absorbable by wᵢ — the model can rescale a feature.” The released loss
cannot do that. losses.py L2-normalizes the
weight vector before the inner product and then squashes the result:
disease_weights_norm = F.normalize(self.disease_weights, p=2, dim=0)
prs_impact = torch.sum(disease_weights_norm * prs_values)
prs_term   = torch.tanh(prs_impact)
‖ŵ‖₂ = 1 is a hard constraint, so the model cannot rescale a feature — it can only
re-allocate a fixed unit budget across diseases. Feature scale therefore is not
absorbed; it decides the answer.

What actually absorbs a constant deflation is Gate D, not the model. A percentile (or
a z-score) is computed against a reference distribution, and a multiplicative deflation
applied equally to the patient and the panel is a monotone transform — it preserves rank
exactly, so the normalised feature is unchanged. The absorption is in the normalisation,
which is another reason Gate D is not optional (§5.5).
Three things keep it from being free, and the first is now the mechanism rather than a
caveat:

The deflation must be consistent between the patient and the reference distribution
(Gate D). Coverage that differs between Maureen and the panel biases the percentile, and
nothing downstream can undo a bias introduced in normalisation. Score the panel through
the same Gate C policy or this guarantee evaporates.
It is not a pure scale: which loci are missing matters, and a few large-weight loci
can deflate a score disproportionately, which breaks the exact rank preservation above.
Over many loci it approximates one.
Fewer loci means a noisier estimate of the same liability. That is variance, not
bias — and variance is far more tolerable in a feature than bias is.

The corresponding trap on the other side: raw sums are not a usable feature vector.
Across the 2,322 production-eligible scores the theoretical magnitude bound
max(|lo|, |hi|) spans roughly twelve orders of magnitude — median 15.9, p95 706, max
2.59 × 10⁷, with 1,818 of 2,322 (78 %) already above 3. Under tanh(⟨ŵ, PRS⟩) with
‖ŵ‖₂ = 1, a vector on those scales saturates the squash, 1 − tanh² ≈ 0, and the
gradient dies. Track A (all-zero PRS) produced no gradient because tanh(0) = 0; feeding
raw sums would produce no gradient from the opposite end, and the “interpretable” disease
weights would converge to a readout of which published score happens to carry the largest
raw magnitude rather than which disease matters. Normalised features are what put
⟨ŵ, PRS⟩ back inside tanh’s live band.
The operational consequence: unplaceable_rows should not be a binary promote/defer
flag. It should be a coverage threshold, chosen empirically by what it does to the
feature vector. The instrument for choosing it already exists — the coverage_v1 payload’s
third quantity (effective variance-weighted information, §5.4) is exactly the right
statistic, and the dual-scorer reconciliation (§5.4) separates the imputation term,
which measures precisely how much a partially-covered score changes when the missing
dosages are filled in. Run that on the affected scores and the threshold stops being a
judgement call.

2. Reference genomes
Every coordinate in this pipeline — in the patient’s gVCF, in a scoring file, in dbSNP —
is meaningless except relative to a specific reference genome build. Mixing builds is
the single easiest way to produce a plausible, entirely wrong score.
2.1 What the reference actually is
The human reference genome is not any one person’s genome. It is a curated haploid
consensus assembled from a handful of anonymous donors (with one donor, RP11,
contributing a majority), maintained by the Genome Reference Consortium. It carries the
reference allele at every position by convention, not by biological privilege — at
plenty of loci the “reference” base is the minor allele in most populations.
This matters directly for us: §5.1’s bug is precisely a case where being
reference-matching is not the same as being effect-free.
2.2 The builds



































BuildReleasedNotesNCBI36 / hg182006Still the original build of 11 catalog scoring files.GRCh37 / hg19Feb 2009The workhorse of the GWAS era. 3,951 of our 5,377 scoring files were authored on it (plus 415 more labelled hg19).GRCh38 / hg38Dec 2013Current production standard. Fixed thousands of assembly errors, modelled centromeres, added alt loci for highly polymorphic regions (HLA).GRCh38.p1 … p142014–2022Patch releases. Patches add fix/novel scaffolds but never move an existing coordinate — so p13 and p14 are coordinate-compatible on the primary assembly.T2T-CHM132022The first truly complete, gapless genome — centromeres, acrocentric short arms, ~200 Mb of new sequence. Not yet our reference: dbSNP, the GWAS corpus, and the PGS Catalog are all still keyed to GRCh38.
GRCh37 and hg19 are the same assembly under UCSC vs GRC naming — with the
irritating exception of the mitochondrial sequence, which differs. Likewise GRCh38 and
hg38. The catalog uses all four spellings, which is why our build handling normalizes
rather than string-matches.
2.3 Naming and assembly flavors
Two orthogonal traps:
Contig naming. UCSC writes chr1, chrX, chrM. Ensembl and the GRC write 1,
X, MT. NCBI writes accessions (NC_000001.11). These name identical sequence.
Every entry point in our code normalizes through
connectors/reference_fasta.py::normalize_chrom (strip a leading chr), and we
standardize on the Ensembl convention because that is what the patient’s gVCF and
the PGS Catalog’s hm_chr column both use.
Assembly flavor. “GRCh38” can mean the primary assembly (chromosomes + unplaced
scaffolds), the full analysis set (primary + alt contigs + decoys), or a no-alt
subset. Alt contigs are alternate versions of polymorphic regions; if reads can align to
both an alt and its primary counterpart, mapping quality collapses and variant calls
quietly degrade. We use the primary assembly — 194 contigs — which matches how the
gVCF was called.
2.4 Liftover, and why we do not do it at score time
Liftover converts coordinates between builds using a chain file of mapped blocks. It
is lossy: some regions have no equivalent, some invert, some map many-to-one. The
GRCh37→GRCh38 shift is large and irregular — on PGS000006, only 3 of 313 loci kept the
same coordinate, with shifts up to 2.87 Mb.
Our position is that liftover is the PGS Catalog’s job, not ours. We download only
the _hmPOS_GRCh38 harmonized files, so every scoring file arrives already on our build.
The patient’s gVCF was called on GRCh38. No conversion happens anywhere in the scoring
path, which removes an entire class of error.
2.5 Our pinned reference
Because the FASTA is the arbiter of what the reference allele is at every scored locus,
it is pinned in code, by checksum, and a mismatch hard-fails rather than falling back.









































BuildGRCh38.p13SourceEnsembl release-109, DNA primary assemblyPathbackend/data/reference/GRCh38/Homo_sapiens.GRCh38.dna.primary_assembly.fa (host-only; backend/data/ is gitignored)sha25678777b0886e8dfa5e14e4957fbbaa53736fcbaa5668d59e09b6b7945fca93d8cContigs194NamingEnsembl (1, not chr1)Pinned atconnectors/reference_fasta.py::PINNED_GRCH38AccessReferenceFasta.ref_base / .ref_bases, via pyfaidx
Validated base-identical to the patient’s gVCF REF field at three
ancestry/clinically-informative loci: one clinically-informative locus,
5:33951588 = C (SLC45A2), 2:135851076 = G (LCT).
Two operational notes. Ensembl ships plain gzip, not bgzip, so the file must be
decompressed to .fa before pyfaidx can index it —
scripts/prs/prepare_reference_fasta.py downloads, verifies, and decompresses in one
step. And the checksum is not verified on every load (hashing 3.15 GB is slow); it is
verified once at pin time and recorded on the mods_prs_run row so any run is
reproducible against the exact bytes used.
2.6 The two build fields inside a scoring file — a live gotcha
A harmonized scoring file carries two different build declarations, and they mean
different things:

#genome_build= — the author’s original build. This is what pgscatalog.org
displays as “Original Genome Build.”
#HmPOS_build= — the build the harmonized positions are on.

Catalog-wide across our 5,377 cached files (scanned from the headers, 2026-07-26):

































genome_build — the author’s originalFilesGRCh373,951GRCh38457hg19415NR (not reported)357hg38182NCBI36 (11) / hg18 (3) / NCBI35 (1)15
HmPOS_build, by contrast, is GRCh38 for all 5,377 — because we only ever download
the GRCh38 harmonized file. Per-row, the same split repeats: chr_position is on the
original build, hm_pos is on GRCh38.
A practical consequence worth knowing: open_scoring_file stores
HmPOS_build or genome_build, so mods_prs_score_manifest.genome_build is uniformly
GRCh38 and the dashboard’s “Genome build” panel is a degenerate one-row table. That
column is not the number pgscatalog.org shows; the table above is.
The gotcha. connectors/pgs_catalog_connector.py::_row_to_variant coalesces
hm_pos → chr_position and hm_chr → chr_name as a fallback when the harmonized field
is blank. For hm_rsID → rsID that fallback is safe, because rsIDs are
build-independent. For position it silently substitutes an original-build coordinate
into a pipeline that assumes GRCh38. Measured 2026-07-26: it fires in 85 of 200 randomly
sampled files, at ~0.0–0.1 % of rows each; the worst case is PGS000016 (atrial
fibrillation, authored on hg19) with 1,316 of 6,730,541 rows. Those rows are counted as
placed_loci, not as unplaceable, so n_no_position under-reports.
Closed (GH #250), before Gate C computed anything. _ColumnIndex now decides once
per file whether the original coordinates share the harmonized frame
(original_coords_share_harmonized_frame: true only when the file is not harmonized at
all, or when both builds resolve to the same assembly — “NR” does not count). A blank
hm_pos on a score authored against another assembly is now an unplaceable row, which is
what it always meant. Gate C counts those rows as unplaceable_row and they never enter
a sum.

3. Scoring files
3.1 Where they come from
The PGS Catalog (EMBL-EBI + University of Cambridge) is
the standardized public repository of published polygenic scores. Each score gets a
stable PGS###### accession, structured metadata (trait, EFO/MONDO mapping, citation,
training cohort, ancestry), and a downloadable scoring file.
Three file flavors exist per score:

























FlavorWhat it isDo we use it?Author-submittedExactly what the authors deposited. 3.2 File structure
A scoring file is a gzipped TSV with a #key=value header. Here is a real one in full —
PGS000004, the Mavaddat 313-variant breast cancer score, annotated:

then a column header and rows:
chr_name  chr_position  effect_allele  other_allele  effect_weight  allelefrequency_effect  hm_source  hm_rsID  hm_chr  hm_pos     hm_inferOtherAllele
1         100880328     T              A             0.0373         0.4097                  liftover   (blank)  1       100414772  (blank)
1         10566215      G              A            -0.0586         0.329                   liftover   (blank)  1       10506158   (blank)
1         110198129     C              CAAA          0.0458         0.7755                  liftover   (blank)  1       109655507  (blank)

Four things are visible in three rows, and each has cost us something:

chr_position ≠ hm_pos. 100880328 vs 100414772 — a 466 kb shift from the
GRCh37→GRCh38 harmonization. Reading the wrong column is a silent catastrophe.
hm_rsID is blank — and not just in these rows: all 313 of them. This score
identifies its variants by position only. A pipeline that joins on rsID matches
literally zero rows here and reports a confident zero.
Row 3 is an indel — C → CAAA, an insertion. Note the effect allele is the
longer one; the shared anchor base C is what makes indel orientation unresolvable
from the reference alone (§5.2).
allelefrequency_effect is present. This is the field that lets a scorer resolve
a strand-ambiguous palindromic SNV — if the effect allele frequency is far from 0.5,
the strand can be inferred.

Optional columns that change everything. Beyond the core schema, a scoring file may
carry is_haplotype, is_diplotype, is_interaction, is_dominant, is_recessive,
dosage_0_weight/dosage_1_weight/dosage_2_weight, variant_description,
locus_name, OR, HR. Any of these means the file is not a plain additive sum,
and quietly summing effect_weight over such a file produces a number that looks fine
and means nothing. Detecting them is the classifier’s first job (§4).
Here is what one of those looks like — PGS004262, a GenoBoost psoriasis score:
chr_name  chr_position  effect_allele  other_allele  dosage_0_weight  dosage_1_weight  dosage_2_weight  ...
6         31274555      T              C            -0.0324954        0.1051552        0.2502743

There is no effect_weight column at all. The weights are per-genotype, and they
are not linear in dosage (−0.032 → +0.105 → +0.250). An effect_weight-based parser
reads zero rows from this file. Fifteen catalog scores are exactly this case, and the
right conclusion is “needs a dedicated calculator,” not “the file is broken” — a
distinction §4.4 encodes deliberately.
3.3 Scale and complexity
The catalog is not uniform. It is two populations of file wearing one format.






























BucketFilesBytes> 50 MB21922.3 GB10–50 MB1,72533.7 GB1–10 MB5432.6 GB< 1 MB2,8900.3 GB
Half the files are under a megabyte; 4 % of them hold 38 % of the bytes. The largest
score by variant count is PGS003162 at 10,318,272 variants (five scores exceed
10 M); the largest by compressed size is PGS005197 — 9,503,677 variants in 185.8 MB.
Those two rankings differ, which is a small but recurring trap: sizing work by file
count, by bytes, and by rows gives three different answers. Across all 5,377 files the
classifier examined 3,452,540,960 variant rows.
The split is historical, not arbitrary: pre-2015 scores are curated lists of genome-wide
significant hits (tens to hundreds of variants, rsID-labelled), and post-2015 scores are
LD-aware genome-wide posteriors (millions of variants, position-only). Any assumption
that holds for one population fails for the other — which is why a 25-score smoke test
once suggested weight_type was uniformly NR, a conclusion the full fleet demolished.
Cost model (measured, after optimization): ~0.98 s per MB of gzip → ~16.7 CPU-hours
for the whole catalog. Sharded six ways on a 16-logical-core box that is ~2.9 h wall.
Two non-obvious facts from profiling a 19.4 MB / 972k-row file:

The time is not I/O. gzip decompression plus readlines is 6 %. Tab-splitting
is 8 %. Per-row dict construction plus PGSVariant allocation is 45 %, and
feature accumulation another 41 %. The lever is Python object allocation, not
decompression.
Therefore: shard by bytes, not by file count, and compute ETA from bytes. Under
largest-first ordering, byte-progress and count-progress diverge wildly — at 1.2 % of
scores the fleet run was already 12.1 % of bytes.

Cache integrity. Five of the 5,377 cached files were truncated by interrupted
downloads (PGS002938, PGS002153, PGS000257, PGS003724, PGS004604); re-downloads were
25–62 % larger. A truncated gzip always fails its CRC/length trailer, so
EOFError: Compressed file ended before the end-of-stream marker detects this
reliably — a partial file can never be silently parsed as complete. Do not assume a
cached scoring file is intact merely because it exists.

A weight is the per-allele effect size the study estimated. What scale it is on is
declared (sometimes) in the #weight_type= header, and getting this wrong is a
biological error the arithmetic cannot catch.

Three things to take from that table:

Case normalization is mandatory. beta + BETA + Beta = 3,699 scores, or 69 %
of the catalog — but only if you lowercase first. A case-sensitive match sees 3,250
and misclassifies 449.
NR is 26 % of the catalog and is not a scale. Roughly one score in four does not
tell you what its numbers mean. Notably, 9 of the 13 scores in our own curated
default set are NR (§4).
The tail is free text. weights.HC171 is not a unit. These need
explicit per-score handling or explicit deferral, never a regex that shrugs.

The theoretical-bounds check. For any additive score, the raw total is
mathematically bounded:
L = Σ min(0, 2·wᵢ)        U = Σ max(0, 2·wᵢ)

because every dosage is in {0, 1, 2}. Every computed score must satisfy L ≤ S ≤ U;
a value outside that interval is a scorer defect, not a biological finding. It is free,
it is computed for every score at classify time (stored as theoretical_lo/_hi), and
it catches whole families of allele-orientation and arithmetic bugs.
It is also one-sided and scale-blind, which is worth internalizing: it cannot detect
an odds-ratio-summed-as-a-beta, and it cannot detect a wrong-but-attainable score. We
learned that concretely — a bounds check over the 40 legacy scores with |raw| > 1000
found all 40 inside their bounds, while every one of them was in fact wrong (§5.1).
Bounds are a floor on correctness, not a ceiling.

3.6 The classification engine
Source: backend/mods_prs_compat.py · Tests: backend/tests/test_mods_prs_compat.py
· Runner: worker task mods_prs_manifest_build, driven by
backend/scripts/prs/build_prs_manifest.py.
Five design properties are worth understanding, because each was paid for:
1. One parser, one accumulator. There is exactly one row parser
(pgs_catalog_connector._row_to_variant) and exactly one feature implementation
(mods_prs_compat._FeatureAccumulator). Both the in-memory path (parse_scoring_file →
score_features) and the streaming path (open_scoring_file → stream_score_features)
drive that same accumulator, and both classifications land in the same
classify_features. This is not tidiness — these counts decide production_eligible, so
if the two read paths could disagree about a score’s features, they could disagree about
whether it is safe to compute. Do not “optimize” by forking a second parse loop.
2. Conservative by presence. For complex-format and inheritance columns, the
classifier flags on the presence of the column, not on confirming that rows use it.
This over-defers a score carrying an unused column — the safe direction. Row-level
refinement is a planned hardening step, not a bug.
3. Precedence is load-bearing. The order is D (unplaceable) > C (dedicated) > D (no usable rows) > B > A, and the placement of the second D check after C is
deliberate: a dosage_N_weight file parses to zero effect_weight rows, and “needs a
dedicated calculator” is the true explanation where “no usable rows” would falsely imply
a broken file. Fifteen catalog scores hit exactly this path. Equally, that check must
come before B and A — under classifier v1 an empty file had every feature count at
zero, fell through to Class A, and was marked production-eligible: a score cleared for
production that computes to nothing.
4. Versioned decisions. Every manifest row carries classifier_version and the
scoring file’s sha256. A change in classifier meaning — or in what it extracts — bumps the
version so a re-run re-classifies rather than skipping rows decided under different rules.
v3 was the 2026-09-22 structural re-classify, v4 the unplaceable_rows threshold
promotion (recomputed in place, no re-read), and v5 (2026-09-26, GH #377) adds the
allele-convention counters below and therefore needs a full re-read.
A bump that is meant to change no decision should be made to prove it:
scripts/prs/verify_classifier_bump.py snapshot before the re-run and compare after it
diff every score’s class, categories and eligibility. v5 moves no counter and promotes no
category, so its diff must be empty — and an empty diff is also how you know the re-run
actually ran.
4b. The allele-convention profile (v5). n_snv_pair_top (A/C + A/G) and
n_snv_pair_bot (C/T + G/T) split a file’s non-palindromic biallelic SNVs in two. On
the forward strand those are the same variants seen from the two strands and occur about
equally often, so top_fraction = top/(top+bot) sits at ~0.5 — measured 0.4991, 0.5017,
0.5018 on three ordinary scores. ~1.0 or ~0.0 means the alleles were written in an A/B
convention (Illumina TOP or BOT), whose strand assignment is made per variant and
recorded nowhere in the file, so about half its rows are reverse-complemented relative to
GRCh38 with nothing saying which half.
Counts, never the ratio — mods_prs_compat.top_fraction derives it on read, the same rule
Gate C’s coverage payload follows. And the profile alone never condemns a file:
PGS005087/5088/5089 are top_fraction = 1.000 with a 0 % complement-only rate, their
alleles being the forward-strand pair at 5,326 of 5,326 checkable loci. The guard needs the
measured complement-only rate too (§5.4). Full reasoning:
`prs_validation/palindrome_orientation_spike.md`.
5. Memory discipline at catalog scale. parse_scoring_file holds the decompressed
text, the split-line list, and every PGSVariant at once — fine for one file, fatal
across 59 GB. The streaming reader yields lazily. Two further optimizations, each
verified behavior-identical against a verbatim reimplementation across 16 real files
(72 → 1.1 M variants, classes A/B/C, zero mismatches):

_ColumnIndex resolves column positions once per file, so _row_to_variant indexes
the split fields rather than building a dict per row — a ~1.3× speedup.
Allele pairs are interned to small integers before per-site storage. A scoring file
has a handful of distinct allele pairs but millions of sites; keeping the pair
strings per site dominated peak memory at 1,040 MB on the 9.5 M-row file. Interning
is exact — distinct pairs get distinct ids — so unlike hashing it cannot under-count
multiallelic sites, which would silently promote a score to eligible.

Cross-validation is still open. The classifier is deliberately structural and
dependency-free, which means it is our reading of the format rather than the reference
implementation’s. GH #237 tracks
cross-validating it against the official pgscatalog libraries.

5. The processing engine
5.1 The bug that defines the design
Everything below is shaped by one defect, found by external audit on 2026-07-12, that
invalidated all 5,368 previously computed scores.
The old genotype store was variant-only: the VCF importer skipped reference blocks,
so a position where the patient matches the reference has no row. The scorer then did
the obvious thing — a scoring locus not found in the store was counted as missing and
contributed nothing.
That is correct only when the effect allele is the alternate allele. When the PGS
effect allele is the reference allele — and a person who is homozygous-reference
therefore carries two copies of the effect allele — the correct dosage is 2 and the
correct contribution is 2 × weight. The pipeline scored 0.
Measured on PGS000019, ~49 % of loci are REF-effect (25 REF vs 26 ALT). At those loci
the dosage map became {0, 1, 0} instead of {2, 1, 0} — an “artificial heterozygote.”
This is a bias, not a constant offset: it distorts different scores by different
amounts depending on how many of their effect alleles happen to be reference.
Three lessons were extracted, and they are worth more than the fix:

“Absent” is ambiguous in a variant-only store. It can mean hom-ref or not
sequenced, and those must never collapse to the same number.
snps_used / snps_in_scoring_file is not coverage. That ratio clustered at
42–52 % across the legacy fleet, and the retired UI colour-coded it as a data-quality
verdict about the published score — presenting a symptom of our own defect as
somebody else’s problem.
A self-check that shares your assumptions cannot fail. The internal reconstruction
that “confirmed” the ~50 % coverage was benign assumed absent = dosage 0, so it
reproduced the bug instead of detecting it. The audit caught it by asking the one
question the check could not.

The response was to wipe rather than quarantine: 9,793 rows deleted on 2026-07-13
(5,368 distinct scores plus superseded re-runs), backed up first to
backend/data/prs_backups/. Scores are fully recomputable from the retained genotypes
plus the scoring files, so keeping known-wrong numbers around bought nothing and risked
a leak. The 8,088,434-row mods_genotype table was untouched.
5.2 Dense callsets
Source: backend/connectors/wgs_dense_callset.py · Locus union:
backend/connectors/pgs_locus_union.py · Worker task: genotype_dense_callset
The fix is to stop treating “absent” as “0” by making absence impossible at the sites we
care about. The mechanism is a dense callset: a genotype record for every locus
some target score needs, whether or not the patient carries a variant there.
“Dense” does not mean all 3.1 billion positions. It means dense over the union of PGS
loci — a site-targeted reconstruction, typically a few million positions, built from
the source gVCF rather than from the variant-only database. This is deliberate:
build_locus_union() collects the (chrom, pos, alleles) sites the target scores
actually reference, deduplicated, and the builder resolves exactly those.
Every target locus resolves to exactly one of four outcomes:






























OutcomeConditionEmittedCALLABLE_HOMREFA confident reference block spans the coordinate.GT 0/0 with a concrete REF (from the FASTA) and the scoring non-ref ALT — so a REF-effect locus becomes dosage-2 eligible.CALLABLE_VARIANTAn explicit, quality-passing variant record.Its genotype.EXPLICIT_MISSINGA no-call, a FAILed record, below-threshold quality, or no record at all../. — routed to the missingness policy, never silently dropped.STRUCTURAL_FAILREF disagrees with the FASTA, contig absent, orientation unresolvable.Nothing. Logged, excluded, never a partial score.
And the Gate A exit invariant is a hard assertion, not a log line:
callable_homref + callable_variant + explicit_missing + structural_fail == union_size

i.e. zero residual implicit-zero. Every locus is accounted for by name. If the
arithmetic does not reconcile, the build raises rather than returning a plausible result.
The callability policy, and the discovery that nearly re-introduced the bug. The
patient’s gVCF is Sequencing.com 30× WGS, reblocked by GvcfReblocker — GATK-style
(END/MIN_DP reference blocks, not DRAGEN RGQ), Ensembl contig naming. The
provisional plan said hom-ref calls should require GQ ≥ 20, which is standard advice.
Measuring the real file showed every PASS reference block carries GQ = 0 —
0 of 159,540 in the first 300k records had GQ > 0, because the reblocker does not
preserve per-site GQ across collapsed blocks. Gating hom-ref on GQ would have rejected
every hom-ref call and silently re-created the exact defect being fixed.
So the policy identifies the caller from the header first, then applies thresholds:

The indel-orientation trap. For equal-length alleles you can ask the FASTA which
allele is the reference — exactly one matches. For an indel you cannot. A deletion
ATTCT → A has an ALT that is the anchor base of the REF, so a per-allele
“does this equal the reference span of its own length?” test matches both alleles.
From a FASTA plus an unordered allele pair, “deletion of TTCT” and “insertion of TTCT”
are genuinely indistinguishable. The first implementation structural-failed all three
real indel sentinels with a misleading reason, and would have quietly dropped every
indel hom-ref locus in a catalog-scale run. The fix: TargetLocus carries explicit
ref/alt when the source knows it, and the FASTA only verifies
(ref == ref_bases(pos, len(ref))) rather than deriving. FASTA-derivation is now gated
on len({len(a) for a in alleles}) == 1. Orientation-unknown indels defer honestly.

reconciles 6/6, zero structural failures):

Autosomal median depth 32 → depth ceiling 96.
A known pathogenic variant, carried in the source report with no rsID at all —
resolved correctly by coordinate, so the position-keyed builder catches exactly
what the legacy rsID-keyed path dropped.
Five somatic tumor loci (BRAF V600E, NRAS Q61K, three indels) → germline
hom-ref GT 0/0, hence REF-effect-eligible.

Both results are biologically correct: a carrier call at the germline site
variant, wild-type in the germline at every somatic locus. That is the check that would
have failed loudly if the reconstruction were wrong.
One boundary worth guarding. The dense-callset path does not read
mods_genotype. It streams the local gVCF directly against the pinned local FASTA. That
is the whole point — reading the source file is precisely what bypasses the variant-only
store that caused the bug. Do not “helpfully” wire the builder onto mods_genotype; it
would reintroduce the defect. A pleasant side effect is zero Cloud SQL egress, since the
only non-patient input is a public reference genome on local disk.

Two footguns that only show up at scale:
Chunk your commits. The first 4.4 M-row ingest accumulated everything into a single
transaction and committed at the very end. A uvicorn --reload (triggered by staging a
200 MB VCF under the watched mount) killed the long-lived transaction and rolled back
everything — hours gone, zero rows durable. The rewrite commits ~100 K records at a
time, each its own short transaction, with per-chunk progress and a printed resume
point. The upsert is idempotent, so a re-run resumes cheaply.
Streaming the file does not mean streaming the working set. The genotype cache
solved the egress problem and created a memory one: each task unpickles the cache into a
~2 GB in-RAM dict. Five concurrent local workers on the 30 GB box hit ENOMEM,
crashed, and churned their tasks; two workers ran clean and finished all 36 tasks.
Fewer workers finished faster, because the only thing quicker than a fast worker is one
that never has to restart. (2026-09-29: history. The cache,
get_patient_genotype_dict_cached, served only the retired compute_prs_pure scorer and
was deleted (GH #481). Gates A, C and D read the dense callset, never mods_genotype
(§5.2), so do not revive it.)
One more, from skipping records: in the VCF importer, skip reference blocks by testing
that ALT is a non-variant (., <NON_REF>, *) — not by testing GT == 0/0.
A genuine hom-ref call at a real variant site has a real ALT and must be kept. Keying the
skip on the genotype silently drops real variants; there is a regression test
(test_parse_vcf_homozygous_ref_emitted) holding that line.

Gate A fixed how the genome is read; this is the arithmetic that reads it. The scorer
never asks “is there a variant row here?” — the question that conflated homozygous
reference with not sequenced. It asks, of the dense callset, which allele is the
reference at this locus, and how many copies of the effect allele does the genotype
name? A GT 0/0 at a REF-effect locus answers two, and that single line is the fix.
Orientation is resolved from the reference allele alone, not from REF+ALT. That is
deliberate: Gate A emits ALT=. for an explicitly-missing locus and the scoring ALT for a
hom-ref one, so a rule that needed the ALT would behave differently on the two.
Every scoring row lands in exactly one of eight outcomes, and the scorer raises rather
than returning a number if they do not sum to the rows it read — the same exit gate Gate A
applies to its four:

The three “not scored for cause” outcomes are kept apart from the two “gap” outcomes
because they mean different things to a reader; collapsing them into one “missing” bucket
is how the retired coverage column came to mean nothing (§5.1).
Two conservative defaults, both recorded on the run rather than baked in.
Palindromic SNVs defer. The complement of an A/T pair is an A/T pair, so both strand
readings fit the data and they give opposite dosages — the one class where a strand error
is silent and inverting. Resolving it needs an allele frequency to compare against, i.e.
a reference panel: Gate D. Palindromes appear in 1,197 of 2,322 scores (51.6 %) and
account for 13,929,705 of 894,528,461 rows — 1.56 % overall.
But the aggregate badly understates the per-score cost, and this document said so for a
day. Measured on the Gate E1 run (mods_polygenic_score, 2026-09-24), among the 1,197
affected scores the deferral takes a median of 10.24 % of their rows, p95 21.49 %,
mean 11.20 % — and 1,088 of 2,321 scores lose more than 5 % of their rows. The
aggregate 1.56 % was right; the per-score figures previously quoted here (median 2.47 %,
p95 17.33 %) were computed on a different denominator and are 4× too low on the median.
The reason is visible the moment you split by score size, and it inverts the “concentrated
in a tail” reading:

The burden sits almost entirely on the small, curated, pre-2015 hit-list scores — which
are precisely the interpretable ones — while the genome-wide LD-posterior scores that
dominate the row count carry almost none. So “1.56 % of rows” is a statement about the big
scores, not about the fleet. Gate D’s palindrome recovery is worth substantially more than
a row-weighted average suggests.

Two earlier revisions got this wrong in opposite directions. One quoted “12.5 % of rows,
median 7.6 % per score” from a 60-score sample; the correction to full-fleet aggregates
then over-corrected the per-score claim. The durable lesson is that a row-weighted
aggregate and a per-score median answer different questions, and for anything that is
consumed per score — which a feature vector is — the per-score distribution is the one
that matters.

Strand flips are measured, not applied. Both sides are GRCh38 and Gate A has already
verified every record’s REF against the pinned FASTA, so a complement-only allele match is
evidence of a problem — an author-strand submission, a harmonization error, a different
variant — rather than a coordinate detail to repair in passing. Applying the flip would
make the problem permanently undetectable: for a single-base pair, accepting complements
resolves all four possible reference bases, so ref_allele_mismatch could never fire
again and the scorer would lose its only structural check that the scoring file and the
genome describe the same variant. So the rows a flip would have rescued are counted as
n_complement_only_match and deferred. Near zero confirms the forward-strand premise; a
large count refutes it. allow_strand_flip=True exists, and says so on the run.
Read that “near zero” per score, not fleet-wide (GH #371, 2026-09-26). E2’s aggregate
is 0.0226 %, but 37 scores sit above 5 % and six near 50 % — the signature of a file
written in Illumina’s A/B allele convention, where the strand is assigned per variant and
recorded nowhere. PGS005393 is the clean case: 53,705 rows, every one A/C or A/G, not a
single C/T, and 49.9 % of them reverse-complemented. For those files the premise is
false, half their ordinary rows are being dropped as ref_allele_mismatch, and their
palindromes are the least safe in the fleet.
Those rows are recoverable, per file and on evidence (GH #376).
ScoringPolicy.strand_flip_recovery_scores names the scores whose complement-only rows may
be flipped — a set of ids rather than a second boolean, because the global
allow_strand_flip is an assumption about the whole catalog and this is a finding about
named files, and a run’s provenance must not let the two look alike. A file qualifies on
both signals: an A/B allele convention (§3.6 4b) and a measured complement-only rate
above 5 %. scripts/prs/strand_recovery_candidates.py computes the set and refuses to call
it final while any manifest row is still at an older classifier. Measured over the full v5
manifest (2026-09-26): 5 scores, 26,885 recoverable rows — 4 further files show the
allele convention but match the reference forward, and 32 exceed the rate without the
convention, and neither group is a candidate. Empty by default — it
recovers coverage, not correctness, it cannot touch a palindromic row, and switching it on
means re-scoring the affected scores, so it is a Gate F decision that can ride E3.
Weight scales are bucketed, not guessed (§3.4). beta/log(OR)/ln(OR)/log(HR) are
additive and computed. A raw odds or hazard ratio is refused — summing ratios is a
category error that produces a plausible number inside the theoretical bounds, so neither
the arithmetic nor the bounds check would catch it. Everything else — NR (1,390 scores)
and the free-text tail — computes with a weight_scale_unverified flag, which Gate F can
gate on. The allow-list is exact strings rather than a regex, because a pattern loose
enough to catch metaGRS would be inventing a scale for a quarter of the catalog.
What it writes. A coverage_v1 metadata payload carrying the three named quantities of
§5.4’s read contract, plus a gate_c block with the outcome histogram, the dosage
histogram, the retained and theoretical bounds, and n_homref_effect_dosage_2 — the count
of loci a hom-ref genotype scored as dosage 2, every one of which the old scorer scored as
0. No ratio is ever stored: coverage fractions are computed on read from numerator and
denominator, so storage and display cannot disagree. No percentile_v1 key is written at
all, because Gate D owns it and an absent key renders as “the scorer did not record a
percentile”, which is the true statement.
Rows are written at validity='quarantined', one commit per score, superseding any earlier
unreleased score for the same (patient, PGS). Measured throughput on the largest catalog
file (PGS005197, 9,503,677 rows): 220 s at a 2.2 MB peak heap — the streaming reader
holds one record, where the in-memory parser peaked at 1,040 MB on that same file (§5.3).

So the panel pass is one stream over the union carrying a per-(sample, score)
accumulator, which factors naturally as a sparse matrix product — dosages
(samples × loci) against oriented weights (loci × scores), chunked by locus block so
neither operand is ever resident. The per-row Python overhead that set E1’s pace

MODS scores the panel, not pgsc_calc. This is the reason the panel is staged
locally rather than the whole job delegated to the witness. A percentile means
something only if the patient and the panel were deflated the same way, and Gate C
deliberately drops missing dosages and defers palindromic SNVs where pgsc_calc
mean-imputes to 2p and resolves palindromes by frequency (§5.4). Scoring the panel
under a different policy than the patient reintroduces exactly the bias Gate D exists
to remove. The witness still runs — on the same panel — and the delta is still a
first-class output.
The circular dependency, and how it dissolves. Palindrome resolution needs allele
frequencies, which need the panel; but the final scoring pass needs palindromes already
resolved. The way out is that the panel yields frequencies before it yields a score
distribution, so Gate D splits: D1 stage the panel and extract per-locus allele
frequencies over the union → D2 score the panel under the now-final policy → D3
fit PCs and the mean/variance regression. E2 then re-scores Maureen under that same
final policy, and only then do z-score and percentile exist.

a 9-score cluster, and enumerating the missing items and walking their sources found it in
minutes. That technique is sound; it was simply pointed at a phantom.

than because the data demands it. Gate C already emits coverage_v1 on the patient side,

backend/mods_prs_panel.py, run as two worker tasks and driven by
scripts/prs/run_gate_d_panel.py (--step d1, then --step d2 --shards N, then
--step merge). Neither task has run against the real panel: that waits on the

kept 16,055,496 records: 14,802,796 SNV sites, of which 255,021 are split multiallelic,
plus 993,947 indel records. It found no multi-ALT records and no REF conflicts, and the
