3. Procedure
The validation suite was built and run in a single session on 2026-05-09. The order matters because each step depends on artifacts from previous Maple phases:
3.1 Inputs assembled

RGCC sensitivities. Already in mods_functional_test_agent_result from prior parsing runs (parser audit 2026-03-18, the patient-specific validation writeup).
PrimeKG drug nodes. Already in mods_kg_node from Phase 3 ingestion (2026-04-15).
Trained checkpoints + inference predictions. Three PrimeKG inference runs were available at session start (v1 from Phase 5.3, A1 from Phase 5.4a). Run B (primekg_corr_1l_400d_v1) inference was generated in this session using the pdr-prep-run skill to produce a phase=inference notebook from the master template; sync to Drive; Colab run; output to inference/<stem>/test_predictions.txt. Two GP-KG inference runs (v3, v4) are from Phase 0.4.

3.2 Script implementation
lib/pdr/code/scripts/compute_metrics_crc.py (~390 lines) implements the full pipeline:

Load RGCC entries with non-null score_raw; dedupe per drug name (mean score, max-priority sensitivity).
Resolve drug names to KG IDs:

--kg primekg: case-fold + alias map → PrimeKG external_id.
--kg gpkg: PubChem PUG REST name → CID (cached) → format as cid<CID + 100M>.


Inner-join RGCC → KG drug ID → model prediction.
Compute Tier 1 (Spearman ρ + p-value) on continuous matched pairs.
Compute Tier 2 (AUROC + AUPR) on the binary positive/negative subset, after dropping moderate.
Write metrics.json + crc_rgcc_metrics.matched.csv (per-drug rank/score for inspection) per checkpoint.

3.3 Bug fixes uncovered en route
Two latent bugs in earlier-shipped infrastructure surfaced during this session and were patched:

backend/scripts/build_pdr2_input_pickle.py:182 — SQL generation was producing ORDER BY ... NULLS LAST DESC (invalid order — DESC must come first). Fixed: col.desc().nullslast().
backend/scripts/build_pdr1_input_csv.py — resolve_drugs() referenced ModsTreatmentDrug.drugbank_id, a column that doesn’t exist (the schema has drug_name + rxnorm_code only). Replaced with a graceful empty-list fallback documented in the function docstring.

Neither bug affected results in this writeup but both blocked the Phase 9 personalization input-builder; the patches unblock that downstream phase.
3.4 Inference subprocess optimization (deferred but documented)
The original Cell 11 of the master training notebook ran test.py once per inference input file, paying the model-load cost (~110 s on PrimeKG: KG load over 8.1M edges, ent2id construction, vocab sidecar) six times for a 6-file inference run. After observing this on the Run B inference log we wrote lib/pdr/code/test_multi.py — a wrapper that loads the model once and loops over test files, reducing inference wall time from ~12 min to ~2 min (~6× faster). The master template’s Cell 11 was rewritten to invoke test_multi.py and Cell 5’s health check was extended to verify it’s present in the Drive snapshot. Run B’s inference predictions used the original (slower) path because the optimization landed after the run was already in progress; future inference runs will use the faster path.

4. Results
4.1 KG drug coverage

Of 112 distinct drug names in Maureen’s RGCC panel:

PrimeKG matches 109 (97%). The 3 unmatched are name-resolution edge cases, not coverage gaps (see §2.3).
GP-KG matches 36 (32%). Of the 76 unmatched, 21 are PubChem-unresolvable RGCC names (typos, brand-name parentheticals, combination cells) and 55 are PubChem-resolved real drugs simply absent from GP-KG’s 1,430-drug node set.

The 55-drug coverage gap is the dominant story: it includes most monoclonal antibodies (Bevacizumab, Cetuximab, Trastuzumab, Atezolizumab, Avelumab, Pembrolizumab, Ramucirumab) and several common cytotoxics (Cisplatin, Carboplatin, Doxorubicin, Etoposide, Cytarabine, Eribulin, Cabazitaxel). For a CRC validation specifically, 4 of the 5 RGCC high-sensitivity drugs are missing from GP-KG: Carboplatin, Cisplatin, Mitomycin, and Oxaliplatin all fall outside GP-KG’s drug node set. Only Pemetrexed survives the join.
This is a structural property of the KG, not a measurement issue. GP-KG was originally constructed for AD-focused link-prediction work (per KG-Predict 2022); its small-molecule selection is biased toward neurology and small-molecule drug-target interaction. PrimeKG was constructed from an integration of 20+ biomedical databases (per Chandak et al., 2023) including DrugBank’s full small-molecule + biologic catalog.

4.4 Run B continuous correlation, drug-by-drug

Each point is one of the 109 matched RGCC drugs, colored by sensitivity category. The 5 high-sensitivity drugs (green, labeled) are concentrated in the upper-middle of the model score range — not at the extreme top, but well above resistant drugs (brown, lower left). The visual ρ ≈ 0.35 is much clearer than a single number conveys: the high-sensitivity drugs aren’t model “winners” in the top-10 sense, but they consistently score above the resistant population, which is exactly what the Tier 1 metric was designed to capture.
The top-3 model picks (annotated) — Liposomal Doxorubicin (rank 2, RGCC moderate 46%), Cetuximab (rank 3, RGCC low 12%), and Sorafenib (rank 5, RGCC resistant 0%) — show that the model’s top picks are not always RGCC’s top picks. This is the classic “in vitro CTC ≠ in vivo response” caveat in action: Cetuximab is a well-established CRC biologic that simply doesn’t kill cells in a 48-hour CTC assay (its mechanism is via EGFR-mediated proliferation arrest, not direct cytotoxicity); Sorafenib is in clinical use for HCC and has CRC trial activity; Doxorubicin is broadly cytotoxic. The model is correctly surfacing drugs known to have CRC research interest from public knowledge, even when the in vitro assay doesn’t see them as killers.

4.6 Two ablations — dim alone, op alone

The five PrimeKG configurations form a partial factorial that lets us isolate two independent effects:
Dim ablation (op fixed at corr). v1 (corr 1L 300d) → Run B (corr 1L 400d) is a clean dim sweep: same op, same depth, same training procedure. Tier 1 ρ jumps from 0.204 → 0.351 (+72% effect size); Tier 2 AUROC jumps from 0.649 → 0.689 (+6%). Embedding capacity dominates the continuous-correlation signal. — ⚠ unrestated (GH #324). Both sides of this ablation were computed on pooled RGCC draws, so the comparison is between two numbers derived the same wrong way. The conclusion may well survive, but it has not been re-measured, and MODS_MISSION_SPEC.md §5.2 leans on it.
Op ablation (dim fixed at 300d). v1 (corr 1L 300d) → A1 (sub 1L 300d) is a clean op sweep: same dim, same depth. Tier 2 AUROC jumps from 0.649 → 0.751 (+16%); Tier 1 ρ stays roughly flat (0.204 → 0.184). The composition operator dominates the binary-discrimination signal but doesn’t help continuous correlation.
Independence. The fact that dim helps Tier 1 without helping Tier 2 (much), and op helps Tier 2 without helping Tier 1, is striking. These are not two views of the same underlying improvement; they are different mechanisms by which the model captures different aspects of the response landscape. The natural follow-up — combining both effects in a single config (sub 1L 400d) — has not been run; we expect it to win on both tiers if the effects are additive (untested).

Reading the table left-to-right: the run with the worst full-ranking CV MRR (A1 at 0.0226, an outlier flagged in an internal session handoff note as a possible measurement artifact) has the best Tier 2 AUROC (0.751). The CV-MRR / Tier 2 ranks are inverted across the three runs.
We had previously suspected A1’s CV anomaly was an artifact of the relation-aware filter in evaluate_model — see the analogous bug we discovered in an internal note on the first GP-KG run. CV MRR underweights what we actually care about (extreme-case discrimination + continuous correlation on real biology) and overweights what is easy to compute (random-triple held-out ranking).
This finding is itself worth surfacing: for drug-repurposing applications, CV-MRR is not a sufficient model-selection metric. Future ablation rounds (Phase 8.5 variant retrain, Phase 9 personalization) should not promote checkpoints to production based on training-time MRR alone.

5. Discussion
5.1 Phase 7.5 closes on PrimeKG
All three PrimeKG checkpoints clear both decision criteria. The strongest single result is Run B’s Tier 1 ρ = 0.351 with p = 1.8 × 10⁻⁴ on n = 109 — a robust positive correlation between the model’s CRC drug ranking (trained on public PrimeKG link-prediction signal) and Maureen’s RGCC drug-sensitivity panel (measured on her own tumor cells). This is the missing baseline that Phase 9 personalization must lift; lift criteria are pre-specified in Phase 9.7 (Tier 1 ρ improvement ≥ 0.05 OR Tier 2 AUROC improvement ≥ 0.03).
We do not have a published comparator for either tier — to our knowledge this is the first patient-specific CRC validation of a public-knowledge-graph link-prediction model. We are establishing the baseline.
5.2 Architecture findings worth their own paragraph
Three findings emerged that are not specific to this validation but speak to how to evaluate KG-completion models for clinical use:
(i) Embedding dim translates directly into patient-specific signal. v1 → Run B is a clean dim ablation; Tier 1 ρ jumped +72% under nothing more than 300d → 400d. The training-time CV MRR for the same change was +5% (0.40 → 0.42). The patient-specific lift is 14× larger than the training-time lift. The model’s representational capacity matters far more for the question we actually care about than for the synthetic held-out-triple task.
(ii) Composition operator changes which extremes the model picks out, independent of capacity. v1 → A1 is an op ablation with dim fixed at 300d. Tier 1 ρ stayed flat (0.204 → 0.184). Tier 2 AUROC jumped +16% (0.649 → 0.751). The sub operator (TransE-style additive composition) produces tighter, more separable score distributions for the extremes; the corr operator (circular correlation, the paper’s choice) produces smoother score landscapes. Different architectures, different qualitative patterns.
(iii) CV MRR is a poor model-selection proxy for clinical generalization. In the three-way ranking of v1, A1, Run B: A1 has the worst CV MRR (0.0226) but the best Tier 2 AUROC. The metric we use to choose between configurations during training does not predict the metric we care about at deployment. This generalizes a finding we previously made for an internal note on the first GP-KG run, where the upstream evaluate_model reported MRR ~0.99 (saturated, filter artifact) while the honest full-ranking eval was 0.07. CV-MRR is not sufficient.
For Phase 9 (personalization) and Phase 11 (PDR2): future runs should be model-selected on RGCC validation tiers, not CV MRR. The Tier 1 + Tier 2 evaluation takes ~10 seconds on a saved checkpoint and should be run on every promotion candidate.
5.3 GP-KG’s coverage gap is a structural property, not a fixable defect
GP-KG passes Tier 1 with the strongest single ρ of any checkpoint (v4 at 0.391). On the 36 drugs it covers, GP-KG is competitive with PrimeKG. But it cannot be scored on Tier 2 because its drug node set excludes 4 of the 5 RGCC high-sensitivity drugs. This is not a result of bad parsing or normalization — PubChem CID resolution succeeded for all 5 (Carboplatin = CID 38904, Cisplatin = CID 5702, Oxaliplatin = CID 5310940, Mitomycin = CID 5746, Pemetrexed = CID 446556). GP-KG simply does not have those nodes; KG-Predict’s 2022 construction selected 1,430 drugs biased toward neurological / general drug-target interaction, not oncology.
The implication: GP-KG cannot serve as the production graph for CRC personalization. Its role going forward is the paper-comparator KG for Phase 0 reproduction — that role is settled. Any new training that targets Maureen’s case must use PrimeKG (or a future composed KG, see §5.5).
5.4 Limitations

n = 5 positives for Tier 2. With only 5 RGCC high-sensitivity drugs, AUROC has high sampling variance. The ranks of Carboplatin, Cisplatin, Oxaliplatin, Mitomycin, Pemetrexed dominate the metric. A future RGCC test panel that adds high-sensitivity drugs would tighten this; we should request expansion of the panel for Maureen’s next draw if practical.
Run B’s checkpoint is the production candidate but the (sub × 400d) cell of the architecture grid was not run. It’s plausible that sub 1L 400d would beat both Run B (Tier 1) and A1 (Tier 2) by combining the dim and op effects. ~5–6 hours of Colab A100 time would resolve this.
In vitro CTC ≠ in vivo response. RGCC measures what kills cells in a 48-hour assay at fixed concentrations. It does not measure pharmacokinetic exposure, drug-drug interactions, immune system involvement, or metastatic-niche effects. Several known prodrug pitfalls apply: Capecitabine (an oral 5-FU prodrug) is typically less active in vitro than 5-FU itself because no liver to metabolize it; we observed this in the Run B matched CSV (Capecitabine RGCC moderate 67%, 5-FU RGCC moderate 72.5%, but the model can’t distinguish them mechanistically). RGCC correlations are supportive, not conclusive.
No pharmacogenomics-aware filtering yet. Maureen has a known inherited pathogenic variant that may affect drug response. The current scoring does not account for this; it ranks drugs against a generic CRC node. Phase 8.5 (variant-aware KG extension) closes this gap.
Single patient. All claims here pertain to Maureen specifically. The patterns we observed (A1 wins Tier 2, Run B wins Tier 1, dim helps Tier 1, op helps Tier 2) may or may not generalize to other patients. Cross-validation against additional RGCC-tested CRC patients would establish whether these are personal idiosyncrasies or general properties; we do not have other patients in the cohort yet.
Drug-name alias map is hand-curated. 30 entries cover the spelling variants and brand names we’ve observed; future patient panels may surface new aliases. The alias map is in source, not configuration; expanding it is a code change.
Spearman ρ is not a fixed test against a “right” ranking. RGCC % cell death is a noisy biological measurement, not a ground-truth ranking. ρ = 1.0 is not a meaningful target; the comparator is “ρ = 0 (no signal).“

5.5 What’s next — three layers of follow-up
Immediate (architecture grid completion). Run primekg_sub_1l_400d_v1 to fill the (sub × 400d) cell at depth 1. Hypothesis: combines the +72% Tier 1 dim effect with the +16% Tier 2 op effect for the best on both tiers. Cost: ~5–6 hours Colab A100. Already memory-feasible (1L sub at 400d ≈ 37 GB, well under 80 GB ceiling).
Near-term (closing Phase 9 + Phase 11).

Phase 9 PDR1 personalization (Maureen Track A — biomarker only). build_pdr1_input_csv.py Track A CSV is staged. Two patient_merge.py adaptations are blocking: the drug filter doesn’t match GP-KG’s CID* IDs, and filter_and_match_disease_nodes_PRS calls a dead UMLS REST endpoint. Both are small patches documented in runs/2026-05-09_phase9/README.md. After patching: train scalars-personalized CompGCN+ConvE, re-run compute_metrics_crc.py, compare against Run B baseline. Decision criterion: Tier 1 ρ improvement ≥ 0.05 or Tier 2 AUROC improvement ≥ 0.03.
Maureen genotype upload + Track B PRS — unblocks the more interesting personalization scenario where PRS scalars actually have nonzero values. Per PDR1’s published Cohen’s d ≈ 1.05 for PRS, this is expected to be the largest personalization lift if it transfers from UK Biobank AD to Maureen-CRC.
PDR2 PrimeKG run — already shown to beat PDR1 v1 on GP-KG by +50% MRR / +88% Hits@10 (an internal note on the first GP-KG run). Run on PrimeKG, score against RGCC, compare to Run B’s ρ = 0.351 baseline.

Long-term (data-boundary exploration via composed KGs).
This is where the canonical KG schema landed in the composition-pipeline foundation commits (Phases A–E of we-need-more-rigor-fuzzy-nygaard.md, mid-2026-05) becomes the primary tool. Three threads:


Diagnostic — which RGCC drugs each KG covers, and why. A natural follow-up to §4.1 is to enumerate, per drug × KG, what predicates / domains exist for that drug node. PrimeKG’s 7,957 drugs come from DrugBank’s full catalog; GP-KG’s 1,430 are a subset. Building a coverage map from the canonical schema (mods_kg_entity joined to mods_kg_relation filtered by domain) tells us not just “is Drug X in this KG?” but “what kind of evidence does this KG carry about Drug X?” — which directly informs whether the KG can support a meaningful link-prediction score for that drug.


Compositional ablation — adding coverage with the composition system. The canonical schema’s mods_kg_composition machinery lets us declaratively define mixes like “PrimeKG ∪ OncoKB variant evidence ∪ CIViC predictive signatures ∪ PharmGKB toxicity edges” without re-ingesting the underlying source data. We can:

Train baseline-PrimeKG (already done — Run B).
Train PrimeKG + OncoKB variant edges — the OncoKB connector landed in commit 672f859 but the variant nodes have not been used for retraining yet.
Train PrimeKG + CIViC + OncoKB + PharmGKB — the Tier 1 MVP composition is seeded as tier1_mvp_with_primekg_v1.
Score each against RGCC. Each successive addition should improve Tier 1 ρ; if it doesn’t, the addition is signal-free for Maureen’s case (or worse, contains conflicting information).

This is a systematic way to test “what does adding source X do for our patient’s signal?” — a question that has been asked qualitatively for years but never answered with a metric. Phase 7.5’s RGCC tiers are the metric.


Boundary discovery — when does adding sources stop helping? Following Translator’s Biolink ecosystem (we already have a translator_connector.py), we can ingest much larger KGs (RTX-KG2 has 140M+ relations across 40+ source databases). The prediction from KG-completion theory is that beyond a certain size, additional relations degrade signal because they introduce noise faster than they add discriminative information (the classic over-smoothing phenomenon, an internal note on the architectural ceiling). Where is that boundary for our use case? RGCC validation gives us the metric to find out, and the canonical schema gives us the levers to compose KGs of varying scope to test against it. Concrete experiment we can run today: train on tier1_mvp_v1 (small, cancer-focused composition) vs rtx_kg2_full (140M+ relations), score both against RGCC, see whether the bigger KG helps or hurts.


The combination of the patient-specific RGCC validation track (Phase 7.5) and the canonical composition schema is, in our view, the most powerful methodological contribution this project can make to drug-repurposing research. It turns the qualitative “more data is better” intuition into a measurable optimization problem with a well-defined objective.

6. Reproducibility
The numbers in this writeup are reproducible from a checkout of the repo at this commit, given the trained checkpoints are present at the documented Drive paths:

results/protein_biomarker_expression_wri.title: Protein Biomarker Expression in MODS
results/protein_biomarker_expression_wri.content:
Protein Biomarker Expression in MODS — Nomenclature, Paper Conventions, and Our Pipeline
Authors: whafa, Claude (Maple project)
Date: 2026-05-18
Status: Audit. No new code; this writeup documents an existing slice of the pipeline that I had only ever touched obliquely. Conclusion up front: Maple emits Maureen’s 84 measured genes to PDR2 as float32 expression values, with a matching protein_names vocabulary, in the exact shape PDR2’s loader consumes — the bool-vs-float worry is unfounded. The interesting questions are upstream (what kind of measurement is in those floats, and whether RNA-percentile is even commensurate with the Olink NPX values PDR2’s paper was trained on).
Companion documents:

pdr_personalization_writeup.md — PDR1 vs PDR2 personalization mechanism reference; the loss function discussed here is fully derived there.
pdr2_track_a_repro_writeup.md — the run that produced the artifact this writeup audits (runs/2026-05-18_maureen_focus_v1/).
pdr_phase8.5_variant_kg_planning.md — variant-aware KG extension. Variant evidence is a different node type than expression and lands in OncoKB/CIViC; not in scope here but addresses a parallel question (genome → tumor causality vs. transcriptome → tumor state).


Summary
A protein biomarker is, in oncology, any protein whose abundance, modification state, or presence/absence in a tumor sample carries clinical signal — drug eligibility, prognosis, or mechanistic insight. The dominant clinical assays produce wildly different value types: IHC gives ordinal intensity scores (0/1+/2+/3+) or percent staining; WTS gives a TPM percentile against a cancer-type cohort; Olink/SomaScan give log₂ relative protein levels (NPX); flow gives positive-fraction percentages. The PDR1 and PDR2 papers built their patient-personalization around Olink plasma proteomics, encoded as continuous float scalars attached to gene self-loops in a knowledge graph.
Maple stores per-gene expression in mods_gene_expression (backend/mods_models.py:1562), populated by the Caris MI Profile WTS parser at backend/connectors/caris_parser.py:743. Maureen’s 84 genes — every protein name in runs/2026-05-18_maureen_focus_v1/maureen_track_a_synthetic_zeros.resolution.json — are TPM percentiles from her single Caris MI Profile WTS panel. All 84 resolve cleanly to canonical NCBIGene CURIEs (build_pdr2_input_pickle.py:209). There are no unmapped protein entries from her data; the number 84 is the count of her measured WTS genes, not the size of an external vocabulary that 84 of N entries successfully match. The pickle the trainer reads contains expr_values: np.ndarray(dtype=np.float32) paired with protein_names: list[str] — type-compatible with what PDR2’s load_patient_data expects.
Where this gets genuinely interesting is the representation gap: PDR2’s paper used Olink NPX (a log₂ scale of plasma protein abundance, typically -3 to +3 with z-score normalization), while Maple’s input is Caris WTS TPM percentile (a 0–100 cohort-relative rank of tumor RNA). PDR2’s loader z-scores both, so the post-normalization shapes look similar, but RNA-from-tumor and protein-from-blood are not the same biological quantity. The model can’t tell the difference; it sees a float and a name. Whether that float means the same thing across patients is a domain question, not a pipeline question.

1. What is a “protein biomarker,” really?
If you’ve been around oncology only at the systems level, the term protein biomarker gets used as if it were one thing. It isn’t. There are at least four assay families in routine clinical use, and they produce values that are mathematically and biologically incommensurate.
1.1 The four assays you’ll see in a real tumor workup








































Assay familyWhat it measuresWhere the sample comes fromNative value typeTypical rangeIHC (immunohistochemistry)Bound antibody → stain intensity on a slice of tumor tissueTumor biopsy blockOrdinal intensity (0, 1+, 2+, 3+) plus percent of stained cells; sometimes combined as H-score (intensity × % up to 300)0–300 or 0–100%WTS / bulk RNA-seq (whole transcriptome sequencing)mRNA abundance per geneTumor biopsy block (FFPE-extracted RNA)Continuous: raw counts → TPM/FPKM → cohort percentile or fold-changeTPM percentile 0–100; fold change ~0.01–100Targeted RNA panels (NanoString nCounter, GeoMx)Same as WTS but with a fixed 770–1800 gene probe set; better at low expressionTumor biopsyNormalized counts or fold-changesimilar to WTSPlasma proteomics (Olink, SomaScan)Actual protein abundance via DNA-tagged antibodies (Olink) or aptamers (SomaScan)Blood drawLog₂ relative abundance (Olink NPX) or RFU (SomaScan)NPX typically -3 to +6
These are not interchangeable. Three of them measure RNA (WTS, NanoString, the panel in your Caris report); one measures protein in tissue (IHC); one measures protein in blood (Olink). The RNA→protein correlation in tumor tissue is famously weak — somewhere around r=0.4 across genes — so an “over-expressed PD-L1” finding from WTS doesn’t necessarily mean “IHC-positive PD-L1” and vice versa. This matters when you want the model to reason about something as concrete as PD-L1 status for ICI eligibility.
1.2 Why oncologists still call all of them “biomarkers”
Because at the level of clinical decision-making, all four can flip the answer to the same question: Is this tumor likely to respond to drug X? PD-L1 IHC at 50%+ unlocks pembrolizumab in NSCLC; HER2 IHC 3+ unlocks trastuzumab in breast; HRD score gates olaparib in ovarian. The clinician folds the underlying assay variability into a clinical heuristic and produces a yes/no. The KG, if it’s faithful to the underlying assay, should not.
Throughout this doc, when we say protein biomarker expression we are talking about the continuous, per-gene measurement that flows into the model — the WTS TPM percentile in our case, the Olink NPX in the papers’ case. The categorical clinical flips (MSI-high, TMB-high, PD-L1 22c3 TPS 1%) live elsewhere in our schema and feed the patient KG through a different path (qualitative BiomarkerRecord edges); we’ll touch them in §3.3 but they are not what the trainer eats as expr_values.

2. How the papers do it
2.1 PDR1: Olink NPX → gene self-loops
PDR1 (Oğuztüzün et al., Journal of Biomedical Informatics, 2025) was built on UK Biobank’s Olink Explore panel — ~3,000 plasma proteins per participant, measured by proximity-extension assay and reported as NPX (Normalized Protein eXpression). NPX is log₂-transformed and inter-plate normalized; for any given protein it sits roughly in the [-3, +3] range, with the cohort mean at zero after normalization.
The mechanism is straightforward and lives in docs/References/PDR1/.../patient_merge.py at the lines our paper-side agent surfaced:
# patient_merge.py, ~line 197
for gene in tqdm(patient_1_columns_to_keep, desc='Adding biomarker self-loops'):
    new_relation = {
        'Head': gene,
        'Relation': self.patient_df[gene].values[0],  # ← the NPX value
        'Tail': gene,
    }
The float NPX value occupies the relation slot of a triple whose head and tail are the same gene node. When the patient-specific KG is serialized to disk, the actual numeric value is replaced with the literal string 'SELF' in the TSV (line 222), and the parallel float lives in scalars_{patient_id}.npy as a torch.float tensor of shape (num_self_loops,).
This is a small but important design choice. It means:

The KG triple format stays canonical (head TAB relation TAB tail).
Numeric edge weights ride a parallel array indexed by edge ID, not stored inline.
There’s no separate protein-expression node type — biomarkers are just gene nodes whose self-loop carries a number.

2.2 PDR2: same encoding, learned weights on top
PDR2 (2026) keeps the encoding identical but adds a learnable head. PersonalizedRepurposingLoss (losses.py lines 39–87 in the PDR2 reference code) takes expr_values as input and learns a per-protein weight vector:
# Sketch, from the agent's audit of losses.py:
expr_term = torch.tanh(torch.sum(protein_weights_norm * expr_values))
loss = base_loss + self.lambda2 * expr_term
The biomarker contribution is a scalar (one number per patient per step) that gates the personalization loss term, with λ₂ controlling its strength (CLI flag --lambda2_biomarker, default 0.01 in our reproduction). The protein_weights themselves are learnable parameters of shape (num_proteins,) and are what gets dumped as the “interpretable” output at the end of fine-tune — the top weights for Maureen’s run were ADORA2A, TSC2, SSTR2, NRG1, CCNE1 (pdr2_track_a_repro_writeup.md).
The key data-type fact: expr_values is a 1D torch.float tensor. Not a categorical index, not a one-hot vector, not a string. A continuous scalar per protein.
2.3 The biomarker vocabulary
The papers do not maintain a curated protein vocabulary file. The “vocabulary” of valid protein/gene names is implicit: it’s the intersection of (a) the column names in the Olink CSVs (uppercased) and (b) the entity IDs in the foundation KG that classify as gene under classify_entity(). PDR2’s classify_entity at lib/pdr2/code/ultra/datasets.py:307 accepts any CURIE prefixed NCBIGene:, HGNC:, HGNC.SYMBOL:, ENSEMBL:, ENSG:, plus a pharmgkb_variants:pharmgkb_gene: form, as a gene. Everything else falls through to the catch-all gene bucket as well (an artifact of the paper’s loose typing), but that doesn’t matter for biomarker matching.
So: the “84 mapped” question, paper-side, would be answered as how many of the Olink protein names appear as gene CURIEs in the foundation KG. Anything that doesn’t appear gets dropped at the self-loop construction step.
2.4 What a patient’s biomarker contribution looks like
A typical PDR1 patient with Olink Explore data contributes on the order of ~50–500 self-loop biomarker edges, plus a few dozen polygenic-risk-score self-loops (one per disease in the criterion), plus diagnosis edges, plus medication edges. The exact count depends on how many Olink proteins map to the foundation KG; ~3,000 input columns funneling down to a few hundred matched gene nodes is plausible based on the Olink Explore catalog overlap with NCBIGene.
Our Maureen run contributes 84. That’s an order of magnitude smaller than a typical Olink patient, and it is the single biggest data-volume gap between Maple’s setup and the paper’s setup.

3. What Maple is doing
3.1 Storage: mods_gene_expression
The canonical home for per-gene expression is ModsGeneExpression:
class ModsGeneExpression(Base):
    __tablename__ = "mods_gene_expression"
 
    gene             = Column(Text, nullable=False)         # "PD-L1", "KRAS", …
    hgnc_id          = Column(Text, nullable=True)          # mCODE HGNC ID
    expression_value = Column(Numeric, nullable=True)       # the float
    expression_unit  = Column(Text, nullable=False)         # "tpm_percentile" | "tpm" | "fold_change" | "livak_ratio"
    cohort           = Column(Text, nullable=True)          # cancer-type cohort the percentile is against
    regulation       = Column(Text, nullable=True)          # "over_expressed" | "under_expressed" | "normal"
    test_type        = Column(Text, nullable=False)         # "caris_mi_profile" | "caris_wts" | "rgcc_onconomics"
    report_date      = Column(Date, nullable=True)
    metadata_        = Column("metadata", JSONB)
Three things to notice:

expression_unit is a string, not an enum. Different lab vendors report different physical quantities (raw TPM, percentile against a cohort, Livak 2^-ΔΔCt fold-change for qPCR). The model doesn’t see the unit — it sees the float. We rely on per-test-type consistency: every Caris MI Profile row carries "tpm_percentile", every RGCC row carries "livak_ratio", and so on. If a future ingester were to dump mixed units into the same test_type, the float column would silently become incoherent.
regulation is a derived categorical computed by the parser (over/under/normal based on a 75/25 percentile threshold or an explicit “Over-expressed” label in the source PDF — see caris_parser.py:805–820). The KG composition step uses only the categorical to decide whether to emit an edge: regulation == "normal" rows are dropped. The actual float still rides along on the edge attributes for the PDR2 pickle path.
One row per gene per report. Multiple reports per patient produce multiple rows; the pickle builder de-duplicates with a priority order (caris_mi_profile > caris_wts > rgcc_onconomics) and a “most recent report wins” rule.

There is a second, parallel storage path for qualitative biomarkers — ModsBiomarkerSeries / ModsBiomarkerValue — that holds things like CEA, CA19-9, MSI, TMB, and the IHC-clone-specific PD-L1 calls (PD-L1 22c3 TPS, PD-L1 SP142, etc.). This path is what the genomic-report parser uses when it pulls a BiomarkerRecord (caris_parser.py:600–740). These do not flow into the expr_values array PDR2 consumes; they currently feed Explorer chips, dashboard pills, and a separate set of KG edges (PRED_HAS_BIOMARKER). The PD-L1 you see in Maureen’s WTS panel and the PD-L1 IHC value from the same Caris PDF are stored separately because they are separate measurements, even though they happen to share a gene name.
3.2 Ingestion: where do values come from?
For Maureen specifically, the answer is one report. The Caris MI Profile parser extracts the WTS table via _parse_expressions() (caris_parser.py:743) with this regex:
expr_pattern = re.compile(
    r"^\s*"
    r"([A-Z][A-Z0-9](../?:[A-Z0-9\-_/]{0,15}))"   # Gene name
    r"\s+"
    r"(\d{1,3})(?:\s*%|\s*(?:th)?\s*(?:percentile)?)?"   # TPM percentile
    r"(?:\s+(Over[-\s]?express\w*|Under[-\s]?express\w*|Normal|"
    r"Down[-\s]?regulat\w*|Up[-\s]?regulat\w*|Low|High|Intermediate))?",
    re.MULTILINE | re.IGNORECASE,
)
For each match: gene symbol uppercased, percentile parsed as Decimal(0..100), regulation either taken from the source label or imputed from the threshold (≥75 → over, ≤25 → under, else normal). The cohort field is set from the diagnosis at the top of the report (colorectal_adenocarcinoma for Maureen).
Other ingesters that can write to mods_gene_expression:

Caris WTS standalone — same parser, different report layout. Currently identical schema output.
RGCC Onconomics — qPCR-based panel via rgcc_parser.py:932. Outputs ResistanceFactorRecord and ImmuneMarkerRecord, which land in ModsResistanceFactor and ModsImmuneMarker rather than ModsGeneExpression. These contribute to the KG via _build_resistance_factor_edges() as additional over_expresses edges, but they are not picked up by build_pdr2_input_pickle.py’s resolve_expression_by_gene() (build_pdr2_input_pickle.py:235). The resistance factors influence the KG topology that the foundation model is trained on; they do not appear in the expr_values vector.

This is a quiet limitation: Maureen has RGCC resistance-factor data that becomes KG edges but not PDR2 input-pickle entries. If we wanted PDR2 to weight her drug-resistance signal, we’d need to either (a) extend resolve_expression_by_gene to also read ModsResistanceFactor, or (b) be content with that signal living only on the structural side. Neither is wrong; we should pick one deliberately.

3.4 KG composition: how the 84 become edges
When the patient KG is composed, _build_gene_expression_edges() iterates the rows and emits:
# patient → over_expresses / under_expresses → gene
eb.add(
    legacy_id, canonical_ids, predicate,
    {
        "source": "mods_gene_expression",
        "gene": expr.gene,
        "expression_value": float(expr.expression_value) if expr.expression_value is not None else None,
        "expression_unit": expr.expression_unit,
        "cohort": expr.cohort,
        "regulation": expr.regulation,
        "test_type": expr.test_type,
        "report_date": expr.report_date,
    },
    "gene", expr.gene,
)
Important: the predicate (PRED_OVER_EXPRESSES or PRED_UNDER_EXPRESSES) is chosen by regulation, not by the raw value. Rows with regulation == "normal" are dropped (line 1216). So Maureen’s KG will have an over-expression edge for every gene with TPM percentile ≥75 and an under-expression edge for every gene with TPM percentile ≤25, but the 50th-percentile rows contribute no edges at the KG-topology layer — they ride along only in the PDR2 input pickle where every measurement carries its float regardless of regulation.
This is a meaningful asymmetry between the KG-composition path and the PDR2-input-pickle path:




















PathIncludes “normal” expression?Encoding of valueKG composition (_build_gene_expression_edges)No — dropped at the regulation filterCategorical predicate (over/under), float in edge metadata for explainability onlyPDR2 input pickle (build_pdr2_input_pickle.py)Yes — every row with non-null expression_valueContinuous np.float32
Both paths are “correct” for what they’re trying to do. The KG path is producing typed edges for the foundation model to learn against, where a “normal” expression edge would be noise; the pickle path is producing the per-patient scalar vector the personalization loss multiplies through, where dropping the median values would zero out the gradient on most genes.
3.5 PDR2 input pickle: the final shape
build_pdr2_pickle() emits a dict that PDR2’s container unpickles directly:
{
    "prs_values":   list[float],      # length = 13 diseases; for Track A, all zeros
    "expr_values":  list[float],      # length = 84 for Maureen; np.float32 → tolist()
    "disease_names": list[str],       # ["C1527249", "C0002395", ...]  (UMLS CUIs)
    "protein_names": list[str],       # ["XPO1", "MAGEA4", "MDM2", ..., "TP53", ...]
}
The arrays are serialized as plain Python lists rather than np.ndarray because of a NumPy-version portability landmine (as_dict() docstring at build_pdr2_input_pickle.py:60): the Vertex container ships NumPy 1.x with PyTorch 2.1.0, but local environments run NumPy 2.x, and a NumPy 2.x np.ndarray pickle references numpy._core which doesn’t exist in NumPy 1.x. Lists serialize identically across versions, and the model code unwraps them via torch.tensor(patient_data['expr_values'], dtype=torch.float) regardless.
Per the docstring at the top of the script: “PDR2’s load step z-scores both vectors at runtime, so the builder emits raw values, not z-scored.” This is the same convention as the paper.

4. Compatibility audit — the float-vs-bool question
You asked specifically: for all I know the training expects a float and we are passing a bool. Walking the type chain:













































LayerTypeSourceSource PDF (Caris report)Decimal string like "85" for TPM percentileCaris report textParser outputDecimal via _parse_decimal()caris_parser.py:801DB columnNumeric (Postgres NUMERIC, arbitrary precision decimal)mods_models.py:1588Pickle builder dictfloat via float(row.expression_value)build_pdr2_input_pickle.py:281Pickle builder arraynp.float32 via np.array(..., dtype=np.float32)build_pdr2_input_pickle.py:102Pickle filelist[float] (Python list, NumPy-portable)build_pdr2_input_pickle.py:74Trainer ingesttorch.tensor(values, dtype=torch.float)PDR2 load_patient_data
Verdict: float-to-float, end-to-end. No bool, no categorical index, no string anywhere in the value channel. Names are strings (which is correct — they’re keys into the entity vocabulary, not values). The regulation classification is a string (also correct — it’s a predicate choice, not a value).
The only place where a boolean coercion could leak in is the regulation filter in _build_gene_expression_edges (drop normal/null), but that filter runs against the KG-composition path, not the pickle path. The pickle takes every row with a non-null expression_value regardless of regulation. So if Maureen had a row stored with regulation = NULL but expression_value = 50.0, that row would miss the KG edge but would appear in expr_values. That’s the worst inconsistency I can find and it isn’t actually a bug — it’s two different ingestion logics, each defensible.
What you should worry about instead is semantic compatibility with the paper’s training assumptions, which is what the next two sections are about.

5. Semantic compatibility: TPM percentile vs Olink NPX
The biggest difference between our pickle and the pickle PDR2 was originally trained against:













































PropertyUKB Olink (paper)Caris WTS (Maple)Sample typePlasmaTumor tissue (FFPE)Molecular speciesProtein (via PEA)mRNANative valueNPX (log₂ relative protein abundance)TPM percentile against cohortRange pre-z-score~[-3, +3], centered ~0[0, 100], centered ~50Range post-z-score~N(0, 1) by constructiondepends on patient’s panel distributionNumber per patient~50–500 mapped~50–200 reported; 84 for MaureenCohort-relative?Inter-plate-normalized but not cohort-relativeYes — percentile is against the cohort distribution
PDR2 z-scores at load time, so both vectors land in a similar numeric range when they hit the model. But z-scoring a TPM percentile is mathematically odd — the percentile is already a rank statistic with a (nearly) uniform distribution over [0, 100], so its z-score has bounded support of roughly [-1.7, +1.7] and a non-Gaussian shape. The model isn’t doing anything explicit with Gaussian assumptions, so this won’t blow up, but it does mean the protein_weights * expr_values product in PersonalizedRepurposingLoss has a different operating range for our data than for the paper’s.
Practical implication: the paper’s default λ₂ = 0.01 was tuned against NPX-shaped inputs. For our percentile-shaped inputs, the effective signal strength of the biomarker term is slightly compressed. Our Track A null result (Δ_MRR = −0.41%) at default λ₂ is consistent with “biomarker term too weak to matter,” which is consistent with the synthetic positive-control test in pdr2_track_a_repro_writeup.md needing λ=1.0 to produce visible shifts. This is not a bug in our pipeline. It might be a tuning step we owe ourselves.

6. Where else could Maureen’s data come from?
The current 84 are all from one Caris MI Profile WTS report. Several plausible additional sources, ordered by how easy they are to land:
6.1 Existing data, currently dropped or not yet composed

RGCC Onconomics resistance factors and immune markers. Already parsed into ModsResistanceFactor and ModsImmuneMarker, already composed into the KG as over_expresses edges, but not included in the expr_values vector PDR2 sees. Extending resolve_expression_by_gene to read these tables would add roughly 10–20 more entries to her vector. The unit story would need attention — ResistanceFactor.value is a percent expression, not a TPM percentile.
The PD-L1 IHC, MSI, TMB, LOH, CMS fields from the same Caris report. Stored as qualitative BiomarkerRecord and routed to mods_biomarker_series. These are clinically the most actionable per-tumor biomarkers and they currently bypass PDR2 entirely. There’s no clean way to fold “MSI-high” into a float channel without a mapping convention (e.g., MSI-high → +1.0, MSI-low → 0.0, MSS → -1.0), and inventing one would diverge from the paper. Worth thinking about as a separate embedding channel rather than a value-channel hack.
Any genes Caris WTS measured but didn’t print on the report. Unknown to me; would require asking Caris for the raw expression matrix rather than the PDF panel. Their service portal sometimes exposes a CSV.

6.2 New tests we could order
In rough order of yield-per-effort:

Olink proteomics from a single blood draw (Olink Explore HT, ~5,400 proteins, or Olink Reveal ~1,000). This is the exact data format the paper was trained against and the most direct way to make Maureen’s pickle look like a UKB participant’s. Cost is in the low thousands for self-pay; turnaround ~6 weeks. Major caveat: it’s plasma, not tumor — so it’s measuring Maureen’s systemic protein state, not her tumor’s. For drug-repurposing modeling, that’s actually closer to the paper’s intent than tumor RNA.
A second Caris WTS at a different timepoint. Adds longitudinal signal (we don’t currently use it, but report_date would let us — see temporal_patient_modeling_planning.md). Wouldn’t increase the per-timepoint count materially but would unlock trajectory features.
NanoString nCounter Pan-Cancer Pathways panel (~770 genes) on existing tumor block. If the integrative clinic still has the FFPE block from her biopsy, this is a relatively cheap add — adds ~10× the gene count vs Caris’s reported panel. Same caveat: it’s RNA, not protein.
SomaScan plasma proteomics (~11,000 aptamers). Larger menu than Olink but less well-validated for clinical use; not what the paper used; probably overkill.
Tumor proteomics by mass spec. Research-grade, hard to get on a clinical sample, would be unique data but not what the foundation model has ever seen.

The Olink option is the most interesting because it would actually answer the question “does Maureen’s biomarker profile match patterns the foundation model learned on UKB?” If we want to do that experiment well, we should do it before retraining the foundation on a Maureen-overlaid graph (a Phase 8.5 follow-up), because adding the data after the model has been trained without it is a strictly worse use of the signal.

7. Open questions and small follow-ups

Is the 75/25 percentile threshold for over/under regulation tuned for colorectal? It’s a fixed constant in caris_parser.py:816–820. Caris’s own definition of “over-expressed” on the PDF can differ from this and we honor their label when present. For panels without explicit labels we’d be silently imposing a generic threshold. Worth confirming with their methodology.
Should “normal” expression rows produce a third edge type? PDR2’s design doesn’t have one; PDR1’s design doesn’t either. The information is in the float on the pickle path, just not in the KG topology. Leaving it.
Resistance factors → PDR2 vector. Decide whether to fold ModsResistanceFactor rows into expr_values. If yes, normalize unit story. If no, document that this is intentional.
Qualitative biomarkers → some kind of model input. PD-L1 IHC, MSI, TMB, HRD — these are first-class clinical biomarkers that currently live entirely outside the PDR2 channel. Possible representations: separate one-hot input channel, separate node types in the KG with edges to the patient, or composition into the criterion alongside disease_weights and protein_weights. Probably worth a dedicated planning doc rather than improvising.
Olink-style plasma proteomics, if Maureen is open to a blood draw. This is the highest-leverage data acquisition we could make, both for paper-faithful retraining and for trajectory tracking.
Audit-replay for the parser. I trust the regex for the layouts I’ve seen, but _parse_expressions will silently miss any row it can’t pattern-match. A small dump of “rows in source PDF text vs rows in mods_gene_expression” per report would catch silent drops. Cheap to write; possibly a worker task.

Appendix B — Glossary

CURIE — Compact URI: a prefix + local ID, e.g. NCBIGene:7157. The lingua franca of biolink-style KGs.
HGNC — HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee. Canonical human gene symbol authority.
H-score — IHC scoring: (1 × %1+) + (2 × %2+) + (3 × %3+), range 0–300.
IHC — Immunohistochemistry. Antibody-stained tissue slides under a microscope.
NPX — Normalized Protein eXpression (Olink). Log₂ relative protein abundance, plate-normalized.
Olink — Proximity-extension assay platform; ~3k–11k proteins per blood sample depending on panel.
PEA — Proximity Extension Assay; the chemistry Olink uses.
SomaScan — Aptamer-based plasma proteomics platform; ~11k aptamers, ~7k unique proteins.
TPM — Transcripts per million. RNA-seq normalization that controls for transcript length and sequencing depth.
TPM percentile — TPM expressed as a rank against a reference cohort. Caris’s standard reporting unit.
WTS — Whole Transcriptome Sequencing. Bulk RNA-seq with no fixed gene panel.


This writeup audits an existing slice of the MODS pipeline. No code changes accompany it. The two practical artifacts produced by reading it are: (1) confirmation that the Maple → PDR2 type chain is float-to-float and matches the paper’s expectations; (2) a short list of follow-ups around resistance-factor inclusion, qualitative-biomarker representation, threshold transparency, and the Olink-blood-draw question — none of which are blocking the current Track A run but all of which would meaningfully expand what the model can learn from Maureen.

8. Update — the fixed feature schema (GH #108, 2026-05-29)
§3.3 above describes the per-patient gene axis: the builder emitted whatever
genes a patient happened to have measured (84 for Maureen). That is fine for one
patient but breaks down the moment we run validation / test patients through
the same model: PDR2’s loss is positional, so patient A’s expr_values[5] (TP53)
and patient B’s expr_values[5] (KRAS) are not comparable, and attribution
weights stop meaning the same thing across patients.
GH #108 introduces a committed, versioned, cross-patient feature schema
(backend/mods_kgia_schema_service.py, table pdr2_feature_schema, descriptor
backend/pdr2_schemas/kgia_schema_v1.json):

Gene axis = the union of assay-observed genes (DISTINCT mods_gene_expression.gene) ∩ canonical-KG gene nodes, ordered by symbol.
Disease axis = supported PRS traits (default_disease_pgs_set()) ∩ KG
disease nodes, ordered by CUI.
Every patient projects onto this fixed axis; unmeasured positions get the
reference_fill (0.0) plus a measured mask. Maureen’s pickle still carries
her 84 measured values — now at fixed positions inside the shared axis, with
the rest filled.
A schema_hash binds a pickle to an exact axis; validate_against_schema
asserts train and inference use identical positions.

Because the axis is universe ∩ KG recomputed per KG snapshot, merging or
growing the KG yields a new schema version with a larger axis — previously
off-KG genes enter automatically (intersection is forward-compatible, not a
lock-out). The --use_ploss channel still can’t route a value through a gene’s
KG node (it’s a global tilt + attribution, §2.2), so the right lever for “let the
model reason about gene X” remains KG node coverage, after which the next
schema version admits it.
The resistance-factor / qualitative-biomarker / cross-assay-unit follow-ups in
§6 and §7 are unchanged by #108; the schema records per-patient assay/unit
provenance so per-assay normalization (Olink NPX ↔ Caris percentile) can be added
when a non-Caris patient lands.
